Summary: On 1 September 1971, two waterbomber aircraft collided while providing forest fire fighting services on a fire 47 NM NW of the Fort Smith Airport (CYSM), NT. Two Consolidated Vultee (CANSO) PBY-5A aircraft (C-FHTN, operated by Northwestern Air Lease, and C-FIDS, operated by Norcanair) collided mid air while responding to a helicopter (Bell 47B3B, C-FOKV) that had crashed near the forest fire. All 4 crew members for both aircraft were fatally injured and both aircraft were destroyed. Transport Canada conducted the aviation safety investigation - file numbers W1801 and W1802.

THE AIRCRAFT WITH 3 FIRE FIGHTERS ON BOARD WAS LANDING ON A SMALL LAKE NEAR A FOREST FIRE. AFTER THE LANDING FLARE, SEVERE TURBULENCE WAS EXPERIENCED CAUSING THE LEFT FLOAT TO STRIKE THE WATER. THE AIRCRAFT BOUNCED ONTO ITS RIGHT WING TIP, THEN ROLLED TO THE LEFT SUBMERGING THE LEFT WING, AND CAME TO REST IN A WING VERTICAL POSITION WITH THE LEFT WING EMBEDDED IN THE MUD AT THE BOTTOM OF THE LAKE. ONE PASSENGER DROWNED BECAUSE HIS SEAT BELT WAS NOT FASTENED. THE CLOSE PROXIMITY OF THE FIRE PRODUCED THE SEVERE LOCAL TURBULENCE

THE AIRCRAFT WAS LANDING IN A CONFINED AREA DURING FIRE FIGHTING OPERATIONS. THE PILOT ELECTED TO EXECUTE A VERTICAL LANDING INTO THE FIRE CUT OVER 50 FOOT TREES. DURING THE DESCENT, THE TAIL ROTOR CONTACTED TREES AND THE AIRCRAFT SLID TO THE GROUND HEAVILY. THE WIND WAS GUSTY AND THE PILOT HAD FLOWN 12 HOURS IN THE LAST 24 HOURS.
AIRCRAFT STALLED AND SETTLED INTO TREES WHEN TURBULENT AND SUBSIDING AIR WAS ENCOUNTERED AFTER TAKE-OFF.

LE PILOTE TENTAIT DE DECOLLER A PARTIR D'UNE ESPACE RESTREINTE QUI N'OFFRAIT QU'UNE SEULE TRAJECTOIRE D'APPROCHE ET QUI ETAIT SITUEE DANS UNE REGION ACCIDENTEE. L'APPAREIL AVAIT PRESQUE SA MASSE MAXIMALE AU DECOLLAGE. LE ROTOR A ACCUSE UNE PANNE DE REGIME ET LES TENTATIVES DE RATTRAPAGE DU PILOTE ONT ETE VAINES. IL SEMBLE QUE LE PILOTE AIT TROP AUGMENTE LE PAS DES PALES. ON N'A DECOUVERT AUCUNE DEFAILLANCE MECANIQUE.

A LA SUITE D'UN ATTERRISSAGE AVEC UN VENT DE 40 A 60 MI/H., LE PILOTE A PRUDEMMENT CONSERVE UNE TRAJECTOIRE FACE AU VENT ET A LAISSE L'APPAREIL DERIVER EN ARRIERE PENDANT 45 MINUTES EN DIRECTION D'UNE BAIE A L'ABRIE DU VENT. AFIN DE MANOEUVRER DANS LA BAIE ET PRES DU QUAI, IL A FALLU FAIRE TOURNER L'AVION. ALORS QUE L'APPAREIL MANOEUVRAIT PAR FORTE HOULE EN ASSIETTE PIQUEE, UN COUP DE VENT VENANT DE L'ARRIERE L'A FAIT CAPOTER.

THE HELICOPTER WAS ENGAGED IN FOREST FIRE FIGHTING AND DEPOSITING WATER WITH A SLING BUCKET. DURING DESCENT TO A LAKE TO REFILL THE BUCKET AND AS A FLARE WAS INITIATED, THE ENGINE RPM STARTED TO DECAY. BEFORE EFFECTIVE EMERGENCY ACTION COULD BE TAKEN, THE BUCKET STRUCK THE WATER AND PULLED THE HELICOPTER DOWN. THE PILOT EVACUATED SAFELY AFTER IMPACT. INVESTIGATION DETERMINED THAT THE ROTORS WERE BEING POWERED AT IMPACT. THE ENGINE MANUFACTURER HAD PREVIOUSLY RELEASED A SERVICE BULLETIN AND OPERATING INFORMATION REGARDING TRANSIENT OVERLOADING THAT MAY CAUSE A REDUCTION IN ENGINE SPEED BELOW OPERATING LIMITS. PILOT FATIGUE MAY BE A FACTOR AS THE PILOT HAD FLOWN SEVEN HOURS MAKING TWENTY DROPS IN THE FOREST FIRE ENVIRONMENT.

THE PILOT WAS ATTEMPTING A GLASSY WATER LANDING IN A WHITEOUT CONDITION CAUSED BY SMOKE FROM FOREST FIRES. THE AIRCRAFT STRUCK THE WATER AND OVERTURNED. THE AIRCRAFT WAS NOT EQUIPPED WITH AN ARTIFICIAL HORIZON AND DID NOT HAVE A VALID CERTIFICATE OF AIRWORTHINESS.

AT HIGH RPM AND AS COLLECTIVE PITCH WAS RAISED FOR A HOVER AND TAKE OFF, A GARBAGE CAN LID WAS DRAWN INTO THE ROTOR DISC. THE LID WRAPPED AROUND A BLADE AND GROUND RESONANCE DEVELOPED. THE PILOT WAS UNABLE TO EFFECT RECOVERY AND THE MACHINE BECAME UNCONTROLLABLE; IT STRUCK THE GROUND AND ROLLED OVER.
A LOUD BANG WAS HEARD ON THE DESCENT TO LANDING. THE AUTOROTATION WAS SUCCESSFUL BUT THE MACHINE ROLLED OVER DUE TO UNEVEN TERRAIN. THE FRONT BEARING IN THE ENGINE FAILED CAUSING STATOR RUB.

THE PILOT ENTERED A HOVER TO HOOK UP WATER BUCKETS. THE MAN ON THE GROUND EXPERIENCED DIFFICULTY HOOKING THE SLING SO THE PILOT ELECTED TO LAND. BECAUSE THE CABLES HAD BEEN LAID OVER THE SKIDS THE PILOT WAS THEN COMMITTED TO LAND, BUT IN A SLIGHTLY DIFFERENT LOCATION BECAUSE THE GROUND MAN WAS TOO CLOSE TO THE ORIGINAL LANDING SITE. AFTER TOUCHDOWN, THE HELICOPTER APPEARED TO BE FIRMLY ON THE GROUND SO POWER WAS REDUCED AND THE PILOT GENTLY GOT OUT OF THE MACHINE. SHORTLY AFTER, IT SLID OFF A ROCK AND STRUCK THE WATER AND DOCK WITH TAIL AND MAIN ROTOR. THE GROUND MAN WAS NOT QUALIFIED; THE PILOT HAD LEFT THE MACHINE WITH THE ENGINE RUNNING AND ROTOR TURNING.

DURING CRUISE AT 2700 FEET, THE PILOT HEARD A LOUD EXPLOSION. AN AUTO-ROTATION WAS INITIATED ONTO A ROAD BUT THE HELICOPTER'S TAIL BOOM CONTACTED A POWER LINE GUY WIRE DURING THE FLARE. THE TAIL BOOM WAS TORN OFF AND DIRECTIONAL CONTROL COULD NOT BE MAINTAINED. AN INDEPENDENT TECHNICAL REPORT OF THE FAILURE ANALYSIS REVEALED THAT THE FUEL INJECTION WHEEL OF THE FUEL SYSTEM HAD FAILED.

SHORTLY AFTER LIFT-OFF AND WHILE COMMENCING CLIMB THE ENGINE LOST POWER. THE PILOT AUTOROTATED TO THE LEFT TO A ROAD. AFTER TOUCHDOWN THE HELICOPTER SLID FORWARD 100 FT AND COLLIDED WITH A RIDGE. THE TAIL BOOM WAS DAMAGED BY THE SUDDEN STOP. INVESTIGATION REVEALED THAT THE LOSS OF ENGINE SPEED WAS DUE TO PARTIAL BLOCKAGE OF THE INJECTION WHEEL FUEL PORTS.
AU COURS D'UN ATTERRISSAGE SUR PLAN D'EAU MIROITANT, LE FLOTTEUR DROIT S'EST ENFONCE PUIS L'APPAREIL A CAPOTE.

THE MACHINE WAS BEING USED FOR FIRE SUPPRESSION. THE WATER BUCKET INADVERTENTLY RELEASED DURING A WATER PICK-UP AND THE PILOT RETURNED TO RETRIEVE IT. AS THE BUCKET WAS HOOKED TO THE RIGHT SKID, THE MACHINE YAWED VIOLENTLY TO THE RIGHT, THE NOSE PITCHED DOWN, THE AIRCRAFT STRUCK THE WATER AND SANK. NO MECHANICAL FAILURE WAS FOUND. DAMAGE TO THE TAIL ASSEMBLY INDICATED THAT THE TAIL ROTOR STRUCK THE WATER IN THE HOVER CAUSING THE BLADES TO FLEX AND SEVER THE TAIL ROTOR ASSEMBLY. THIS IS CONSISTENT WITH THE SEQUENCE OF EVENTS DESCRIBED BY THE PILOT. THIS METHOD FOR BUCKET RECOVERY IS NON-STANDARD AND THE COMPANY HAD NOT DEVELOPED A PROCEDURE FOR PREVENTION OF LOSS OR RECOVERY OF WATER BUCKETS.

SHORTLY AFTER TAKE-OFF THE PILOT REPORTED THE LEFT ENGINE WAS ON FIRE AND RETURNED TO HIS DEPARTURE POINT. THE LANDING WAS ACCOMPLISHED WITHOUT INCIDENT. FIRE TRUCKS EXTINGUISHED THE FIRE. THE ENGINE COMPARTMENT WAS BURNT OUT AHEAD OF THE FIREWALL AND THE TAIL CONE OF THE ENGINE NACELLE WAS BURNT OFF. THE MAIN HYDRAULIC HIGH PRESSURE LINE FROM THE ENGINE PUMP TO THE FIREWALL HAD SEPARATED AND THE ESCAPING FLUID HAD IGNITED ON CONTACT WITH THE HOT EXHAUST AND THE EXHAUST FLAME.

THE AIRCRAFT ON AN AERIAL FIRE SUPPRESSION OPERATION ENTERED A STEEP NOSE DOWN ATTITUDE, CRASHED AND BURNED AFTER TAKING OFF FROM A LAKE. THE OPERATION HAD STARTED AT 0515 CDT WITH THE AIRCRAFT LANDING TO REFUEL AT 1142 AFTER 6.27 HRS OF FLIGHT TIME. AT ABOUT 1820, AFTER FLYING ANOTHER 5:40 HRS, THE AIRCRAFT LANDED ON THE LAKE WHERE THE CO-PILOT DIP-CHECKED THE FUEL TANKS FOR CONTENTS. THE PILOT RADIOED ON TAKE-OFF THAT HE WAS RETURNING TO BASE TO REFUEL BUT ADVISED ON CLIMB-OUT THAT THERE HAD BEEN A MISUNDERSTANDING AS TO THE FUEL REMAINING AND THAT HE WOULD STAY WITH THE FIRE FOR "A COUPLE MORE HOURS". WITNESSES HEARD A "SPUTTERING ENGINE" OR "ENGINE OFF" SOUND BEFORE THE CRASH. IT IS BELIEVED THAT AN ASYMMETRIC FUEL LOAD CAUSED AN INTERRUPTION OF FUEL FLOW TO THE RIGHT ENGINE. CREW FATIGUE WAS PROBABLY A FACTOR IN THE LOSS OF CONTROL OF THE AIRCRAFT SINCE THERE WAS A CREW DISAGREEMENT ABOUT THE FUEL ON BOARD AFTER DIPPING, DISTRACTION FROM FLYING THE AIRCRAFT IS ALSO  A POSSIBLE FACTOR.

WHILE THE PILOT WAS ON APPROACH THE FLAPS RETRACTED, LIKELY DUE TO EXCESSIVE AIRSPEED. HE LOST DIRECTIONAL CONTROL WHILE CONCENTRATING ON EXTENDING THE FLAPS, AND THE AIRCRAFT TOUCHED DOWN WITH SIDE MOTION, SKIPPED AND OVERTURNED. THE OCCUPANTS ESCAPED FROM THE RIGHT DOOR BEFORE THE AIRCRAFT SANK. THE AIRCRAFT WAS 5 HOURS OVERDUE FOR INSPECTION, AND THE RIGHT DOOR LATCH WAS BROKEN. BEFORE THE FLIGHT, THE PASSENGERS HAD INSISTED THAT THE DOOR BE REMOVED AND REINSTALLED OFF THE LATCH. IF THE AIRCRAFT HAD NOT BEEN FLOWN WITH THE DOOR OPEN IT IS LIKELY THAT ESCAPE WOULD HAVE BEEN IMPOSSIBLE.

THE APPROACH TO LAND WAS BEING FLOWN IN VARIABLE WIND CONDITIONS; A THREE-POINT TOUCHDOWN WAS MADE USING LEFT UP-AILERON TO COMPENSATE FOR A LEFT CROSSWIND. SHORTLY AFTERWARDS A GUST LIFTED THE RIGHT WING AND THE AIRCRAFT GROUNDLOOPED TO THE RIGHT, SLIDING SIDEWAYS ALONG THE RUNWAY. THE LEFT GEAR COLLAPSED WHICH ALLOWED THE LEFT WING TO STRIKE THE SURFACE AND SUSTAIN SUBSTANTIAL DAMAGE . THE AIRCRAFT CAME TO REST ON THE GRASS AREA. THE PILOT'S EXPERIENCE OF ONLY 10 HOURS ON TAILWHEEL AIRCRAFT WAS PROBABLY A CONTRIBUTING FACTOR IN THIS ACCIDENT.

THE HELICOPTER WAS LIFTING OFF WITH A LOAD OF WATER IN A MONSOON BUCKET WHEN THE REAR OF THE RIGHT SKID SNAGGED A CABLE FROM THE BUCKET. THE PILOT WAS UNABLE TO MAINTAIN CONTROL, AND THE HELICOPTER ROLLED AND STRUCK THE WATER. THE PILOT WAS PICKING UP WATER DESPITE A 2 FT SWELL DUE TO THE URGENCY OF THE FIRE-FIGHTING OPERATION. HE FAILED TO SEE THE CABLE BECAUSE OF THE BLACK WATER BACKGROUND.

THE NEWLY-LICENCED COMMERCIAL HELICOPTER PILOT WAS ATTEMPTING TO FLY TWO FIRE FIGHTERS AND SOME EQUIPMENT OUT OF A SWAMPY AREA. THE WIND WAS LIGHT, THE TEMPERATURE WAS 20 DEG C AND THE MACHINE WAS JUST UNDER MAXIMUM GROSS WEIGHT. THE PILOT LIFTED OFF AND TRIED TO SIMULTANEOUSLY TRANSITION TO FORWARD FLIGHT WITHOUT PERFORMING A HOVER CHECK. HE WAS THEN FORCED TO OVERPITCH TO CLEAR THE SURROUNDING TREES. THE RESULTING DETERIORATION IN RPM CAUSED THE PILOT TO ATTEMPT A FORCED LANDING WITH ONLY PARTIAL CONTROL OF THE HELICOPTER. DURING THE TOUCHDOWN THE MAIN ROTOR SEVERED THE TAILBOOM.

A WATER BUCKET WAS SLUNG BENEATH THE HELICOPTER TO CARRY FIRE RETARDANT FROM THE MIXING SITE TO A FOREST FIRE. THE PILOT FLEW TO THE REFUELLING SITE AND SET THE BUCKET ON THE GROUND WITHOUT DISCONNECTING THE SLING, THEN MOVED BACK OVER THE BUCKET INTENDING TO LAND BEHIND IT. ABOUT ONE FOOT ABOVE THE GROUND THE HELICOPTER STARTED TO ROLL TO THE RIGHT. THE PILOT APPLIED LEFT CYCLIC AND RAISED THE COLLECTIVE PITCH LEVER BUT THE HELICOPTER CONTINUED TO ROLL RIGHT AND PITCH FORWARD TILL IT BECAME INVERTED AND FINALLY CAME TO REST ON ITS SIDE. THE CAUSE OF THE ACCIDENT WAS UNDETERMINED.

THE PILOT WAS ON FOREST FIRE SPOTTING IN A STEEP NARROW MOUNTAIN VALLEY. HE FIRST FLEW AT A HIGH ALTITUDE WHERE THERE WAS ADEQUATE ROOM TO MANOEUVRE BUT DECIDED TO GO LOWER TO GET A BETTER LOOK. AFTER ENTERING THE VALLEY, THE AIRCRAFT BECAME "BOXED IN" AND WAS UNABLE TO OUTCLIMB THE RISING TERRAIN AND STALLED WHEN THE PILOT ATTEMPTED A TURN.

A78P0069: THE AIRCRAFT DEPARTED FROM THE SQUAMISH AIRPORT AT APPROXIMATELY 1915 PST ON A LOCAL PLEASURE FLIGHT WITH THE POSSIBILITY OF LOOKING FOR ACCESS ROADS TO SNOWMOBILING AREAS. THE AIRCRAFT WAS OBSERVED ON TAKE-OFF TO USE MORE RUNWAY THAN NORMAL. AT APPROXIMATELY 1925 PST A "BIRD DOG" INVESTIGATING A FOREST FIRE REPORTED SEEING REMAINS OF AN AIRCRAFT IN THE FIRE. THE AIRCRAFT HAD BEEN FLYING TOWARDS RISING TERRAIN WHEN THE LEFT WING STRUCK A TREE AND WAS TORN OFF AT THE WING ROOT. THE CABIN SECTION WAS CONSUMED BY A POST-IMPACT FIRE. WEATHER CONDITIONS WERE GOOD FOR VFR FLIGHT. THE AIRCRAFT WAS ESTIMATED TO BE AT OR ABOVE ALL UP WEIGHT AT THE TIME OF THE CRASH. THE WEIGHT COMBINED WITH THE HIGH AMBIENT TEMPERATURES AT 3300' ALTITUDE WOULD REDUCE AIRCRAFT CLIMB PERFORMANCE. ALTHOUGH THE ACTUAL CAUSE IS UNDETERMINED; THE CIRCUMSTANCES ARE CONSISTENT WITH THE FACT THAT THE AIRCRAFT WOULD HAVE DIFFICULTY OUTCLIMBING THE RISING TERRAIN.

THE HELICOPTER DEPOSITED THE SLING LOAD THEN LANDED ALONGSIDE. AS A CREW UNLOADED THE NET ONE MEMBER FROM THE GROUND PARTY RAISED THE HOOK ABOVE HIS HEAD. THE ROTOR STRUCK THE HOOK, CAUSING INJURY TO THE PERSON AND DAMAGING THE ROTOR BLADES.

A78P0093: AFTER DELAYING DUE TO POOR WEATHER THE PILOT WITH 4 PASSENGERS AND FREIGHT DEPARTED FROM DRAGON LAKE ON A CHARTER FLIGHT TO ANOTHER LAKE ABOUT 65 MILES TO THE EAST. THE PILOT CALLED 30 MINUTES LATER AND STATED THAT HE WOULD BE LATE RETURNING BECAUSE OF WEATHER. THE BURNING WRECKAGE WAS LOCATED SOME HOURS LATER BY A RANGER INVESTIGATING A REPORTED FOREST FIRE. INVESTIGATION REVEALED THAT AT TAKE-OFF THE AIRCRAFT WAS 359 LBS OVERWEIGHT, AND THE C OF G WAS 1.5 INCHES AFT OF THE AFT LIMIT. AFTER 45 MINUTES OF FLIGHT THE AIRCRAFT WOULD BE 200 LBS OVERWEIGHT, AND THE C OF G WOULD BE 0.5 INCH AFT OF THE LIMIT. WEATHER IN THE AREA WAS INFLUENCED BY AN UPPER TROUGH WITH A MOIST AND STABLE AIR MASS. WEATHER OBSERVED BY RESIDENTS AND TRUCKERS INDICATED LOW CEILING AND VISIBILITY, WITH FOG OBSCURING SOME HILLS. VFR FLIGHT COULD NOT BE SUCCESSFULLY CARRIED OUT IN THE CONDITIONS DESCRIBED. AN AIRCRAFT, LIKELY THE ACCIDENT AIRCRAFT, WAS SEEN FLYING WEST NEAR THE ACCIDENT SITE 40 TO 45  MINUTES AFTER TAKE-OFF. DENSE BLACK SMOKE WAS REPORTED BY A TRUCKER TRAVELLING THROUGH THE AREA 10 TO 15 MINUTES AFTER THE SIGHTINGS. THE AIRCRAFT HAD STRUCK TREES WHILE INVERTED IN A NOSE LOW, WINGS LEVEL ATTITUDE WITH A HIGH RATE OF DESCENT. A SEVERE POST-IMPACT FIRE DESTROYED THE CABIN OF THE AIRCRAFT. IT IS CONCLUDED THAT THE PILOT LOST CONTROL IN INSTRUMENT CONDITIONS.

LE DECOLLAGE A ETE EFFECTUE A PARTIR D'UNE SECTION ABRITEE DE LA RIVIERE. LORSQUE L'APPAREIL A ETE PRIS PAR UN FORT VENT QUI SOUFFLAIT EN RAFALE AU-DESSUS DES ARBRES IL S'EST CABRE ET S'EST INCLINE A GAUCHE. LE PILOTE A REPRIS LA MAITRISE DE SON APPAREIL ET A DECIDE DE CONTINUER LE VIRAGE A GAUCHE POUR REVENIR SE POSER EN VENT ARRIERE. APRES UN VIRAGE DE 180 DEGRES, IL A DU PIQUER VERS LA RIVIERE POUR EVITER LES ARBRES. L'AVION AVAIT PARTIELLEMENT COULE LORSQUE LES OCCUPANTS ONT ETE REPECHES PAR UN BATEAU.

THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNING FROM A FIRE BOMBING MISSION AND WAS FORCED TO OVERSHOOT DUE TO A LIGHT PLANE ON THE RUNWAY. ON THE SECOND APPROACH THE PILOT MISJUDGED HIS TOUCHDOWN AND LANDED A FEW FEET SHORT OF THE LIP OF THE RUNWAY. AFTER STRIKING THE THREE INCH LIP THE AIRCRAFT CONTINUED THE LANDING ROLL. SEVERAL HUNDRED FEET LATER THE LEFT GEAR COLLAPSED AND THE AIRCRAFT SWERVED OFF THE RUNWAY COMING TO REST IN A PARALLEL DITCH WITH THE LEFT WING ON THE GROUND. THE TRUNNION WAS FOUND TO HAVE FAILED FROM PRE-EXISTING CRACKS POSSIBLY CAUSED BY A VERY HARD LANDING REPORTED SOME YEARS BEFORE. (LP 117/79)

WHILE IN CRUISE FLIGHT THE PILOT NOTICED A SEVERE TAIL ROTOR VIBRATION AND IMMEDIATELY FORCED LANDED THE HELICOPTER INTO A SWAMP. AFTER SHUTDOWN THE PILOT NOTICED A DAMAGED HORIZONTAL STABILIZER AND BROKEN TAIL ROTOR DRIVE SHAFT MOUNTING BRACKET. LATER INVESTIGATION REVEALED THAT THE TAIL ROTOR LEADING EDGE CAP STRIP HAD PEELED OFF. THE STRIP PEELING OFF CAUSED THE INITIAL VIBRATION WHICH IN TURN CAUSED THE DAMAGE. THERE WAS ALSO EVIDENCE OF A POSSIBLE PREVIOUS TAIL ROTOR STRIKE.

A79C0068: THE AIRCRAFT WAS BEING USED TO TRANSPORT A FIRE CREW AND EQUIPMENT TO THE SITE OF A NEW BUSH FIRE. THE PILOT SELECTED A LANDING AREA BUT DID NOT LIKE THE "FEEL" ON TOUCHDOWN AND MOVED AWAY TO EITHER FIND A NEW AREA OR ATTEMPT ANOTHER LANDING IN THE SAME AREA. THE WIND WAS GUSTING TO 20 MPH AS HE LIFTED OFF AND MOVED TO THE RIGHT AWAY FROM THE LANDING AREA. THE PILOT APPLIED LEFT PEDAL TO COUNTERACT THE NORMAL YAW AS POWER WAS APPLIED BUT SOON FOUND THAT FULL LEFT PEDAL WOULD NOT STOP THE YAW. HE APPLIED SOME LEFT CYCLIC AND DECREASED COLLECTIVE MOMENTARILY. THE YAW CONTINUED AND THE PILOT APPLIED FULL POWER. THE YAW RATE INCREASED, THE AIRCRAFT ROTATED RAPIDLY AND CRASHED INTO THE LAKE. THE PILOT HAD FLOWN 22 OF HIS TOTAL OF 58 HOURS ON TYPE IN THE PREVIOUS THREE DAYS AND HAD FLOWN 7 HOURS THE DAY OF THE ACCIDENT.

APRES S'ETRE POSE DANS UNE PETITE CLAIRIERE SUR LE SOMMET D'UNE MONTAGNE, LE PILOTE S'EST APERCU QUE L'APPAREIL N'ETAIT PAS DE NIVEAU. IL A DONC REDECOLLE POUR AMORCER UN VIRAGE A GAUCHE ET SE POSER AILLEURS. PENDANT LE VIRAGE, LE ROTOR DE QUEUE A HEURTE UN ARBRE, CE QUI A PROVOQUE UNE PERTE DE MAITRISE EN DIRECTION. LE PILOTE A COUPE LES GAZ ET A ESSAYE DE SE POSER. LES PATINS DE L'HELICOPTERE SE SONT ROMPUS EN HEURTANT LE SOL LORS DU VIRAGE ET L'APPAREIL S'EST COUCHE SUR LE COTE.

A79W0053: THE FLOAT-EQUIPPED HELICOPTER WAS BEING USED TO TRANSPORT GEOLOGICAL EXPLORATION CREWS FROM A MAIN CAMP TO A NEARBY DRILLING SITE. AFTER LANDING ON A LAKE, THE PILOT WAS WATER TAXIING THE HELICOPTER TO A SMALL DOCK TO DISCHARGE PASSENGERS. WHILE THE PILOT WAS OCCUPIED WITH DOCKING, A MEMBER OF THE GROUND PARTY IN THE AREA PROCEEDED DOWN THE GANG PLANK TO THE DOCK; HE WAS STRUCK ON THE HEAD AND FATALLY INJURED BY THE MAIN ROTOR BLADES.

THE AIRCRAFT WAS BEING USED TO SUPPLY FIRE-FIGHTING CREWS. THE PILOT STATED THAT HE WAS ON A LOW PRECAUTIONARY APPROACH TO A CLEARING, AND WHEN HE PULLED PITCH TO GO AROUND THE ROTOR RPM FELL OFF. HE WAS UNABLE TO REGAIN RPM, AND PULLED MORE PITCH TO CUSHION THE LANDING. THE BLADES STRUCK TREES AND THE AIRCRAFT CAME TO REST ON ITS SIDE. THE MACHINE WAS DESTROYED BY THE FOREST FIRE BEFORE IT COULD BE RECOVERED FOR EXAMINATION.

THE PILOT WAS AWARE OF THE FACT THAT HE WAS LOW ON FUEL BUT THE FUEL GAUGE INDICATED THAT THERE WAS SUFFICIENT FUEL TO AIR TAXI TO THE FUEL DRUM. THE ENGINE FLAMED OUT DUE TO FUEL EXHAUSTION AND THE AIRCRAFT LANDED HEAVILY ON A ROAD WITH A 15 DEGREE SLOPE.

THE PILOT WAS ATTEMPTING A STEEP DESCENDING TURN TO LAND ON A POORLY MARKED PAD ON A LAKE SHORE. THE SURFACE OF THE LAKE WAS GLASSY CALM AT THE TIME. THE PILOT FLARED AT WHAT HE THOUGHT WAS 50 FT ABOVE THE SURFACE, HOWEVER THE HELICOPTER STRUCK THE WATER BEFORE THE RATE OF DESCENT AND FORWARD SPEED HAD BEEN ARRESTED. THE HELICOPTER ROLLED INVERTED AND TRAPPED THE PILOT IN THE WRECKAGE. HE MANAGED TO FREE HIMSELF AND ESCAPE TO THE SURFACE THROUGH A HOLE IN THE BROKEN BUBBLE OF THE AIRCRAFT. THE PILOT ATTRIBUTED HIS ESCAPE TO PRIOR SCUBA TRAINING. (LP 194/79, LP 195/ 79)

A79P0070: AFTER ASSESSING THE AREA AND CARRYING OUT A DUMMY FIRE BOMBING RUN, THE PILOT COMMENCED CLIMBING TO DEMONSTRATE A SECOND RUN FOR THE TANKER PILOTS. HE GAINED ALTITUDE IN A WIDER VALLEY THEN FLEW UP THE NARROW VALLEY WHERE THE FIRE WAS LOCATED. AS HE FLEW TOWARDS THE MOUNTAIN RIDGE THE PILOT REALIZED THAT THE AIRCRAFT COULD NOT OUTCLIMB THE RISING TERRAIN AND THAT THE VALLEY WAS TOO NARROW TO TURN. HE SELECTED THE MOST FAVOURABLE AREA AVAILABLE FOR THE CRASH LANDING. AS THE AIRCRAFT SETTLED INTO THE TREE TOPS THERE WAS AN EXPLOSION AND IT BURST INTO FLAMES. THE ELEVATION OF THE FIRE WAS 5500 FT AND THE TOP OF THE RIDGE WAS 8000 FT. THE DISTANCE FROM THE FIRE TO THE RIDGE WAS APPROXIMATELY 1 MILE. THE PILOT REPORTED THAT HE ASSESSED HIS ALTITUDE AS QUITE ADEQUATE TO CLEAR THE RIDGE, BUT THAT AFTER PASSING THE FIRE NOTICED A DECREASE IN AIRSPEED AND RATE OF CLIMB WHICH COULD SUGGEST THE PRESENCE OF SUBSIDING AIR.

THE STUDENT PILOT WAS ON A SOLO FLIGHT WITH INSTRUCTIONS TO REMAIN IN THE VALLEY. INSTEAD HE ELECTED TO FLY TOWARDS HIGHER TERRAIN IN THE AREA OF A FOREST FIRE, WHERE A BIRD-DOG AIRCRAFT HAD CRASHED SEVERAL DAYS EARLIER. HE ENTERED THE SAME VALLEY AND ATTEMPTED TO OUTCLIMB THE RAPIDLY RISING TERRAIN. THE AIRCRAFT EVENTUALLY COLLIDED WITH TREES.

A FIRE DEVELOPED IN THE RIGHT ENGINE AS THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNING FROM A FIRE FIGHTING OPERATION. THE PILOT CARRIED OUT THE "FIRE-FEATHER" PROCEDURE AND LANDED ON A LAKE WHERE A HELICOPTER WITH A MONSOON BUCKET EXTINGUISHED THE FIRE. THE SOURCE OF THE FIRE WAS HOT EXHAUST RELEASED INTO THE NACELLE DUE TO SEPARATION OF THE EXHAUST MANIFOLD FROM #5 CYLINDER.

ON THE FIRST DAY OF THE FIRE FIGHTING SEASON THE AIRCRAFT WAS BEING FLOWN AGAINST A GRASS FIRE THAT WAS THREATENING BUILDINGS ON THE EDGE OF THE TOWN AND AIRPORT. DESPITE BEING WARNED TWICE ABOUT HIGH TREES ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE FIRE THE PILOT MADE HIS RUN BELOW TREE TOP HEIGHT. THE TANKER STRUCK THE TREES AS THE PILOT PULLED UP INTO A STALL. THE AIRCRAFT ROLLED LEFT THROUGH 270 DEG AND CRASHED ON ITS RIGHT WING TIP; IT CARTWHEELED AND EXPLODED INTO FLAMES.

THE PILOT HAD JUST COMPLETED A CHECK FOR A FOREST FIRE AND WAS CLIMBING AWAY WHEN HIS HELICOPTER EXPERIENCED A POWER LOSS. HE AUTOROTATED INTO THE TREES BELOW. THE HELICOPTER WAS SUBSTANTIALLY DAMAGED. SUBSEQUENT INVESTIGATION REVEALED FAILURE OF THE FIRST STAGE PLANETARY GEAR SYSTEM IN THE TRANSMISSION.

THE PILOT HAD BEEN FLYING FOR 8 HOURS FIGHTING A LARGE FOREST FIRE SLINGING A MONSOON BUCKET. WHILE PICKING UP A BUCKET FULL OF WATER THE ENGINE SUDDENLY FAILED AND THE FULL BUCKET DRAGGED THE HELICOPTER INTO THE RIVER, CAUSING DAMAGE TO THE ENGINE AND TAIL ROTOR DRIVE SYSTEM. THE CAUSE OF THE ENGINE FAILURE WAS ATTRIBUTED TO A FAILED SPUR ADAPTER GEAR SHAFT IN THE ENGINE.
THE PILOT MISJUDGED AND TOUCHED DOWN 10 FT SHORT OF THE HARD SURFACE. THE MACHINE ROLLED FORWARD AND STRUCK AN EXPOSED 5 1/2 INCH RUNWAY LIP. THE IMPACT CAUSED THE LEFT MAIN GEAR TO COLLAPSE.

AS THE HELICOPTER LIFTED TO A LOW HOVER, IT DRIFTED TO THE RIGHT, AND THE RIGHT SKID SNAGGED ON A TREE STUMP. THE HELICOPTER YAWED RIGHT AND ROLLED ONTO ITS RIGHT SIDE. THE HELICOPTER WAS BEING USED TO TRANSFER FIRE FIGHTING PERSONNEL BETWEEN UNPREPARED LANDING SITES. WIND IN THE AREA WAS GUSTY AND VARIABLE AT THE TIME OF THE OCCURRENCE.

THE HELICOPTER WAS ENGAGED IN FIRE-FIGHTING. WHILE POSITIONING OVER A SLING LOAD THE REAR LEFT SKID CAUGHT THE NET. WHEN THE PILOT PULLED UP, THE HELICOPTER TILTED TO THE LEFT DUE TO THE UNBALANCED LOADING, AND THE MAIN ROTOR STRUCK THE GROUND. THE PILOT HAD BEEN ON LONG DUTY HOURS, POOR ACCOMMODATION AND IMPROPER MEALS.

THE PILOT WAS ATTEMPTING TO DROP FOUR FIREFIGHTERS AS CLOSE TO A SPOT FIRE AS POSSIBLE AT DUSK IN AN ATTEMPT TO PUT OUT THE FIRE BEFORE DARK. THE HELICOPTER HAD BEEN BROUGHT INTO A HOVER CLOSE TO THE INTENDED LANDING AREA AND BECAUSE THERE WAS NO HEADSET FOR THE REAR SEAT PASSENGER THE PILOT TURNED HIS HEAD TO DESCRIBE THE CONDITION OF THE LANDING AREA TO HIM, THUS DIVERTING HIS ATTENTION FROM FLYING THE AIRCRAFT. THE HELICOPER MOVED SLIGHTLY AND THE MAIN ROTOR BLADES STRUCK A FIRE-DARKENED TREE THAT WAS DIFFICULT TO SEE IN THE POOR LIGHT. THE PILOT HAD BEEN FLYING STEADILY 7 TO 8 HOURS A DAY FOR A SHORT TIME AND THE ACCIDENT OCCURRED AT THE END OF AN 8-HOUR DAY. BY HIS OWN ADMISSION THE PILOT WAS SUFFERING FROM FATIGUE.

THE HELICOPTER WAS IN A HOVER FOR A WATER BUCKET PICKUP WHEN THE ENGINE LOST POWER. IT STRUCK THE WATER TAIL FIRST AND ROLLED OVER TO THE RIGHT. SUBSEQUENT INVESTIGATION REVEALED THAT THERE WAS WATER IN THE FUEL CONTROLLER.

THE HELICOPTER WAS BEING USED TO MOVE FUEL DRUMS FROM ONE LOCATION TO ANOTHER IN PREPARATION FOR THE FIRE SEASON. THE AIRCRAFT WAS DEPARTING FROM AN AREA COVERED WITH 2 FOOT GRASS MAKING IT VERY DIFFICULT FOR THE PILOT TO SEE THE LANYARD ON THE GROUND. THE PILOT HAD LANDED THE HELICOPTER AHEAD OF THE LOAD AND ATTACHED THE LANYARD AND AS HE LIFTED OFF HE COULD NOT SEE IT. AS HE LIFTED TO A HOVER, THE LANYARD SNAGGED THE REAR OF THE RIGHT SKID, THE HELICOPTER ROLLED TO THE RIGHT AND MAXIMUM LEFT CYCLIC FAILED TO STOP THE ROLL. THE MAIN ROTOR STRUCK THE GROUND AND THE HELICOPTER CAME TO REST ON ITS SIDE.

A80C0074: THE HELICOPTER WAS EMPLOYED IN FIRE SUPPRESSION AND CREW TRANSPORTATION. WHILE IT WAS WATER BUCKETING, GROUND CREW SAW THE BUCKET DROP AND THEN HEARD A LOUD SQUEAL. THE HELICOPTER DESCENDED RAPIDLY AND DISAPPEARED FROM VIEW. THEN THEY SAW BILLOWING SMOKE AND HEARD AN EXPLOSION. THE TWO OCCUPANTS DIED ON IMPACT. FIRE CONSUMED MOST OF THE MACHINE. THE INVESTIGATION REVEALED THAT THE TRANSMISSION SIDE OF THE INPUT DRIVE SHAFT HAD FAILED AT AN ESTIMATED 200 FT AGL. THE HELICOPTER STRUCK TREES, THEN THE GROUND AT A HIGH SINK RATE AND LOW ROTOR RPM. THE DISTANCE FROM WHERE THE BUCKET WAS DROPPED TO THE POINT OF IMPACT INDICATES THAT THE PILOT MAY HAVE ATTEMPTED TO STRETCH THE GLIDE TO REACH A CLEARING JUST BEYOND THE IMPACT POINT.

WHILE ON A FIRE FIGHTING OPERATION THE PILOT SET HIS WATER BUCKET DOWN BESIDE HIS REFUELLING DRUM, MOVED AHEAD A FEW FT AND LANDED. REALIZING HE MIGHT BE SITTING ON THE CABLES TO THE BUCKET, THE PILOT LEANED OUT THE DOOR TO PEER UNDER THE HELICOPTER, LEAVING THE ENGINE RUNNING AT 100% RPM. THE HELICOPTER LIFTED OFF AND DRIFTED RIGHT. THE CABLES TO THE WATER BUCKET SNAGGED ON THE FUEL DRUM, CHECKING THE MOVEMENT OF THE HELICOPTER TO THE RIGHT BY PULLING ON THE HOOK ON THE BELLY OF THE AIRCRAFT. THIS CAUSED THE RIGHT DRIFT TO BECOME A ROLLING TENDENCY TO THE RIGHT, WHICH THE PILOT WAS UNABLE TO CHECK. THE AIRCRAFT ROLLED ONTO ITS RIGHT SIDE AND WAS SUBSTANTIALLY DAMAGED.

THE PILOT WAS ON A LOW-LEVEL FIRE-CONTROL MISSION. HE HAD JUST COMPLETED A WATER-DROP, TURNED THROUGH 270 DEGREES AND CLIMBED TO APPROXIMATELY 150 FT ABOVE TREE-TOP LEVEL. THE AIRCRAFT LEVELLED OUT AND AS THE THROTTLE WAS RETARDED THE ENGINE QUIT. THERE WAS INSUFFICIENT TIME TO DETERMINE CAUSE AND THE PILOT FORCE LANDED STRAIGHT AHEAD INTO THE TREES. THE AIRCRAFT WAS DESTROYED AND THE PILOT RECEIVED MINOR INJURIES. IT WAS DETERMINED THAT FUEL WAS CRITICALLY LOW. THE SMALL AMOUNT REMAINING MIGRATED IN THE TURN, CAUSING THE ENGINE TO DRAW AIR AND FAIL.

THE AIRCRAFT WAS BEING USED TO SLING A WATER BUCKET TO HOT SPOTS DURING A FIRE-FIGHTING OPERATION. WATER WAS BEING PICKED UP FROM A VERY SHALLOW MARSHY POND AND THE BUCKET WAS PICKING UP DEBRIS FROM THE BOTTOM WHICH PREVENTED THE BUCKET DOORS FROM CLOSING PROPERLY. WHEN THE LEAKAGE FROM THE BUCKET BECAME EXCESSIVE THE PILOT SET THE BUCKET DOWN AND LANDED BESIDE IT TO INVESTIGATE. THE ENGINE WAS LEFT RUNNING AT 100% RPM, FLAT PITCH, HYDRAULIC CONTROL BOOSTERS ON AND FRICTION OFF THE CYCLIC AND COLLECTIVE CONTROLS. AS HE WAS REACHING INTO THE BUCKET TO CLEAR THE DOORS HE THOUGHT THE REAR OF THE SKIDS WERE SINKING INTO THE SOFT GROUND. HE HURRIEDLY MOVED BACK TO THE PILOT'S SEAT AND AS HE PULLED PITCH TO LIFT THE HELICOPTER HE WAS SWINGING HIS LEFT LEG OVER THE CYCLIC CONTROL. THE HELICOPTER LIFTED AS IT MOVED BACKWARDS RAPIDLY, THE HEELS OF THE SKIDS CAUGHT IN THE SOFT GROUND, TEARING BOTH SKIDS FROM THE CROSS MEMBERS. THE AIRCRAFT TIPPED TO THE RIGHT, THE MAIN ROTOR  STRUCK THE GROUND AND THE HELICOPTER ROLLED ONTO ITS SIDE.

A80W0058: AFTER DUMPING A 300-GALLON WATER BUCKET, THE PILOT WAS CLIMBING THROUGH 800 FT AGL AT 40 KNOTS WHEN THE ENGINE LOST POWER. HE ATTEMPTED AN AUTOROTATION LANDING INTO SURROUNDING TREES WHICH RESULTED IN SUBSTANTIAL DAMAGE TO THE HELICOPTER. A FIRE BROKE OUT IN THE ENGINE COMPARTMENT WHICH CONSUMED THE MACHINE. THE PILOT WAS NOT INJURED AND WAS EVACUATED FROM THE FIRE SCENE BY HELICOPTER. SUBSEQUENT EXAMINATION OF THE BURNED REMAINS FAILED TO DISCLOSE ANY REASON FOR THE LOSS OF POWER. THE PILOT'S CYCLIC CONTROL WAS NOT FITTED WITH A DECEL BUTTON GUARD, BUT THERE WAS NO EVIDENCE TO INDICATE THAT THIS CAUSED THE POWER LOSS.

THE HEAVILY LOADED HELICOPTER WAS BEING FLOWN VERY LOW AND AT A SLOW SPEED DURING AN INSPECTION OF A BURN AREA AS PART OF A FIRE FIGHTING OPERATION. THE PILOT HAD JUST PULLED COLLECTIVE IN A CLIMBING TURN TO THE RIGHT WHEN SUDDENLY TAIL ROTOR CONTROL WAS LOST AND THE AIRCRAFT YAWED TO THE RIGHT. TORQUE WAS OBSERVED TO CLIMB THROUGH 100% AND PROBABLY WENT MUCH HIGHER AS THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO STOP THE ROTATION BY APPLICATION OF LEFT PEDAL. THIS HIGH TORQUE PROBABLY WAS THE REASON FOR THE LOSS OF TAIL ROTOR CONTROL AS NO EVIDENCE OF ANY MECHANICAL FAILURE WAS FOUND.

THE AIRCRAFT WAS ON A LOW-LEVEL WATER BOMBING FLIGHT. THE PILOT HAD JUST TURNED ONTO FINAL APPROACH FOR THE WATER-DROP 2 MILES FROM THE FIRE. HE WAS FACING INTO THE SUN AND HAD THE AIRCRAFT SET UP IN A NOSE HIGH ATTITUDE VERY CLOSE TO THE TREE TOPS. HE FELT THE AIRCRAFT SINKING AND APPLIED MORE POWER BUT THE LEFT WING STRUCK TREE TOPS, THE AIRCRAFT ROTATED 180 DEGS AND CRASHED INTO THE TREES. THE PILOT WAS NOT INJURED AND THERE WAS NO FIRE.

WHILE IN CRUISE FLIGHT A LOUD BANG WAS HEARD AND THE ENGINE FAILED. AN AUTOROTATION WAS CARRIED OUT INTO 50-FT TREES. ENGINEERING REPORT LP 279/80 CONCLUDED THAT #1 CONNECTING ROD FAILED IN OVERLOAD DURING NORMAL OPERATION AFTER FATIGUE CRACK PROPAGATION HAD SUFFICIENTLY WEAKENED THE ROD. THE FATIGUE INITIATED AT A GALLED AREA ON THE BORE OF THE ROD AT THE CRANKSHAFT END. ENGINE OVERSPEED AND/OR OVERTORQUING OF THE ENGINE ARE TWO PROBABLE CONTRIBUTING FACTORS THAT MAY HAVE PRODUCED THE GALLING. NO MATERIAL DEFICIENCIES WERE FOUND CONTRIBUTORY TO THE FAILURE.

THE PILOT WAS ENGAGED IN FIRE-FIGHTING AND WAS APPROACHING THE FIRE AREA AT AN ALTITUDE OF ABOUT 100 TO 150 FT WITH A BUCKET OF WATER IN THE SLING. AS HE SLOWED DOWN TO ABOUT 20 KTS THE ENGINE SUDDENLY LOST POWER. AN AREA OF LOW TREES IMMEDIATELY TO THE RIGHT OF THE HELICOPTER WAS SELECTED FOR A FORCED LANDING. THE PILOT DID A DESCENDING 180 DEG TURN TOWARD HIS SELECTED LANDING AREA AND JETTISONED THE BUCKET JUST PRIOR TO ENTERING THE TREES. EXAMINATION OF THE ENGINE COMPRESSOR REVEALED AN ADVANCED STATE OF EROSION  TO SEVERAL STAGES OF THE COMPRESSOR BLADES AND STATORS. DURING A TEST RUN THE ENGINE EXPERIENCED A STALL DURING ONE OF THE TEST REQUIREMENTS. IN ALL PROBABILITY THE PILOT EXPERIENCED A COMPRESSOR STALL DUE TO THE LOSS OF COMPRESSOR EFFICIENCY AT TOO LOW AN ALTITUDE TO CLEAR THE STALL PRIOR TO ENTERING THE TREES.

THE HELICOPTER CREW HAD COMPLETED A WATER DROP AND WAS RETURNING TO CAMP WHEN THE CRASH OCCURRED. WITNESSES REPORTED HEARING A BANG, CRACK AND A BOOM AND SEEING BLACK SMOKE. EVIDENCE FOUND DURING THE INVESTIGATION AT THE SITE INDICATED THAT THERE HAD BEEN AN AERIAL BREAK-UP. LABORATORY ANALYSIS OF THE MAIN ROTOR BLADES CONFIRMED THAT A BLADE HAD FAILED IN FLIGHT BY DUCTILE BENDING OVERLOAD. IT COULD NOT BE DETERMINED WHY THE MAIN ROTOR BLADE FAILED. (LP 223/80, LP 224/80, LP 225/80, LP 226/80)

A81C0041: AS THE WATER BOMBER PROBE WAS LOWERED BY THE CO-PILOT AT ABOUT 75 KTS, THE AIRCRAFT SWUNG VIOLENTLY LEFT. THE RUN WAS ABORTED WHILE THE MACHINE TURNED 90 DEG AND SINCE WATER WAS SEEN IN THE NOSE COMPARTMENT THE CAPTAIN ELECTED TO BEACH THE AIRCRAFT. ROCKS AND A STEEP BANK ON THE SHORELINE MADE SUCCESSFUL BEACHING IMPOSSIBLE AND THE AIRCRAFT SANK AFTER THE CREW EVACUATED.  THE LEFT NOSEWHEEL DOOR HAD TORN OFF AND WAS THE PROBABLE CAUSE OF THE UNCONTROLLABLE SWING.

A81C0050:  THE HELICOPTER WAS BEING USED TO LOGISTICALLY SUPPORT FIREFIGHTING OPERATIONS. AFTER MOVING SOME FUEL AND EQUIPMENT THE PILOT WAS ASKED TO DUMP SOME WATER ON A HOT SPOT. THE BUCKET WAS HOOKED UP AND THE PILOT, WHO HAD NOT DONE ANY BUCKETING ON HIS OWN, WENT FOR HIS FIRST PICK-UP. DURING THE FILLING OF THE BUCKET A CABLE CAUGHT OVER THE SKID. AS LIFT-OFF WAS ATTEMPTED THE HELICOPTER NOSED OVER INTO THE WATER.

AS THE PILOT WAS ATTEMPTING TO FILL THE WATER BUCKET, THE CABLE SLIPPED OVER THE FRONT OF THE RIGHT SKID. FLYING FROM THE LEFT SEAT, HE WAS UNAWARE OF THE PROBLEM UNTIL HE TRIED TO LIFT THE FULL BUCKET. THE AIRCRAFT WAS PULLED OVER ON ITS RIGHT SIDE BEFORE HE WAS ABLE TO RECOVER. THE PILOT STATED THAT HE HAD RECEIVED A 45 MIN CHECK-OUT WITH THE WATER BUCKET BEFORE BEING SENT TO WORK AT THE NORTHERN FORESTRY SITE. THE FIRST AND ONLY OTHER TIME HE HAD FILLED A BUCKET WAS UPON HIS ARRIVAL AT THE SITE THE PREVIOUS EVENING.

WHILE IN CRUISE AT 600 FT AGL THE PILOT ELECTED TO MANUALLY LEAN HIS ROUGH RUNNING ENGINE. THE ENGINE STOPPED AND AN AUTOROTATION WAS CARRIED OUT INTO A SWAMP WHERE THE HELICOPTER ROLLED ONTO ITS RIGHT SIDE. INDVERTENT SELECTION OF THE MIXTURE TO "IDLE CUT OFF" CAUSED THE ENGINE STOPPAGE. THE REASON FOR THE ROUGH RUNNING ENGINE WAS NOT DETERMINED.

THE PILOT, WHO HAD FLOWN OVER 30 HRS DURING THE PREVIOUS 3 DAYS, WAS ENGAGED IN MOVING MEN AND EQUIPMENT DURING FOREST FIRE OPERATIONS AND WAS ATTEMPTING TO LAND AT A FIRE CAMP TO PICK UP ANOTHER CREW. THE PILOT HAD LANDED AT THIS CAMP BEFORE AND WAS CONCERNED ABOUT THE POORLY CONSTRUCTED LOG PAD. IT WAS UNEVEN WITH LARGER LOGS AT THE FORWARD AREA WHICH HAD A TENDENCY OF DUMPING THE TAIL ROTOR INTO THE TREES AND BUSHES LINING THE RIVER BANK BEHIND THE PAD. FEARING A TAIL ROTOR STRIKE THE PILOT DECIDED TO LAND AHEAD OF THE PAD AND WHILE MANEUVERING TO GET THE SKIDS FIRMLY ON THE GROUND THE LEFT SKID BEARPAW SNAGGED ON A STUMP CAUSING A DYNAMIC ROLL-OVER.

TREES LOCATED UPWIND OF THE HELIPAD NECESSITATED A 120 DEG TURN OVER THE PAD AND A DOWNWIND DEPARTURE. DURING THE TURN THE TAIL ROTOR STRUCK THE TREES AND SEPARATED. THE HELICOPTER YAWED TO THE RIGHT AND CAME TO REST AT THE EDGE OF THE PAD.

A81W0077:  DURING A WATER-BUCKETING OPERATION, THE PILOT EXPERIENCED A LOSS OF POWER AT LOW ALTITUDE, AND AUTOROTATED INTO A SHALLOW LAKE. DURING THE AUTOROTATION THE BUCKET AND LANYARD, WHICH HAD NOT BEEN JETTISONED, STRUCK AND DAMAGED THE TAIL ROTOR AND BOOM. SUBSEQUENT EXAMINATION DETERMINED THE ENGINE FAILED AS A RESULT OF A RESTRICTED FUEL FLOW. A DEFECTIVE FUEL BOOST PUMP WAS GENERATING METAL PARTICLES WHICH PLUGGED THE MAIN FUEL STRAINER. A FILTER BYPASS VALVE FAILED TO OPEN DUE TO OVERTORQUING ON INSTALLATION, RESULTING IN FUEL STARVATION AND SUBSEQUENT LOSS OF POWER.

A81C0071:  THE PILOT HAD COMPLETED TWO SUCCESSFUL WATER PICKUP RUNS, BUT ON PROBE EXTENSION DURING THE THIRD PICK-UP, THE A/C PITCHED FORWARD VIOLENTLY, NOSED DOWN, AND SANK IN THE LAKE. INVESTIGATION SHOWED THE RIGHT BOMBING DOOR HAD OPENED DURING THE PICKUP RUN. THE MASSIVE DRAG LOADS INDUCED BY THE OPEN DOOR AND THE SUBSEQUENT NOSE DOWN WERE SUFFICIENT TO WRENCH THE A/C WINGS AND ENGINE FROM THEIR TOWER MOUNTING. THE THROUGH BOLTS ATTACHING THE HYDRAULIC ACTUATOR TO THE DOOR TORQUE TUBE WERE FOUND SHEARED. MECHANICAL LINKAGES BETWEEN THE TORQUE TUBE AND THE DOOR WERE INTACT, INDICATING THE BOMB DOOR WAS NOT IN THE OVER-CENTER LOCKED CONDITION WHEN IT OPENED. CAUSE OF THE UNLOCKED CONDITION COULD NOT BE POSITIVELY DETERMINED; HOWEVER, THE A/C HAD A REPORTED HISTORY OF HYDRAULIC PROBLEMS. IT HAD BEEN PREVIOUSLY NOTED THAT PROBE EXTENSION PRODUCED MOVEMENT IN THE BOMB DOOR ACTUATORS, BUT REPAIRS UNDERTAKEN HAD NOT SUCCESSFULLY RESOLVED THIS PROBLEM.

THE PILOT WAS ON A RETURN FLIGHT TO A FIRE WHEN THE HELICOPTER EXPERIENCED AN ELECTRICAL FAILURE. WHEN HE AND HIS ENGINEER DISCOVERED THE GENERATOR HAD FAILED, THEY DECIDED TO FLY THE SHORT DISTANCE TO THE MAIN FIRE BASE TO UNDERTAKE REPAIRS. THE ENGINE WAS STARTED WITH EXTRA BATTERIES WHICH WERE DISCONNECTED AFTER THE START. THE PILOT USED HIS TOT AND AIRSPEED TO JUDGE ENGINE PERFORMANCE DURING THE FLIGHT. WITHIN SIGHT OF DESTINATION, HALFWAY ACROSS A LAKE, THE HELICOPTER WAS BUFFETED AND DROPPED AS IF IN TURBULENCE. A LOSS OF RPM FOLLOWED, AND THE PILOT INITIATED A 180 DEG AUTOROTATION TO A SWAMPY AREA ON THE LAKE SHORE. SUSPECTING FUEL COMTAMINATION, SAMPLES WERE ANALYSED BUT FOUND SATISFACTORY. FURTHER INVESTIGATION FAILED TO DETERMINE ANY REASON FOR THE FAILURE.

AS HE APPROACHED THE LANDING AREA TO DISEMBARK TWO FIREFIGHTERS AND THEIR EQUIPMENT THE PILOT SAW THE FIRE BOSS DIRECTING HIM TO THE TOUCHDOWN SITE. HE ARRESTED DESCENT AT ABOUT 10 FT FOR ANOTHER SITE SURVEY, THEN CONTINUED DOWN. HE HEARD A SUDDEN LOUD NOISE AND FELT THE HELICOPTER START TO ROTATE. HE STOPPED THE ROTATION AND LOWERED THE HELICOPTER TO THE GROUND. SUBSEQUENT INSPECTION REVEALED THAT THE TAIL ROTOR HAD STRUCK A POST AND TWISTED THE AFT SECTION OF THE TAIL BOOM FROM THE HELICOPTER.

THE PILOT WAS RETURNING FROM A FOREST FIRE RECONNAISSANCE FLIGHT WHEN HE PICKED UP A DAMAGED WATER BUCKET. HE THEN DROPPED INTO A SMALL LAKE AND FILLED THE BUCKET WITH WATER FOR STABILIZATION AND USE BACK AT THE CAMP. ENROUTE HE REALIZED THAT HE WOULD HAVE NO WATER LEFT WHEN HE ARRIVED AT HIS DESTINATION, SO HE DECIDED TO REFILL THE LEAKING BUCKET FROM A LAKE CLOSER TO CAMP. ON THE SECOND PICKUP, THE NUMBER 2 ENGINE SPOOLED DOWN AS THE PILOT STARTED TO LIFT OFF FROM THE HOVER. HE DID NOT RECOGNIZE THE PROBLEM IN SUFFICIENT TIME TO PREVENT THE MAIN ROTOR RPM FROM DETERIORATING; THE MACHINE SLOWLY SETTLED IN THE WATER. REALIZING THAT HE WAS UNABLE TO REGAIN FLIGHT, HE ALERTED THE PASSENGERS AND ROLLED THE HELICOPER TO THE LEFT TO STOP THE MAIN ROTOR. AFTER THE OCCUPANTS EVACUATED THE HELICOPTER, IT ROLLED ONTO ITS RIGHT SIDE IN THE SHALLOW WATER. THE CAUSE OF THE ENGINE MALFUNCTION REMAINS UNDETERMINED.

AS THE PILOT PICKED THE HELICOPTER UP INTO A HOVER AFTER REFUELLING FROM FUEL OIL DRUMS, A GUST OF WIND DRIFTED IT TO THE RIGHT. THE RIGHT REAR BEAR PAW STRUCK THE FUEL DRUM CAUSING THE HELICOPTER TO ROLL TO THE RIGHT; THE MAIN ROTOR STRUCK ROCKS AND THE HELICOPTER ROLLED ONTO ITS RIGHT SIDE.

DURING A STEEP APPROACH, THE PILOT REALIZED HE WAS TOO FAST AND DECIDED TO GO AROUND. AS HE ROLLED ON THROTTLE AND PUSHED DOWN ON COLLECTIVE TO REGAIN RPM, THE RATE OF DESCENT INCREASED. THE PILOT PULLED UP ON COLLECTIVE BUT THE AIRCRAFT SETTLED RAPIDLY INTO THE TREE TOPS AND MUSKEG.

A81C0096: THE PILOT LIFTED OFF FROM A PAD ON A RIVERBANK AND AS HE APPLIED FORWARD CYCLIC THE A/C BEGAN TO SINK. HE RE-ENTERED THE HOVER, CHECKED THE ENGINE GAUGES AND AGAIN APPLIED FORWARD CYCLIC. THE HELICOPTER DESCENDED AS IT MOVED FORWARD, THE SKIDS CONTACTED THE RIVER, AND THE HELICOPTER ROLLED INTO THE WATER. A TEARDOWN OF THE ENGINE REVEALED FOD DAMAGE TO THE COMPRESSOR ASSEMBLY AND CONTAMINATION ON THE ROTOR BLADES AND STATOR VANES OF SUFFICIENT MAGNITUDE TO RESULT IN REDUCED ENGINE PERFORMANCE. THE HELICOPTER WAS BEING USED FOR FIRE CONTROL DUTIES AND HAD BEEN OPERATING IN AN AREA OF SANDY TERRAIN AND SMOKE-FILLED AIR.

THE FLOAT-EQUIPPED HELICOPTER WAS APPROACHING A HELIPAD AT A FIRECAMP WHEN THE PILOT INITIATED AN OVERSHOOT. HE THEN CIRCLED, AND BEGAN WHAT APPEARED TO BE A LOW, FLAT APPROACH TO A RUN-ON LANDING ON A CALM RIVER SURFACE. DURING THE APPROACH THE LEFT FLOAT COLLIDED WITH A SANDBAR, THE PILOT LOST CONTROL AND THE A/C CAME TO REST ON ITS SIDE 150 FT FROM ITS INITIAL IMPACT POINT. THE PILOT HAD FLOWN 35 HRS IN THE PRECEEDING 3 DAYS. HE HAD EXPRESSED CONCERN OVER A STICKING THROTTLE EARLIER IN THE DAY. POST-CRASH EXAMINATION OF THE THROTTLE BOX REVEALED AN AREA OF WEAR THAT COULD HAVE CAUSED THE THROTTLE TO BIND AT HIGH RPM. IT IS PROBABLE THAT THE INITIAL OVERSHOOT, AND SUBSEQUENT SELECTION OF THE FLAT APPROACH AND RUN-ON LANDING, WERE A RESULT OF A STUCK THROTTLE. (LP 295/81)

WHILE LOWERING FIRE FIGHTING EQUIPMENT INTO A CLEARING USING A LONG LINE OF INADEQUATE LENGTH THE TAIL AND MAIN ROTORS CONTACTED TREES. THE LOAD WAS RELEASED AND THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO RETURN TO BASE CAMP. A LOUD BANG WAS HEARD AND THE HELICOPTER BEGAN TO ROTATE UNCONTROLLABLY TO THE RIGHT. THE HELICOPTER IMPACTED IN A HEAVILY TREED AREA. IT WAS DETERMINED THAT INITIAL TREE CONTACT DAMAGED THE TAIL ROTOR DRIVE SHAFT WHICH LATER FAILED.

AS THE WIND DIRECTION CHANGED DURING THE NIGHT A FOREST FIRE STARTED THREATENING TO OVERRUN AN EXPLORATION CAMP. THE PILOT AND TWO PASSENGERS TOOK OFF IN DARKNESS TO INVESTIGATE THE POSSIBILITY OF RELOCATING THE CAMP ON AN ISLAND ABOUT 1/2 MI AWAY. AFTER TAKE-OFF THE PILOT REALIZED THAT THE THICK SMOKE AND DARKNESS WOULD PRECLUDE HIS FLYING TO THE ISLAND SO HE DECIDED TO RETURN TO THE TAKE-OFF POINT. WHILE HE COULD SEE SOME LIGHTS FROM THE CAMP THE SMOKE AND DARKNESS MADE THE APPROACH DIFFICULT. HE WAS TOO HIGH ON THE FIRST ATTEMPT, BUT THE SECOND APPROACH SEEMED CORRECT UNTIL HE TOUCHED DOWN IN THE WATER ON THE RIVER. AS THE HELICOPTER ROLLED RIGHT THE PILOT AND PASSENGERS CLIMBED OUT AND SWAM ASHORE.

A81P0077:  THE PILOT WAS PERFORMING A WATERBOMBING DEMONSTRATION USING A NEWLY CONSTRUCTED 600 GALLON MONSOON BUCKET. AFTER PARTIALLY FILLING THE BUCKET IN A MOUNTAIN LAKE AT THE 4500 FT LEVEL, HE STARTED DOWN THE MOUNTAIN SLOPE AT 60 TO 70 KTS TOWARD THE FIRE AREA. A SHORT TIME LATER, A LOUD BANG WAS HEARD AND THE A/C STARTED TO SHAKE AND YAW TO THE RIGHT. THE BUCKET HAD FLOWN UP AND STRUCK THE TAILBOOM, SEPARATING THE GEAR BOX AND ROTOR FROM THE A/C. THE PILOT FLEW THE HELICOPTER SEVEN MILES FURTHER DOWN THE SLOPE BEFORE MAKING A FORCED LANDING INTO THE TREES. INVESTIGATION SHOWED THAT THE STAINLESS STEEL BAND SECURING THE BOTTOM OF THE BUCKET HAD FAILED, RESULTING IN INSTANTANEOUS LOSS OF THE WATER. THE BOTTOM OPEN, THE BUCKET STREAMED LIKE A DROGUE AND STRUCK THE TAIL. THE PILOT HAD NOT CHECKED THAT THE BUCKET HAD BEEN INSTALLED WITH ATTACHMENT CABLES SEVEN FEET LONGER THAN NORMAL FOR HIS A/C. THE FAILED LOWER BAND WAS NOT RECOVERED; HOWEVER, EXAMINATION OF THE UPPER BAND  SHOWED EVIDENCE OF POOR MANUFACTURING TECHNIQUES THAT WOULD WEAKEN THE ASSEMBLY. IF SIMILAR WORKMANSHIP HAD BEEN EMPLOYED THROUGHOUT, THE LOWER BAND WOULD HAVE BURST WITH THE ADDITION OF THE LOAD OF WATER.

THE HELICOPTER LIFTED OFF FROM A CONFINED AREA AND HAD REACHED A HEIGHT JUST ABOVE THE TREES WHEN THE ROTOR RPM BEGAN TO DECAY. IT SETTLED INTO THE TREES AND ROLLED OVER ONTO ITS SIDE APPROXIMATELY 150 FT FROM THE POINT OF DEPARTURE. DUE TO THE HIGH DENSITY ALTITUDE, THERE WAS LITTLE EXTRA POWER AVAILABLE FOR A VERTICAL LIFT OFF. ON REACHING THE TOP OF THE TREES, THE PILOT, IN ORDER TO LOOK FOR OTHER TRAFFIC, ALLOWED HIS ATTENTION TO BE DIVERTED FROM THE OPERATION OF THE HELICOPTER, AND OVERPITCHED THE ROTOR BLADES CAUSING A LOSS OF RPM.

A81C0104: THE PILOT WAS ENGAGED IN WATER BOMBING OPERATIONS, AND LANDED ON A LAKE TO PICK UP WATER. THE LAKE PROVED TO BE TOO SMALL, AND ON TAKE-OFF THE AIRCRAFT WAS UNABLE TO CLEAR TREES ON SHORE; IT STRUCK THE TREES, CRASHED AND BURNED.

THE HELICOPTER HAD LANDED ON A ROCKY RIDGE TO OFF-LOAD A FIRE-FIGHTING CREW. THE PILOT REPORTED THAT AS THE LAST PASSENGER STEPPED DOWN FROM THE A/C, A STRONG GUST OF WIND ROLLED THE HELICOPTER TO THE RIGHT. THE MAIN ROTOR STRUCK A TREE AND THE HELICOPTER SLID, ON ITS SIDE, DOWN THE RIDGE TO THE BOTTOM OF A RAVINE. AT THE TIME, THE WINDS WERE REPORTED TO BE GUSTING TO 60 MPH.

A81P0086:  AFTER 7 FIRE FIGHTING FLIGHTS TOTALLING 52 MIN FLYING TIME, THE PILOT RETURNED TO REFUEL. AS ANOTHER HELICOPTER WAS BEING REFUELLED, HE DECIDED TO COMPLETE ANOTHER FIRE RETARDANT CHEMICAL DROP. ON HIS RETURN TO THE REFUELLING AREA, HE FOUND A HELICOPTER DEPLANING FIRE FIGHTING CREWS. RELYING ON HIS FUEL GAUGE READINGS HE ATTEMPTED ONE MORE 7 MIN FLIGHT TO DROP ANOTHER LOAD. UP TO THIS POINT, THE HELICOPER HAD BEEN AIRBORNE FOR 59 MIN WITH AN INITIAL LOAD OF 175 LBS OF FUEL. AS HE CLIMBED TOWARDS THE FIRE, THE ENGINE FLAMED OUT. HE RELEASED THE BUCKET AND INITIATED AN AUTOROTATION. TO CLEAR A MAJOR POWER LINE, HE ALLOWED THE MAIN ROTOR RPM TO DECAY; A HEAVY LANDING RESULTED.

WHILE ON PATROL AT A HEIGHT OF 150 FT ABOVE GROUND, THE PILOT HEARD A LOUD BANG FOLLOWED BY A POWER LOSS. HE AUTOROTATED INTO A CLEARING AND MADE A HARD LANDING RESULTING IN SUBSTANTIAL DAMAGE TO THE AIRCRAFT. DURING THE INVESTIGATION IT WAS LEARNED THAT THERE WAS SEVERE DAMAGE TO THE COMPRESSOR SECTION. THE EROSION PATTERN SHOWED SIGNS OF DETERIORATION OF STATOR VANES WHICH RESULTED IN THE FAILURE OF ONE OR MORE THIRD STAGE STATOR VANES AND DAMAGE TO THE FOURTH AND FIFTH STAGE ROTOR BLADES. THE AIRCRAFT HAD BEEN OPERATED IN A SANDY ENVIRONMENT FOR SOME TIME, AND HAD ACCUMULATED A TOTAL OF 1565 HRS ON THE COMPRESSOR SINCE OVERHAUL. THE SPECIAL 300 HR INSPECTIONS REQUIRED BY THE MANUFACTURER WHEN AIRCRAFT ARE OPERATED IN DUSTY CONDITIONS HAD NOT BEEN CARRIED OUT.

A81Q0087: PEU APRES LE DECOLLAGE D'UN PLAN D'EAU APRES ECOPAGE, L'AVION A HEURTE UN ARBRE MORT QUI DEPASSAIT LES AUTRES DE 25 A 30 PIEDS. LE PILOTE N'A PAS VU L'ARBRE ET N'A PU DE CE FAIT EVITER LA COLLISION. LA TRAJECTOIRE DE VOL, FACE AU SOLEIL COUCHANT AVEC EN PLUS UN PARE-BRISE SALE, REDUISAIENT LA VISIBILITE VERS L'AVANT DE L'EQUIPAGE. APRES LA COLLISION, L'AVION S'EST DEROUTE VERS L'AERODROME LE PLUS PROCHE OU L'ATTERRISSAGE S'EST EFFECTUE EN TOUTE SECURITE.

APPROACHING THE LANDING SITE LOCATED ON A RAILROAD SIDING WITH A SLING LOAD, THE HELICOPTER PILOT NOTED OBSTRUCTIONS, INCLUDING A BOX CAR, SOME DRUMS OF FUEL, BAGS OF SEED, FERTILIZER AND A SIGN POST. HE RELEASED THE SEED/FERTILIZER BUCKET SLING LOAD AND MOVED LEFT TO LAND ADJACENT TO IT. HE FORGOT ABOUT THE SIGN POST AND ALLOWED THE MAIN ROTOR TO STRIKE THE POST. ON IMPACT THE HELICOPTER TAIL BOOM SWUNG UNCONTROLLABLY TO THE RIGHT AND STRUCK THE BOX CAR. THE PILOT WAS ABLE TO SET THE HELICOPTER DOWN, HOWEVER TWO MAIN ROTOR BLADES WERE DESTROYED AND THE TAIL ROTOR GEAR BOX TORN OUT.

A81W0113:  WHILE PICKING UP A BUCKET OF WATER FROM THE LAKE ADJACENT TO A FOREST FIRE, THE HELICOPTER PILOT EXPERIENCED A LOSS OF DIRECTIONAL CONTROL, AND IMMEDIATELY JETTISONED THE BUCKET. THE HELICOPTER ROTATED TWICE TO THE RIGHT BEFORE THE PILOT COULD SECURE BOTH ENGINES, AND MADE A HEAVY AUTOROTATION LANDING INTO 4-5 FT OF WATER. THE PILOT AND PASSENGER ESCAPED AND CLIMBED ONTO THE CABIN ROOF. ANOTHER CREW WITNESSED THE ACCIDENT AND ARRANGED FOR A RESCUE. IT WAS DETERMINED THAT THE "WHITE" TAIL ROTOR PITCH LINK HAD FAILED, WITH CONSEQUENT LOSS OF TAIL ROTOR PITCH CONTROL. ANALYSIS OF THE FAILURE (LP 355/81) INDICATED THAT PREMATURE WEAR OF THE ROD END BEARING HAD PRODUCED ABNORMAL LOADING AND FATIGUE INITIATION. THE INVESTIGATORS NOTED IT WAS FORTUNATE THAT THE PICK-UP WAS BEING DONE NEAR THE SHORE. THEY FURTHER COMMENTED ON THE INADVISABILITY OF CARRYING UNNECESSARY PASSENGERS ON HAZARDOUS FIRE-FIGHTING OPERATIONS, AND THE NECESSITY OF WEARING FLOTATION GEAR AT ALL TIMES.

A81Q0105:  THE PILOT AND A FORESTRY ENGINEER WERE ON A FOREST FIRE SURVEY FLIGHT; THE AIRCRAFT STRUCK TREES ALONG RISING TERRAIN LOCATED BETWEEN TWO RELATIVELY HIGH-CLIFFED HILLS.ON-SCENE INVESTIGATION REVEALED THAT THE AIRCRAFT INITIALLY CONTACTED A TREE WITH THE RIGHT FLOAT AND THE GROUND WITH THE LEFT WING TIP, INDICATING A STEEP BANK TO THE LEFT. THE AIRCRAFT THEN STRUCK THE SURFACE, CARTWHEELED FOR ABOUT 150 FT, AND BURST INTO FLAMES. A DETAILED EXAMINATION OF THE WRECKAGE WAS NOT POSSIBLE DUE TO THE SEVERITY OF THE DAMAGE. HOWEVER, A PIECE OF A PROPELLER BLADE WAS EXAMINED, AND IT WAS DETERMINED THAT THE ENGINE WAS TURNING AT HIGH RPM AT TIME OF IMPACT. (LP 391/82)WEATHER INFORMATION FOR THE AREA, INDICATED IFR CONDITIONS WITH CLOUD CEILINGS OF 600 FT OR LESS, AND VISIBILITIES OF 0 TO 1 MI IN FOG.THE ELT FAILED TO FUNCTION BECAUSE OF A DEPLETED BATTERY PACK WHICH WAS 2 YRS PAST ITS EXPIRY DATE.

FOLLOWING A ROUTINE WATER BOMBING MISSION, THE PILOT COULDN'T EXTEND THE LEFT MAIN LANDING GEAR BY EITHER MANUAL, OR EMERGENCY PROCEDURES. HE SUCCESSFULLY LANDED HIS A/C AT BASE, WITH THE LANDING GEAR RETRACTED. THE UPLOCK ASSEMBLY WAS LOCKED AND JAMMED DUE TO A BOLT AND BEARING MISALIGNMENT.

THE PILOT LIFTED THE HELICOPTER INTO A HOVER THEN MOVED FORWARD TO GAIN SPEED FOR TRANSLATION. THE MACHINE RAPIDLY ROTATED 2 OR 3 TIMES AND THE MAIN ROTORS STRUCK TREES BESIDE THE TAKE-OFF PATH. THE HELICOPTER CRASHED ON ITS LEFT SIDE SHEARING OFF THE SKID GEAR AND SEPARATING THE MAIN ROTOR. THE PILOT WAS ON STANDBY FOR THE FORESTRY SERVICE AND WAS TASKED TO MOVE A CREW OF 4 MEN TO A NEW FIRE SITE. THE PILOT ASSUMED THE "CREW" WAS A UNIT DESIGNED TO SUIT THE LOAD CAPACITY OF THE HELICOPTER; THEREFORE HE ALLOWED THE MEN TO LOAD THEIR OWN EQUIPMENT. A WATER BUCKET WAS ALSO TO BE SLUNG BELOW THE MACHINE. UNFORTUNATELY, THE TOTAL LOAD EXCEEDED THE HELICOPTER'S MAX ALLOWABLE WEIGHT. THE PILOT ASSUMED HIS LOAD WAS WITHIN LIMITS AND LIFTED OFF THE PAD. AS LONG AS HE REMAINED IN GROUND EFFECT IN THE HOVER, THE TAIL ROTOR WAS ABLE TO MAINTAIN CONTROL. WHEN THE PILOT MOVED AWAY FROM THE PAD AND PULLED UP TO CLEAR THE BUCKET, HE ALSO MOVED OUT OF GROUND EFFECT. ONCE DONE,  ADDITIONAL POWER WAS NEEDED, BUT THE TAIL ROTOR WAS UNABLE TO PROVIDE THE REQUIRED ANTI-TORQUE FORCE. DESPITE THE APPLICATION OF FULL PEDAL AND DOWN COLLECTIVE, THE MACHINE CONTINUED TO SPIN OUT OF CONTROL UNTIL IMPACT.

FOLLOWING REFUELLING, THE PILOT FORGOT TO REMOVE THE FUEL NOZZLE FROM THE HELICOPTER'S FUEL FILLER NECK. WHEN HE ATTEMPTED TAKE-OFF, THE NOZZLE REMAINED WEDGED IN THE FILLER NECK AND THE HELICOPTER LIFTED THE DRUM, PUMP, AND HOSE OFF THE GROUND. HE LOST CONTROL, AND THE HELICOPTER LANDED ON ITS LEFT SIDE, 150 FT FROM THE HELIPAD. THE PILOT HAD BEEN ENGAGED IN FOREST FIRE CONTROL OPERATIONS, AND HAD FLOWN 38 HRS IN FOUR DAYS - 9 OF WHICH WERE ON THE DAY OF THE ACCIDENT AFTER ONLY 6 HRS OF INTERRUPTED SLEEP. IT IS LIKELY THAT FATIGUE LED THE PILOT TO FORGET TO REMOVE THE FUEL NOZZLE.

AHE TANKER, FULLY LOADED WITH FIRE RETARDANT, WAS BEING LED IN ON A LOW LEVEL FIRE SUPPRESSION BOMBING RUN BY A SMALL SPOTTER A/C. THE SPOTTER PILOT OVERSHOT THE TURN ONTO THE FINAL LEAD-IN LINE AND ASKED THE TANKER PILOT IF HE COULD TIGHTEN UP HIS TURN. FOLLOWING THE RUN OVER THE FIRE, THE SPOTTER PILOT PULLED UP TO OBSERVE THE TANKER'S RETARDANT DROP. THE TANKER FAILED TO APPEAR. IT HAD CRASHED NEAR THE TURN ON POINT TO THE LEAD-IN LINE. INVESTIGATION REVEALED THE LOAD CARRIED BY THE TANKER PLACED THE C OF G AT THE AFT LIMIT. IN ALL PROBABILITY, THE PILOT TIGHTENED UP HIS TURN ONTO THE LEAD-IN LINE AS REQUESTED, CAUSING THE A/C'S TAIL HEAVY STATUS TO ASSUME COMMAND. THE PILOT LOST CONTROL AND DID NOT HAVE SUFFICIENT POWER OR ALTITUDE TO RECOVER.

DURING FIRE FIGHTING OPERATIONS, THE PILOT WAS FILLING A WATER BUCKET FROM A SMALL POND. AS HE FLEW AWAY, THE BUCKET APPARENTLY SNAGGED AND HE WAS UNABLE TO JETTISON THE LOAD; THE HELICOPTER WENT OUT OF CONTROL AND ROLLED ON ITS SIDE INTO THE POND. THE SAME PILOT HAD SUCCESSFULLY COMPLETED NUMEROUS WATER PICK-UPS AT THE SAME POND WITHOUT DIFFICULTY. INVESTIGATION REVEALED TWO ITEMS WHICH MAY HAVE CONTRIBUTED TO THE ACCIDENT. THE POND CONTAINED A LARGE AMOUNT OF DEBRIS, INCLUDING SOME OLD CARS, AND THROUGHOUT THE COURSE OF THE WATER BOMBING FLIGHTS, THE GROUND FIRE FIGHTERS WERE ALSO PUMPING WATER OUT OF THE POND NEARBY LOWERING THE WATER LEVEL NEAR THE HIDDEN DEBRIS. THE PILOT WAS MILITARY-QUALIFIED IN THE BELL 212. HIS ATTEMPT TO JETTISON THE BUCKET MAY HAVE BEEN UNSUCCESSFUL AS THE JETTISON BUTTON IN THE 206 IS IN A DIFFERENT POSITION THAN THE 212. IT IS POSSIBLE HE REVERTED TO HIS PREVIOUS EXPERIENCE IN REACTING TO THIS EMERGENCY.

WHILE ON A FLIGHT FROM WATSON LAKE, YUKON, TO FORT NELSON, BC, THE HOMEBUILT A/C BROKE UP. WITNESSES ON THE GROUND REPORTED HEARING AN A/C FLYING OVERHEAD, FOLLOWED BY AN EXPLOSION-LIKE NOISE. AN AIR SEARCH LOCATED PORTIONS OF THE A/C SCATTERED ALONG A 3 MI WRECKAGE PATH. THE SEARCH WAS SEVERELY HAMPERED BY DENSE BUSH AND LOW VISIBILITY CAUSED BY SMOKE FROM A DISTANT FOREST FIRE; TO DATE, SUBSTANTIAL PORTIONS OF THE A/C HAVE NOT BEEN LOCATED. THE FAILURE TO LOCATE MUCH OF THE WING MADE IT DIFFICULT TO DETERMINE THE BREAK-UP SEQUENCE. EVIDENCE SUGGESTS THE WING FAILED BY DOWNWARD BENDING AS A RESULT OF HIGH NEGATIVE "G" LOADS - INDICATIVE OF FAILURE OF THE HORIZONTAL TAIL. EVIDENCE ALSO SUGGESTS THE VERTICAL FIN AND RUDDER SEPARATED EARLY IN THE BREAK-UP SEQUENCE. ALL FRACTURE SURFACES EXAMINED WERE CONSISTENT WITH OVERLOAD FAILURE; THERE WAS NO EVIDENCE OF PRE-CRACKING OR PROGRESSIVE FAILURE. THE WEATHER AT THE TIME OF THE OCCURENCE WAS REPORTEDLY BELOW VFR. SMOKE HAD  REDUCED VISIBILITY TO ABOUT 1/4 MILE. OTHER PILOTS FLYING IN THE AREA REPORTED WIND GUSTING TO 40 KTS WITH MODERATE MECHANICAL TURBULENCE. THESE CONDITIONS, COUPLED WITH THE PILOT'S LACK OF INSTRUMENT FLYING EXPERIENCE AND THE THORP T-18'S SENSITIVE FLIGHT CONTROLS, COULD HAVE LED TO OVERCONTROLLING OR A LOSS OF CONTROL. THIS, IN TURN COULD HAVE RESULTED IN EXCEEDING THE DESIGN LIMITS FOR THE A/C, AND STRUCTURAL FAILURE. EYEWITNESSES REPORTED THE A/C LANDED VERY HEAVILY IN WATSON LAKE. EXAMINATION OF THE LANDING GEAR LEGS REVEALED THEY WERE BOTH BENT OUTWARDS AND TO THE REAR. THESE BENDS WERE NOT THE RESULT OF THE ACCIDENT AS THE LANDING GEAR ASSEMBLY STRUCK THE GROUND INVERTED. RATHER, IT IS POSSIBLE THE BENDING RESULTED FROM THE HARD LANDING. IF SO, SOME FORM OF UNNOTICED STRUCTURAL DAMAGE MAY HAVE OCCURRED DURING THE LANDING THAT LED TO A FAILURE IN FLIGHT. INVESTIGATORS DETERMINED THE A/C WAS NOT BUILT TO THE SPECIFICATIONS AND STANDARDS REQUIRED BY THE DESIGNER. A  NUMBER OF ENGINEERING DRAWINGS HAD NOT BEEN COMPLIED WITH, AND NUMEROUS MODIFICATIONS CONSIDERED CRITICAL BY THE DESIGNER WERE NOT INCORPORATED. THESE INCLUDED STRENGTHENING OF THE MAIN TAIL PLANE SPAR AND MODIFICATIONS TO THE MASS BALANCE WEIGHTS TO REDUCE THE PROBABILITY OF FLUTTER. INVESTIGATORS CONCLUDED THE A/C WAS NOT AIRWORTHY AT THE TIME OF THE ACCIDENT AND THE BREAK-UP MOST PROBABLY WAS THE RESULT OF THE BUILDER'S FAILURE TO ADHERE TO DESIGNER SPECIFICATIONS. IT IS PROBABLE THE INITIAL FAILURE WAS CAUSED BY FLUTTER, AND IT IS POSSIBLE THAT THE BREAK-UP WAS INFLUENCED BY THE PREVAILING WEATHER AND THE EARLIER HARD LANDING. LP 333/82

A83P0033: THE PILOT WAS ENGAGED IN A WATER SLINGING OPERATION. ON 3 OR 4 OCCASIONS, ANOTHER PILOT ENGAGED IN THE SAME OPERATION SAW HIM HAVING PROBLEMS WITH THE BUCKET. JUST PRIOR TO THE ACCIDENT, THE HELICOPER WAS ON THE GROUND AND THE PILOT WAS KNEELING BESIDE THE BUCKET. FOUR MIN LATER, WHEN THE SECOND PILOT RETURNED FROM HIS DROP, HE SAW THE HELICOPTER LYING ON ITS SIDE. EXAMINATION OF THE WRECKAGE REVEALED THAT THE HELICOPTER CONTACTED THE GROUND IN AN ATTITUDE OF APPROXIMATELY 45 DEG NOSE-DOWN, AND 30 DEG OF BANK TO THE RIGHT. THE AFT SECTION OF THE RIGHT SKID, WITH BEAR PAW ATTACHED, HAD SEPARATED FROM THE FUSELAGE ATTACHMENT AND HAD ONE OF THE WIRE CABLES FROM THE BUCKET WRAPPED AROUND IT. THE DRAG MARK ON THE UPPER SURFACE OF THE SKID AND A PERMANENT SET-BEND IN ONE CABLE, INDICATED THAT ONE CABLE WAS DRAPED OVER THE SKID AT TAKE-OFF. THE BUCKET HAD BEEN JETTISONED, BUT UNFORTUNATELY, HAD SNAGGED ON THE SKID AT LIFT-OFF; THE LATERAL C OF G SHIFTED DRASTICALLY TO THE  RIGHT, EXCEEDING THE CYCLIC CONTROL LIMITS.

THE PILOT HAD JUST UNLOADED RETARDANT ON A FIRE; WHEN HE APPLIED POWER, THE ENGINE FAILED TO RESPOND EXCEPT IN SURGES. HE DECLARED AN EMERGENCY AND LANDED ON AN OLD LOGGING ROAD. THE A/C WAS ALMOST STOPPED WHEN THE LEFT WING CAUGHT A SMALL TREE CAUSING IT TO VEER OFF THE ROAD; IT RAN OVER SOME LOGS AND BOULDERS, WENT UP ON ITS NOSE AND FELL BACK TO AN UPRIGHT POSITION. THE ENGINE TROUBLE WAS CAUSED BY A SPLIT IN THE #7 CYLINDER HEAD BETWEEN THE SPARK PLUG HOLES. IT WAS DETERMINED THAT THE CRACK ORIGINATED NEAR THE EXHAUST PORT AS A RESULT OF THERMAL STRESSES OVER A LONG PERIOD. (LP 362/83).

THE PILOT WAS INVOLVED IN A FIRE-FIGHTING OPERATION FROM A COMPANY AERODROME. DURING ONE TAKE-OFF ATTEMPT, THE A/C BECAME AIRBORNE AFTER A GROUND RUN OF APPROXIMATELY 2000 FT, THEN SETTLED BACK ONTO THE RWY. THE PILOT DECIDED TO ABORT THE TAKE-OFF, AND APPROACHING THE RWY END, ATTEMPTED A GROUNDLOOP TO THE RIGHT. THE A/C LEFT THE SIDE OF THE RWY, 100 FT FROM THE END, AND CAME TO REST ON THE BANK OF A SMALL POND. THE RWY BEING USED WAS 2900 FT LONG WITH A 2% UPSLOPE. AMBIENT TEMPERATURE WAS 26 DEG C AND THE WIND WAS VARYING UP TO 110 DEG, AND GUSTING FROM 5 TO 15 KTS. IT WAS REPORTED THAT AT THE TIME OF TAKE-OFF, THE WIND GAVE A TAILWIND COMPONENT TO THE A/C. AS WELL, THE A/C WAS OPERATING 1325 LBS ABOVE THE MAXIMUM AUW OF 7200 LBS. THE COMBINATION OF RWY UPSLOPE, ABOVE STANDARD TEMPERATURES, TAILWIND AND OVERWEIGHT CONDITION, RESULTED IN THE REQUIRED TAKE-OFF DISTANCE EXCEEDING THE AVAILABLE RWY LENGTH. IT IS APPARENT THAT THE PILOT DID NOT GIVE ADEQUATE CONSIDERATION  TO THESE FACTORS WHEN PLANNING THIS PARTICLUAR TAKE-OFF.

THE PILOT WAS ON A WATER BOMBING MISSION IN SUPPORT OF A FIRE FIGHTING OPERATION. THE THIRD DROP OF THE DAY WAS MADE AT A LOW ALTITUDE OF AROUND 50 FT AGL, ABOVE SOME TREES. THE PILOT WAS LINING UP FOR HIS FINAL RUN-IN, WHEN AT THE LAST MOMENT, THE FIRE CONTROLLER DIRECTED HIM TO THE RIGHT OF THE BLAZE. TO MANOEUVRE TO THE NEW DROP ZONE NECESSITATED AN ABRUPT HEADING CHANGE OF 60 DEG AND A BANK ANGLE OF UP TO 45 DEG. THE PILOT REPORTED THAT WHEN HE LOST CONTROL OF THE A/C, IT SEEMED TO FALL OUT OF THE TURN; THE RIGHT WINGTIP HIT SOME TREES. THE STALL SPEED OF THIS A/C IS 78 MPH. THIS WOULD INCREASE RAPIDLY TO THE OPERATING SPEED OF 105 MPH IN AN ABRUPT TURN. THE PILOT MAY HAVE HAD DIFFICULTY RECOGNIZING THIS, RESULTING IN THE STALL AND LOSS OF CONTROL. EVERYTHING HAPPENED SO QUICKLY AND AT SUCH LOW ALTITUDE, THAT THE PILOT WAS UNABLE TO JETTISON THE LOAD OR EFFECT A RECOVERY.

A83C0060:  WHILE THE HELICOPTER PILOT WAS PICKING UP WATER WITH A BUCKET THE TAIL ROTOR FAILED; HE MANAGED TO LAND THE MACHINE IN SHALLOW WATER AND KEEP IT UPRIGHT. INSPECTION OF THE MACHINE REVEALED THAT THE TAIL ROTOR GEARBOX AND TAIL ROTOR ASSEMBLY HAD BEEN RIPPED FROM THE TAIL ROTOR PYLON. THESE PARTS WERE FOUND RESTING ON THE BOTTOM OF THE RIVER BELOW THE TAILBOOM OF THE HELICOPTER. A LARGE SECTION OF ONE OF THE TAIL ROTOR BLADES WAS RECOVERED SOME DISTANCE FROM THE MAIN WRECKAGE. THE TAIL ROTOR BLADE SEPARATED UNDER NORMAL OPERATING LOADS DUE TO FATIGUE CRACKING AND ULTIMATE OVERLOAD RUPTURE OF THE FATIGUE-WEAKENED SECTION. THE FATIGUE INITIATED ON THE INSIDE SURFACE OF THE BLADE SPAR LOCATED AT A CORROSION PIT WITHIN A LOCALIZED REGION OF CORROSIVE ATTACK. THE CORROSIVE ATTACK AND PITTING WERE DIRECTLY ASSOCIATED WITH A HIGH LOCAL CONCENTRATION OF PHOSPHOROUS. THE SOURCE OF THE PHOSPHOROUS WAS A PHOSPHORIC ACID METAL PREP SOLUTION USED TO BOND A U-CHANNEL OF THE BLADE TO  THE INSIDE OF THE SPAR. (LP 286/83).

THE PILOT WAS ENROUTE TO BASE WHEN THE STARBOARD ENGINE FAILED; HE FEATHERED THE PROPELLER AND SHUT DOWN THE ENGINE. ABOUT 12 MIN LATER, THE PORT ENGINE ALSO FAILED. HE MADE A FORCED LANDING IN A SWAMP AREA AND COLLIDED WITH A STAND OF TALL EVERGREENS. TECHNICAL EXAMINATION REVEALED THAT THE ENGINES FAILED DUE TO FUEL EXHAUSTION. AS THE FUEL GAUGES WERE NOT CALIBRATED ACCURATELY, THEY INDICATED AN AMOUNT GREATER THAN WAS ACTUALLY ON BOARD.

THE PILOT SIMULATING A FIRE-FIGHTING OPERATION USING A SLING AND MONSOON BUCKET. AFTER A SUCCESSFUL DROP HE RETURNED TO THE LAKE FOR MORE WATER. OVER THE LAKE THE MONSOON BUCKET OR SLING STRUCK A POWER CABLE STRUNG OVER THE LAKE. THE HELICOPTER WAS APPARENTLY BROUGHT TO A SUDDEN STOP, AND AS A RESULT, THE MAIN ROTOR BLADE SEVERED THE TAIL BOOM. THE HELICOPTER FELL TO THE WATER AND SUBMERGED INVERTED. BEFORE HE COULD BE RESCUED, THE PILOT DROWNED. THERE WAS NO EVIDENCE OF ANY COMPONENT FAILURE TO PREVENT THE SUCCESSFUL CONTINUATION OF THE PRACTICE SESSION. THE WIRE STRIKE WAS PROBABLY THE RESULT OF THE PILOT'S INADEQUATE MONITORING OF HELICOPTER'S ALTITUDE. HE WAS AWARE OF THE WIRES, IN FACT HE HAD WARNED ANOTHER PILOT ABOUT THEM SHORTLY BEFORE THE ACCIDENT.

A84W0045: THE AIRCRAFT DEPARTED CALGARY EN ROUTE TO THE MOSSE MOUNTAIN AREA TO CARRY OUT A PRACTICE WATER BOMBING RUN.  UPON REACHING THE PRACTICE AREA, THE PILOT CONTACTED THE BIRD DOG PILOT ON THE FORESTRY FREQUENCY.  AFTER THE INITIAL RADIO CONTACT, NO OTHER TRANSMISSIONS WERE MADE.  WHEN THE PILOT OF A SECOND AIRCRAFT ARRIVED AT THE PRACTICE AREA, HE FOUND THAT THE FIRST AIRCRAFT HAD FAILED TO SHOW UP.  WITNESSES IN THE AREA REPORTED SEING AN AIRCRAFT ON FIRE SPINNING TO THE GROUND.  THE LEFT WING OF THE AIRCRAFT WAS FOUND AT A GAS WELL SITE.  THE REMAINDER OF THE AIRCRAFT CRASHED INTO THE TREES APPROXIMATELY HALF A MILE WEST OF WHERE THE LEFT WING HAD SEPARATED. THE INVESTIGATION DETERMINED THAT THE FAILURE OF THE LEFT WING WAS DUE TO A PROGRESSIVE FATIGUE CRACK IN THE FRONT, LOWER SPAR CAP OF THE LEFT WING.  THE FATIGUE CRACK PROGRESSED FROM A MACHINING GROOVE OR CUT ACROSS THE SPAR CAP APPROXIMATELY ONE-SIXTEENTH OF AN INCH DEEP.  AS THE HISTORY OF THE AIRCRAFT COULD NOT  BE ESTABLISHED, THE ORIGIN OF THE MACHINING CUT COULD NOT BE DETERMINED.  SINCE THE OUTBOARD EDGES OF THE CUT ARE UNDER A RIVETED SECTION OF SKIN, IT IS PROBABLE THAT THE CUT WAS MADE EITHER DURING OVERHAUL OR MANUFACTURE. THE LEFT WING AND OTHER PARTS FOUND AT THE GAS WELL SITE SHOWED NO EVIDENCE OF ANY FIRE DAMAGE, AND NEITHER ENGINE SHOWED ANY SIGN OF AN IN-FLIGHT FIRE.  IT CAN BE CONCLUDED THAT ANY IN-FLIGHT FIRE OCCURRED AFTER THE LEFT WING HAD FAILED. THE INVESTIGATION COULD NOT DEFINITELY DETERMINE WETHER OR NOT THE WING FAILURE WAS PILOT INDUCED.  DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT TESTS SHOW THAT, IN THIS AIRCRAFT TYPE, THERE IS A SEVERE PITCHING-UP MOMENT WHEN THE LOAD IS DUMPED.  THIS PITCHING-UP MOMENT IS INCREASED AS THE AIRCRAFT'S SPEED IS INCREASED AND AS THE AMOUNT OF FLAP IS DECREASED.  IF THE PILOT HAD INADVERTENTLY JETTISONED THE LOAD, THE PITCH-UP MOMENT AND RESULTANT INCREASED G LOADING COULD HAVE CAUSED THE WING FAILURE.  A LABORATORY EXAMINATION OF THE BOMB  DOOR ACTUATORS SHOWED THAT THE DOORS WERE CLOSED AT IMPACT. THE AUTOPSY REVEALED THAT THE PILOT'S BLOOD-ALCOHOL LEVEL AT THE TIME OF THE ACCIDENT WAS 1.1 GRAMS PER LITRE.  ALTHOUGH THIS AMOUNT OF ALCOHOL WOULD HAVE ADVERSELY AFFECTED HIS ABILITY TO FLY THE AIRCRAFT, IT IS NOT POSSIBLE TO DETERMINE WETHER THIS FACT HAD ANY BEARING ON THE CAUSE OF THE ACCIDENT. THE FOLLOWING LABORATORY REPORTS WERE COMPLETED:  LP 246/84 - BOMB DOOR ACTUATORS;  LP 247/84 - DROP SELECTOR SWITCH;  AND LP 249/84 - WING SPAR FAILURE. FINDINGS: CAUSE RELATED: 1.  THE LEFT WING WAS WEAKENED DUE TO A FATIGUE CRACK WHICH INITIATED AT A MACHINING CUT IN THE FACE OF THE FORWARD LOWER SPAR CAP. 2.  THE SEQUENCE OF EVENTS DURING THE FLIGHT, RESULTING IN THE WING FAILURE, COULD NOT BE DEETERMINED. OTHER: 1.  THE PILOT'S BLOOD ALCOHOL LEVEL WAS 1.1 GRAMS PER LITRE.

A84P0028: THE AIRCRAFT LEFT PENTICTON ON ITS SECOND FLIGHT OF THE DAY TO OBSERVE A FIRE IN THE MOUNTAINS SOUTH OF PENTICTON.  A SEARCH WAS INITIATED WHEN CONTACT WITH THE AIRCRAFT COULD NOT BE MADE.  A MILITARY SEARCH AND RESCUE AIRCRAFT VISUALLY LOCATED THE AIRCRAFT A FEW HOURS LATER ON THE SOUTH SLOPS OF THE OLALLA CREEK VALLEY AT AN ELEVATION OF ABOUT 5,600 FEET ABOVE SEA LEVEL.tHE AIRCRAFT STRUCK TREES IN A LEFT TURN ON A HEADING LEFT OF THE ORIGINAL TRACK. ON IMPACT WITH THE GROUND, THE AIRCRAFT CARTWHEELED, AND THE FORWARD CABIN AREA WAS DESTROYED.  EXAMINATION OF THE AIRCRAFT INDICATED THAT THE LANDING GEAR AND FLAPS WERE RETRACTED AND THAT THE ENGINE WAS PRODUCING SUBSTANTIAL POWER. RATHER THAN CLIMBING TO ALTITUDE BEFORE PROCEEDING ON TRACK, THE PILOT, AS ON THE FIRST FLIGHT, LIKELY CHOSE TO CRUISE CLIMB ALONG THE TRACK EXCHANGING AIRSPEED FOR ALTITUDE.THE TEMPERATURE AT THE ACCIDENT SITE WAS ABOUT 19 DEGREES CELSIUS, CONSIDERABLY WARMER THAN THE TEMPERATURE EXPERIENCED  ON THE FIRST FLIGHT.  IN ADDITION, IT IS LIKELY THAT LOCALIZED VERTICAL DRAFTS WOULD HAVE BECOME MORE FREQUENT AND STRONGER AS THE DAY PROGRESSED. WITH AIRCRAFT PERFORMANCE DEGRADED BECAUSE OF THE TEMPERATURE INCREASE AND THE PRESENCE OF VERTICAL DRAFTS, IT IS LIKELY THAT THE PILOT WAS NOT ABLE TO CLIMB ABOVE THE TERRAIN AND THE TREES WERE STRUCK DURING A TURN TO REVERSE TRACK. FINDINGS: CAUSE RELATED: 1. A CRUISE CLIMB ON TRACK WAS LIKELY ATTEMPTED. 2. AIRCRAFT PERFORMANCE WAS DEGRADED BECAUSE OF RELATIVELY HIGHER TEMPERATURES AND VERTICAL DRAFTS. 3. THE AIRCRAFT COULD NOT CLIMB OVER THE TERRAIN AND STRUCK TREES DURING AN ATTEMPT TO REVERSE COURSE. OTHER: -NIL-

FOLLOWING A WATER BOMBING OPERATION, THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED TO BUFFALO NARROWS TO RELOAD.  THE PILOT CALLED NORTH BATTLEFORD FLIGHT SERVICES AND REPORTED THAT THE AIRCRAFT WAS ON FINAL WITH THE GEAR DOWN.  ON TOUCHDOWN, THE AIRCRAFT SETTLED ON ITS BOMB BAY DOORS AND PROPELLERS AND SKIDDED TO A HALT.  THE GEAR SELECTOR WAS FOUND IN THE DOWN POSITION BY COMPANY MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL, BUT THE LANDING GEAR WAS IN THE UP AND LOCKED POSITION, AND THE GEAR DOORS WERE CLOSED. ALTHOUGH TE PILOT CONTENDED THAT THE GEAR WAS SELECTED AND CONFIRMED DOWN, NO EVIDENCE OF ANY SYSTEM MALFUNCTION COULD BE FOUND. NUMEROUS GEAR CYCLING TESTS WERE CONDUCTED FOLLOWING THE ACCIDENT, AND ALL WERE SUCCESSFUL. FINDINGS: CAUSE RELATED: 1.  THE AIRCRAFT WAS LANDED WITH THE LANDING GEAR RETRACTED. 2.  NO EVIDENCE OF LANDING GEAR SYSTEM MALFUNCTION COULD BE FOUND. OTHER: -- NIL --

THE HELICOPTER, WHICH WAS ENGAGED IN FOREST FIRE CONTROL DUTIES, HAD LANDED AT AN AIRSTRIP FOR REFUEL.  REFUELLING WAS FROM 45-GALLON FUEL DRUMS, AND THE PILOT HAD LANDED CLOSE TO THE DRUMS.  AFTER REFUELLING, AS THE HELICOPTER ENTERED A HOVER, THE PILOT HEARD A "BEEP" FROM EITHER THE ENGINE OUT WARNING OR THE LOW ROTOR RPM WARNING SYSTEM.  AS HE GLANCED DOWN AT THE INSTRUMENT PANEL IN AN ATTEMPT TO DETERMINE THE REASON FOR THE BEEP, THE HELICOPTER DRIFTED TO THE RIGHT, AND THE RIGHT SKID GEAR CAME INTO CONTACT WITH THE FUEL DRUMS.  DYNAMIC ROLL-OVER OCCURRED, AND THE HELICOPTER WAS SUBSTANTIALLY DAMAGED. THE HELICOPTER WAS IN GOOD MECHANICAL CONDITION AND HAD NO KNOWN UNSERVICEABILITIES PRIOR TO THE ACCIDENT.  AN EXAMINATION OF THE MACHINE AND ITS RELATED SYSTEMS FAILED TO UNCOVER ANY DEFICIENCIES THAT COULD HAVE CONTRIBUTED TO THE ACCIDENT.  WHEN BOTH WARNING SYSTEMS WERE BENCH TESTED, THEY FUNCTIONED NORMALLY;  NO REASON FOR THE REPORTED BEEP COULD BE FOUND.  THE  HELICOPTER WAS EQUIPPED WITH "HIGH SKID GEAR", A FACTOR WHICH WOULD HAVE ENHANCED THE AIRCRAFT'S SUSCEPTABILITY TO DYNAMIC ROLL-OVER, ONCE THE SKIDS HAD STRUCK THE FUEL DRUMS. THE PILOT WAS OPERATING THE HELICOPTER IN A DEMANDING ENVIRONMENT, AND HE HAD FLOWN 23 HOURS IN THE PREVIOUS THREE DAYS.  CONDITIONS WERE SUCH THAT IT WAS VERY DIFFICULT TO GET PROPER REST.  THE HEAVY FLYING SCHEDULE, COUPLED WITH THE LACK OF PROPER REST, LEFT THE PILOT FATIGUED AND REDUCED HIS ALERTNESS.  THE PILOT DID NOT NOTICE THE HELICOPTER DRIFTING TO THE RIGHT AND COULD NOT REACT IN TIME TO TAKE CORRECTIVE ACTION BEFORE THE SKIDS STRUCK THE FUEL DRUMS. FINDINGS: CAUSE RELATED: 1.  THE PILOT WAS FATIGUED DUE TO A HEAVY FLYING SCHEDULE AND LIMITED REST IN THE THREE DAYS PRIOR TO THE ACCIDENT. 2.  THE PILOT'S ATTENTION WAS DIVERTED TO THE INSTRUMENT PANEL DURING THE HOVER. 3.  THE HELICOPTER'S RIGHT SKID GEAR WAS ALLOWED TO CONTACT FUEL DRUMS, A CONDITION WHICH CONTRIBUTED TO DYNAMIC  ROLL-OVER. OTHER: - NIL -

THE PILOT AND THREE PASSENGERS WERE ON A RECONNAISSANCE FLIGHT IN MOUNTAINOUS TERRAIN, IN SEARCH OF SMOULDERING FIRES, AND THE PILOT HAD DESCENDED TO LOW LEVEL TO INSPECT SOME LIGHTNING STRIKE AREAS. THE WIND SPEED WAS 35 TO 40 KNOTS WITH GUSTS, WHICH CAUSED MODERATE TO SEVERE TURBULENCE.  THE TURBINE ENGINE (ALLISON 250-C20B) LOST POWER WHILE THE HELICOPTER WAS FLYING AT 200 TO 250 FEET ABOVE GROUND LEVEL (AGL) AT A SPEED OF ABOUT 40 KNOTS.  THE PILOT AUTOROTATED AND HEADED, WITH THE WIND, TOWARD THE CLEARED BUT STUMP- RIDDEN OVERRUN AREA OF A NEARBY AIRSTRIP.  THE MAIN ROTOR RPM DECREASED, AND TAIL ROTOR AUTHORITY WAS LOST AS THE HELICOPTER REACHED THE SELECTED LANDING AREA.  THE HELICOPTER TOUCHED DOWN, THE RIGHT SKID STRUCK A STUMP AND BROKE, AND THE MAIN ROTOR BLADES SEVERED THE TAIL BOOM. THE COMPRESSOR DISCHARGE PRESSURE LINE (PC LINE) FROM THE PC AIR FILTER TO THE COMPRESSOR SCROLL FAILED AT THE AIR FILTER CONNECTION. THE FUEL TO THE ENGINE IS CONTROLLED BY  REGULATED AIR PRESSURE, AND THE LOSS OF AIR PRESSURE WOULD CAUSE THE ENGINE TO GO TO FLIGHT IDLE.  LABORATORY EXAMINATION OF THE PC AIRLINE REVEALED THAT THIS PART FAILED BECAUSE OF HIGH CYCLE FATIGUE.  FATIGUE INITIATED ON THE SURFACE OF THE TUBE UNDERNEATH THE ATTACHMENT NUT SLEEVE IN AREAS OF CORROSSION PITTING.  ANALYSIS OF THE CORROSION BY-PRODUCTS INDICATED EXPOSURE TO A MARINE OR INDUSTRIAL ENVIRONMENT. THE POWER LOSS OCCURRED AT LOW ALTITUDE, AT LOW AIRSPEED, IN MODERATE TO SEVERE TURBULENCE, AND OVER ROUGH TERRAIN, CONDITIONS THAT, VIRTUALLY PRECLUDED THE SAFE RECOVERY OF THE HELICOPTER ONCE THE ENGINE WENT TO FLIGHT IDLE.  THE TAIL WIND ON LANDING FURTHER AGGRAVATED THE SITUATION. THE FOLLOWING LABORATORY REPORT WAS COMPLETED:  LP 279/84 - PC LINE FAILURE - HUGHES 500 D. FINDINGS; CAUSE RELATED: 1.  THE PC AIRLINE FAILED IN FATIGUE IN AREAS WEAKENED BY CORROSION PITTING;  AS A RESULT, AIR PRESSURE WAS LOST AND THE ENGINE WENT TO IDLE. THIS TUBE AND ASSOCIATED FITTINGS WERE TO BE INSPECTED USING A 10X MAGNIFYING GLASS NO LATER THAN 31 JULY 1986, AND THEREAFTER ON A PERIODIC BASIS WHENEVER THE TUBE IS REMOVED DURING A COMPRESSOR WASHING.

Apres avoir quitte Charlo (Nouveau-Brunswick) en direction de Sorel, le pilote rencontre pour une deuxieme journee consecutive des conditions meteorologiques defavorables. La veille, il etait revenu atterrir a Charlo, mais cette fois-ci il continue vers sa destination. En cours de route, il tente en vain a plusieurs reprises de communiquer avec la station d'information de vol (FSS) de Mont-Joli. Apres environ une heure de vol, les conditions continuent a se deteriorer. Le pilote decide d'effectuer une approche en campagne dans un champs avoisinant. A l'atterrissage, la roulette de nez s'embourbe, l'oleo brise et l'appareil glisse une centaine de pieds avant de s'immobiliser. L'enquete a revele qu'avant son depart, le pilote avait recu un expose meteorologique complet a la station d'information de vol (FSS) de Charlo. Generalement, il pouvait s'attendre a des conditions tres variables le long de sa route, avec des plafonds entre 1 000 pieds et 4 000 pieds au-dessus du  niveau de la mer (ASL) et des visibilites reduites jusqu'a un demi-mille par endroits. L'itineraire prevu (Charlo-Quebec-Sorel) traverse une chaine de montagnes orientee N.-E./S.-O. L'elevation moyenne du terrain varie entre 1 200 pieds et 1 800 pieds au-dessus du niveau de la mer (ASL) avec points culminants s'elevant jusqu'a 2 300 pieds au-dessus du niveau de la mer (ASL). Tel que prevu, les conditions se sont deteriorees a mesure que le vol progressait vers l'ouest. Le pilote a quand meme continue croyant qu'il s'agissait d'un phenomene local et esperant que les conditions s'amelioreraient. Par ailleurs, la visibilite reduite et le plafond bas l'ont contraint a descendre pour rester en vol visuel. Puisqu'il survolait une region montagneuse, cette decision lui a cause deux problemes principaux. En premier lieu, il n'a pas pu maintenir une altitude pertinente et securitaire au-dessus du terrain et, par surcroit, la portee de ses communications a diminue  considerablement. Ne pouvant communiquer avec les stations d'information de vol (FSS) environnantes, il n'a pu verifier si, en realite, les conditions allaient s'ameliorer. Lorsque le pilote s'est rendu compte que poursuivre le vol devenait trop dangereux, les conditions s'etaient deteriorees a un point tel qu'il n'osait plus faire demi-tour ou derouter. La seule option possible etait d'effectuer une approche en campagne. Presse par le temps, il a choisi parmi les champs environnants. Malheureusement, le secteur qu'il survolait etait accidente et les champs etaient cahoteux et detrempes. A l'atterrissage, la surface a entraine une deceleration rapide, la roulette de nez s'est embourbee et l'oleo avant n'a pu resister a la charge. CONCLUSIONS Faits etablis se rapportant aux causes: 1. Le pilote n'a pas su reconnaitre les dangers associes au survol de regions montagneuses dans des conditions meteorologiques marginales. 2. Le pilote a poursuivi le vol malgre des conditions  meteorologiques qui justifiaient de faire demi-tour ou de derouter beaucoup plus tot. 3. En retardant la prise de decision, le pilote a ete force d'atterrir dans un secteur peu propice. 4. La surface du champ etait trop irreguliere et detrempee pour permettre un atterrissage securitaire. Autres faits etablis: -Neant-

Shortly after take-off, the pilot reported that the engine was losing power and he was carrying out an emergency landing. Nothing further was heard from the helicopter. The wreckage was discovered about two hours later; all five occupants of the helicopter were fatally injured. The Canadian Aviation Safety Board determined that the engine experienced an internal fire which led to an uncontained engine failure. An in-flight fire occurred as a result of the number one turbine wheel disintegrating. The flight departed Revelstoke, British Columbia with four fire-fighters on board en route to a fire near Beatrice Lake. Approximately 25 minutes after take-off, a Forestry Services Duty Officer received a radio transmission from the helicopter pilot indicating that an engine failure had occurred and that the helicopter was going down. A while later, a helicopter on a fire-spotting patrol located the wreckage. There were no survivors. The helicopter struck the ground at high  speed at a flight path angle of 33 degrees, in a very steep, left-bank attitude. The examination of the engine (Allison 250-C-28B) found that the turbine assembly gas producer outside casing was ruptured and the first stage turbine wheel was missing. The engine was shipped to the Canadian Aviation Safety Board Engineering Facility for a complete analysis. Investigators were unable to recover any part of the missing turbine wheel from the wreckage. The field investigation revealed that the fuel control lever was in the cut-off position. This was consistent with the pilot's twist grip position of the collective lever. The lower turbine shield was penetrated by debris from the first stage turbine wheel which severed the fuel lines of the fuel pump and fuel control unit. This would have allowed fuel to spray freely about on the engine until the pilot was able to shut off the fuel. The first stage turbine nozzle assembly was found to have phosphorus in the form of a surface  deposit diffused into the diaphragm at the air cooling hole. A pressure check of the number eight oil sump was performed during the engine teardown, and leakage was observed at the sump during the test. Recovered fuselage components, which included the cabin doors, indicated smoke and soot residue present on the interior surfaces. The baggage compartment in which two litres of gasoline were stowed showed signs of an in-flight fire. Medical evidence indicated that smoke and fire were present in the cabin area of the helicopter, prior to the helicopter striking the ground. ANALYSIS: The pilot initiated an autorotation when the engine failure occurred. The engine fuel control unit was found in the cut-off position and the twist grip throttle on the collective was closed as would normally be expected following an engine failure. It could not be determined how much more of the emergency check-list had been completed beyond this action or if collective had been applied  before ground contact. The engine failure was caused by the failure of the number one turbine wheel. Although the engine was extensively damaged, it was evident that the wheel had departed from the engine while the helicopter was in flight. The phosphorus deposits are indicative of an internal oil fire. An oil fire will occur in the area of the number one turbine wheel if oil from the number eight bearing lubrication system is allowed to escape past the labyrinth seal. Once the oil is past the seal, it contacts the hot turbine wheel, vaporizes, and flows outwards. Upon reaching the area of the first stage nozzle turbine cooling air holes, it is mixed with the air passing through the holes. Because the temperature is above the flash-point of the oil, the mixture ignites. The air passing through the air holes creates a blow-torch effect, applying flame to the rim of the wheel disc. Although the turbine wheel was not recovered, examination of engines which failed in  similar circumstances revealed that fatigue cracks appeared, progressed, and produced wheel failure. The engine manufacturer ascribed this to thermal fatigue. The manufacturer's technical data reports suggest that the source of the leak may have been as a result of improper assembly. The investigation did not reveal any evidence that would support this suggestion. This particular engine did not have high oil consumption, nor was there any evidence of smoke coming from the engine. Once the wheel had failed and disintegrated, there was nothing to stop the pieces as they flew out through the side of the engine. The hot shrapnel introduced an ignition source for any combustible material in its path. It set fire to both the engine fuel supply system and the baggage compartment's contents.
