The aircraft was dispatched to engage in water bombing at the site of a large forest fire. After completing one successful water pick-up from an open bay, the aircraft was directed to a lake closer to the fire. During the water pick-up, the pilot rejected the take-off, and the aircraft porpoised and came to a stop. The crew shut down the engines but decided to restart them to beach the aircraft. When the aircraft started to move forward, it began to fill with water through a hole in the forward hull. The engines were shut down, and the aircraft sank. The two crew members escaped through the cockpit overhead escape hatches. The lake was surrounded by hills and had a dog-leg to the left. There was a gusty cross-wind from the right producing about a one-foot chop. After take-off, the water bombers were turning left to stay over water in order to avoid having to climb over the hills at the shoreline. This aircraft was a different Canso than the one normally flown  by this crew. It had slightly different handling and performance characteristics. On the water, the aircraft was nose heavy and had a tendency to turn right. The crew was planning to turn left after the water pick-up to follow the lake. The take-off run used more of the available space than they expected, and the crew attempted to turn left while still on the water, but the aircraft would not turn. The particular characteristics of this aircraft and the cross-wind from the left contributed to the inability of the crew to turn the aircraft on the water. When the aircraft would not turn, the pilot elected to reject the take-off, and the aircraft began to porpoise. Reducing power would tend to pitch the nose up, and this, together with the wind and wave conditions, led to the porpoise. Although the crew had been briefed on the procedure to recover from a porpoise, they did not take effective recovery action. The porpoise oscillations increased in intensity until the  aircraft sustained hull damage. The Canso is a World War II vintage aircraft which has been modified as a water bomber. Each Canso used by the operator had different handling characteristics of varying degree. The crew was experienced but normally flew the same aircraft. When assigned to this aircraft, they were not briefed on its characteristics. FINDINGS: Cause Related: 1. The crew was not familiar with the different performance and handling characteristics of this aircraft. 2. During the water pick-up, the aircraft used more of the available distance than the crew anticipated. 3. Because of the aircraft characteristics on the water and a cross-wind from the right, the crew was unable to turn the aircraft to the left to follow the contour of the lake. 4. The crew elected to reject the take-off because of steeply rising terrain straight ahead. 5. During the rejected take-off procedure, the aircraft entered a porpoise from which the crew was unable to recover. Other: -Nil-

The pilot of the float-equipped aircraft, with a fire warden and one other passenger on board, was conducting an aerial forest fire spotting flight. After circling a fire, he turned up a sloping mountain valley to turn around for another pass over the fire. The valley was narrow, and the pilot was unable to turn the aircraft. The pilot initiated a climb; however, the aircraft contacted trees on the upward slope of the valley and nosed over 400 feet below the top of the valley and just beyond a clearing in the trees. The fire warden was killed, and the pilot and one passenger were seriously injured. The plane's ELT signals were picked up, the wreckage was spotted, and the injured were airlifted to hospital. Under the existing conditions of temperature and altitude, the aircraft could not safely turn around in or climb out of the confined mountain valley. The aircraft was not equipped with shoulder harnesses, nor were they required; however, medical evidence indicates that  the injuries suffered resulted from unrestrained flailing of the occupants' upper bodies. The pilot had misjudged both the turning space available in the mountain valley and the aircraft's climb capability. Once the aircraft was in the valley, ground contact could not be avoided. The aircraft could have been force-landed in a nearby clearing, likely with less serious consequences. The occupants' injuries would have been less serious had the shoulder harnesses been available and worn. FINDINGS: Cause Related: 1. The pilot misjudged the turning space available and the aircraft's climb capability. 2. A more suitable forced-landing area was not used. 3. The occupants' injuries would have been minimized had shoulder harnesses been available and used. Other: -Nil-

A85P0023:  The pilot of the helicopter which was equipped with a "monsoon bucket" had been scooping water from a fast-flowing river for about three and one-half hours and was dropping it on a nearby forest fire. As the bucket was being filled, the current carried it under the helicopter and attempted to sweep the bucket downstream. In an attempt to hold the bucket against the current, the pilot applied power to the helicopter. The tail rotor struck the water, and the helicopter rotated violently into the water. During the crash, the pilot was thrown against the side of the cockpit. The helmet he was wearing was cracked from the force of the impact. The pilot's shoulder harness was not worn. During previous operations, the pilot had been able to judge the speed of the current and had picked up the bucket just as it was full and passed beneath the helicopter. On this attempt, the bucket was swept out in front of the helicopter and began to pull on the hoist line. Instead of moving  ahead to keep the bucket perpendicular to the helicopter, the pilot attempted to lift the bucket. He felt a juddering in his controls, which he thought was caused by pulling the bucket across the rocks on the river bottom. In actual fact, it was the tail rotor blades striking the water. When the tail rotor dug in and broke the tail rotor drive, the helicopter immediately rotated to the right and crashed. The fact that the pilot's head struck the side of the cockpit with such force as to break his helmet indicates that he might have suffered serious injury without the protection of the helmet. The shoulder harness was not used because the pilot felt he would not be able to observe the slung load adequately. FINDINGS: Cause Related: 1. The pilot attempted to lift the bucket against a strong current with the helicopter not centered over the load and he allowed the tail rotor to strike the water. Other: 1. The pilot might have suffered a severe head injury had he  not been wearing a helmet. 2. The pilot's shoulder harness was not in use.

THE HELICOPTER WAS WORKING IN SUPPORT OF FOREST FIRE OPERATIONS AND WAS BEING FLOWN WITH THE PILOT'S DOOR REMOVED. THE HELICOPTER WAS ON A LANDING PAD BEING UNLOADED, WHEN A LOSS OF CONTROL OCCURRED. THE HELICOPTER SLID OFF THE PAD BACKWARDS IN A NOSE-HIGH ATTITUDE AND ROLLED DOWN A STEEP SLOPE. THE PILOT SUSTAINED MINOR INJURIES WHEN HE JUMPED CLEAR OF THE HELICOPTER. THE LANDING AREA WAS A MAN-MADE CLEARING ON A HILLTOP. THE TREES HAD BEEN CLEARED IN A HORSESHOE SHAPE, WHICH ALLOWED MINIMUM ROTOR CLEARANCE. LOGS WERE PLACED SO THAT THE REAR OF THE SKIDS RESTED ON A LOG WHILE THE FRONT OF THE SKIDS MADE GROUND CONTACT. ACCORDING TO THE PILOT WHO WAS MONITORING THE OFF-LANDING, AN ENGINE OVERSPEED OCCURRED, AND THE HELICOPTER PITCHED UP, VEERED RIGHT, AND SLID OFF THE PAD BACKWARDS.  EXAMINATION OF THE HELICOPTER, ITS ENGINE AND ACCESSORIES DID NOT REVEAL ANY EVIDENCE OF FAILURE OR MALFUNCTION. THE REASON WHY THE HELICOPTER PITCHED UP AND ROLLED OFF THE PAD WAS NOT  DETERMINED. FINDINGS: CAUSE RELATED: 1. THE HELICOPTER PITCHED UP AND ROLLED OFF THE PAD FOR UNDETERMINED REASONS. OTHER: -NIL-

ENGINE SPOOLED DOWN AS BUCKET WAS BEING PULLED FROM WATER. FOLLOWING RELEASE OF THE BUCKET, THE AIRCRAFT STRUCK A RIVER EMBANKMENT THEN BECAME AIRBORNE AGAIN. AUTOROTATION WAS CARRIED OUT ONTO A SANDBAR BUT AIRCRAFT ROLLED OVER AT IMPACT.

THE HELICOPTER THAT WAS FITTED WITH A 300-GALLON UNDERSLUNG BUCKET WAS ENGAGED IN FIRE FIGHTING DUTIES. PRIOR TO PICKING UP A LOAD OF RETARDANT, THE PILOT FLEW OVER TO A BEAVER POND TO SEE IF THE WATER WAS DEEP ENOUGH TO PICK UP WATER. WHILE FLYING OVER THE BEAVER POND AT LOW ALTITUDE, THE PILOT HEARD A LOW ROTOR WARNING HORN AND SENSED THE ENGINE SPEED (LYCOMING T53-13B) WAS INCREASING. THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO MAKE A PRECAUTIONARY AUTOROTATIONAL LANDING IN THE BEAVER POND, AND A HARD LANDING OCCURRED. THE BELL MODEL 205A-1 MANUAL STATES THAT, IF AN ENGINE OVERSPEED OCCURS, THE PILOT SHOULD COMPLETE THE ENGINE FUEL CONTROL MALFUNCTION PROCEDURE. IF ALTITUDE AND TIME DO NOT PERMIT COMPLETION OF THIS PROCEDURE, AN AUTOROTATION SHOULD BE CARRIED OUT. THE BEAVER POND WAS THE ONLY CLEAR AREA AVAILABLE TO CARRY OUT AN AUTOROTATIONAL LANDING. IN ORDER TO REMAIN WITHIN THE CONFINES OF THE BEAVER POND, THE PILOT WAS FORCED TO FLARE AT ABOUT 30 FEET ABOVE THE GROUND TO REDUCE HIS  FORWARD SPEED TO ZERO. FROM THIS HEIGHT, THRE WAS INSUFFICIENT ROTOR SPEED AVAILABLE TO CUSHION THE LANDING, AND A HARD LANDING OCCURRED. THE ENGINE WAS DISASSEMBLED, AND IT WAS DISCOVERED THAT THE BEVEL GEARS DRIVING THE TACHOMETER AND GOVERNOR WERE DAMAGED AND DISENGAGED. THIS WOULD HAVE CAUSED THE ENGINE TO ENTER AN OVERSPEED CONDITION, AND THE DISENGAGEMENT OF THE TACHOMETER DRIVE WOULD CAUSE THE LOW RPM LIGHT TO ILLUMINATE. LABORATORY ANALYSIS CONCLUDED THAT THE TACHOMETER DRIVE BEARING SLEEVE BUSHING WAS NOT PROPERLY INSTALLED AT THE TIME OF THE LAST BUSHING REPLACEMENT. THE IDENTITY OF THE AGENCY WHICH PERFORMED THE SLEEVE BUSHING REPLACEMENT WAS NOT DETERMINED, AS THERE WAS NO RECORD OF ANY WORK HAVING BEEN DONE ON THIS COMPONENT IN THE AVAILABLE AIRCRAFT LOG-BOOKS. THE FOLLOWING LABORATORY REPORT WAS COMPLETED: LP 194/85 - ACCESSORY DRIVE GEAR ASSEMBLY, BELL 205A-1. FINDINGS: CAUSE RELATED: 1. THE TACHOMETER DRIVE BEARING SLEEVE BUSHING WAS NOT PROPERLY  INSTALLED AT THE TIME OF THE LAST BUSHING REPLACEMENT. 2. THE BEVEL GEARS IN THE ENGINE, WHICH DRIVE THE TACHOMETER AND THE GOVERNOR BECAME DISENGAGED, CAUSING THE ENGINE TO ENTER AN OVERSPEED CONDITION. 3. IN ACCORDANCE WITH RECOMMENDED PROCEDURE, THE PILOT CARRIED OUT AN AUTOROTATION INTO THE ONLY CLEAR AREA AVAILABLE. 4. IN ORDER TO REMAIN WITHIN THE CONFINES OF THE BEAVER POND, THE PILOT FLARED AT ABOUT 30 FEET TO REDUCE HIS FORWARD SPEED TO ZERO. 5. A HARD LANDING OCCURRED AS A RESULT OF INSUFFICIENT ROTOR SPEED BEING AVAILABLE TO CUSHION THE LANDING. OTHER: 1. THERE WAS NO RECORD OF THE BEARING SLEEVE BUSHING BEING REPLACED IN THE ENGINE LOG BOOKS.

De retour d'une patrouille de surveillance des feux de foret, le pilote, qui etait seul a bord, voulait executer un atterrissage court sur la piste 03 de l'aeroport de Maniwaki. Il s'est presente en finale a une vitesse oscillant entre 65 et 70 noeuds, pleins volets sortis, train sorti et moteur au ralenti. En approche finale, le taux de descente s'est accru. Le pilote a brutalement remis pleins gaz, le moteur a eu des rates puis s'est arrete. Le pilote a tire sur le manche; le taux de descente s'est encore accru et l'appareil a touche a 200 pieds environ avant le seuil de la piste. Les jambes du train d'atterrissage principal se sont rompues apres l'impact. L'avion a glisse sur le ventre et s'est immobilise a quelque 130 pieds avant le seuil de piste. Les conditions meteorologiques signalees par un observateur a l'aeroport etaient les suivantes: ciel clair, temperature 20 degres Celsius, vents nord nord-ouest: 11 a 19 noeuds. On n'a releve aucune defectuosite technique  du moteur (Avco Lycoming 540-J3C5D) anterieure a l'accident. Ce moteur peut toutefois avoir des rates, voire s'etouffer, si la remise des gaz est brutale plutot que d'etre progressive. La diminution normale de la vitesse du vent a l'approche du sol a provoque une baisse de la vitesse indiquee et, en consequence, une diminution de la portance. L'avion s'est enfonce et le pilote s'est rendu compte qu'il n'atteindrait pas la piste. Lorsqu'il a remis brutalement les gaz, le moteur s'est etouffe. En tirant instinctivement sur le manche, il a provoque une autre hausse marquee du taux de descente et l'avion qui a brutalement touche le sol avant le seuil de piste. CONCLUSIONS Faits etablis se rapportant aux causes: 1. Afin de contrer un taux de descente eleve et de rallonger son approche, le pilote a fait une remise des gaz trop brusque, et le moteur s'est etouffe. 2. En tirant sur le manche, le pilote n'a fait qu'augmenter le taux de descente et l'avion a brutalement touche  le sol avant le seuil de piste. Autres faits etablis: -Neant-

The helicopter was flying in support of fire suppression operations and was transporting three fire-fighters and their equipment a short distance along the fire line. The pilot was preparing for descent when the engine emitted a strange noise, then lost all power. The pilot turned toward a swampy clearing and attempted to arrest the rate of descent. The aircraft continued descending and crashed through small trees, coming to rest on its side. All four occupants suffered serious injuries. Cause Related: 1. The engine lost power when the second stage turbine wheel stub shaft failed. 2. The stub shaft failed probably from a mechanism involving seal hang-up and rub, with subsequent torsional overload failure of the shaft. 3. When the engine failed, there was no suitable area for the pilot to make an autorotational landing. Other: -Nil-

The helicopter was engaged in forest fire suppression and had just completed two successful water uplift flights. On the third water uplift, as the helicopter transitioned from hover to forward flight, it struck an unmarked 5/8 inch cable suspended across the river. The cable contacted the windshield then the main rotor blades, causing the helicopter to vibrate violently. The pilot reduced power, and the helicopter settled into the water. The cable was attached to trees and was approximately seven feet above the water on one side and 20 feet high on the other side. There were high broken clouds, and the wind was from the south at 20 knots. The visibility was 20 miles, and the temperature was 22 degrees Celsius. The pilot had checked the area for obstructions but did not see the cable. During the uplift, the rotor wash sprayed water on the windshield which resulted in some reduction in forward visibility.

Le pilote et l'observateur effectuaient la patrouille incendie pour le compte de la Societe de conservation du Nord-Ouest. Environ cinquante-cinq minutes apres le decollage, l'helicoptere s'est ecrase sans que le pilote n'envoie de message de detresse. L'appareil a heurte les arbres a haute vitesse et s'est immobilise au sol en position legerement inversee, sur le cote gauche. Il a ensuite ete detruit par un incendie qui a ete alimente par le carburant contenu dans les reservoirs. Les deux occupants ont ete tues au moment de l'impact. Faits etablis se rapportant aux causes: 1. La poutre de queue s'est rompue en vol pour une raison indeterminee. Autres faits etablis: 1. Plusieurs defectuosites n'avaient pas ete rectifiees avant le vol.

The pilot, with a forestry official as passenger, was on a fire patrol in the float-equipped aircraft out of Fort McMurray, Alberta. The aircraft had been flying for approximately two hours, at an altitude of 3,500 feet agl, when the engine lost power as fuel was exhausted from the left tank. Adequate power could not be restored, and the pilot force-landed the aircraft in muskeg. In an attempt to restore power, the pilot switched the fuel selector to the "both" position, and power was restored momentarily before the engine again lost power. The right tank was then selected, and the pilot noted that the fuel flow was seven gallons per hour. He then placed the auxiliary fuel pump switch to emergency. The engine continued to run unevenly and at low power. The auxiliary fuel pump was then switched off, and the mixture control was pushed into the rich position. No change was made to the throttle setting, which remained where it had been for cruise power. As the aircraft was  losing both airspeed and altitude, and as power could not be restored, the pilot prepared for a forced landing. One lake, about five miles away, appeared to be within gliding distance. The pilot maintained an airspeed of 80 to 85 mph as he approached the lake, but it became apparent that he would undershoot by about one-quarter of a mile. Full flap was lowered just prior to touchdown, and the aircraft landed heavily in the muskeg. The fuel system was checked, and no usable fuel was found in the left tank, but there was a considerable quantity in the right tank. The engine was started with the tank selector on the right tank, and the engine ran normally. The owner's manual for this aircraft recognizes that a fuel tank may be completely exhausted in flight and gives a recommended procedure for restarting the engine. The auxiliary fuel pump should be switched on immediately and left in the emergency position for at least three to five seconds to ensure adequate  fuel flow. The pilot did not switch the pump on immediately and did not leave it on long enough to purge the fuel lines of air. FINDINGS: Cause Related: 1. The engine lost power because of fuel starvation. 2. The recommended procedure to restart the engine was not followed. 3. The engine would not produce normal power because of inadequate fuel flow and the presence of air in the fuel line. Other: -Nil-

The pilot departed the terminal parking area on a short fight to the forestry helipad for fuel. The helicopter was passing over the centre of the airfield at a height of 50 feet and at 10 to 15 mph airspeed, when the engine-out horn and light came on, and the engine lost all power. The pilot made an autorotative landing, but the helicopter landed hard, and the tail boom and skids were damaged. The aircraft lost power because of lack of fuel. The aircraft manufacturer's handbook indicates that a successful autorotation from 50 feet at 15 mph is not possible without damaging the helicopter.

The Firecat, operating as Tanker 62, departed Williams Lake at approximately 1400 Pacific daylight time (PDT) for a fire-suppression flight to McBride, British Columbia. On arrival at destination, Tanker 62 was positioned as the number two drop aircraft and was in a holding pattern until conditions were suitable to complete the run to the fire area. Following a short delay, the pilot of Tanker 62 was asked by the fire-control officer if he was next, and this was acknowledged by Tanker 62. The fire-control officer then described the fire-suppression run required, and, when this transmission was not acknowledged by Tanker 62, the fire-control officer attempted to communicate with Tanker 62 but was unsuccessful. During this time, another Firecat pilot noticed a small fire a short distance from the main fire. The secondary fire was subsequently confirmed to have been started by the crash of Tanker 62. The pilot was fatally injured. FINDINGS: Cause Related: 1. The pilot lost  control of the aircraft for undetermined reasons. Other: -Nil-

A87A0010: The aircraft was engaged in water bombing a forest fire located near the threshold of runway 22 at Gander Airport. The aircraft was over the airport at an altitude of 200 feet above ground level (agl) en route to the fire with the fifth load, when the left engine (Pratt and Whitney R-1830-92) started to run rough and lose power. The captain continued to the fire, dropped the load, and turned for a landing on runway 31. After landing and carrying out a 180-degree turn, the captain leaned the mixture on the left engine to try to smooth it out, but it stopped. The captain continued taxiing to the Forestry Department ramp using the brakes for steering. After turning onto the ramp, the captain let the aircraft roll under its own momentum approximately half-way across the ramp. When he applied the brakes again to turn the aircraft, they did not respond. At this time, the co-pilot also applied brakes, but the aircraft continued straight ahead toward the edge of the ramp  without any braking action. When the captain realized that the aircraft would not turn or stop, he shut down the right engine. The aircraft struck an auxiliary power cart at the edge of the ramp, rolled down a slope into a ditch, and the nose gear broke off when it struck the ramp access road. The aircraft swung 15 degrees to the left and came to rest with the right wing 24 feet from the Forestry Department building. CONCLUSIONS: Findings: 1. The cylinder hold-down studs for the number two cylinder failed because of fatigue cracking. 2. The failure of the piston skirt was a result of overload and was secondary to the release of the cylinder. 3. The captain taxied the aircraft to the maintenance facility on one engine, contrary to an unwritten company policy, because he felt that it was urgent to have the aircraft repaired quickly so he could return to fight the fire. 4. The captain taxied the aircraft too fast, resulting in the brakes becoming overheated and  ineffective. 5. The downslope on the ramp combined with the tail wind increased the aircraft speed as it crossed the ramp. Causes: The engine power loss occurred because the cylinder hold-down studs failed as a result of fatigue cracking. After landing, the captain taxied the aircraft on one engine at too great a speed, which resulted in the brakes becoming overheated and ineffective.

A87Q0012: A garbled radio call led the pilot of an aircraft to investigate a possible aircraft in distress.  The investigating aircraft discovered a small forest fire started by a crashed aircraft.  Both occupants of the downed aircraft were fatally injured.The Canadian Aviation Safety Board determined that the float-equipped aircraft crashed when the pilot was unable to reach a suitable landing area following a complete engine failure at low altitude.

The helicopter had been chartered to perform fire-control duties to the east of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, where a number of fires were burning. On arrival in the area, the pilot landed, contacted the fire chief, and was assigned the job of bucketing water to one of the fires. The pilot departed to the only water source in the area, a small beaver pond. After arriving at the pond, the pilot lowered the bucket, which was attached to a 15-foot lanyard, but the water was too shallow for the bucket to sink. The pilot manoeuvred the helicopter to an area where the water appeared to be deeper and again lowered the bucket. The bucket sank, and, as the pilot applied collective to raise the load and commence forward flight, he noticed a sudden rise in turbine outlet temperature (TOT). While checking the mirror to ensure that the cable had not snagged over the skid, the pilot felt a "jerk", and the helicopter rolled right and struck the water. The pilot, who had been wearing a  protective helmet and shoulder harness, was able to extricate himself and swim to shore; he was rescued about four hours later. CONCLUSIONS: Findings: 1. While filling the bucket, the pilot's attention was momentarily diverted, and the aircraft moved to the right. The bucket could not move in concert because of dense weeds, and the cable pulled the aircraft over. 2. The pilot was wearing a protective helmet and shoulder harness which probably prevented serious injuries. 3. There was no procedure in place to ensure that radio communication between the helicopter and the fire-control centre was maintained; as a result, rescue was delayed. 4. The ELT did not function because of low battery output. Causes: When the aircraft moved to the right, the water-filled bucket could not move as quickly because of dense weeds, and the cable tightened and pulled the aircraft over.

A87C4034: The aircraft was engaged in fire suppression and had just picked up a load of water from a nearby lake, when the pilot felt a severe vibration coming from the left engine. The pilot jettisoned the load, feathered the propeller, and shut down the engine. Only two of three propeller blades feathered, but the pilot was able to return to Thompson and land safely. Since manufacture, the propeller (Hamilton Standard model 43E60) had accumulated 84 hours in service. During disassembly, it was determined that the blade bushing screws and the blade drive pins that secure the blade bushing to the number two (unfeathered) blade, had failed in shear. The blade thrust washer had a radial crack running completely through it. The manufacturer examined the propeller and found the number two blade to be deformed slightly rearward. This varied from the other two blades, and, as there was no evidence of leading edge damage, was indicative of static blade impact. The damage is  typical of a blade struck during towing or service equipment operations; the strike could have occurred at any time prior to this incident. The thrust washer initially cracked at blade impact and eventually the crack propagated completely through the washer. The sharp edges of the crack scraped out an area inside of the barrel arm and caused the thrust washer to jam against the wall. This resulted in enough resistance that the torque required to change blade angle became greater than the shear strength of the blade bushing screws and the blade drive pins. The screws and pins eventually sheared, and the blade bushing separated from the blade. The blade, now independent of the remaining two blades, assumed a different pitch angle which resulted in excessive propeller vibration. CONCLUSIONS: Findings: 1. The number two blade was deformed slightly rearward because of static blade impact. 2. The blade thrust washer cracked at impact and eventually jammed, causing the number  two blade bushing screws and drive pins to shear. 3. The blade bushing separated from the number two blade resulting in a different blade pitch angle and excessive propeller vibration. Causes: The number two propeller blade had previously received static impact damage. The twin-engined helicopter was dispatched to pick up a forest fire protection crew which was threatened by an approaching fire. The crew was located on a rock outcropping approximately 15 feet above the surface of a small lake. On arrival at the site, the pilot balanced the helicopter with one wheel on the rock outcropping and the other over the lake surface, and the fire protection crew began to board. The helicopter crewman, who occupied the left seat in the cockpit, left his position and entered the passenger cabin to assist in the loading. Shortly thereafter, the number two engine lost power, and the pilot directed the personnel on board to exit the aircraft. Following the evacuation, the aircraft began to slowly descend and drift sideways over the lake. The pilot was unable to arrest the descent, and the aircraft settled into the lake. The uninjured pilot exited the helicopter and was rescued immediately by another helicopter and crew. The accident occurred at lat  56o06'N, long 103o44'W* at 2215 central standard time (CST)**, during the hours of daylight. The accident site is approximately 1,250 feet above sea level (asl).*** 3.1 Findings: 1. The crewman inadvertently moved the number two fuel shut-off switch to the closed position when he exited the flight crew compartment. 2. The number two engine stopped because of fuel starvation when the number two fuel shut-off solenoid valve closed. 3. The helicopter was unable to maintain flight on the remaining engine. 4. A suitable landing area was not used to board the passengers and equipment. 5. The fuel shut-off switches were not externally guarded. 6. The pilot was certified and qualified for the flight in accordance with existing regulations. 7. The aircraft was certified, equipped, and maintained in accordance with existing regulations and approved procedures. 8. There was no evidence found of any airframe failure or system malfunction prior to or during the flight. 9. The weight and centre of gravity were within the prescribed limits. 3.2 Causes: The number two fuel shut-off switch was inadvertently moved to the closed position.

A87Q0022: L'helicoptere etait utilise dans le cadre d'une operation de lutte contre un incendie de foret. Le pilote avait quitte la base du lac Grosse Roche (Quebec) dans des conditions de vol a vue (VFR) avec le plein de carburant et trois passagers a bord. Alors que l'helicoptere franchissait 300 pieds-sol en montee a une vitesse d'environ 70 noeuds, le moteur (Allison 250C20B) a decelere graduellement et l'helicoptere a effectue un mouvement de lacet a gauche. Le voyant d'alarme d'extinction moteur s'est allume et l'avertisseur d'alarme a retenti. Le pilote a immediatement entame une descente en autorotation vers l'aire la plus convenable puis il a averti les passagers qu'il y avait une panne moteur. Lorsque l'helicoptere est arrive pres de la cime des arbres, le pilote a tire sur la commande de pas cyclique pour reduire la vitesse vers l'avant et il a tire sur la commande de pas collectif pour diminuer la vitesse descensionnelle. L'helicoptere s'est pose brutalement dans les  arbres, il a pris feu et il a ete detruit. Les deux occupants en places avant ont subi des blessures graves tandis que les passagers en places arriere, coinces dans l'epave, ont peri dans l'accident. Faits etablis: 1. Le moteur a subi une perte de puissance pour une raison qui n'a pu etre determinee. 2. La majeure partie du circuit de carburant a ete detruite dans l'ecrasement et dans l'incendie qui a suivi. 3. La contamination du carburant n'a pas ete un facteur contributif. 4. La turbine ne presentait aucun signe de dommage anterieur a l'impact. Causes: Le moteur de l'helicoptere a decelere pour une raison qui n'a pu etre determinee.

The pilot was flying at an altitude of about 50 to 75 feet above the water for a retardant drop on a fire burning on an island in Lake LaBerge, Yukon. The aircraft flew through the smoke, and, as it emerged, the left wing struck a pine tree. The flying characteristics of the aircraft were not affected, and the aircraft was flown back to Whitehorse without difficulty. The pilot had been warned by radio of a tree-top that rose above the general height of the trees in the fire area. He noticed one tree-top off to his right as he approached the fire and assumed that it was the one about which he had been warned. The tree struck by the aircraft protruded about 15 feet above the surrounding trees. The altitude at which the aircraft flew for the retardant drop allowed it to clear the trees on the island with the exception of one or two isolated protruding tree-tops. The pilot believed he had the protruding tree-top mentioned in the radio warning in sight. He did not see the  other protruding tree-top ahead of the aircraft because it was obscured by smoke until just before impact. During the retardant run, the pilot did not fly at a sufficient altitude to ensure that the aircraft would clear all obstacles. FINDINGS: Cause Related: 1. The pilot did not see the protruding tree-top because it was obscured by smoke. 2. The pilot flew at an altitude that would just clear the trees because he believed he had located and would miss a protruding tree-top known to be on the island. Pendant la passe d'epandage, le pilote n'a pas maintenu une altitude suffisante pour s'assurer que l'avion franchirait tous les obstacles. CONCLUSIONS Faits etablis se rapportant aux causes: 1. Le pilote n'a pas vu la cime d'un arbre qui depassait les autres parce que la fumee la cachait. 2. Le pilote a vole a une altitude qui permettait juste d'eviter les arbres, croyant avoir apercu la cime de l'arbre dont on lui avait parle et qui n'etait pas sur sa trajectoire. A87W0051: The pilot, flying the helicopter on a forestry contract, was dropping water from a water bucket onto a small forest fire. On the second trip, the pilot slowed down to near the hover, about 100 feet above the trees. Forestry ground personnel requested him to move to the right to get over the fire before he dropped the load. As the pilot made the correction, the helicopter started rotating to the right and eventually struck the trees. After the impact, the pilot escaped through the right rear door; the helicopter burst into flames and was destroyed by fire. Examination of the burnt wreckage did not show any mechanical problems. The capacity of the bucket had been reduced to 70 gallons, which resulted in a calculated gross weight of 3,165 pounds, which is the maximum all-up weight at which the helicopter could hover out of ground effect under the conditions existing at the time. A torque of 98 per cent had been required to lift the bucket out of the river, which was 300  feet below the altitude of the fire. While the helicopter was approaching the fire, its airspeed was below 10 knots and decreasing. The pilot reported that he heard the low-rotor-warning horn shortly after losing control. When questioned after the accident, the pilot was unable to recall what control inputs he had made while looking outside the helicopter and positioning the bucket over the fire. Although the pilot reported that he had dumped the water from the bucket before the helicopter started spinning, witnesses on the ground observed water splashing out of the bucket during the rotating descent. The bucket was destroyed by the post-crash fire, and it could not be determined whether the water had been dumped before the impact. On the day before the occurrence, under similar conditions, the pilot had lost control of the helicopter, which then spun to the right a number of turns before the pilot regained control. After the accident, the pilot was unable to describe  the proper technique required to recover from loss of tail-rotor effectiveness. While hovering out of ground effect, an unanticipated right yaw or loss of tail-rotor effectiveness can occur. A 1 per cent decay in main rotor rpm will result in a 3 per cent decay in tail-rotor rpm. When main-rotor rpm decays because the pilot pulls more pitch, this rpm decay is amplified proportionately for the tail rotor until tail-rotor effectiveness is lost. In this case, while the helicopter was at low forward airspeed and at low altitude, the pilot's attention was diverted during a critical manoeuvre, and he inadvertently allowed the helicopter to start rotating to the right. The pilot did not then take the appropriate corrective action, and, as the speed of the rotation increased, he increased the collective pitch, causing the main rotor rpm to decay and tail-rotor effectiveness to be lost. CONCLUSIONS: Findings: 1. The helicopter was being hovered out of ground effect at the  maximum weight possible under the existing conditions. 2. The pilot's attention was diverted during a critical manoeuvre, and he inadvertently allowed the helicopter to start rotating to the right. 3. The pilot did not understand or use the proper technique to recover from loss of tail-rotor effectiveness. 4. The pilot increased the collective pitch, causing the main rotor rpm to decay and tail-rotor effectiveness to be lost. 5. The pilot lost control of the helicopter which then crashed. Causes: When the helicopter began to rotate to the right, the pilot did not use the correct recovery technique; as a result, control was lost, and the helicopter crashed.

The helicopter was on a flight to home base at Bluff Lake, British Columbia after a day of flying forestry personnel to various forest fires. The engine suddenly lost power, and the pilot immediately entered an autorotation and transmitted a MAYDAY message stating that his engine had failed and that he was making a forced landing. As there were no suitable landing areas, the pilot selected a spot where the jack pine trees appeared to be less dense and landed the helicopter. The aircraft shook violently as the main rotor blades chopped through the trees, and one tree penetrated the helicopter's fuselage in the back seat area, rupturing the fuel cell. The helicopter came to rest in a nose-down attitude with the left skid touching the ground and the end of the tail boom 14 feet up in the trees. The helicopter was substantially damaged, but the pilot was unhurt. The pilot was wearing a shoulder harness and safety helmet, both of which helped prevent any injury during the  violent descent through the trees. The engine (Allison 250-C20) was removed for examination after the accident. The compressor had accumulated 999.9 hours toward its scheduled overhaul time of 3,500 hours. The compressor section had two blades missing from the second stage stators, and there was evidence of damage to all sections aft of the second stage. Laboratory analysis of the compressor section revealed that the second stage stator blades had failed in overload following extensive fatigue cracking. There was also significant erosion damage which reduced the blade thickness. When the stator blades failed, damage resulted to the compressor blades, and the engine lost power. The following laboratory report was completed: LP240/87 - Compressor Failure Bell 206B, C-GCHK. CONCLUSIONS: Findings: 1. There was significant erosion damage to the second stage stator blades which reduced the blade thickness. 2. Two second stage compressor stator blades failed in overload  following extensive fatigue cracking. 3. The engine lost power in flight, forcing the pilot to land into the trees. 4. The pilot was wearing a shoulder harness and safety helmet and escaped unhurt. Causes: Two stator blades failed, resulting in damage to the compressor and causing the engine to lose power.

The aircraft was returning from a 1 hour and 15 minute flight where it had been used in the direction of tanker aircraft on fire suppression activities. The pilot unintentionally landed wheels up, and the aircraft skidded along the runway on its belly. The pilot had 46 years flying experience; however, during the last five years his flying had been limited to flying the Cessna 310 as a "bird dog" on fire suppression activities. He relied on memory for all vital action checks. The first item on his memorized pre-landing check was 'flaps', after which the remaining items were checked in sequence. On the accident flight, he was attempting a flapless landing because of a 30-degree crosswind. On the Cessna 310P aircraft, a landing gear warning horn sounds when power is reduced to 12 inches of manifold pressure. On the accident flight, the pilot flew a low, power-on approach using approximately 17 inches of manifold pressure. When the power was reduced during the landing  flare, the landing gear warning horn sounded, but, by this time, the propellers had struck the runway. The pilot's decision to carry out a flapless landing meant that the first item on the memorized check-list was not performed, and, as a result, the rest of the pre-landing check was not done. The use of a printed vital-action check-list would have reminded the pilot to lower the landing gear on the approach. CONCLUSIONS: Findings: 1. The pilot did not use a printed vital-action check-list. 2. The pilot did not use his usual memorized pre-landing check-list and did not lower the landing gear. 3. The pilot carried out the approach with the power set above the minimum landing gear warning horn setting, and the aircraft landed gear up. Causes: The pilot forgot to lower the landing gear.

A Bell 206 and a Bell 205 were positioned on adjacent helipads approximately 100 feet apart and facing in opposite directions, and a maintenance vehicle was parked close to the Bell 205. When both helicopters received dispatches to a fire, an engineer backed the vehicle clear of the helipad. The engineer then left the vehicle to assist a passenger to close the door of the Bell 205. The vehicle, left idling and unattended, rolled backwards, in a gradual 180-degree turn, and struck the tailboom of the idling Bell 206.

The aircraft was returning to Prince Albert, Saskatchewan after being used for fire suppression. On approach to Prince Albert, the pilot selected the landing gear down, but the left main gear did not extend and could not be extended by emergency means. The aircraft was flown to La Ronge where the pilot carried out an intentional wheels-up landing. The aircraft suffered substantial damage to the belly pod and both propellers. Findings: 1. The left main outboard gear door horn attachment fitting failed as a result of a high-cycle fatigue. 2. The fatigue initiation was probably the result of excessive compression of the hinge "ears", caused by overtightening of the through bolt or misrigging of the gear door linkages. 3. The gear door actuator became detached as a result of the failure, which prevented the gear doors from opening and the left landing gear from extending. 4. There is no manual means to release the main landing gear uplock hook. Causes: The left main  outboard gear door horn attachment fitting failed as a result of a high-cycle fatigue. Initiation of the fatigue was probably caused by overtightening of the through bolt or misrigging of the gear door linkages.

The pilot and an observer were departing on a forest-fire patrol. At about 200 to 300 feet above ground level (agl), during the initial climb, the engine (Lycoming 0-320-E3D) began to run rough and then lost all power. While the pilot was looking for a place to land, the engine regained full power. The pilot decided to turn right and execute a left teardrop turn to land downwind on the departure runway. During the left turn, the engine lost all power again. The pilot lowered the nose to maintain airspeed, and, as he banked left to attempt to avoid trees along the cleared runway area, the left main wheel and the nosewheel struck the ground. The left main wheel axle broke, and the wheel came off. About the time the aircraft struck the ground, the engine regained full power, and the aircraft became airborne. The right wing struck trees, but the pilot maintained control and climbed to circuit altitude to assess the damage. At this time, the engine was running normally. The  pilot decided to stay in the circuit so he could land should any further engine problems develop, and he selected the left fuel tank in order to lighten the left wing for landing. Approximately two and one-half hours later, the pilot landed successfully on the runway, and, as the aircraft came to a stop, it swung 90 degrees to the left. The complete fuel system was examined for indications of water or contamination, and none was found. Examination of the aircraft did not reveal the cause of the power loss. CONCLUSIONS: Findings: 1. The engine lost power during initial climb, then returned to full power. 2. The engine lost power again as the pilot attempted to return to the runway, then regained full power about the same time the left wheel and the nosewheel struck the ground. 3. The pilot did not use the throttle setting when the engine lost power. 4. After the initial engine problems, the aircraft flew for about two and one-half hours with normal engine operation. Causes: The cause of the engine power loss could not be determined.

Apres avoir effectue une patrouille de feux de forets en compagnie d'un observateur, le pilote est revenu a son point de depart. Durant la course a l'atterrissage, le train avant et le train droit se sont affaisses. L'avion a glisse vers la droite puis s'est immobilise sur le nez et l'aile droite en bordure de la piste, a 3 200 pieds du seuil de piste. Personne n'a ete blesse, et les dommages structurels a l'appareil ont ete concentres en-dessous du fuselage et de la nacelle droite. Durant l'etape vent arriere, le pilote a commande la sortie du train d'atterrissage; il affirme avoir constate en etape de base que les trois voyants verts du train etaient allumes et que l'indicateur du train avant pres du palonnier indiquait la position sortie. En courte finale, le pilote a selectionne pleins volets et a commence l'arrondi a 90 noeuds. Selon le pilote, l'impact des roues principales avec la piste a ete assez dur. L'avion a roule au sol normalement pendant 5 a 10 secondes.  Le pilote a commande la rentree des volets, puis l'appareil s'est affaisse sur le nez tout en bifurquant sur la droite. Apres l'immobilisation de l'appareil, le pilote a constate que les voyants lumineux du train d'atterrissage etaient eteints. Selon l'observateur d'experience assis sur le siege avant droit, l'avion aurait roule sur la piste sur une distance estimee entre 1 000 et 1 500 pieds. D'apres les marques sur la piste, il a ete estime que l'avion a originalement touche des roues a environ 1 500 pieds du seuil. Les marques sur la piste ont etabli que l'helice droite et le train avant ont heurte le sol simultanement a environ 2 800 pieds du seuil de piste. Par contre, l'helice gauche a laisse ses empreintes dans l'asphalte 15 pieds plus loin, durant le deportement de l'avion sur le nez vers la droite. Les deformations aux extremites des pales d'helices ont confirme que la puissance des deux moteurs n'avait pas ete entierement reduite. Le vent soufflait de face a  environ sept noeuds. L'avion a ete place sur des verins hydrauliques afin de subir des essais et des verifications. On a constate que la biellette, qui relie le train d'atterrissage droit a la boite d'engrenages dans le poste de pilotage, etait pliee sous compression, alors que la biellette du train gauche etait intacte. La biellette du train avant etait repliee a 90 degres vers le haut et l'arriere, et le boulon de la rotule d'articulation etait cisaille. Une portion de ce boulon cisaille a ete retrouvee dans une cavite du logement de la roulette de nez. Le train gauche est reste sorti, alors que le train droit, en s'affaissant, a lourdement endommage sa trappe. Le train avant, en s'affaissant, est rentre entierement dans son logement, et les deux trappes se sont refermees normalement. Les volets etaient rentres et le levier de commande de train etait abaisse. Les dommages structurels etaient trop importants pour etablir si les ajustements sur les biellettes et  les microcontacts rencontraient les tolerances prescrites par le constructeur. Sur ce genre d'appareil, la selection des volets et des roues se fait de la console du centre, et les commandes se trouvent a la meme hauteur, non loin l'une de l'autre. The pilot, accompanied by three initial attack firefighters, was conducting a patrol over a forested area. While cruising at 1,000 feet above ground level the engine chip detector warning illuminated. The pilot initiated a right turn toward a field, and suddenly the engine out aural warning sounded several times. The pilot experienced a loss of altitude and observed a decreased indication of rotor rpm and N1 (gas producer) rpm. The pilot shut down the engine (Allison 250-C20) and entered autorotation at 80 mph, while heading toward the field. When the helicopter was over the centre of the field, at 60 mph, the pilot turned into wind and touched down with very little forward motion. On landing, the main rotor blades cut off the tail boom just aft of the horizontal stabilizer. The occupants were uninjured and evacuated normally. Examination of the helicopter did not reveal any mechanical discrepancies. An engine teardown determined that the engine chip light illuminated  because a two and one-half bearing in the gearbox module failed. Examination of the two and one-half bearing and matching spur adaptor gearshaft by the CASB Engineering Laboratory indicated that the failure was a result of spalling fatigue. It was not possible to determine the cause of the spalling. It was not possible to test run the engine due to the damaged bearing; however, an examination of the engine components and accessories indicated no cause for the loss of power. There was an adequate supply of clean fuel of the correct grade in the helicopter, and no water was found in the fuel system. A fuel sample taken from the main fuel filter housing was examined by the CASB Engineering Laboratory, and their analysis found that the fuel had a gum content of 36 milligrams per 100 millilitres (mg/ml) as compared to the specification for Jet B fuel of 14 mg/ml. This condition is characteristic of weathered fuel and, although it may result in excessive exhaust smoke, does  not reduce engine performance. The operator indicated that the barrels of fuel used were two years old. The pilot had been employed with the company for six months and had received training in autorotative landings from the chief pilot. The field in which the landing was made was several acres in size, with a level surface of short grass. As there was no physical reason to cause the tail boom to be cut off, it was concluded that the pilot used an incorrect technique during the autorotational landing. The cause of the loss of engine power could not be determined. The following laboratory reports were completed: LP 108/88 - Examination of 2 1/2 Bearing/Spur Adaptor Gearshaft; and LP 131/88 - Examination of Fuel Samples. CONCLUSIONS: Findings: 1. The engine lost power in flight. 2. A two and one-half bearing in the gearbox module failed as a result of spalling fatigue, the cause of which was not determined. 3. The pilot used an improper landing technique, and, as a  result, the tail boom was cut off on touchdown. Causes: The engine lost power for undetermined reasons. The pilot used an incorrect landing technique.

The helicopter was engaged in fire-fighting operations west of Buffalo Narrows, Saskatchewan. The helicopter had picked up a bucket of water from a small lake and was about 30 feet above the surface, with a forward speed of 25 knots, when the engine lost all power. The aircraft lost altitude, and the bucket contacted the lake surface, pitching the aircraft nose-down. The pilot was able to recover from the 40-degree nose-down attitude and landed the helicopter on the lake surface. The helicopter remained floating in shallow water for a short period of time, then slowly listed over onto its right side. The two occupants waded to shore and were rescued a short time later. Findings: 1. The engine lost all power because the carburettor airbox control valves closed, shutting off air to the engine. 2. The carburettor airbox control valves had been lockwired to the cold position. 3. The lockwire had failed, allowing the interconnecting rod to vibrate, eventually causing the rod  end bearing to fail, and the control valves moved to the closed position. 4. The carburettor heat control rod had been removed and had not been replaced. Causes: The engine lost all power because of an unauthorized modification to the induction airbox.
