A93C0092: WHILE IN CRUISE FLIGHT, THE CREW OF A SIKORSKI S-58D HELICOPTER HEARD A LOUD BANG, FOLLOWED BY A ROUGH RUNNING ENGINE AND A MAJOR LOSS OF POWER.  THE CREW LANDED THE HELICOPTER SAFELY IN A MUSKEG AREA AND WERE NOT INJURED.  PRELIMINARY INDICATIONS ARE THAT THE POWER LOSS OF THE WRIGHT R1820 ENGINE WAS CAUSED BY A BROKEN NUMBER 7 CYLINDER EXHAUST VALVE.  THE COMPANY WILL BE ISSUING A SDR TO TRANSPORT CANADA.

A93Q0127: LORS D'UNE MANOEUVRE D'ECOPAGE, L'APPAREIL A TOUCHE UN HAUT-FOND. DES DOMMAGES A LA COQUE ONT ETE CONSTATES SUITE A L'ATTERRISSAGE A L'AEROPORT DE CHIBOUGAMAU.  APRES INSPECTION, L'APPAREIL A DECOLLE VERS QUEBEC OU IL SERA REPARE ET REMIS EN SERVICE.

A93C0105: THE CANADAIR CL215 AIRCRAFT, C-GUMW, DEPARTED THE AIRPORT TO PARTICIPATE IN NEARBY FOREST FIRE FIGHTING OPERATIONS.  UPON REACHING A CRUISING ALTITUDE OF 2,000 FEET ASL, THE LEFT ENGINE BEGAN TO VIBRATE AND BACKFIRE.  THE PILOT CARRIED OUT A PRECAUTIONARY SHUT DOWN OF THE LEFT ENGINE AND RETURNED TO THE LYNN LAKE AIRPORT.  MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL TRACED THE PROBLEM TO A STUD THAT HAD FALLEN OUT OF THE CARBURETTOR, CAUSING AN AIR LEAK WHICH DISTURBED THE FUEL MIXTURE TO THE ENGINE.  THE CARBURETTOR WAS REPLACED AND THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A NORTH CENTRAL HELICOPTERS LTD. BELL 204B HELICOPTER, C-FCYW, WAS BEING USED TO TRANSPORT A NINE-MAN FIRE-SUPPRESSION TEAM FROM A FIRE LINE AT THE PRIMROSE AIR WEAPONS RANGE TO THEIR CAMP AT ARSENAULT LAKE.  THE PILOT WAS IN THE FINAL STAGES OF LANDING, WITH THE HELICOPTER APPROXIMATELY 2 FEET ABOVE GROUND LEVEL, WHEN A LOUD NOISE WAS HEARD AND THE HELICOPTER BEGAN TO YAW SLOWLY.  THE PILOT CONTROLLED THE YAW BY REDUCING THROTTLE AND COMPLETED THE LANDING WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.  THE PILOT AND HIS PASSENGERS WERE NOT INJURED.  INSPECTION REVEALED THAT THE HELICOPTER TAIL ROTOR DRIVE SYSTEM SUFFERED A FAILURE OF THE 42-DEGREE GEARBOX.

A93C0170: THE PROVINCE OF MANITOBA CANADAIR CL-215 WATER BOMBER WAS ON A WATER-BOMBING MISSION.  THE AIRCRAFT HAD SCOOPED WATER FROM A LAKE AND JUST BEFORE BECOMING AIRBORNE, STRUCK A SUBMERGED ROCK.  THE TAKE-OFF WAS COMPLETED AND THE AIRCRAFT LANDED SAFELY AT ITS DESTINATION LAND BASE.  THE AIRCRAFT HAD SUFFERED CONSIDERABLE DAMAGE TO THE LOWER HULL.  AT THE TIME AND LOCATION OF THE OCCURRENCE, THE WEATHER WAS CLOUDY WITH RAIN SHOWERS AND THE WIND WAS ABOUT 15 TO 20 KNOTS.  THE CREW HAD MADE A SUCCESSFUL SCOOP BEFORE THE OCCURRENCE RUN AND OTHER AIRCRAFT HAD MADE SCOOP RUNS IN THE LAKE ON THE PREVIOUS DAY.  IT WAS ONLY AFTER SEVERAL PASSES OVER THE LAKE THAT ANOTHER AIRCRAFT WAS ABLE TO LOCATE THE ROCK.  THIS INCIDENT WAS NOT REPORTED EARLIER FOR UNDETERMINED REASONS.

A93Q0131: SUITE A UNE VARIATION DE PUISSANCE DU BMEP (BRAKE MEAN EFFECTIVE PRESSURE), L'EQUIPAGE A CONSTATE LA PERTE D'UN CYLINDRE SUR LE MOTEUR #2.  LE MOTEUR A ETE MIS EN DRAPEAU ET L'APPAREIL A ATTERRI A SAINT-HONORE SANS AUTRE INCIDENT.

THE BELL 206B JETRANGER WAS CRUISING ABOUT 120 MPH AT 1,500 FT AGL, WHEN A BIRD STRUCK THE WINDSHIELD CENTRE POST.  THE BIRD, A LOON, SMASHED OUT PART OF THE WINDSHIELD AND ENTERED THE COCKPIT.  THE LOON WAS FATALLY INJURED.THE PILOT DID NOT SEE THE LOON BEFORE THE STRIKE.  THE HELICOPTER CONTINUED TO ITS DESTINATION AT REDUCED SPEED.  MAINTENANCE ARE TO INSPECT AND REPAIR THE HELICOPTER AS REQUIRED.

THE CESSNA 210 WAS ON A LOCAL FIFTEEN-MINUTE FLIGHT WITH THE PILOT AND 1 PASSENGER.  WHEN THE AIRCRAFT DID NOT RETURN TO BASE, ANOTHER AIRCRAFT WAS DISPATCHED AND OBSERVED NEARBY SMOKE COMING FROM THE WRECKAGE OF THE CESSNA.  THE CESSNA HAD STRUCK POWER LINES THAT CROSSED A RIVER, AND HAD CRASHED INTO AN ADJACENT WOODED AREA.  THE AIRCRAFT WAS COMPLETELY DESTROYED BY A POST-IMPACT FIRE AND THE PILOT AND PASSENGER WERE FATALLY INJURED.

A93W0105: AT THE FIRST POWER REDUCTION AFTER SCOOPING WATER FROM A LAKE, THE RIGHT ENGINE SHUT ITSELF DOWN AND AUTO-FEATHERED.  THE CREW COMPLETED THE ENGINE SHUTDOWN CHECKLIST AND RETURNED TO NORMAN WELLS.MAINTENANCE FOUND THAT THE ENGINE HAD SEIZED.  THEY CHANGED THE SEIZED ENGINE OVERNIGHT AND RETURNED THE CL215 TO SERVICE.

A93W0120: THE "BIRD DOG" AIRCRAFT ADVISED THE CREW OF THE CL-215 THAT THERE WAS A TRAIL OF SMOKE BEHIND THEIR RIGHT ENGINE.  THE CREW OBSERVED A LARGE OIL LEAK ON THE PROPELLER AND NOSE CASE.  THEY SHUT DOWN AND SECURED THE ENGINE AND LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.MAINTENANCE REPLACED A DEFECTIVE GASKET AND RETURNED THE AIRCRAFT TO SERVICE.

C-FTGU, A CESSNA 305C (L-19 BIRDDOG) AIRCRAFT, WAS ON A LOCAL TRAINING FLIGHT WITH AN INSTRUCTOR PILOT AND A PILOT TRAINEE ON BOARD.  THE AIRCRAFT DEPARTED THE DEBERT AIRPORT AT 15:20 ADT AND PROCEEDED TO THE TRAINING AREA WITH THE PILOT TRAINEE AT THE CONTROLS.  THE PURPOSE OF THE FLIGHT WAS TO TYPE CHECK THE PILOT TRAINEE ON THE L-19 AIRCRAFT AS WELL AS A CONVERSION FROM TRICYCLE TO CONVENTIONAL LANDING GEAR AIRCRAFT.  AFTER CONDUCTING SOME AERIAL WORK IN THE TRAINING AREA THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED TO THE AIRPORT FOR A FULL STOP LANDING.THE WIND AT THE TIME WAS REPORTED TO BE 230 DEGREES AT 5 TO 10 KNOTS.  HOWEVER, RUNWAY 28 WAS SELECTED FOR THE LANDING BECAUSE OF GLIDER OPERATIONS BEING CONDUCTED FROM RUNWAY 23.  WHEN THE AIRCRAFT WAS ON SHORT FINAL THE WINDSOCK WAS OBSERVED TO BE NEARLY LIMP AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS TRACKING DOWN THE EXTENDED CENTRELINE WITH MINIMAL CONTROL INPUT CORRECTIONS.THE AIRCRAFT TOUCHED DOWN 200 FEET FROM THE THRESHOLD, BOUNCED BACK INTO THE AIR, AND THEN REPORTEDLY SETTLED ONTO THE RUNWAY WITH THE WEIGHT DISTRIBUTED CORRECTLY ON THE WHEELS AND TRACKING DOWN THE RUNWAY CENTRELINE.  DURING THE ROLL OUT THE AIRCRAFT STARTED TO DRIFT TO THE LEFT AND THE INSTRUCTOR PILOT FELT CORRECTING PRESSURE ON THE RIGHT RUDDER PEDAL.  HOWEVER, BY THE TIME HE REALIZED THAT NOT ENOUGH RIGHT RUDDER WAS BEING APPLIED AND ATTEMPTED TO ASSIST THE PILOT TRAINEE, THE SWING TO THE LEFT HAD ALREADY DEVELOPED AND HE WAS UNABLE TO PREVENT THE AIRCRAFT FROM GROUND LOOPING.THIS WAS THE PILOT TRAINEE'S FIRST LANDING IN A CONVENTIONAL LANDING GEAR AIRCRAFT.  THE INSTRUCTOR PILOT FEELS THAT IT WOULD HAVE BEEN MORE PRUDENT IF THE INTRODUCTION TO CONVENTIONAL LANDING GEAR AIRCRAFT HAD BEEN CARRIED OUT IN AN AIRCRAFT WITH MORE FORGIVING CHARACTISTICS.

A94W0080: ON INITIAL CLIMB OUT THE #2 ENGINE OF THE DOUGLAS A-26C STARTED TO BACKFIRE.  THE PILOT REDUCED POWER AND RETURNED TO LAND AT WHITEHORSE WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT. FIRE RETARDENT WAS NOT JETTISONED. MAINTENANCE ADJUSTED THE VALVE LASH ON THE INTAKE VALVE OF #2 CYLINDER OF THE RIGHT ENGINE.

A94W0087: THE NUMBER FOUR ENGINE BACKFIRED THREE TIMES IN CRUISE FLIGHT. THE CREW SHUT DOWN THE ENGINE AND CONTINUED TO YELLOWKNIFE WHERE THE DC-6 LANDED WITHOUT INCIDENT. ERS WAS NOT REQURESTED. MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL FOUND THE NUMBER NINE CYLINDER TO BE DEFECTIVE.

A94C0120:  THE CESSNA 337F SKYMASTER AIRCRAFT, C-FFXS, WAS BEING USED FOR AERIAL RECONNAISANCE IN SUPPORT OF PROVINCIAL FOREST FIRE MANAGEMENT.  THE PILOT HAD BEEN AIRBORNE FOR APPROXIMATELY 3 HRS 45 MINS WHEN THE REAR ENGINE BEGAN TO RUN ROUGHLY AND THEN QUIT.  THE PILOT WAS UNABLE TO MAINTAIN ALTITUDE AND TRANSMITTED A "MAYDAY" MESSAGE OVER THE RADIO.  THE PILOT RECEIVED INFORMATION ABOUT A NEARBY MINING AIRSTRIP AND BEGAN TO HEAD TOWARDS IT.  SHORTLY THEREAFTER THE FRONT ENGINE SPUTTERED ONCE AND THEN ALSO QUIT.  NEITHER ENGINE WOULD RESTART AND THE PILOT CARRIED OUT A FORCED LANDING IN THE SHALLOW WATER NEAR THE SHORE OF A LAKE.  THE PILOT EVACUATED THE AIRCRAFT SUCCESSFULLY AND THE AIRCRAFT REMAINED UPRIGHT BUT BECAME PARTIALLY SUBMERGED WITH THE WINGS REMAINING OUT OF THE WATER.  THE PILOT SUSTAINED MINOR INJURIES AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS SUBSTANTIALLY DAMAGED.IT WAS REPORTED THAT THE FUEL SELECTORS WERE SELECTED TO THE MAIN TANKS WHICH WERE EMPTY; HOWEVER, THE AUXILLARY FUEL TANKS REMAINED FULL OF FUEL.  THE OCCURRENCE AIRCRAFT WAS A CESSNA 337F WHICH HAS BOTH MAIN FUEL TANKS AND OPTIONAL AUXILLARY FUEL TANKS.  THE "F" MODEL 337 HAS ONE SET (2) OF FUEL GUAGES TO INDICATE BOTH THE MAIN AND AUXILLARY FUEL QUANTITY AND THE FUEL SELECTOR HAS AN ADDITIONAL POSITION TO SELECT FUEL FROM THE AUXILLARY TANKS.  THE MAJORITY OF THE PILOT'S EXPERIENCE WAS GAINED IN "G" MODEL CESSNA 337 AIRCRAFT WHICH HAVE A DIFFERENT FUEL SYSTEM WITH THE AUXILLARY FUEL INCORPORATED IN THE MAIN FUEL SYSTEM AND FUEL SELECTORS WITH POSITIONS FOR LEFT, RIGHT, AND OFF ONLY.  IT WAS REPORTED THAT THE FUEL MISMANAGEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN PREVENTED THROUGH INCREASED AWARENESS OF DIFFERENCES BETWEEN VARIOUS MODELS OF THE SAME AIRCRAFT TYPE.

A94C0165:  THE PILOT OF THE CANADAIR CL215 AMPHIBIOUS AIRCRAFT, C-GOFR, WAS RETURNING AFTER A FIRE BOMBING MISSION WHEN AT 5,000 FEET AND 35 MILES NORTH OF PICKLE LAKE THE LEFT ENGINE LOST POWER.  THE LEFT ENGINE BEGAN TO VIBRATE HEAVILY ACCOMPANIED BY A LOUD NOISE AND THE BMEP INDICATION WENT TO ZERO.  THE ENGINE WAS FEATHERED AND SECURED.  THE PILOT LANDED THE AIRCRAFT AT PICKLE LAKE WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.  THE ENGINE WAS FOUND TO HAVE SUFFERED SERIOUS INTERNAL FAILURE AND WAS REPLACED.  THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNED TO SERVICE AND AN SDR WAS SUBMITTED TO TRANSPORT CANADA.

A94P0151.  SHORTLY AFTER THE TAKE-OFF OF THE DOUGLAS DC-6B, ONE OF THE LOW-TENSION LEADS ON THE #4 ENGINE BECAME DISCONNECTED.  THE COCKPIT ENGINE ANALYZER INDICATED THAT ONE CYLINDER WAS NOT FIRING.  THE CREW SECURED THE #4 ENGINE AND RETURNED TO ABBOTSFORD FOR A PRECAUTIONARY LANDING.  ERS WAS NOT REQUESTED, AND THE AIRCRAFT LANDED WITHOUT DAMAGE OR INJURY.

A94W0124:  THE BELL 206B HELICOPTER WAS BEING UTILIZED TO TRANSPORT A TWO-PERSON INITIAL ATTACK FIRE CREW TO A RECENTLY SPOTTED FOREST FIRE.  SHORTLY AFTER TAKE-OFF, AT AN ALTITUDE OF APPROXIMATELY 300 FEET ABOVE GROUND, THE ENGINE LOST ALL POWER.  THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO AUTOROTATE TO THE ONLY AVAILABLE ROAD; HOWEVER, THE HELICOPTER OVERSHOT, STRUCK TREES AND CRASHED BESIDE THE ROAD.  THE PILOT SUSTAINED FATAL INJURIES AND THE TWO PASSENGERS RECEIVED SERIOUS INJURIES.  THE HELICOPTER WAS DESTROYED.

A94Q0142: LE CESSNA 182, EN PATROUILLE DE FEU, A SUBI UNE PERTE DE PUISSANCE EN VOL. LE PILOTE A ESSAYE DE REPARTIR LE MOTEUR MAIS SANS SUCCES. LE PILOTE A FAIT UN ATTERRISSAGE FORCE DANS UN MARECAGE. AU TOUCHE DE LA ROUE DE NEZ L'AERONEF S'EST RETOURNE. LE PILOTE ET LE PASSAGER SONT SORTIS INDEMNES ET ONT ETE EVACUE ASSEZ RAPIDEMENT PAR HELICOPTERE.L'APPAREIL ETAIT EN CROISIERE A 3,500 PIEDS LORSQUE LA PERTE DE PUISSANCE EST SURVENUE. UN EXAMEN DE L'APPAREIL A REVELE QUE LES RESERVOIRS CONTENAIENT DE L'ESSENCE ET QUE LE FILTRE DU GASCOLATOR ETAIT PROPRE. AUCUNE ANOMALIE N'A ETE DECELEE AVEC LE MOTEUR. CEPENDANT LES CONDITIONS METEOROLOGIQUES ETAIENT PROPICES AU GIVRAGE DE CARBURATEUR AINSI QUE LE FAIBLE TAUX DE PUISSANCE UTILISE DANS LE VOL DE CROISIERE. DE PLUS, LE PILOTE N'A PAS UTILISE LE RECHAUFFE CARBURATEUR.

A94P0174:  THE #2 ENGINE OF THE AEROSTAR 600 LOST POWER JUST AFTER TAKE-OFF.  THE AIRCRAFT WOULD NOT MAINTAIN ALTITUDE AND THE PILOT MADE A FORCED LANDING WITH THE GEAR UP, COMING TO REST ABOUT 400 FEET BEYOND THE DEPARTURE END OF RWY 34, AND STRIKING SOME OF THE APPROACH LIGHTS OF RWY 16.  THE TWO CREW WERE NOT INJURED.AT THE TIME OF THE ACCIDENT, THE DENSITY ALTITUDE WAS ABOUT 5,000 FEET AND THERE WAS POSSIBLY A WIND SHEAR.  AN INSPECTION OF THE ENGINE REVEALED THAT THE SCAT HOSE (PART #920029-01) BETWEEN THE AIR FILTER AND THE CARBURETTOR HAD COLLAPSED.

A94P0202:  WHILE THE GRUMMAN FIRE-CAT (C-GHNU) WAS CRUISING AT 6,500 FEET, THE PILOT NOTICED THAT THE PERFORMANCE ON THE #1 ENGINE WAS CONSIDERABLY LOWER THAN NORMAL, AND HE FELT WORSENING AIRFRAME VIBRATIONS.  HE THEN SAW OIL STREAMING FROM THE #1 ENGINE BREATHER PIPE, WHEREUPON HE FEATHERED THE #1 ENGINE.  HE CONTINUED WITH THE SHUT DOWN PROCEDURES FOR THE #1 ENGINE BUT INADVERTANTLY ACTIVATED THE FIREWALL SHUTOFF SWITCHES FOR THE #2 ENGINE.  FACED WITH NO POWER ON EITHER ENGINE, THE PILOT WAS NOW COMMITTED TO FORCE-LAND IN THE FRASER RIVER.THE AIRCRAFT LANDED ON THE RIVER AND WAS SUBSTANTIALLY DAMAGED BY THE WATER IMPACT, WHICH ACTIVATED THE ELT.  THE PILOT ESCAPED WITH MINOR INJURIES AND WAS RESCUED BY HELICOPTER.  THE AIRCRAFT WAS LATER TOWED TO THE SHORELINE.THE OPERATOR CARRIED OUT AN ENGINE TEAR DOWN AND REPORTED THAT THE #3 PISTON HAD A HOLE IN IT; APPARENTLY, A HOT SPOT FORMED ON THE PISTON CAUSING EROSION AND BREAK THROUGH.

A94O0232:  DURING THE AERIAL SPRAY OPERATION THE PILOT FELT RUDDER OPERATION STIFFENING.  MOMENTS LATER BOTH THE RUDDER AND ELEVATORS SEIZED.  THE ONLY CONTROLS AVAILABLE TO THE PILOT WERE THE AILERONS.  THE PEZETEL M-18 DROMADER RETURNED TO KAPUSKASING WITH THE BIRDDOG AIRCRAFT FLYING ALONGSIDE.  THE LANDING WAS UNEVENTFUL AND EMERGENCY SERVICES WERE STANDING BY.  A PRELIMINARY INSPECTION BY THE OPERATOR REVEALED A POSSIBLE FAILURE OF THE REAR SPAR OF THE VERTICAL FIN.

A94C0201: THE SASKATCHEWAN AIR SERVICES CANSO, C-FUAW, WAS RETURNING FROM A LOCAL WATER BOMBING MISSION.  ABOUT 40 MILES FROM LA RONGE THE RIGHT ENGINE BEGAN EMITTING SMOKE AND RAN VERY ROUGHLY.  THE ENGINE WAS SHUTDOWN AND AN EMERGENCY DECLARED. THE AIRCRAFT LANDED SAFELY AT LA RONGE. POST FLIGHT INSPECTION REVEALED A BLOWN CYLINDER HEAD.

A95Q0010:  UNABLE TO KEEP RUNWAY CENTER LINE, THE PILOT OF THE B747 ABORTED THE TAKE-OFF FROM RUNWAY 29 AT MIRABEL AT 2206Z.  RUNWAY CONDITIONS WERE REPORTED TO BE FAIR AT 100% SNOW, 1/8 OF AN INCH THICK, 20% ICE PATCHES AND A JBI OF .35.  THE WEATHER WAS CEILING 1300 FEET OBSCURRED, VISIBILITY OF 1 1/2 MILE IN LIGHT SNOW AND WINDS WERE CALM.WHILE TAXIING THE PILOT INDICATED TO THE TOWER THAT HE HAD A HOT BRAKE INDICATION AND REQUESTED AN INSPECTION BE DONE AT 2217Z.  THE TOWER ADVISED THE FIRE HALL DISPATCHER OF THE REQUEST AT 2218Z.  THE AIRCRAFT TAXIING ON ALPHA STOPPED AT ALPHA 3 INTERSECTION.URGENCE 1 VEHICULE ALREADY ON GOLF TAXIWAY WAS ADVISED AT 2220Z, AND VIA HOTEL AND ALPHA CAME UP FROM THE BACK OF THE B747.  AT 2221Z THE PILOT WAS ADVISED THAT THE INSPECTION VEHICULE WAS EN ROUTE.  AT 2225Z, THE PILOT INQUIRED AGAIN ABOUT AN INSPECTION VEHICULE, UNAWARE THAT URGENCE 1 HAD PARKED BEHIND THE AIRCRAFT AND THAT PERSONNEL WERE ALREADY UNDER THE AIRCRAFT CHECKING OUT THE BRAKES.BECAUSE OF THE PILOT'S SECOND DEMAND FOR AN INSPECTION VEHICULE, THE TOWER ACTIVATED THE CRASH BELL ALERT TO NOTIFY THE FIRE HALL OF THE IMMEDIATE NEED FOR A VEHICULE.  THE FIRE HALL DISPATCHER, AWARE THAT THE FIRE CREW WERE ALREADY ON SITE, WAS CONFUSED BY THE CRASH BELL DEMAND FROM THE TOWER.RUNWAY 29 WAS SWEPT AGAIN AND THE B747 DEPARTED MIRABEL AT 2337Z. URGENCE 1 VEHICULE CREW OMITTED TO CONTACT GROUND CONTROL OF THEIR PRESENCE ON THE AIRPORT TAXIWAYS AND THEREFORE THE TOWER WAS UNAWARE THAT URGENCE 1 WAS RESPONDING TO THE B747'S CALL.AS LONG AS FIRE CREW ARE INSIDE THE VEHICULE THEY CAN COMMUNICATE WITH THE TOWER AND WITH THE FLIGHT CREW.  WHEN OUTSIDE THE VEHICULE, THEY CAN ONLY COMMUNICATE WITH THE FIRE HALL DISPATCHER, WHO CAN THEN RELAY THEIR MESSAGE VIA THE TOWER.THE FIRE HALL INTERVENTION PROCEDURE WILL BE REVISED BECAUSE OF THE POTENTIAL DANGER OF FIRE CREWS WORKING IN PROXIMITY OF THE AIRCRAFT WITHOUT THE FLIGHT CREW'S KNOWLEDGE.

A95A0082: A95A0083: THE CREW OF THE CANADIAN MILITARY CL601, MILITARY 144613, DID A GO-AROUND AFTER A HARD LANDING FROM A FLAPLESS APPROACH.  A VISUAL INSPECTION FROM THE GROUND REVEALED A SEVERELY DAMAGED RIGHT MAIN LANDING GEAR WHICH EVENTUALLY SEPARATED FROM THE AIRCRAFT IN FLIGHT.  AN INFLIGHT FIRE STARTED IN THE FUSELAGE AREA NEAR THE MISSING GEAR LOCATION.AN EMERGENCY LANDING WAS CARRIED OUT IN SHEARWATER AND, ON LANDING, THE AIRCRAFT DEPARTED THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE RUNWAY.  A POST INPACT EXPLOSION AND FIRE IN THE CENTRE FUEL TANK WAS QUICKLY EXTINGUISHED BY THE FIRE CREW.THE CREW OF THE AIRCRAFT, WHO SUFFERED FROM BRUISING AND SMOKE INHALATION,  EVACUATED THROUGH THE OVER WING EXITS.THE CANADIAN MILITARY HAVE CONVENED A BOARD OF INQUIRY.

A95C0080:  THE DEHAVILLAND CS2F-1 TRACKER AIRCRAFT WAS IN THECLIMB AFTER TAKE-OFF ON A LOCAL FIRE MANAGEMENT TRAINING FLIGHT WHEN THE RIGHT ENGINE AND PROPELLER STRUCK A BIRD (BELIEVED TO BE A GOOSE).  THE ENGINE AND COWLING WERE DAMAGED AND A SIGNIFICANT ENGINE OIL LEAK WAS VISIBLE.THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO FEATHER THE PROPELLER PRIOR TO SHUTTING DOWN THE ENGINE; HOWEVER, THIS WAS UNSUCCESSFUL.  THE PILOT THEN ELECTED TO KEEP THE RIGHT ENGINE OPERATING AND RETURNED TO THE AIRPORT FOR A LANDING WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.INSPECTION REVEALED THAT THE BIRDSTRIKE HAD SEVERED THE OIL LINE TO THE PROPELLER GOVERNOR WHICH RESULTED IN INSUFFICIENT OIL TO MOVE THE PROPELLER TO THE FEATHER POSITION.  THE LINE WAS REPLACED, THE COWLING DAMAGE REPAIRED, AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A95A0098: THE CL215, C-FAYN, WAS AT 2500 FEET ASL WHEN THE PILOT NOTICED A FLUCTUATING OIL PRESSURE AND A LARGE AMOUNT OF OIL LEAKING FROM THE #1 ENGINE.  HE SHUT DOWN THE ENGINE AND RETURNED TO STEPHENVILLE FOR AN UNEVENTFUL LANDING.MAINTENANCE DETERMINED THAT THE LEAK WAS CAUSED BY A FAULTY OIL SCREEN GASKET.  A SB (#859) WAS ISSUED IN 1952 RECOMMENDING THE REPLACEMENT OF ALL GASKETS WITH THE SAME PART NUMBER AS THE ONE FOUND ON THE AIRCRAFT. THESE OLD GASKETS WERE TOO THIN AND THEY WERE REPLACED BY A THICKER ONE.  THE OPERATOR FOUND MORE OF THESE OLD GASKETS IN THEIR AIRCRAFT STORES.  ALL THE OLD GASKETS ARE BEING DESTROYED AND ALL AIRCRAFT ARE BEING CHECKED AND THE GASKETS ARE BEING REPLACED IF NECESSARY.

A95C0097:  A SASKATCHEWAN GOVERNMENT CS2F-2 TRACKER, C-GEQD, DEPARTED PRINCE ALBERT ON A LOCAL TEST FLIGHT. SHORTLY AFTER TAKE-OFF THE PILOT NOTICED A FIRE WARNING LIGHT ACCOMPANIED BY FUMES IN THE COCKPIT.  THE PILOT SHUT DOWN THE RIGHT HAND ENGINE, DISCHARGED THE FIRE EXTINGUISHER BOTTLE AND RETURNED TO LAND AT PRINCE ALBERT.  ERS WERE ADVISED.  THE AIRCRAFT SUSTAINED MINOR WIRING DAMAGE. THE PILOT WAS UNINJURED.MAINTENANCE INSPECTION REVEALED SHORTED AND BURNED WIRES IN THE FUSELAGE ALONG WITH ELECTRICAL OVERHEAT DAMAGE TO THE RIGHT HAND NACELLE FIRE WARNING CONTROL BOX.

A95C0101:  THE BELL B206L1 LONGRANGER HELICOPTER HAD JUST DISEMBARKED TWO FIREFIGHTERS AND SOME EQUIPMENT AT A TEMPORARY HELIPAD THAT WAS CONSTRUCTED FROM LOGS.  DURING THE SUBSEQUENT LIFT-OFF THE PILOT NOTICED ONE OF THE FIREFIGHTERS URGENTLY WAVING AT HIM.  THE PILOT BEGAN TO DESCEND TO LAND THE HELICOPTER ON THE PAD AGAIN.  DURING THE DESCENT THE HELICOPTER ROLLED OVER TO THE RIGHT, THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO CONTROL THE AIRCRAFT ATTITUDE USING CYCLIC; HOWEVER HE WAS UNSUCCESSFUL AND THE HELICOPTER STRUCK THE GROUND.  THE PILOT MANAGED TO EGRESS THROUGH THE CRACKED FRONT BUBBLE WINDSCREEN BEFORE THE HELICOPTER WAS CONSUMED BY A POST-CRASH FIRE.  THE AIRCRAFT WAS DESTROYED, BUT THE PILOT ESCAPED WITH MINOR INJURIES.IT WAS INDICATED THAT ONE OF THE LOGS THAT MADE UP THE LANDING SURFACE OF THE PAD, BECAME CAUGHT ON THE BEARPAW ON THE LEFT LANDING SKID.  AS THE HELICOPTER LIFTED OFF, THE END OF THE SNAGGED LOG REMAINED ATTACHED TO THE LEFT SKID AND ROSE WITH THE AIRCRAFT TOWARDS THE VERTICAL POSITION.  WHEN THE PILOT ABORTED THE TAKE-OFF AND TRIED TO LAND AGAIN, THE LOWER END OF THE LOG WEDGED IN THE GROUND PREVENTING FURTHER DESCENT OF THE LEFT SKID.  THE RESTRICTED MOVEMENT ON THE LEFT SIDE OF THE HELICOPTER INITIATED A RIGHT ROLL WHICH QUICKLY EXCEEDED THE CONTROL CAPABILITIES OF THE AIRCRAFT.

A95C0107:  THE CANADAIR CL215 WATER BOMBER, C-GOFR, HAD JUST LIFTED OFF FROM A WATER PICK-UP ON A LAKE WHEN THE PILOTS NOTICED A POWER LOSS ON THE RIGHT ENGINE.  THE WATER LOAD WAS JETTISONED, AND ENGINE POWER RETURNED TO NORMAL; HOWEVER, THE RIGHT ENGINE OIL PRESSURE WAS NOTED TO BE DECREASING AND EVENTUALLY STABILIZED AT 60 PSI.  THE CREW DECIDED TO RETURN TO BASE AND ADVISED THAT THEY HAD AN ENGINE PROBLEM.  THE PILOT OF A "BIRD DOG" OBSERVER AIRCRAFT THAT WAS OPERATING IN THE AREA FLEW OVER TO OFFER ASSISTANCE AND ADVISED THE CL215 CREW THAT THEY HAD SMOKE AND FLAMES COMING FROM THEIR RIGHT ENGINE.  ALTHOUGH THE CREW HAD NO COCKPIT INDICATION OF AN ENGINE FIRE,THEY SHUT DOWN THE RIGHT ENGINE AND LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.  THE ENGINE WAS REPLACED AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNED TO SERVICE.  FURTHER INFORMATION MAY BE OBTAINED DURING ENGINE TEARDOWN.

A95W0087: A GROUP OF THREE HELI-TACK SPECIALISTS (HTS), WHOSE LIVES WERE ENDANGERED BY A RAPIDLY ADVANCING FOREST FIRE, WERE BEING RESCUED FROM A SEISMIC LINE BY A BELL 212 HELICOPTER EQUIPPED WITH A HELI-TACK RAPID EXTRACTION 150 FOOT LINE, SUSPENDED FROM INSIDE THE HELICOPTER. DURING THE EXTRACTION, THE BOTTOM HTS LET GO AND RAN TO SAFETY DOWN THE CUT LINE. THE SECOND HTS WAS FATALLY INJURED WHEN HE STRUCK AND BECAME LODGED AT THE 40-FOOT LEVEL OF AN ASPEN TREE, AND THE THIRD HTS SUFFERED A BROKEN LEG. VISIBILITY AND FLIGHT CONDITIONS DETERIORATED RAPIDLY IN THE RESCUE ZONE BECAUSE OF SMOKE, FLAMES, AND FLYING ASH.

A95C0106:  THE BELL 206B JETRANGER HELICOPTER HAD LANDED ON A TEMPORARY HELIPAD DURING FIRE-FIGHTING OPERATIONS.  THE LANDING PAD, WHICH WAS SITUATED ON A LAKE SHORELINE, CONSISTED OF TWO LOGS WITH THE REAR LOG SUPPORTED ON TOP OF SMALL SUPPORT CROSS LOGS AT EACH END.AFTER THE HELICOPTER LANDED WITH THE LANDING GEAR SKIDS ACROSS THE TWO LOGS, THE SINGLE PASSENGER DEPARTED AND THE PILOT REMAINED AT THE CONTROLS WITH THE AIRCRAFT RUNNING AWAITING THE PASSENGER'S RETURN.  SUDDENLY THE REAR OF THE AIRCRAFT DROPPED AND THE PILOT IMMEDIATELY TRIED TO CORRECT WITH CYCLIC HOWEVER THERE WAS A LOUD BANG AND SIGNIFICANT VIBRATION SO THE PILOT SHUT DOWN THE ENGINE.THE REAR LOG HAD SLIPPED OFF THE SUPPORTS AND THE TAIL ROTOR HAD CONTACTED THE WATER RESULTING IN THE LOSS OF A TAIL ROTOR BLADE AND SIGNIFICANT DAMAGE TO THE TAIL BOOM.  THE PILOT REMAINED UNINJURED.

A95C0112:  THE MANITOBA GOVERNMENT AIR DIVISION CANADAIR CL215 WAS CONDUCTING FIRE SUPPRESSION WORK IN THE VICINITY OF THE PAS, MB.WHILE SCOOPING WATER, THE CREW NOTED A DECREASE IN THE PERFORMANCE OF THE LEFT ENGINE.  ONCE AIRBORNE, THE PERFORMANCE DECREASED FURTHER.  THE CREW DUMPED THE WATER LOAD, SECURED THE ENGINE, AND RETURNED TO BASE AT THE PAS, LANDING WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.MAINTENANCE ENGINEERS FOUND THAT THE LEFT ENGINE #6 CYLINDER HAD FAILED.  THE CYLINDER WAS REPLACED AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A95C0115:  WHILE ENGAGED IN FIRE SUPPRESSION DUTIES, THE BELL 206B JET RANGER WAS LIFTING OFF FROM A LOG PAD.  THE LEFT SKID OF THE HELICOPTER SNAGGED A LOG, AND THE PILOT USED RIGHT CYCLIC TO BREAK FREE.  WHEN THE HELICOPTER BROKE FREE, IT MOVED TO THE RIGHT, AND STRUCK A TREE.  THE PILOT HOVERED JUST ABOVE THE GROUND WHILE THE PASSENGERS DISEMBARKED TO PREPARE A LANDING PAD.  HE THEN LANDED THE HELICOPTER WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.  THERE WERE NO REPORTED INJURIES, BUT THE HELICOPTER SUSTAINED DAMAGE TO ITS MAIN ROTOR BLADES.

A95W0091:  WHILE ON APPROACH FOR LANDING, THE CREW OF THE DC-6B AIRCRAFT PERFORMED A PRECAUTIONARY SHUT DOWN OF THE NO.1 ENGINE BECAUSE OF VIBRATIONS AND ABNORMAL SOUNDS. THE AIRCRAFT WAS LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.MAINTENANCE ADVISED OF A NO. 1 ENGINE CYLINDER FAILURE.

A95W0094: THE BELL 212 WAS ON A FORESTRY CONTRACT AND TASKED WITH MOVING A FIRE CAMP TO A DIFFERENT LOCATION.  THE FIRST TRIP CONSISTED OF CAMP EQUIPMENT.  THE SECOND TRIP CONSISTED OF LINE BOSSES, FIRE FIGHTERS, AND OTHER EQUIPMENT.  THE THIRD TRIP CONSISTED OF 15 FIRE FIGHTERS.  THE PILOT HAD COMMENCED THE TAKE-OFF RUN AND WAS NOW FLYING OVER SMALL TREES TOWARD HIGHER TREES WHEN HE EXPERIENCED THE HELICOPTER SETTLING.  POWER WAS ADDED, BUT THE MAIN ROTOR RPM STARTED TO DECAY.  THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO REGAIN THE LOST ROTOR RPM BY MILKING THE COLLECTIVE LEVER, BUT THE RPM STILL DECAYED, AND THE LOW ROTOR WARNING HORN ACTIVATED.A PARTIAL LEFT TURN WAS MADE TOWARD LOWER TREES, BUT THE ROTOR RPM FURTHER DECAYED, AND THE HELICOPTER SETTLED HEAVILY INTO THE TREES AND ROLLED ONTO ITS SIDE, COMING TO A STOP.THE PILOT AND PASSENGERS VACATED THE SUBSTANTIALLY DAMAGED HELICOPTER WITHOUT INCIDENT, OR SERIOUS INJURIES.  A SMALL POST CRASH FIRE IN ONE OF THE ENGINES WAS QUICKLY EXTINGUISHED.  IT WAS DURING THE POST CRASH EGRESS THAT THE PILOT BECAME AWARE THAT HE HAD 15 VERSUS 14 PASSENGERS ON BOARD.

A95Q0104: LE CESSNA 182 EFFECTUAIT UNE PATROUILLE DE FEU.  L'AERONEF A ETE RETROUVE SUR LE FLANC D'UNE MONTAGNE PAR "RECHERCHE ET SAUVATAGE" SUITE A L'ALERTE DE LA RADIOBALISE DE DETRESSE (ELT). LE PILOTE AVAIT SUBI DES BLESSURES MORTELLES.

A95C0132: C-GSKI WAS BEING USED IN LONGLINING WHEN THE PILOT NOTED A LOSS OF ENGINE POWER.  THE LOAD WAS DROPPED AND THE PILOT INITIATED AN AUTOROTATION.  A HARD LANDING RESULTED, CAUSING DAMAGE TO THE TAIL BOOM AND OTHER COMPONENTS.  THE AIRCRAFT WILL HAVE TO BE SLUNG OUT FOR REPAIR.MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL SUSPECT A CRACKED P2 LINE ON THE FCU OR CONTAMINATED FUEL.

A95C0139:  THE BELL-205A-1 HELICOPTER, C-GNMR, WAS OPERATING ON CONTRACT TO THE PROVINCIAL MINISTRY OF NATURAL RESOURCES IN SUPPORT OF FOREST FIRE SUPPRESSION ACTIVITIES.  THE PILOT DEPARTED, WITH THE SEVEN PASSENGERS AND THEIR EQUIPMENT ON BOARD, FOR A LOCAL FLIGHT TO DROP OFF THE FIRE-FIGHTING CREW.  THE VISIBILITY WAS REPORTED TO BE THREE QUARTERS OF A MILE IN SMOKE AS THE FLIGHT BEGAN; HOWEVER, AS THE HELICOPTER WAS HEADING NORTH FROM LEAF RAPIDS AND TRAVERSING THE CHURCHILL RIVER THE VISIBILITY DETERIORATED RAPIDLY AND THE PILOT ATTEMPTED A RIGHT TURN TO RETURN FOR LANDING. THE HELICOPTER DESCENDED IN THE TURN, THE MAIN ROTOR BLADES STRUCK THE WATER AND THE AIRCRAFT CRASHED INTO THE RIVER.  THE PILOT AND FOUR PASSENGERS EXITED THE AIRCRAFT AND WERE RESCUED; HOWEVER, THREE PASSENGERS SUFFERED FATAL INJURIES.  THE AIRCRAFT WAS DESTROYED.

A95O0134: SHORTLY AFTER DEPARTURE ON THE FIRST FLIGHT OF THE DAY, THE RIGHT ENGINE (PRATT & WHITNEY R-2800) ON THE CANADAIR CL215-1A10 AIRCRAFT BEGAN TO INDICATE A LOSS OF POWER FOLLOWED BY A REDUCTION IN ENGINE OIL PRESSURE. THE FLIGHT CREW SHUTDOWN THE ENGINE AND RETURNED TO CHAPLEAU WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.AN EXAMINATION OF THE ENGINE REVEALED NO REMARKABLE INDICATIONS FOR THE POWER LOSS BUT MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL SUSPECT A POSSIBLE MAIN BEARING FAILURE. THE ENGINE WAS REPLACED AND IS SCHEDULED TO BE SENT TO AN OVERHAUL FACILITY FOR FURTHER INSPECTION.THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A95W0132:  DURING THE DEPARTURE, THE PILOT MANOEUVRED THE BELL 212, WITH BUCKET TRAILING, OVER THE LOCAL COMMUNITY, TO AVOID FIXED WING TRAFFIC. DURING THIS MANOEUVRE, THE HOOK APPARENTLY SWIVELLED ALLOWING THE BUCKET TO FALL FREE. THE BUCKET PUNCTURED TWO HOLES IN THE ROOF OF THE ARCTIC COLLEGE BUILDING.

A95C0153:  AIR CANADA 123, A BOEING 767-233, WAS 80 NM NORTH OF WINNIPEG AT FL390, EN ROUTE FROM TORONTO TO EDMONTON, WHEN THE FORWARD CARGO HOLD FIRE INDICATOR ILLUMINATED.  THE CREW ACTIVATED THE CARGO HOLD FIRE EXTINGUISHER SYSTEM (WHICH DIRECTS FIRE RETARDANT INTO BOTH FORWARD AND REAR CARGO HOLDS), AND DIVERTED THE FLIGHT TO WINNIPEG.  THE CREW CARRIED OUT AN UNEVENTFUL LANDING AND STOPPED ON RUNWAY 18, WITH ERS STANDING BY.  MAINTENANCE OPENED AND CHECKED BOTH CARGO HOLDS, AND FOUND NO EVIDENCE OF FIRE.  ALL CARGO AND BAGGAGE WAS REMOVED FROM BOTH CARGO HOLDS, AND THE AIRCRAFT RESUMED THE FLIGHT TO EDMONTON UNDER THE OPERATOR'S M.E.L., WITH THE CARGO HOLD FIRE DETECTION AND SUPPRESSION SYSTEMS INOPERATIVE.  THERE WERE NO REPORTED INJURIES AND THERE WAS NO REPORTED DAMAGE. THE OPERATOR PLANS TO CHECK THE CARGO HOLD FIRE DETECTION SYSTEM ON THE AIRCRAFT'S ARRIVAL IN EDMONTON.

A95W0135: THE BELL 205A-1 WAS IN CRUISE FLIGHT WHEN THE PILOT NOTICED AN INCREASE IN VIBRATION, AND A CHANGE IN THE ROTOR SOUND. HE IMMEDIATELY LANDED THE HELICOPTER ON A CUT-LINE, AND AFTER INSPECTION, REPORTED THAT A 1.5 FOOT SECTION OF MAIN ROTOR BLADE HAD DELAMINATED INBOARD OF THE TAB. A SUBSEQUENT REPORT FROM MAINTENANCE INDICATED THAT A THREE FOOT SECTION OF THE BLADE WAS MISSING. ANALYSIS OF THE BLADE HAS REVEALED THAT THE FAILURE WAS DUE TO A FATIGUE MODE OF PROGRESSIVE CRACKING THROUGH THE TRAILING EDGE EXTRUSION. THE FATIGUE CRACKING INITIATED FROM A CORROSION PIT ON THE AFT EDGE OF THE EXTRUSION.

A95Q0171:  QUINZE MINUTES APRES LE DECOLLAGE DE BAIE COMEAU VERS LE NORD-OUEST POUR UNE OPERATION DE LUTTE CONTRE LES INCENDIES, L'EQUIPAGE S'EST APERCU D'UNE PERTE D'HUILE SUR LE MOTEUR #1 DU CL-215.  LE MOTEUR A ETE FERME PAR PRECAUTION ET L'AERONEF EST RETOURNE ATTERRIR A BAIE COMEAU SANS AUCUN PROBLEME.  LES SERVICE D'URGENCE ONT ETE AVISES.  L'INSPECTION A REVELE UNE FUITE D'HUILE D'UN JOINT D'ETANCHIETE (O'RING) DU REFROIDISSEUR D'HUILE (OIL COOLER).  LE JOINT A ETE CHANGE, DE L'HUILE RAJOUTE ET L'APPAREIL A ETE REMIS EN SERVICE.

A95Q0168:  WHILE ON FIRE SUPPRESSION OPERATIONS, THE CL-215'S ENGINE #1 BACKFIRED.  THE ENGINE WAS SHUTDOWN AND SECURED.  THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED TO BAIE COMEAU WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.  MAINTENANCE FOUND THAT CYLINDER #14 HAD FAILED.  THE CYLINDER WAS REPLACED AND THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A95Q0175: ALORS QUE LE PILOTE EFFECTUAIT DE L'ARROSAGE POUR LES FEUX DE FORET, LE MOTEUR DE L'HELICOPTERE (BELL 204B) QU'IL PILOTAIT A SUBI UNE DECELERATION EN VOL.  LE PILOTE A POSE L'APPAREIL EQUIPE DE FLOTTEURS SUR L'EAU APRES AVOIR LARGUE LA CHARGE QU'IL TRANSPORTAIT.  L'APPAREIL N'A SUBI AUCUN DOMMAGE.LE TRANSPORTEUR AERIEN A DECIDE DE TRANSPORTER SON HELICOPTERE PAR VOIE TERRESTRE JUSQU'A SA BASE DE CALGARY OU IL TENTERA DE DETERMINER LA SOURCE DE LA DEFAILLANCE DU MOTEUR.INFO A SUIVRE.

A96Q0057:  PEU DE TEMPS APRES LE DECOLLAGE, LE MOTEUR DROIT DU CL215 S'EST MIS A VIBRER ET A AVOIR DES RETOURS DE FLAMMES.  LE PILOTE A REDUIT LA PUISSANCE PUIS A MIS L'HELICE EN DRAPEAU.  LE PILOTE EST REVENU ATTERRIR A L'AEROPORT JEAN LESAGE SANS AUTRE PROBLEME.  LES SERVICES D'URGENCE AVAIENT ETE MIS EN DISPONNIBILITE.  L'EXAMEN DU MOTEUR A REVELE QUE LE CABLE D'UNE BOUGIE DU CYLINDRE 17 ETAIT DEFECTUEUX.

A96C0086:  THE PILOT OF THE TRACKER CS2F-2, C-GEQD HAD EXPERIENCED A FALSE LEFT ENGINE  FIRE WARNING LIGHT ON A PREVIOUS FLIGHT.  MAINTENANCE CHANGED A FIRE DETECTION LOOP AND RELEASED THE AIRCRAFT FOR A TEST FLIGHT.  SHORTLY AFTER TAKE OFF, THE PILOT WAS ALERTED TO A FIRE WARNING ON THE SAME ENGINE.  THE PILOT SECURED THE ENGINE AND AN UNEVENTFUL LANDING WAS MADE IN LA RONGE.  MAINTENANCE DISCOVERED A SECOND UNSERVICEABLE FIRE DETECTION LOOP.  THE AIRCRAFT HAS BEEN REPAIRED AND RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A96Q0086:  L'HELICOPTERE BELL 212 ETAIT EN FINAL POUR UNE ZONE RESTREINTE AVEC, A SON BORD, DES COMBATTANTS CONTRE LES INCENDIES FORESTIERS.  ALORS QUE LE PILOTE SE PREPARAIT A ATTERRIR, UN DES COMBATTANTS L'A AVISE QUE LE ROTOR PRINCIPAL VENAIT DE FRAPPER LES ARBRES.UNE INSPECTION VISUELLE A ETE EFFECTUE APRES L'ATTERRISSAGE DANS UNE ZONE DE PLUS GRANDE DIMENSION.  LE SERVICE D'ENTRETIEN DE LA COMPAGNIE A MENTIONNE QUE LE ROTOR PRINCIPAL DEVRA ETRE CHANGE.  DE PLUS, UNE INSPECTION DU SYSTEME D'ENTRAINEMENT DEVRA ETRE EFFECTUE AVANT DE REMETTRE L'APPAREIL EN SERVICE.TRANSLATION:A96Q0086:  THE BELL 212 HELICOPTER WAS ON A FINAL APPROACH FOR A CONFINED AREA LANDING WITH A GROUP OF FOREST FIREFIGHTERS ON BOARD.  AS THE HELICOPTER WAS ABOUT TO LAND, ONE OF THE FIREFIGHTERS INFORMED THE PILOT THAT THE MAIN ROTOR HAD STRUCK SOME TREES.A VISUAL EXAMINATION OF THE HELICOPTER WAS CONDUCTED FOLLOWING A LANDING IN A LESS CONFINED AREA.  THE COMPANY'S MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL HAVE ADVISED THAT THE MAIN ROTOR WILL REQUIRE REPLACEMENT.  IN ADDITION, AN EXAMINATION OF THE DRIVE TRAIN WILL BE CONDUCTED PRIOR TO RETURNING THE HELICOPTER TO SERVICE.

A96C0096:  THE DC-6A (C-FCZZ) WAS ON A LOCAL FOREST FIRE SUPPRESSION FLIGHT OUT OF LA RONGE, WHEN THE #1 ENGINE BEGAN TO RUN ROUGH.  THE CREW ELECTED TO SHUT DOWN AND SECURE THE AFFECTED ENGINE AND MAKE A PRECAUTIONARY LANDING IN LA RONGE.  AFTER AN UNEVENTFUL LANDING, MAINTENANCE CHANGED THE FRONT PLUGS AND AN IGNITION COIL.

A96Q0091: A95Q0091:  L'APPAREIL, UN HUGHES 500C, EFFECTUAIT UNE APPROCHE POUR UN HELI-SURFACE TEMPORAIRE A FLANC DE MONTAGNE.  APRES UNE PASSE A 200 PIEDS AU-DESSUS DU POINT D'ATTERRISSAGE, LE PILOTE A DECIDE D'EFFECTUER L'APPROCHE VENT ARRIERE PUISQUE C'ETAIT LA SEULE OPTION. EN COURTE FINALE, L'APPAREIL A EFFECTUE UN MOUVEMENT DE LACET VERS LA DROITE ALORS QU'ELLE ETAIT EN STATIONNAIRE A UNE HAUTEUR DE 30 A 40 PIEDS.  LE PILOTE A TENTE DE CORRIGER MAIS L'APPAREIL S'EST ENFONCE.  LE PILOTE A UTILISE LE COLLECTIF POUR ABSORBER L'IMPACT AU SOL.L'APPAREIL S'EST IMMOBILISE SUR LE COTE GAUCHE EN PIQUE.  PERSONNE N'A ETE BLESSEE.  LORS DE L'APPROCHE, LE VENT SOUFFLAIT A UNE VELOCITE DE 10 NOEUDS AVEC DES RAFALES A 15 NOEUDS.TRANSLATION:A96Q0091:  THE HELICOPTER, A HUGHES 369, WAS CONDUCTING AN APPROACH TO A TEMPORARY HELIPAD ON THE SIDE OF A MOUNTAIN.  AFTER OVERFLYING THE HELIPAD AT AN ALTITUDE OF 200' OBOVE THE PAD, THE PILOT DETERMINED THAT HIS ONLY OPTION WAS TO CONDUCT A DOWNWIND APPROACH TO THE SITE.  ON SHORT FINAL AND WHILE IN A 30 TO 40' HOVER, THE HELICOPTER YAWED TO THE RIGHT.  THE PILOT WAS UNABLE TO CONTROL THE YAW AND THE HELICOPTER STRUCK THE GROUND.  THE PILOT WAS ABLE TO CUSHION THE LANDING BY RAISING COLLECTIVE.THE HELICOPTER CAME TO REST ON ITS LEFT SIDE.  THERE WERE NO INJURIES.AT THE TIME OF THE APPROACH, THE WIND WAS 10 KNOTS WITH GUSTS TO 15.

A96C0100:  THE CANADAIR CL215 (C-GMAK) WAS CARRYING OUT FOREST FIRE SUPPRESSION OPERATIONS WHEN AN ABNORMALLY HIGH OIL CONSUMPTION WAS NOTED ON THE LEFT ENGINE.  THE CREW ELECTED TO CEASE OPERATIONS AND RETURN TO THOMPSON UNDER A REDUCED POWER SETTING.  CONTINUED HIGH OIL CONSUMPTION THREATENED OIL EXHAUSTION AND PROMPTED THE CREW TO SHUT DOWN THE AFFECTED ENGINE AND DIVERT TO GILLAM WHERE AN UNEVENTFUL LANDING WAS MADE.MAINTENANCE FOUND A CRACKED CYLINDER ON THE LEFT ENGINE.

A96Q0093:  L'APPAREIL, UN AS 350D, EFFECTUAIT DE L'ARROSAGE POUR LES FEUX EN FORET EN UTILISANT UN PANIER POUR TRANSPORTER L'EAU. DANS LE BUT DE REMPLIR LE PANIER, LE PILOTE A PRESENTE L'APPAREIL EN FINALE AU DESSUS DU LAC ET EN TENTANT D'ELIMINER LA VITESSE RESIDUELLE, IL A EFFECTUE UN ARRONDI TRES PRONONCE. LE ROTOR DE QUEUE A ALORS TOUCHE A L'EAU.LE ROTOR DE QUEUE AINSI QUE SA BOITE D'ENGRENAGE SE SONT SEPARES DE L'APPAREIL QUI A COMMENCE A TOURNER VERS LA GAUCHE.L'APPAREIL S'EST IMMOBILISE SUR LE COTE GAUCHE DANS ENVIRON 6 PIEDS D'EAU ET DE BOUE. LE PILOTE EST SORTI INDEMNE.TRANSLATION:A96Q0093:  THE HELICOPTER, AN AEROSPATIALE AS 350D, WAS ENGAGED IN A FOREST FIRE SUPPRESSION OPERATION AND WAS SLINGING A WATER BUCKET.  DURING AN ATTEMPT TO FILL THE WATER BUCKET, THE PILOT FLEW THE HELICOPTER ON A FINAL APPROACH TO A LAKE.  IN ORDER TO ELIMINATE ALL HIS FORWARD SPEED, THE PILOT EXECUTED A PRONOUNCED FLARE.  DURING THE FLARE, THE TAIL ROTOR CONTACTED THE WATER.THE TAIL ROTOR AND ITS GEAR BOX SEPARATED FROM THE HELICOPTER WHICH THEN COMMENCED YAWING TO THE LEFT.  THE HELICOPTER CAME TO REST ON ITS LEFT SIDE IN APPROXIMATELY 6' OF WATER AND MUD.  THE PILOT ESCAPED UNINJURED.

A96P0134:  DURING THE LAST WATER-BOMB RUN, THE PILOT OF THE CONAIR FIRECAT SAW OIL VENTING FROM THE #1 ENGINE BREATHER; ALL ENGINE INSTRUMENTS WERE INDICATING NORMAL.  ON CLIMBOUT FROM THE TARGET, THE PILOT OBSERVED A RISE IN ENGINE OIL TEMPERATURE AND A DECREASE IN ENGINE OIL PRESSURE.  PASSING 2,800 FEET, HE FEATHERED THE #1 ENGINE.  HE CONTINUED THE CLIMB TO 8,500 FEET, AND LANDED ABOUT 10 MINUTES LATER AT WHITEHORSE WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT. A SUSPECTED MASTER ROD BEARING FAILURE NECESSITATED AN ENGINE CHANGE.

A96C0116: THE CONSOLIDATED VULTEE, PBY-5A, DEPARTED REPULSE BAY ON A FIREFIGHTING MISSION.  THE CREW SHUT DOWN THE RIGHT ENGINE WHEN THEY NOTICED SMOKE AND OIL TRAILING FROM THE ENGINE.  THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNED TO REPULSE BAY FOR AN UNEVENTFUL LANDING.A MAINTENANCE INSPECTION REVEALED THAT THE #12 CYLINDER HAD FAILED.

A96A0111: THE CL215 AIRCRAFT WAS ENROUTE FROM DEER LAKE TO GANDER WHEN ELECTRICAL PROBLEMS WERE EXPERIENCED.  THE CREW ADVISED GANDER TOWER THAT THEY MAY EXPERIENCE A COMMUNICATIONS FAILURE DUE TO ELECTRICAL PROBLEMS, THAT THERE WAS SOME SMOKE IN THE REAR OF THE AIRCRAFT, AND THAT NO ASSISTANCE WAS REQUIRED.  THE AIRCRAFT LANDED WITHOUT INCIDENT AT 19:40 NDT.  AS A PRECAUTION, ERS HAD BEEN PLACED ON STANDBY BY THE TOWER.MAINTENANCE FOUND AN ELECTRICAL SHORT IN ONE OF THE INVERTERS.

A96C0123:  THE BELL 204B HELICOPTER (C-GRGA) WAS ENGAGED IN FOREST FIREFIGHTING OPERATIONS AND THE PILOT WAS ATTEMPTING TO LAND ON A HELIPAD TO PICK UP A FIRETEAM LEADER. THE HELIPAD HAD BEEN CUT INTO THE FOREST ON THE SIDE OF A LAKE.  THE LANDING AREA SLOPED UPWARDS FROM THE LAKE SHORE AND WAS COVERED IN LARGE BOULDERS.  BECAUSE OF THE SLOPE OF THE HELIPAD, A LARGE LOG HAD BEEN PLACED IN THE ONE CLEAR AREA OF THE PAD TO SUPPORT THE AFT PORTION OF HELICOPTER'S SKIDS. THE REMAINDER OF THE HELIPAD WAS UNUSABLE BECAUSE OF STUMPS AND OTHER DEBRIS.THE FIRETEAM LEADER CLEARED SOME DEBRIS BUT AFTER REPEATED UNSUCCESSFUL ATTEMPTS TO LAND, THE PILOT OF A BELL 206 PILOT REQUESTED THE PILOT OF THE 204 TO MAKE AN ATTEMPT TO RECOVER THE FIRE TEAM LEADER.  THE PILOT OF THE OCCURRENCE HELICOPTER TOUCHED DOWN INITIALLY BUT WAS CONCERNED THAT THE HELICOPTER WAS POSITIONED TOO FAR BACK ON THE LOG AND WOULD SLIP BACKWARDS IF THE COLLECTIVE WAS LOWERED FURTHER.  THE FIRETEAM LEADER ALSO OBSERVED THAT THE BEARPAWS WERE BEHIND AND APPEARED TO BE TOUCHING THE LOG.  HE USED HIS HAND HELD RADIO TO INFORM THE PILOT.THE PILOT RAISED THE COLLECTIVE AND LIFTED THE HELICOPTER INTO THE HOVER.  HE REPORTED THAT THE HELICOPTER BEGAN A HUMPING MOTION AND HE HEARD A BANGING.  HE THEN LOWERED THE COLLECTIVE TO LAND BUT ROTATED BACK ON THE LOG STRIKING THE TAIL ROTOR.  THE HELICOPTER YAWED TO THE RIGHT, ROLLED OVER ON ITS RIGHT SIDE AND CRASHED.THE FIRETEAM LEADER OBSERVED THE HELICOPTER BEGIN TO BOUNCE VIGOROUSLY AND RAN FOR SAFETY INTO THE TREE LINE.  HE HEARD THE HELICOPTER CRASH AND THEN RESCUED THE SERIOUSLY INJURED PILOT WHO WAS TRAPPED IN THE AIRCRAFT.  THREE WITNESSES WERE ORBITING THE SITE IN THE BELL 206.  THE WITNESSES OBSERVED THAT THE HELICOPTER'S TAIL BOOM WAS LOW AND HAD DESCENDED INTO THE ROCKS ON LANDING.  THEY THEN OBSERVED THE TAIL ROTOR SLOWING DOWN AS THE HELICOPTER LIFTED OFF.  THEY OBSERVED THE HELICOPTER THEN SLEW TO THE RIGHT, ROLL OVER AND CRASH.

A96A0142:  THE CL-215 AIRCRAFT WAS MAKING A WATER PICK-UP ON THE CHURCHILL RIVER WHEN THE #2 ENGINE LOST POWER.  THE PICK-UP WAS ABORTED AND THE AIRCRAFT LANDED ON THE RIVER WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.MAINTENANCE DETERMINED THAT THE IMPELLER IN THE #2 ENGINE HAD FAILED.

A96C0149   THE CANADAIR CL-215 WAS ENROUTE FROM LA RONGE TO LOWER FISHING LAKE WHEN THE LEFT ENGINE BEGAN TO RUN ROUGH.  THE CREW ELECTED TO SHUT DOWN THE AFFECTED ENGINE AND RETURN TO LA RONGE.  THE AIRCRAFT LANDED SAFELY AND THERE WERE NO INJURIES.  MAINTENANCE DETERMINED THAT A CYLINDER HAD FAILED AND THAT THE ENGINE REQUIRED CHANGING.

A96Q0121:  L'APPAREIL CL-215 ETAIT A COMBATTRE UN FEU DE FORET LORSQUE LE MOTEUR DE DROITE (P&W R-2800) A SUBI UNE PERTE DE PUISSANCE. L'EQUIPAGE A PRIS LES MESURES APPROPRIEES ET EST REVENU ATTERRIR SANS AUTRE INCIDENT A SA BASE DE DEPART. LES SERVICES D'URGENCE ETAIENT EN ATTENTE.IL A ETE DETERMINE QU'UNE VALVE ETAIT DEFECTUEUSE. LA VALVE SERA CHANGEE ET L'APPAREIL REMIS EN SERVICE.

A96P0179:  WHEN THE RAMP CREW OPENED THE AFT PIT DOOR OF THE BOEING 737-200 AND STARTED TO UNLOAD THE CARGO, THEY DETECTED A STRONG ODOUR.  THE ERS WAS REQUESTED AND THE FIRE CREW DISCOVERED A LIQUID-SOAKED BOX CONTAINING TWELVE 375ML PLASTIC BOTTLES.  THE BOTTLES CONTAINED BUTYL-METHYL-ETHER "OCTANE BOOSTER" - A CLASS 3 FLAMMABLE LIQUID.THE SHIPPER WAS MERCURY MARINE OF BURNABY, B.C., AND THE CONSIGNEE WAS RC MARINE OF KITIMAT, B.C.,  TRANSPORT CANADA DANGEROUS GOODS PERSONNEL HAVE BEEN ADVISED.  MORE INFORMATION TO FOLLOW.

A96C0168:  THE CESSNA 337G, C-FIGS, WAS RETURNING FROM AN AERIAL APPLICATION (FORESTRY) BIRD DOG MISSION.  THE PILOT NORMALLY EXTENDS THE LANDING GEAR ON THE DOWNWIND CIRCUIT LEG, BUT ON THIS OCCASION, HE REPORTEDLY FORGOT TO DO SO.  THE PILOT COMPLETED A (POWER-ON) SHORT-FIELD APPROACH TO THE GRAVEL RUNWAY, AND TOUCHED DOWN WITH THE LANDING GEAR RETRACTED.  THE GEAR WARNING HORN REPORTEDLY ACTIVATES WHEN THE POWER IS REDUCED TO IDLE.  NEITHER THE PILOT NOR THE ONE PASSENGER WERE INJURED.  THE AIRCRAFT SUSTAINED DAMAGE TO ITS BELLY AND PROPELLERS.

A96Q0154: PEU APRES LE DECOLLAGE L'APPAREIL CL-215 A SUBI UNE PERTE DE PUISSANCE DU MOTEUR DROIT. L'EQUIPAGE A EFFECTUE LES PROCEDURES D'URGENCE APPROPRIEES ET EST REVENU POSER L'APPAREIL SANS AUTRE INCIDENT A L'AEROPORT DE DEPART. IL A ETE DETERMINE QUE LA POMPE A ESSENCE ETAIT DEFECTUEUSE. LA POMPE A ETE CHANGEE ET L'APPAREIL REMIS EN SERVICE.

A97W0125: THE DOUGLAS A26C LOST POWER ON ONE ENGINE ON DEPARTURE FROM WHITEHORSE, YUKON. THE PILOT DROPPED THE LOAD OF FIRE RETARDENT AND RETURNED TO THE AIRPORT WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT. ERS WAS ON STANDBY.MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL CHANGED ONE CYCLINDER, AND RETURNED THE AIRCRAFT TO SERVICE.

A97W0155:  THE NUMBER THREE ENGINE ON THE DC4 BEGAN TO BACKFIRE DURING A FIRE DROP. THE FLIGHT CREW REDUCED THE POWER ON THE ENGINE AND SUBSEQUENTLY SECURED IT DUE TO CONTINUED ROUGH RUNNING. THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED TO FORT SIMPSON WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT. MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL FOUND THAT THE OIL SCREEN WAS CONTAMINATED WITH METAL AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS FERRIED TO THE HAY RIVER MAINTENANCE BASE FOR AN ENGINE CHANGE.

A97C0134: A97C0234: A RISK OF COLLISION OCCURRED BETWEEN TANKER 261, A CANADAIR CL215, AND BIRD DOG 1, AN AERO COMMANDER 500B.BIRD DOG 1 WAS DOING A LEAD-IN FOR TANKER 261, TO A FIRE TWO MILES WEST OF HUDSON, ON.  BIRD DOG 1 STARTED THE LEAD IN RUN EAST TO WEST.  THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO KEEP SIGHT OF A HELICOPTER WHICH WAS ALSO WORKING IN THE AREA.  WHEN BIRD DOG 1 COMPLETED THE LEAD-IN LINE, THE PILOT PULLED UP INTO A CLIMBING TURN TO CLEAR THE AREA, AND HE WAS ADVISED BY THE CREW OF TANKER 261 THAT HE WAS COMPROMISING SEPARATION BETWEEN THEIR TWO AIRCRAFT.  BIRD DOG 1 HAD PASSED UNDER TANKER 261 DURING THE LEAD-IN, AND THE CREW OF TANKER 261 BRIEFLY LOST SIGHT OF BIRD DOG 1.WHEN THE CREW OF TANKER 261 OBSERVED BIRD DOG 1'S CLIMBING TURN, THEY MANOEUVRED TO INCREASE SEPARATION BETWEEN THE TWO AIRCRAFT.

A97P0207:  The pilot of the Bell 206B helicopter (serial number 478) was engaged in transporting survey crews in the Bear Valley area, about 45 nautical miles (nm) north of Mackenzie, British Columbia. On the morning of the accident, he had begun flying at about 0645 Pacific daylight time (PDT). A survey crew contacted the pilot by radio at about 1200 and requested a pick-up for about 1400; they also informed the pilot of a 100- to 150-foot ceiling and a visibility of about 300 metres (1000 feet). At about 1445, the pilot was attempting to locate the survey crew at the 5100-foot elevation, but low cloud, fog, and precipitation prevented him from making visual contact with the landing area. The pilot was in two-way radio contact with the ground crews and remarked that the lower pick-up pad was fogged in and that he could not see the trees or ground below him. The pilot continued manoeuvring in the area, searching for the landing pad. Witnesses on the ground then saw the helicopter appear from the base of the low cloud, in a right-hand, descending turn, roughly in a 40-degree nose-down and 40-degree right-bank attitude before it struck trees and collided with the terrain at 5200 feet above sea level (asl), inside a cirque. The pilot was fatally injured, and the helicopter was destroyed by impact forces and a post-crash fire.The helicopter was manufactured in 1969, and maintenance records reveal that the helicopter was certificated, equipped, and maintained in accordance with existing regulations and approved procedures. As of 26 July 1997, it had 11 640 hours of flight time, and the Allison 250-C20B engine had 10 003 hours. The helicopter's weight and centre of gravity at the time of the accident are not conclusively known, but based on the day's previous activities, it is estimated that the weight and balance were within the prescribed limits and that there was sufficient fuel on board for the flight.The helicopter struck the rocky surface at a high impact angle and was damaged by an intense post-crash fire, except for the aft section of the tail boom, the tail rotor assembly, two doors, and fragments of the skid gear. No flight or engine instruments were recovered, except for the face of the engine torque gauge. The TSB Engineering Branch examination of this dial did not reveal any impact-related reading. All flight controls were destroyed by impact and fire. The main rotor gearbox and the engine gearbox were also destroyed by fire. An examination of the gears and bearings that remained did not reveal any anomaly or indication of pre-impact distress or malfunction. The aircraft systems were examined to the degree possible, and no sign of a malfunction was found.Four days before the accident, the pilot had experienced smoke in the cockpit resulting from an electrical short circuit in the directional gyro (DG). Company maintenance personnel in Mackenzie removed the DG and inspected the associated wiring loom and cannon plug; the helicopter was then test-flown and returned to the Bear Valley camp without the DG installed. The removal of the DG did not affect the airworthiness of the helicopter. The DG was not required for the pilot to navigate in visual meteorological conditions (VMC), since a magnetic compass was installed in the helicopter as standard equipment. The absence of the DG could have affected the pilot's ability to fly in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). The accident helicopter was not authorized to fly under instrument flight rules (IFR) conditions.Witnesses recalled that when the helicopter departed on this trip, waves of low cloud and fog were moving through the area, and the visibility had diminished to about one mile in drizzle; the sky condition at the drop site was described as a solid overcast around 600 feet above ground level (agl). These weather conditions reportedly persisted throughout the day. Witnesses also reported that there was very little wind at the time of the accident, that light rain was falling, and that the fog and low cloud coming up the slope caused an overcast ceiling of about 300 feet agl. About two hours after the accident, the same weather conditions prevented another helicopter from landing at the accident site. The weather reporting station nearest the accident area is 45 nm away in Mackenzie. At 1300, the automated weather observation system (AWOS) at Mackenzie had recorded a measured ceiling of 700 feet overcast and a visibility of more than 9 miles. At 1400 the sky condition was 500 feet scattered, 1600 feet broken, and 2800 feet overcast, and the visibility was more than 9 miles, in very light drizzle. In the hour between these reports, four special observations recorded a broken ceiling as low as 500 feet. Based on witnesses accounts, however, the weather conditions at the accident site were significantly different from the Mackenzie AWOS. This was likely because of the distance and the mountainous terrain, which is known to create unpredictable local weather conditions.The 45-year-old pilot had recently begun his career in aviation, and had accumulated about 400 hours of total flying time. He held a Canadian commercial helicopter pilot licence (CPL-H), endorsed for the Bell 47 and 206 helicopters, for daylight flying only, and a valid medical certificate. The pilot did not hold an instrument rating, nor was it required, since this operation was to be conducted under visual flight rules (VFR). The pilot had attended a course on pilot decision making in April 1997. His only exposure to instrument flying was during basic training toward his CPL-H.In early May 1997, the pilot had successfully completed the operator's Upgrade Training Program, which included mountain-flying and reduced-visibility training, and his pilot proficiency check. On May 12 he began as a base pilot in Mackenzie, and on July 2 the pilot assumed his duties at the Bear Valley camp. The Bear Valley contract was the pilot's first commercial assignment and his first exposure to remote-base and self-dispatch operations. He was expected to make routine operational decisions involving customer requirements, weather, helicopter serviceability, and the suitability of the terrain, although he could easily consult with the operations bases in Prince George or MacKenzie. On July 7 he experienced a main rotor blade strike during a confined-area approach in the Bear Valley area. The next day, the company chief pilot carried out an evaluation flight and debriefing with him before he returned to the Bear Valley operation and continued his assignment.The pilot had flown about 120 hours in the 30 days before the accident and at least 16 hours in the last 3 days; he was scheduled to begin his time off the following day. An examination of the pilot's flight time/days off records revealed at least 12 instances in the previous 70 days where his flight- and duty-times exceeded the limits specified in the Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs Sections 700.16, 720.16, and 720.17 ). During the 30 days before the accident, the pilot did not have the required 8 hours of rest on five occasions and had exceeded the 14-hour duty time limit on eight occasions, the most recent being on the day before the accident.It is apparent from his records that the pilot had been filling in the forms incorrectly. If filled in correctly, these records would have allowed the pilot and the operator to accurately maintain and monitor his flight time and duty time to prevent him from exceeding the daily and cumulative limits specified in the CARs.On 28 April 1992, Transport Canada (TC) conducted a regional audit of Northern Mountain Helicopters Incorporated (NMH) and identified several areas of non-conformance, mainly regarding pilot training records, flight- and duty-time records, and aircraft journey log entries. As a result of this audit, the company pledged to undertake a plan to rectify the areas of concern. TC carried out another in-depth audit of the company between May 11 and May 22, 1998, which focussed on the 18-month period from October 1996 to May 1998. The purpose of the audit was to assess the operator's level of conformance with the regulations and standards governing the operations of Canadian air operators. The results of this 1998 audit noted that significant changes in the company structure and operations following the 1992 audit were insufficient to address all of the noted deficiencies.In the six-year period between the audits, the TC Centre (TCC) in Prince George, British Columbia (B.C.), had carried out maintenance inspections and audits of several NMH bases. These inspections/audits and their results were recorded in the Prince George TCC, but were not forwarded to the TC Pacific Region office in Vancouver, and the 1998 audit did not reflect the Prince George inspections. The inspections carried out by the TCC identified frequent maintenance-related deficiencies; TCC inspectors later assessed most of the company's responses to these findings as satisfactory.Nevertheless, in January 1996 a TCC audit of the NMH aircraft and maintenance facilities identified 17 deficiencies, several of which were recurring since the audit carried out in January 1994. As a result, TC Airworthiness sent a letter to NMH stating that TC was alarmed at the results, and warned that the Approved Maintenance Organization Certificate, number 144-90, would be suspended if the company did not meet the requirements of the letter. The certificate was not suspended at that time.In December 1997, about five months after the accident, TC Pacific Region issued NMH two Notices of Suspension, one each for the Canadian Air Operator Certificate, number 1518, and the Approved Maintenance Organization Certificate, number 144-90, because TC determined that the company had failed to comply with the conditions required for the issuance of these certificates. Following response by NMH to the conditions of the suspensions, TC later withdrew the Notices of Suspension.At the time of the 1998 audit, NMH offered domestic, non-scheduled international, and aerial work air services from the main base at Prince George, B.C., and from eleven sub-bases in B.C., one sub-base in Ontario, and two international operational bases in Sudan and Congo. NMH operated a mixed fleet of about 70 aircraft and held Air Operator Certificate number 1518. The operator employed about 130 pilots and operated under Subparts 702, 703, and 704 of the CARs in diverse flight operations such as general charter, heli-logging, forest fire management, aerial construction, and seismic support.As a result of the 1998 audit, a total of 54 airworthiness findings and 17 operational findings were made, several of which TC assessed would have had an impact on flight safety. TC technical inspectors noted several deficiencies in the areas of technical records, maintenance schedules, defect deferral, maintenance dispatch, and quality assurance. According to TC, the airworthiness findings suggested that the company had less-than-acceptable control over various components on the maintenance system and that, as evidenced by the number and seriousness of the findings, the company had made little effort to comply with all aspects of the (then) new CARs.TC operational inspectors identified several areas of concern resulting from the audit. The most important of these were the lack of effective flight and duty time monitoring, and poorly kept pilot training records. These deficiencies had the potential to adversely affect flight safety. The TC auditors found that the flight crew training program was lacking in several areas, notably in training for flight in reduced visibility. Further, pilot training records were found to have been inaccurate and incomplete. The TC auditors found that the system in place for tracking pilot flight and duty times was extraordinarily inaccurate and ineffective. As well, the auditors made five findings regarding company pilots exceeding the flight- and duty-time limitations contained in the CARs. Three of these findings concerned the accident pilot: he had less than the required minimum rest periods on five occasions; he had duty time in excess of the maximum on five occasions; and he had been given only two days of rest in the 31-day period before the accident (OP-09-01 to OP-09-03).In partial summary, the audit revealed the following about the operator:	1.	the maintenance control system did not comply with Commercial Air Service Standards;	2.	company aircraft were not maintained in accordance with an effective maintenance control system that met the requirements of CAR Part VII - Commercial Air Services, Subpart 6 - Aircraft Maintenance Requirements for Air Operators;	3.	pilots had not completed the required ground- and flight-training programs;	4.	the system to monitor flight time, duty time, and rest periods was not followed; and,	5.	each pilot was not provided with the required time free from duty.On 4 June 1998, as a result of this audit, TC issued the operator a Notice of Suspension under Section 7.1(1)(b) of the Aeronautics Act, effective 8 June 1998. To avoid further action against the operator's Air Operator Certificate, TC required the operator to comply with the conditions specified in the Notice of Suspension within 30 days. On 8 June 1998, a Special Inspection Team from TC examined the operator's compliance with the conditions. In summary, TC found that the operator had "co-operated on all levels with a clear understanding of deficiencies identified." As well, TC noted that "steps were already being taken to correct deficiencies and prevent future occurrence." Accordingly, the Notice of Suspension was withdrawn.Nevertheless, the operator's responses to the operational finding concerning the accident pilot (OP-09-01 to 03) were all assessed as unacceptable by TC in July 1998. The TC inspector noted that the operator's responses put into question the operator's grasp of the flight- and duty-time limitations. The inspector also noted that more was needed to educate the flight crews about flight and duty times and to enforce the limitations of the CARs. TC has continued to monitor the operator since that time and has assessed as satisfactory the operator's response to each deficiency noted since.Fatigue is a debilitating phenomenon which slows reaction time, reduces concentration, and can lead to errors of attention. The performance and judgement of an individual suffering from fatigue becomes degraded, and one common effect is an increase in that individual's willingness to take risks and a tendency to finish tasks more quickly. The two most common causes are insufficient rest and a lack of sleep. Research shows that, although individual needs vary, the majority of the population requires between 7.5 and 8.5 hours of sleep in a 24-hour period. If people obtain less than their requirement, they develop a sleep debt, which is cumulative. This occurs when insufficient quantity of sleep continues over several consecutive days. For example, missing one hour of sleep per day for four days has about the same effect as missing fours hours of sleep in one night. Furthermore, the impact of sleep debt is compounded when it is combined with a long day.On the ground, spatial orientation is sensed by the combination of vision, muscle sense, and specialized organs in the inner ear, which sense linear and angular accelerations. Vision is the strongest of the orienting senses, and in visual flight, the pilot relies on regular visual references with the ground and horizon to control the aircraft attitude and altitude. If a pilot is in cloud, the visual reference to the ground and horizon is lost. As a result, the available cues (solely from the external forces on the body) often produce spatial disorientation in flight, because the pilot has a false impression of aircraft attitude and motion. Under these conditions, the pilot is completely dependent on the flight instruments and learned flying skills for control of the aircraft. Inexperienced pilots with little instrument time are particularly susceptible to spatial disorientation when they are confronted with no external visual attitude references. Without suitable flight instruments or skills, a disoriented pilot would quickly lose control of the aircraft. Research found in the FAA Advisory Circular 60-4A, shows that a pilot can take as long as 35 seconds to re-establish full control of an aircraft by using instruments alone. In that period, the pilot spends at least five seconds recognizing that a hazard exists, determining the necessary corrective action, and responding to it. Instrument flight training in itself does not prevent disorientation, rather it provides the pilot with the ability to overcome it.The pilot may have decided to attempt the crew pick-up in adverse weather conditions because of his reluctance to leave the survey crews stranded and his desire to do well in his first unsupervised assignment. His assessment of the potential risks involved may have been influenced by his limited experience.The survey crews saw the helicopter emerge from the low clouds in an extreme flight attitude, which was not consistent with controlled flight in this type of helicopter. The crews' description of the brief flight path before impact, as well as wreckage and impact characteristics, indicate that the pilot had insufficient time or altitude to prevent the collision with the terrain. Such a loss of control most likely was the result of spatial disorientation.While the possibility exists that a mechanical malfunction did occur, no definitive conclusions about the mechanical condition of the helicopter can be drawn from the available wreckage. The remainder of the analysis will focus on the possible human performance aspects of this accident.The absence of the DG, while not affecting the pilot's ability to navigate in VMC, could have limited his ability to maintain control in IMC. Although the weather conditions reported by ground observers were not consistent with VMC, the actual in-flight conditions experienced by the pilot are not conclusively known. It is probable the pilot encountered the same conditions as those that were observed and that, as a result, he rapidly became disoriented.The pilot had, on occasion, exceeded the limitations concerning flight time, duty time, and rest periods. As well, several days before the accident, he had entered into a period when, although individuals can vary, the average person would have experienced serious cumulative sleep debt. Although the pilot recorded a normal sleep period immediately before the day of the accident, it is possible that the effect of the recent sleep debt may have adversely affected his performance or decision-making ability. It could not be determined if fatigue-related factors contributed to the circumstances of this accident; nonetheless, the workload and schedule of the pilot included periods when the risk of fatigue-related performance decrements would have been elevated.TC audit findings show that the operator had not exercised effective operational control of the company's maintenance and operational activities. In particular, the method for tracking pilot flight and duty time was ineffective and inaccurate. This allowed the accident pilot to exceed the maxima, and it prevented the operator from monitoring and regulating the pilot appropriately. Such lack of operational control and administrative support may have increased the burden of workload on the accident pilot, perhaps exacerbating his overall stress and fatigue levels and diminishing his judgement.The TC audit of the company in 1992 revealed several areas of non-conformance, and the company pledged to rectify the areas of concern. However, it was not until the regulatory audit from 11 to 22 May 1998, following this occurrence, that TC carried out another audit of the company.TC issued repeated warnings of suspension of the company's maintenance and operational activities during the period between the audits, ultimately precipitating the most recent Notice of Suspension of the Air Operator Certificate in June 1998. Following the 1992 Transport Canada audit, deficiencies related to the company's air operator certificate and the approved maintenance organization certificate, were either not eliminated or were allowed to re-emerge.1.	The weather in the vicinity of the accident made it unlikely that the flight could be completed in visual meteorological conditions.2.	The helicopter emerged from the low cloud base in a steep, nose-down turn, and there was insufficient altitude and time to prevent the aircraft from striking the ground.3. 	The pilot likely experienced spatial disorientation and lost control of the helicopter.1.	The pilot's work/rest schedule increased the probability of him making fatigue-related errors in both aircraft handling and judgement.2.	According to the company records, the pilot had, on several occasions, exceeded the legislated flight- and duty-time limitations of the CARs.3.	Transport Canada audits carried out after the accident revealed deficiencies in the company's control of maintenance and operational activities.4.	Following the 1992 Transport Canada audit, deficiencies related to the company's air operator certificate and the approved maintenance organization certificate, were either not eliminated or were allowed to re-emerge.5.	The pilot had no formal instrument flying training or experience beyond that provided in his commercial helicopter flight training syllabus. 1.	The pilot was licensed and qualified for VFR flight.2.	The pilot did not hold an instrument rating nor was one required for the planned operation.3.	Records indicate that the helicopter was certified, equipped and maintained for the operation.4.	No indication was found of any pre-impact failure of the helicopter, its engine or systems. This report concludes the Transportation Safety Board's investigation into this occurrence. Consequently, the Board authorized the release of this report on 17 August 2000.

A97Q0172:  L'EQUIPAGE DU CANADAIR CL215 A DECOLLE DE L'AEROPORT DE MANIWAKI. A97A0157: THE BELL 206L (LONGRANGER) HELICOPTER WAS ON A FOREST FIRE MAPPING FLIGHT WHEN THE PILOT HEARD A LOUD BANG ACCOMPANIED BY A SHARP YAW TO THE LEFT. A98W0102: The crew of the S61 had been bucketing water during a forest fire suppression operation from a small relatively shallow pond. The crew had experienced some difficulties with the bucket and had just returned to the bucketing operation after a short stop at Kerby Lake airfield for maintenance action with the bucket.The first officer was flying the helicopter from the left seat as is normal in the S61 during vertical reference work. The initial approach was described as normal, and as the helicopter slowed it began to settle while still in forward motion. The pilot applied power and as he did so the nose dropped. The Captain who was in the right seat realised that the aircraft was settling and was about to jettison the bucket when the aircraft struck the water. After water impact the helicopter rolled to the right. The left emergency window was jettisoned before the helicopter submerged however the pilots were unable to exit the helicopter before they themselves were submerged. The water, although shallow was turbid resulting in near zero visibility for the pilots as they attempted to exit the helicopter. Neither pilot had difficulty orienting themselves to the cockpit environment. The co-pilot exited first and the captain was then able to exit.It was reported that the engines were producing adequate power at the time of the accident and that the torque was responding as would be expected during the final seconds of flight.The S61 helicopter will enter a state known as ?settling with power'. Once the helicopter begins to settle with power, the application of additional power will only serve to aggravate the situation and increase the rate of descent.

A98W0123: THE PILOT WAS LANDING THE BELL 206B HELICOPTER AT THE ROSE LAKE, YUKON FOREST FIRE STAGING AREA. HE APPROACHED THE SITE INTO A FIVE KNOT WIND, COMPLETED A 180 DEGREE HOVER TURN AND ATTEMPTED TO SET DOWN NEAR A PILE OF BUNDLED FIRE HOSES. AS HE WAS MANOEUVRING TO PLACE THE SKIDS IN A STABLE POSITION ON THE GENTLY SLOPING GROUND, THE HELICOPTER BEGAN TO DRIFT TO THE RIGHT AND THE RIGHT SKID SNAGGED A SMALL THREE-INCH-HIGH STUMP THAT WAS PROTRUDING FROM THE GROUND AT A 45 DEGREE ANGLE. AS THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO DISENGAGE THE STUMP, HE BECAME CONCERNED ABOUT THE SAFETY OF A FIRE FIGHTER WHO WAS SITTING ON THE FIRE HOSES, BELOW THE ROTOR DISC AND TO THE LEFT OF THE HELICOPTER. THE PILOT BELIEVES HE APPLIED UP COLLECTIVE AT THAT MOMENT, AND THE HELICOPTER ROLLED RAPIDLY ONTO THE RIGHT SIDE. THE PILOT AND THE FIRE FIGHTER WERE UNINJURED; HOWEVER, A FORESTRY PASSENGER OCCUPYING THE LEFT COCKPIT SEAT SUSTAINED MINOR FACIAL INJURIES. THE HELICOPTER WAS DESTROYED.THE HELICOPTER WAS FITTED WITH SHOULDER HARNESSES AND HEAD RESTRAINTS IN BOTH FRONT SEATS. THE PILOT WAS WEARING A HELMET AND A SHOULDER HARNESS. THE PASSENGER WAS NOT WEARING A HELMET OR THE AVAILABLE SHOULDER HARNESS.THE PILOT REPORTED THAT A COMBINATION OF A LACK OF SLEEP, A LACK OF PROPER NOURISHMENT, AND MULTIPLE DISTRACTIONS HAD REDUCED HIS ALERTNESS AND CONTRIBUTED TO THE DYNAMIC ROLLOVER. HE HAD STAYED AT THE FIRE CAMP THE PREVIOUS NIGHT, AND HE HAD RECEIVED LITTLE OR NO SLEEP BECAUSE HE HAD SLEPT ON A ROCKY SURFACE WITHOUT A FOAMY. HE HAD BEEN DISPATCHED ON AN "INITIAL ATTACK" PRIOR TO EATING A PROPER BREAKFAST, HE HAD BEEN RECEIVING MULTIPLE VERBAL MESSAGES AND INSTRUCTIONS FROM FORESTRY PERSONNEL THROUGHOUT THE MORNING, AND HE HAD BEEN UNABLE TO DISCUSS THE LANDING AT THE STAGING AREA WITH HIS PASSENGER, ON THE INTERCOM, BECAUSE OF THE VHF-FM RADIO CONVERSATIONS THAT WERE IN PROGRESS BETWEEN AGITATED FORESTRY PERSONNEL AT THE TIME OF THE ACCIDENT. HE REPORTED THAT HE HAD ELECTED TO LAND CLOSE TO THE BUNDLED HOSES IN ORDER TO REDUCE PERSONNEL MOVEMENT AROUND THE HELICOPTER AND THEREBY REDUCE THE CHANCE OF ACCIDENTAL PERSONNEL OR EQUIPMENT CONTACT WITH THE MAIN ROTOR.

A98W0130: THE CONAIR FIRECAT DEPARTED WHITEHORSE, YT ON A WATER BOMBING FLIGHT TO A NEARBY FOREST FIRE. DURING THE CLIMB-OUT THE PILOT OBSERVED HIGH OIL TEMPERATURE ON THE NO. 1 ENGINE (WRIGHT R-1820), AND OIL AND SMOKE DISCHARGING FROM THE BREATHER TUBE. THE ENGINE THEN BEGAN TO RUN ROUGH AND LOSE POWER. THE PILOT COMPLETED AN IN-FLIGHT SHUT DOWN OF THE ENGINE, DUMPED THE LOAD OF FIRE RETARDANT AND RETURNED TO WHITEHORSE WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT. MAINTENANCE EXAMINATION DETERMINED THAT THE ENGINE HAD SUSTAINED A MAIN BEARING FAILURE.

A98W0127: THE DOUGLAS B-26C WATER BOMBER HAD DEPARTED CARMACKS, YT AND WAS EN ROUTE TO A NEARBY FOREST FIRE WHEN THE NO. 2 ENGINE (PRATT AND WHITNEY R-2800) BEGAN TO RUN ROUGH. THE PILOT SECURED THE ENGINE, DUMPED THE LOAD OF FIRE RETARDANT, AND DIVERTED TO WHITEHORSE, WHERE THE AIRCRAFT LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT. ERS WAS STANDING BY. MAINTENANCE EXAMINATION DETERMINED THAT THE ENGINE HAD SUSTAINED AN INTERNAL FAILURE AS EVIDENCED BY A LARGE AMOUNT OF METAL IN THE OIL SCREEN. THE ENGINE WAS CHANGED AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A98W0141: WHEN THE FUEL MIXTURE OF THE  PRATT & WHITNEY R2800 ENGINE WAS LEANED IT BACKFIRED. THE CREW SECURED THE ENGINE AND CARRIED OUT A PRECAUTIONARY LANDING AT HIGH LEVEL. MAINTENANCE DETERMINED THAT THE EXHAUST VALVE STEM ON #17 CYLINDER HAD FAILED AND SUBSTANTIALLY DAMAGED THE CYLINDER AND BOTH SPARK PLUGS. THE CYLINDER AND PLUGS WERE REPLACED AND THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A98C0145: THE CREW OF AN ONTARIO MINISTRY OF NATURAL RESOURCES, CANADAIR  CL215 6B11 (CL415) AIRCRAFT, C-GBFY, HAD COMPLETED THEIR LAST DROP ON A FIRE IN THE VICINITY OF SIOUX LOOKOUT.  THE AIRCRAFT FLAPS HAD BEEN SET AT 15 DEGREES FOR THE DROP, AND WHEN THE FLAPS WERE RETRACTED, THE FLAP SYSTEM INDICATED THAT THE RIGHT FLAP RETRACTED FULLY, BUT THE LEFT FLAP REMAINED EXTENDED BY APPROXIMATELY 3 DEGREES.  THE CREW USED APPROXIMATELY 50 PERCENT AILERON TRIM TO COUNTER THIS FLAP CONDITION WHILE FLYING AT 100-110 KNOTS.  THE CREW RETURNED TO DRYDEN WHERE THEY CONDUCTED A SUCCESSFUL FLAPLESS LANDING.  THE OPERATOR AND THE AIRCRAFT MANUFACTURER HAVE DETERMINED THAT A FLAP INTERCONNECT CABLE WAS IMPROPERLY ROUTED DURING MANUFACTURE.  THE SUBJECT CABLE FAILED DURING NORMAL OPERATING LOADS.  THE ASYMMETRIC  FLAP SENSING AND LOCK-OUT SYSTEM FUNCTIONED NORMALLY AND THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN FLAP SETTINGS WAS RESTRICTED TO APPROXIMATELY 3 DEGREES.   THE AIRCRAFT MANUFACTURER HAS CONTACTED  OWNERS AND OPERATORS OF THE CL215 6B11 (CL415) MODEL AIRCRAFT AND ADVISED THEM TO INSPECT FOR A SIMILAR CONDITION.  THE IMPROPER FLAP INTERCONNECT CABLE ROUTING HAS NOT BEEN REPORTED ON ANY OTHER AIRCRAFT, TO DATE.  THE MANUFACTURER REPORTS THAT THE MAJORITY OF AIRCRAFT FROM THE PRODUCTION RUN HAVE BEEN INSPECTED AND THERE HAVE BEEN NO REPORTS OF OTHER AIRCRAFT WITH THE IMPROPER CABLE ROUTING.

A98C0154: THE CREW OF A SASKATCHEWAN GOVERNMENT NORTHERN AIR OPERATIONS DEHAVILLAND CS2F-2 TANKER AIRCRAFT, C-GEHP, EXPERIENCED A HOT GENERATOR WARNING FOLLOWED BY A GENERATOR FAIL WARNING.  THEY CONDUCTED A PRECAUTIONARY SHUT-DOWN OF THE AFFECTED ENGINE AND RETURNED TO LA RONGE WHERE THEY ACCOMPLISHED AN UNEVENTFUL LANDING.  COMPANY MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL DETERMINED THAT THE NO.1 GENERATOR HAD FAILED CAUSING THE GENERATOR DRIVE SHAFT TO SHEAR.

A98P0204:    The pilots of the Conair Aviation Ltd. DC-6A (C-FCZZ) experienced a backfire on the number two engine during cruise from High Level, Alberta to Abbotsford.  They performed a scope check which identified  the number twelve cylinder spark plugs were not firing.  The pilots carried out the company mandatory shut down procedures and shut the engine down in flight. The aircraft landed without further incident.  No injuries or damage were reported.Company maintenance replaced the number twelve cylinder spark plugs, ignition leads and coil.  They performed an engine ground run and systems check prior to releasing the aircraft back into service.

A98W0146: The Bell 204B was conducting water bucket operations during forest fire suppression. It was reported that the helicopter collective froze during a water pick-up. The pilot was unable to control power application and the aircraft contacted the water and rolled inverted. The pilot sustained minor injuries.During and after the recovery of the helicopter, the flight control systems were examined. There was no evidence of any binding or jamming of any control rods or cables. The collective hydraulic servo and irreversible valve were recovered and forwarded to the TSB Engineering facility for analysis.

A98P0205:    The pilots of the Conair Aviation Ltd DC-6 (C-GIBS) experienced two backfires on the number 1 engine, shortly after leaning the mixture, during cruise from Abbotsford to Whitehorse.  They selected the mixture to rich, reduced the engine power and performed a scope check which revealed that the spark plugs were operating correctly.  The pilots performed the company mandatory shut down procedures and shut the engine down in flight when the engine backfired a third time.  The aircraft landed without further incident.  No injuries or damaged were reported.Company maintenance found the number five cylinder cracked.  They changed the cylinder and performed engine ground runs and systems checks prior to releasing the aircraft back into service.

A98W0154: THE BELL 212 HELICOPTER WAS ON A TRAINING FLIGHT WITH THE PILOT AND SIX PASSENGERS ON BOARD. WHILE IN A TURN AT 500 AGL THE PILOT EXPERIENCED AN AIRFRAME SHUDDER, THE HELICOPTER WAS LEVELLED, AND THE PILOT NOTED THAT THE TURBINE OUTLET TEMPERATURE ON NO. 1 ENGINE WAS CLIMBING. THE ENGINE WAS SHUT DOWN AND THE HELICOPTER LANDED STRAIGHT AHEAD. THERE WAS NO DAMAGE AND NO INJURIES. THE COMPANY REPORTED A PROBLEM WITH THE COMPRESSOR, AND AN SDR WILL BE SUBMITTED TO TRANSPORT CANADA.

A98P0210:   The pilots of the Conair Aviation Ltd. DC-6 (C-GIBS) noticed a lower than normal BMEP indication on the number 3 engine while in cruise from Kamloops to Abbotsford.  They performed a scope test which revealed the number 5 cylinder spark plugs were not operating.  The pilots carried out the company emergency checklist and shut the engine down.  The aircraft landed without further incident.  No injuries or damage were reported.Company maintenance found the number 5 cylinder on the number 3 engine to be defective.  They changed the cylinder and performed system checks prior to releasing the aircraft back into service.

A98P0217:   The pilot of Conair Aviation Ltd. Firecat (C-FEFK) experienced a rough running number 2 engine during climb-out after a retardant drop.  He carried out the company emergency procedures and shut down the engine.  The aircraft landed without further incident.  No injuries or damage were reported.Company maintenance found an ignition coil to be defective.  They changed the coil and performed maintenance checks prior to releasing the aircraft back into service.

A98P0223:   WHILE ENGAGED IN FIRE-FIGHTING ACTIVITIES, the pilot of the Tundra Helicopters HU-369D (C-GDSI) experienced A LOSS OF engine power AND MAIN ROTOR RPM DECAY while FILLING a water bucket ON A 100-FOOT LONG-LINE from a river.  THE PILOT NOTED BOTH AUDIO AND VISUAL CONFIRMATION OF THE POWER LOSS AND lowered the collective LEVER; ENGINE power AND RRPM THEN RETURNED.The pilot then raised the collective and again experienced a SIMILAR loss of ENGINE power AND RRPM.  He repeated this action a number of times before noting a rhythmic power surge.   The tail of the helicopter swung from side to side during the power changes.  The pilot then experienced violent engine surges.  He attempted to land with the long-line still attached and the bucket in the water.  Approximately 30 feet above the water, the helicopter nosed over when the slack was taken up in the long-line. Just prior to impact, the pilot applied LEFT pedal so that the impact would be on the right side of the helicopter.  The helicopter crashed inTO the river and was washed downstream before GROUNDING in shallow water.  The helicopter was destroyed BUT The PILOT WAS NOT INJURED.Numerous other helicopters were using the same fuel station AROUND THE TIME OF THE ACCIDENT, and there were no reports of FUEL contamination.THE HELICOPTER WAS RECOVERED FROM THE RIVER AND TRANSPORTED TO AN EXAMINATION FACILITY.  An insitu examination of the engine and it's systems did not reveal any deficiencies.  An approved facility conducted bench checks on the fuel control, governor, bleed valve, fuel pump, and fuel nozzle.  ALTHOUGH these components HAD BEEN contaminated by water and sand, they did function and were not identified as contributing to the engine power loss or fluctuations.  The approved facility performed an engine tear down and, although it was contaminated by water and sand, did not discover any deficiencies that could be identified as contributing to the engine power loss or fluctuations.

A98W0170: DURING TAKE-OFF, AT ROTATION, THE CREW OF THE DOUGLAS DC-6A, C-FCZZ EXPERIENCED MAJOR FLUCTUATIONS IN THE BMEP (BRAKE MEAN EFFECTIVE PRESSURE) INDICATOR, AND HEARD A MUFFLED BACKFIRE. AS ALL OTHER INDICATIONS WERE OKAY AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS PERFORMING WELL, THEY CARRIED ON TO THEIR DESTINATION AND CARRIED OUT AN UNEVENTFUL LANDING. MAINTENANCE CHANGED THE IGNITION COIL AND "Y" LEAD ON NO. 18 CYLINDER ON NO. 3 ENGINE. THE AIRCRAFT WAS RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A98C0176: AFTER A WATER PICK-UP IN THE CL215, C-FYXG, THE PILOT NOTICED THE BMEP NEEDLE BOUNCING AND LEFT ENGINE CYLINDER HEAD TEMPERATURE DROPPING OFF TO ZERO. THE ENGINE BACKFIRED AND THE CREW SHUT DOWN THE ENGINE. THE EXHAUST VALVE FAILED ON THE NO.8 CYLINDER AND IS BEING REPLACED.

A98C0180: AFTER RETURNING FROM A FIRE PATROL MISSION, THE PILOT OF THE CESSNA 337,C-GDQU, DID NOT REALIZE THAT THE LANDING GEAR WAS NOT DOWN PROIR TO THE FULL FLAP LANDING. THE POWER SETTING PRIOR TO LANDING WAS REPORTEDLY ABOVE THE SETTING AT WHICH THE LANDING GEAR WARNING HORN IS TRIGGERED. NO INJURIES.

A98A0127: A98A0127: Three Grumman TBM-3 water bombers departed Miramichi enroute to Woodstock to put on a water bombing demonstration.  Approximately 15 minutes into the flight C-GLEK experienced a complete engine failure.  (The pilot reported hearing two loud bangs followed by oil covering the windscreen and a complete power loss)  The pilot of the lead aircraft directed C-GLEK towards a clear cut area, however, because of large stumps in the clear cut, the pilot elected to over-fly the clear cut area and carry out a controlled crash into the trees rather than risk going end-over-end in the clear cut area.  The pilot was able to exit the aircraft by himself but was later taken to the hospital where he was held overnight for observations.The TSB will be attending an engine tear-down and will up-date the summary with the findings.

A98C0185: Saskatchewan Northern Air Operations Bird Dog 5, a Beech B-55 Baron, was in the circuit at La Ronge, SK. On the second landing, the pilot reportedly rounded out higher than normal, then touched down and bounced the aircraft.  On the second touchdown, the aircraft landed on its nosegear first.  The nosegear bent and then broke, and the aircraft came to rest on the runway, on its main gear and its nose.  The aircraft sustained substantial damage to its landing gear, gear doors, engines, propellers, and nose.  The pilot was not physically injured.  The landing gear was examined by company engineers and no pre-existing fault was found.
