A98P0231: The Conair S2P Firecat C-FOPU was 15 miles west of Penticton when the pilot noticed low oil pressure and high oil temperature on the number 1 engine. The pilot immediatly shut the engine down and diverted to Penticton where the engine was removed and replaced with an overhauled unit.

A98Q0138: LE B90 EFFECTUAIT DES ORBITES A 3 000 PIEDS ASL AU-DESSUS D'UN FEU DE FORET QUI SEVISSAIT SUR LE VERSANT DE LA FALAISE QUI BORDE LE FLEUVE ST-LAURENT.  LE PASSAGER, UN <POINTEUR> DE LA SOCIETE DE PROTECTION CONTRE LES FEUX (SOPFEU), ASSIS A DROITE DU PILOTE, A DEMANDE A CE DERNIER DE SURVOLER LES ABORDS DE LA VOIE FERREE SITUEE PRES DU FLEUVE AFIN D'EVALUER LA MENACE POUR LE TRANSPORT FERROVIAIRE QUE POUVAIT REPRESENTER L'INCENDIE. LE PILOTE S'EST ELOIGNE VERS LE FLEUVE ET A DESCENDU A 500 PIEDS ASL AVANT DE SUIVRE AU-DESSUS DE L'EAU LE CHEMIN DE FER EN DIRECTION OUEST.  IL AVAIT L'INTENTION D'EFFECTUER UN VIRAGE A DROITE POUR PERMETTRE AU PASSAGER DE MIEUX OBSERVER LE SECTEUR.  LES VOLETS ETAIENT RENTRES ET LA VITESSE ETAIT 160 NOEUDS.  PENDANT LE VIRAGE, LE PILOTE A JUGE QU'IL N'Y AVAIT PAS ASSEZ D'ESPACE ENTRE LE RELIEF ASCENDANT ET L'APPAREIL POUR COMPLETER LA MANOEUVRE.  APRES AVOIR CONCLU QUE SA MARGE DE MANOEUVRE ETAIT SUFFISAMMENT REDUITE POUR QU'UN DEMI-TOUR FASSE DECROCHER L'AVION LORS DU VIRAGE, IL A DECIDE DE TENTER DE FRANCHIR LA CRETE DROIT DEVANT.  A CETTE FIN, IL A MIS PLEIN GAZ PUIS A AFFICHE LA VITESSE QUI PERMETTAIT LA MEILLEURE PENTE DE MONTEE.  L'AILE DROITE A HEURTE UN ARBRE A ENVIRON 400 PIEDS DU SOMMET.  LE PILOTE A ALORS CABRE L'APPAREIL AFIN DE REDUIRE LES FORCES DE DECELERATION.  UN INCENDIE A ECLATE PEU DE TEMPS APRES LA COLLISION AVEC LE SOL.  LE PILOTE A DU DETACHER ET TIRER LE PASSAGER INCONSCIENT HORS DE LA CABINE.  LES OCCUPANTS ONT EVACUE L'AERONEF PAR LA PORTE PRINCIPALE SANS AUTRE PROBLEME.  LE VENT SOUFFLAIT DU SUD-OUEST A 15 NOEUDS ET LA VISIBILITE ETAIT PLUS DE 15 MILLES.  LE PILOTE N'A RAPPORTE AUCUNE ANOMALIE OU DEFAILLANCE.

A98C0188: WHILE LANDING IN A CONFINED AREA DURING FOREST-FIRE OPERATIONS, THE TAILROTOR OF THE B-204B, C-GEAI, CONTACTED TREES. DAMAGE WAS LIMITED TO THE TAIL ROTOR AND TAIL ROTOR DRIVE AREA WITH REPORTEDLY NO EXTERNAL DAMAGE. tHERE WERE NO INJURIES.

A98W0181: THE AEROSPATIALE AS 350B (HELICOPTER) WAS ON APPROACH TO LAND AT A FIRE CAMP AND AT APPROXIMATELY 20 FEET AGL CONTROL WAS LOST. THE HELICOPTER CAME TO REST ON ITS SIDE, AND THE TAIL BOOM SEPARATED. THE PILOT AND PASSENGERS (5) WERE MEDI-VACED TO THE SLAVE LAKE HOSPITAL FOR TREATMENT AND OBSERVATION, (ONE PASSENGER SUFFERED SERIOUS INJURIES).INVESTIGATORS HAVE BEEN DISPATCHED TO THE SCENE.

A98C0190: The Northern Air Operations CL215, C-FAFO, was engaged in fire fighting operations. After a water pick-up the crew observed abnormal instrument readings from the left engine and then smoke and oil emanating from the top of the left engine cowling. The crew shut the engine down as a precautionary measure and returned to La Ronge, SK. Maintenance found a cracked cylinder on the left engine.

A98P0248: The Bell 212 helicopter pilot was delivering fuel barrels on a 50-foot long line to a site near a tractor. During the manoeuvre, he inadvertently swung the tail rotor into nearby trees, causing substantial damage to the tail rotor blades. The damage was not immediately obvious to the pilot; however, he noted a vibration after he had delivered the load an was enroute to Mica Creek. He landed there without further incident.

A99P0005:  The Air Canada A-340 (C-FYLU / ACA896) had just began the take-off roll on runway 08R at Vancouver International Airport, when at about 80 knots, the pilots received a warning light in the cockpit, indicating that a refuelling panel/door was open.  The pilots aborted the take-off below 100 knots; the pilot intentionally decelerated the aircraft slowly, using the all the remaining runway before vacating it at the far end at taxiway "D5".The pilots then stopped the aircraft on taxiway "D".  At that time, two airport fire trucks were returning along taxiway "D" to the fire hall after training exercises, and when they passed alongside the stationary aircraft, the fire crews saw smoke and flames coming from the right main landing gear.  Moments later, they saw flames from the left landing gear.They quickly approached that aircraft and commenced to spray the wheel assemblies with water; the fires were extinguished in seconds. The fire crew, however, were not able to communicate directly with the flight crew to inform them of the fire, but a Vancouver International Airport Authority supervisor arrived and began to speak to the pilots using the ground intercom system.  At the same time the flight crew were talking to their company and the Vancouver ground control, and were not aware of the fires, until the VIAA supervisor spoke to them.After a 15-minute monitoring period by ERS to ensure the gear assemblies were safe for the aircraft to continue moving, the aircraft was towed to the gate with the passengers on board.The aircraft was later towed to the company maintenance facility for inspection.  No fire damage or defect was found.  It is likely that the long roll-out after the RTO contributed to the brake overheat condition.  The operator reports that the refuelling panel/door had not been latched properly at the last refuelling.  More information to follow.

A99Q0066: L'équipage du CL215, effectuait un vol d'entraînement. Pour fin d'exercice, l'hélice du moteur droit avait été mise en drapeau (feather). Lors de la tentative de dévirer l'hélice (unfeathering) une défectuosité du sélecteur de dévirage (unfeathering switch ) empêcha l'hélice de quitter la position drapeau. L'équipage était donc dans l'impossibilité de redémarrer le moteur. L'équipage a procédé à la liste de vérification et déclaré une urgence auprès du service du contrôle de la circulation aérienne. L'aéronef s'est posé sans difficulté à l'aéroport Int'l Jean Lesage. Le service d'entretien a remplacé le sélecteur de dévirage (unfeathering switch) et après avoir complété un point fixe (run up) pour fin de vérification, l'appareil a été remis en service.

A99A0061: The TBM aircraft was working out of the Brockway, NB Airport fighting a forest fire in the vicinity of Lawrence Station, NB. When the pilot reduced power to the cruise power setting, after climbing out from dropping a load on the fire, the engine stopped. The aircraft was substantially damaged during the forced landing in a clear cut area, the pilot sustained minor injuries. An examination of the engine was carried out and no pre-impact mechanical discrepancies were found that could have caused the engine to stop.  The magneto drive shaft was spun by hand and both magnetos fired normally. The magneto switch was tested and found to function normally.  An examination of the aircraft fuel system did not reveal any discrepancies.  The carburetor was sent to an overhaul facility for examination and testing and no discrepancies were found that would have caused the engine to stop.

A99C0089: TANKER 252, A CANADAIR CL-215, WAS ON APPROACH AT WINNIPEG AFTER FIRE-SUPPRESSION ACTVITIES IN THE MANIGOTAGAN AREA.  WHEN THE CREW SELECTED THE LANDING GEAR DOWN, A WARNING HORN SOUNDED AND THE GEAR DID NOT INDICATE DOWN AND LOCKED.  THE CREW PULLED UP AND FLEW TO THE PRACTISE AREA, AND THE CREW CONSULTED COMPANY MAINTENANCE.  THE CREW THEN RETURNED TO WINNIPEG AND LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT, WITH ERS STANDING BY.  MAINTENANCE FOUND THAT THE LEFT LANDING GEAR WIRING HAD BEEN PINCHED BY THE CAM ROLLER HOUSING, WHICH HAD LED TO AN UNSAFE GEAR INDICATION.  THE WIRING HARNESS WAS RE-ALIGNED AND THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED TO SERVICE.

A99Q0091L'équipage du CL-215 immatriculé C-GFQB effectuait un vol dans le cadre d'une intervention de feux de forêts. Lors de la montée initiale, suite à un écopage, l'équipage a ressenti une vibration. L'équipage a donc discontinué l'écope et pris de l'altitude. À ce moment, l'équipage a remarqué une baisse de puissance sur le moteur droit et a arrêté le moteur en plaçant l'hélice en position drapeau. Toutefois, une des pales ne s'est pas positionnée en  drapeau. L'équipage a effectué la liste de vérification et l'appareil s est posé sans difficulté à l'aéroport de La Tuque. Aucune urgence n'a été déclarée.Le service d'entretien a constaté que la rondelle de butée du chanfrein (Bevel Thrust washer) était défectueuse, ce qui empêchait la pale de l'hélice à se positionner en drapeau. L'hélice a été changée et l'appareil a été remis en service. L'hélice défectueuse a été envoyée chez BL Aviation pour une révision. Un SDR a été émis à l'intention de Transports Canada.

A99C0097: THE MANITOBA GOVERNMENT AIR SERVICES CANADAIR CL215 WATER BOMBER, C-GUMW, DEPARTED THUNDER BAY EN ROUTE TO ITS HOME BASE AT GIMLI, MB.  SHORTLY AFTER TAKEOFF, THE CREW FELT A SLIGHT VIBRATION, AND NOTED THAT THE BMEP (POWER OUTPUT) OF THE RIGHT ENGINE HAD DECLINED.  THE CREW DIVERTED THE FLIGHT BACK TO THUNDER BAY, WHERE THEY LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.  MAINTENANCE FOUND A CRACKED CYLINDER IN THE BACK ROW OF THE ENGINE.  THE CREW REPORTED THAT THE ENGINE HAD FUNCTIONED NORMALLY DURING THE PRE-TAKEOFF RUNUP.

A99W0096: THE BELL 204B WAS ENGAGED IN FOREST FIRE SUPPRESSION. WHILE TRANSITING FROM THE WATER PICKUP AREA WITH A FULL BUCKET TO THE DROP ZONE, THE CAST ALUMINUM TOP OF THE WATER BUCKET FAILED, AND DROPPED THE BUCKET OFF INTO THE BUSH. THE HELICOPTER RETURNED TO BASE AND LANDED WITHOUT INCIDENT. THE BUCKET WAS RECOVERED BY A LOCAL RESIDENT AND IS BEING EXAMINED AND REPAIRED.  MORE INFORMATION WHEN AVAILABLE.

A99W0095: THE PILOT HAD ENTERED A HOVER ON THE FORESTRY PAD LOCATED ON THE EDGE OF A LAKE. AS HE ATTEMPTED TO BACK OUT AND TURN RIGHT, THE BELL 206 HELICOPTER DRIFTED INTO TREES ON THE NORTH SIDE OF THE PAD. THE PILOT ALLOWED THE HELICOPTER TO SETTLE INTO THE WATER. A PASSENGER ATTEMPTED TO EXIT ON THE RIGHT SIDE, AND THE PILOT ROLLED THE HELICOPTER ON ITS LEFT SIDE. ALL THE OCCUPANTS EXITED WITHOUT INJURY. THE HELICOPTER CAME TO REST IN FOUR FEET OF WATER ON ITS LEFT SIDE.

A99C0127: The helicopter was on the second flight of the day, flying contract missions for the Fire Management and Forest Protection Branch of the Province of Saskatchewan. The pilot was bucketing hot spots on a fire that was almost out. The pace was leisurely and pilots in the area were picking their own targets. The pilot of the S55B/T was making right-hand circuits from the fire line to a nearby lake. He estimated that he had dumped 10 to 15 buckets on the fire when he returned to a bay in the lake to charge the bucket for the next drop. The bucket was in the water, suspended on a 20-foot line below the helicopter. The pilot had moved the helicopter off to the side and had his head out the side window to watch the progress of the fill, and he was not in a position to monitor the engine gauges.While hovering 10 to 15 feet above the water's surface, with the throttle in the full-open position, the pilot heard the engine begin to spool down. He did not have time to tell if the engine had stopped completely or if it had decelerated to flight idle, but it was apparent that the helicopter would not maintain its altitude. The pilot pulled the collective to arrest the descent, and then rolled the throttle off in an attempt to reduce the main rotor revolutions per minute (rpm). He did not have time to pull the fuel shut-off or to pull the rotor brake before the helicopter struck the water. The helicopter settled onto its left side, and the main rotor blades were substantially damaged. When it was apparent that the helicopter was sinking, the pilot departed the helicopter and swam to the nearest shoreline. He did not think to reach for his life jacket that was stored overhead in the cockpit of the helicopter. The pilot, who was wearing his helmet, suffered a blow to the head during the occurrence and experienced some soreness in his neck afterwards.

A99P0070:   The Bell 206 Helicopter (C-FBQG) was manouvering above a steep hill side in support of a heli-logging operation, when the Chokers attached to the end of the external load Longline became snagged on a large log.  Witnesses reported that the helicopter reached extreme pitch attitudes before the Chokers released.  The Longline subsequently snagged another log.  The pilot appeared to lose control of the helicopter and experienced Dynamic Roll Over while attached to the ground by the Longline/external load. The Helicopter struck the ground, rolled over, and came to rest, held up by the Longline, on the hill side .  Ground crews reached the aircraft in time to temporarily put out a post-crash fire with the aircraft fire extinguisher, however a second fire ensued.  Without other appropriate fire fighting equipment, the ground crew were forced to quickly extricate the trapped pilot.  The fire consumed the aircraft, but was extinguished by a company helicopter (S61) which later transported the injured pilot to the Hope, B.C. hospital.  The pilot, who was wearing a helmet, received serious injuries to his right arm and torso.  His helmet displayed extensive impact damage and likely prevented serious head injuries. Preliminary information revealed no mechanical failure of the helicopter prior to impact.   NMH report:REPORT 99091A   07/27/99 		(Preliminary prepared 07/12/99)JUNE 18, 1999BELL 206B-IIC-FBQGHELI-LOGGING SUPPORTBOSTON BAR B.C. AREAComplete pilot records are available from the Flight Training department. Total time approximately 2,400 hours, total time on type - 500 hours, long line training (1998) - .6 hours, long line experience - 50 hours. At 17:10 on June 18, 1999 helicopter C-FBQG crashed while conducting support activities for a Sikorsky SK-61 Heli-logging operation near Boston Bar B.C. The crash site was at approximately 3000ASL, and the temp was 20C.  The exposure of the impact sight (slope) was westerly and while the winds were variable the interviews indicate they were upslope at about 20knots.  There were no passengers on board the helicopter at the time, the pilot sustained multiple injuries (serious) and the aircraft was destroyed in a post impact fire.At the time of the mishap the pilot was in the process of delivering bundles of chokers to the riggers on the hill.BACKGROUNDAlthough the pilot had been working in support of this particular heli-logging operation since May 30 1999, this was the first day that he was required to fly close support for the SK-61. Previously his activities involved crew set outs and pickups of both fallers and riggers, and limited longline delivery of choker bundles. On this particular day, the logging had shifted to a block that was much closer to the log delivery landing and therefore required a more continuous supply of choker delivery to the riggers. At the time of the mishap the SK-61 had just finished refueling at the service landing and was heading back up the hill, and the Bell 206 was delivering the last three bundles of chokers (for the day) to the riggers. There was one-half of a logging cycle (35 minutes) left to be completed that day.OCCURRENCEOf the three riggers working in the area of the accident, two had received their choker deliveries. The helicopter was bringing a bundle for the third rigger, and had two more hooked to the carousel for riggers on an adjacent block. As the helicopter arrived at the site the third rigger was getting a drink of water from his packsack. As he turned back he noticed the helicopter appeared to be sitting in a vertical hover, with the bundles resting on the ground, downslope from his ribbon stick (target for choker delivery). The helicopter was facing the slope as if the pilot was trying to locate the rigger or ribbon stick. A brief radio conversation occurred advising the pilot where the target was and the pilot acknowledged that he now had a visual confirmation. The rigger indicated during the post accident interview, that at that point the helicopter seemed to start nosing over and turning to the right as if the aircraft was going to move the choker bundles in that direction. As this movement began the aircraft rapidly pitched nose down and began a downward arc. It was later found that the bundles had not cleared the hill. The stringers used to attach the bundles to the carousel hooks had become caught between two large logs. See Investigation photographs included with this report.  As the aircraft continued in this downward arc it also rotated to the right 180 degrees (around the mast) until it was facing back up the longline, in a pronounced nose up, tail down attitude.The aircraft seemed to hang in this position, and was described as fluttering, wobbling, or waffling. After only a matter of seconds the aircraft seemed to launch over backwards, turning to the left while doing so, and impacted the slope in a nose down, left yawing manner. At this point the rigger who had virtually been looking thru the pilot's door, dove for cover as blades and other items began to be thrown in all directions.Investigation found that of the three carousel hooks being used at the time, one appears to have released, another was damaged and the stringer nubbin would have been released, and the third was actually ripped off of the carousel.When the noise of the impact subsided, the rigger radioed there was an aircraft down and he needed help. This call was the activation mechanism of the Heli-log Emergency Response Plan. He then ran downslope to the aircraft, which was resting on its left side, being held there by the longline, which was still attached to the helicopter (the carousel was caught in logs further upslope). See photographs.POST IMPACT The pilot was still restrained by the seatbelt and shoulder harness and did not appear to be conscious. The rigger began to check the pilot for a determination of injuries and was joined at that time by the other two riggers. At this point it was noted that there were flames visible around the turbine outlet area. One rigger directed the aircraft's Halon Fire Extinguisher at the flames while the second turned off the fuel valve itself. Due to the fact that the instrument panel had been torn back and to the right it is difficult to know whether this action had any effect. The three riggers began to administer first aid to the pilot who was starting to regain consciousness.A Supervisor, Maintenance Engineer, and another First Aid Attendant arrived at the site with the spine board and Level 3 First Aid Kit. It was noted that flames were again visible, not only from around the turbine area but also spreading to the hillside itself. The fire extinguisher was again directed at the flames but found to be exhausted and was of no further use. A decision was then made to immediately remove the pilot from the wreckage due to the increasing danger of fire and/or explosion. This was accomplished and the pilot was moved some 30 feet across the 60% slope where first aid was continued and attachment to the spine board carried out. Due to the increasing heat from the fire, a radio call went out for the SK-61 to bring it's Bambi Bucket and drop some water onto the fire.When the SK-61 arrived the injured pilot had been moved another 30 feet across slope and was being shielded from the fire and water by a large log and the crewmembers themselves. Two water drops were made which reduced the flame and heat substantially and the SK-61 returned to the service landing to reattach the longline and Emergency Stretcher Slinging Gear. Upon it's return the pilot and spine board were secured in the Ferno Stretcher and slung some 200 yards further up the hill to a landing where the ambulance and a number of vehicles were located. The First Aid attendants continued to stabilize the pilot for further transportation while the SK-61 returned to the service landing to drop the long line and install floorboards. Upon it's return, the injured pilot was then loaded internally into the SK-61 which then departed for the Fraser Canyon Hospital in Hope BC.  All persons involved in the emergency response, whether it be on the hill, in the SK-61, or back at the service landing did a commendable job under very adverse conditions and this cumulative action no doubt lead to the survival of the pilot. Only one and one-half hours had elapsed from the time of impact until the time of admittance to the Hospital in Hope. Due to complications involving internal injuries the pilot was transferred later that evening to the Chilliwack General Hospital where he underwent seven hours of surgery.Compound fractures to the right arm above and below the elbow were the most obvious injuries, however the rupture of the diaphragm combined with the resultant intrusion of various internal organs proved to be the most serious, and life threatening injury.

A99W0113: WHILE IN CRUISE FLIGHT AT 3 500 FT ASL THE PILOT OF THE BELL 205 OBSERVED A HELICOPTER APPROACHING FROM THE FOUR O'CLOCK POSITION. THE PILOT PULLED UP AND A BELL 206 PASSED UNDERNEATH. THE BELL 206 WAS OBSERVED TO BE C-GQKU, OWNED BY ULTRA  HELI. LTD. THE RADIO FREQUENCY WAS REPORTED TO BE BUSY AT THE TIME OF THE OCCURRENCE.

A99W0111: THE PILOT OF THE BRITTEN-NORMAN ISLANDER BN-2A-9, C-FTAM, WAS EN ROUTE TO FORT MCMURRAY, AB WHEN HE DECIDED TO STOP AT A WINTER STRIP TO PICK UP SOME COMPANY MATERIAL THAT HAD PREVIOUSLY BEEN LEFT BEHIND. THE STRIP WAS DRAGGED TWICE SUCCESSFULLY TO DETERMINE IF THE SURFACE WAS FIRM ENOUGH FOR A LANDING.  ON THE THIRD APPROACH, A LANDING WAS CARRIED OUT, AND AFTER A GROUND ROLL OF ABOUT 75 TO 100 FEET THE NOSE WHEEL SUNK INTO THE SOFT SURFACE AND WAS BENT BACKWARDS. THE AIRCRAFT CAME TO A STOP, SUBSTANTIALLY DAMAGED. THERE WERE NO INJURIES TO THE PILOT.

A99W0114: WHILE IN CRUISE FLIGHT EN ROUTE TO A FIRE CAMP, THE PILOT OF THE BELL 204B HELICOPTER DETERMINED THAT A LOSS OF ANTI-TORQUE PEDAL OPERATION HAD OCCURRED. THE PILOT ASSESSED THE LOW SPEED CONTROLLABILITY OF THE HELICOPTER AND THEN DECLARED AN EMERGENCY. A RUN-ON LANDING WAS CONDUCTED ON A GRAVEL LEASE ROAD, WITH FIRE FIGHTING, MEDICAL EQUIPMENT, AND PERSONNEL IN PLACE. THE HELICOPTER CAME TO REST NEAR THE LEFT SHOULDER OF THE ROAD, AND THE PASSENGER RAPIDLY DEPLANED WITHOUT INJURY. THE OPERATOR REPORTS THAT THE FAILURE WAS A RESULT OF SEPARATION OF THE PITCH CHANGE SHAFT IN THE TAIL ROTOR ASSEMBLY. AN SDR WILL BE SUBMITTED TO TRANSPORT CANADA.

A99C0170: THE PILOT OF THE BELL 204B, C-GSHB, WAS ARRIVING AT A FIRE CAMP IN THE VICINITY OF CROSS LAKE, MB, TO PICK UP FIREFIGHTERS AT A NEWLY-CONSTRUCTED PAD.  THE PILOT MANEUVERED TO AVOID AN AREA CONTAINING PEOPLE, AND HAD DIFFICULTY IN MAINTAINING SIGHT OF THE PAD. JUST BEFORE TOUCHDOWN, THE TAIL ROTOR OF THE HELICOPTER STRUCK A TREE BRANCH, WHICH HAD NOT BEEN VISIBLE TO THE PILOT ON APPROACH TO THE SITE.  THE PILOT LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT, AND INSPECTED THE AIRCRAFT.  THE PILOT REPORTEDLY CONSIDERED THE AIRCRAFT SAFE FOR A FERRY FLIGHT AND FLEW THE AIRCRAFT TO NORWAY HOUSE WITH NO PASSENGERS.  ENGINEERS THERE FOUND DAMAGE TO THE TAIL ROTOR.  THEY REPLACED THE TAIL ROTOR, DRIVESHAFT AND ASSOCIATED GEAR BOXES IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE BELL REPAIR SCHEDULE.THE ACCIDENT WAS REPORTED ON 21 JULY 1999.  COMPANY OFFICIALS ADVISED THAT PERSONNELL INVOLVED WITH THE OCCURRENCE HAD BEEN INVOLVED WITH FIRE WORK IN THE FIELD AND HAD FOUND IT DIFFICULT TO REPORT THE OCCURRENCE AT AN EARLIER DATE.

A99W0126: The pilot of the Bell 212 Helicopter was conducting fire suppression. While descending vertically to a small pond and as the bucket entered the water, the helicopter began to settle with power. The pilot attempted to recover by pushing the nose forward to gain airspeed. In doing so, the bambi bucket, which was attached by a 100 foot long line, entered the water. As the bucket rolled forward and filled it acted as an anchor point on the long line. The helicopter settled into small trees at the edge of the pond. The low rotor warning horn sounded just as the helicopter touched down. On touch down the main rotor blades contacted trees. Debries from the trees struck the helicopter and broke some of the side windows and the windshield. The helicopter was substantially damaged; the pilot, who was wearing a helmet, was not injured.The weather was; temperature-24 deg C, wind - light and veriable, visibility - 10 miles in haze and smoke, density altitude - 2300 ft.The pilot had flown for 7.3 hours on the day of the occurrence and had been working 12 hour duty days. On the prior two duty days he had flown 9.2 hours. His last day off was 8 days ago. He reported that he was well rested and that he had not experienced any problems with the helicopter. His last fuelling of the helicopter was about 25 minutes before the accident. He had fuelled to about 1100 pounds and estimated that he had 800 pounds of fuel remaining at ground impact.

A99W0131: THE BELL 204B HELICOPTER WAS BEING HOT REFUELLED WHEN A FIRE STARTED. THE PILOT SHUTDOWN THE ENGINE AND EXITED THE HELICOPTER AND ESCAPED WITHOUT INJURY. A DRY CHEMICAL FIRE EXTINGUISHER AND WATER WERE USED TO CONTROL AND EXTINGUISH THE FIRE. THE HELICOPTER HAD BEEN GROUNDED PRIOR TO COMMENCING THE REFUELLING. IT WAS REPORTED THAT THE FUELLER INADVERTENTLY LIFTED THE NOZZLE AND FUEL SPRAYED INTO THE ENGINE INTAKE. THERE WERE NO INJURIES BUT THE HELICOPTER WAS SUBSTANTIALLY FIRE DAMAGED.

A99W0133: The loaded McDonnell Douglas A26B was on the takeoff roll departing Fort McMurray for a fire about 60 miles N. Prior to liftoff, the crew noticed electrical arcing behind the instrument panel and smelled smoke. The electrical system was shut down, and the takeoff continued until the aircraft had attained sufficient altitude that the load could be dumped. The crew turned the electrical system on, declared an emergency, and landed without incident. Maintenance has advised that a wire had chafed behind the instrument panel, and was arcing onto an instrument case. Further information to follow when maintenance has determined which wire had shorted, and an SDR will be submitted to Transport Canada.

A99C0177: The pilot of a Bell 205A was coming in to pick up his second bucket of water. It was reported the water was very glassy and the helicopter came in a little too fast. The tail rotor struck the water disabling the tail rotor system. When the helicopter leveled off the tail rotor came out of the water and it started an uncommanded yaw to the right. The pilot reduced power and then set the helicopter on the water where it rolled onto its right side. The pilot escaped without injury. The aircraft sustained substantial damage.

A99Q0141: L'équipage du CL215 effectuait le démarrage du moteur gauche afin de repositionner l'aéronef sur l'aire de trafic. Pendant le démarrage, l'équipage a été avisé par le personnel au sol qu'il y avait un retour de flammes dans le moteur. La procédure de démarrage a été complétée tel que requis selon la procédure d'urgence . Après avoir complété le démarrage, le personnel au sol a avisé l'équipage que tout semblait normal. Une fois l'appareil repositionné sur l'aire de trafic, le moteur a été arrêté. Cinq minutes plus tard un fumée noire sortait de l'échappement du générateur. Le personnel au sol a utilisé un extincteur afin de combattre l'incendie. Selon le personnel d'entretien, le feu s'est déclaré suite à une fracture du corps de la pompe d'accélération  occasionnant une  fuite de carburant à l'intérieur de la section accessoire du moteur. Le carburateur et plusieurs lignes d'alimentation en carburant ont été changées ainsi que le harnais électrique des instruments moteurs. Un SDR sera émis.

A99C0172: The De Havilland CS2F-2, C-GEQD, was inbound to Prince Albert on a fire-control flight when the the pilot received a fire indication on the right engine. The fire bottle was discharged and the right engine was shut down. The aircraft landed safely and was able to clear the runway onto to a taxi ramp. It was then towed away. Further inspection by maintenance staff revealed that there was no fire and that a faulty wiring harnesss set off the alarm.

A99W0151: WHILE CONDUCTING A WATER PICK UP ON AGNES LAKE, THE CREW EXPERIENCED A FIRE WARNING FOR THE NO.1 ENGINE. THE PILOT SHUT DOWN THE ENGINE AND CAME TO A STOP IN THE WATER. THE FIRE EXTINGUISHED ITSELF. EXAMINATION DETERMINED THAT AN EXHAUST STACK ON THE NO.1 P&W R-2800 ENGINE HAD DETACHED AND ALLOWED HOT EXHAUST GASSES TO MELT A PUSH-ROD COVER RESULTING IN OIL LEAKAGE AND THE SUBSEQUENT FIRE.

A99P0106:   THE BELL 206B C-FPOC WAS PICKING UP WATER FROM A LAKE/SWAMP WHEN IT LOST POWER.  THE PILOT MANAGED TO LAND THE HELICOPTER ON AN OLD BEAVER DAM. HOWEVER BEFORE THE MAIN ROTOR BLADES HAD COME TO A COMPLETE STOP, THE HELICOPTER ROLLED ON TO IT'S RIGHT SIDE, SLID BACKWARDS AND INTO THE LAKE.THE PILOT GOT OUT AND HELD ON TO THE H.F. ANTENNA, TRYING TO KEEP THE HELICOPTER FROM SLIDING FURTHER INTO THE LAKE, BUT AS THE HELICOPTER FILLED UP WITH WATER THE ANTENNA BROKE OFF AND IT SUNK OUT OF SIGHT.

A99C0216: The Athabaska Airways Bell206B, C-GCNC, was landing on a road intersection to refuel about 50 metres from the helicopter pad at Uranium City, SK. The pad was occupied by other helicopters. The pilot had been assigned the intersection several times before and was aware of powerlines close to the landing point. The pilot did not see an unused telephone line and a wire-strike occurred while the pilot was manoeuvring to position near the refuelling point. Replacement of the vertical fin, tail rotor blades, tail rotor drive shaft and free-wheeling unit were required.

A99C0208: THE SOWIND AIR PIPER PA-31-350, C-GHMK, WAS EN ROUTE FROM ST. ANDREWS, MB, TO BERENS RIVER.  ABOUT 40 NM SOUTH OF BERENS RIVER, THE PILOT NOTED A NOISE AND YAW FROM THE LEFT ENGINE. THE ENGINE LOST POWER, SMOKE WAS OBSERVED, AND THE COWLING WAS DISRUPTED.  THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO SECURE THE ENGINE, BUT WAS NOT ABLE TO FEATHER THE PROPELLER.  THE PILOT COMPLETED A FORCED LANDING ABOUT FIVE NM NORTH OF PRINCESS HARBOUR.  AFTER LANDING, THE NINE PASSENGERS AND ONE INFANT DEPARTED THE AIRCRAFT VIA THE EMERGENCY EXIT. THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO EXTINGUISH THE FIRE IN THE LEFT ENGINE WITH THE HAND-HELD FIRE EXTINGUISHER, BUT WAS NOT SUCCESSFUL, AND THE FIRE CONSUMED THE AIRCRAFT FORWARD OF THE HORIZONTAL TAIL.  THE FIRE WAS SUBSEQUENTLY EXTINGUISHED BY A WATER BOMBER OPERATING IN THE AREA. EXAMINATION OF THE AIRCRAFT REVEALED THAT THE #2 CYLINDER OF THE LEFT ENGINE HAD DEPARTED THE ENGINE CASE.

A99C0224: The pilot of a Bell 204B helicopter, C-GVVI, was hauling netted loads in the vicinity of Trout Lake, Ontario.  On the second load, the pilot lifted off and had travelled approximately 2 miles from his take-off point, when the load detached from the helicopter cargo hook.  The cargo net dropped to the ground damaging the fire-fighting equipment contained therein.  The cargo release controls involve two switches on the cyclic control for the machine and both switches must be simultaneously activated to release the load.  The pilot reported that he did not activate the cargo release switches and he did not have his hand on the cyclic in a manner that would have caused inadvertent activation of the switches. The person who was hooking the load to the helicopter reported that he employed the normal procedure of pulling back on the lanyard in an attempt to confirm that the load was properly secured in the hook. After the flight, the cargo hook was inspected and found to be in an open condition. Company maintenance personnel completed functional testing of the cargo hook and its electrical control mechanism and they found that the hook functioned normally in all respects.  The helicopter was returned to service and has been operating in the sling-load role without further problems.

operation: AIR TRANSPORT; FIRE FIGHTING / FIRE MANAGEMENT
Summary: A99C0244: A loss of separation occurred approximately 18 miles west of Wawa, Ontario.  Both aircraft were in radio contact with the Winnipeg Marathon-Sector controller in Winnipeg. The first aircraft, a CL215T, was southeast bound on V13, was level at 5 thousand, and had reported by Marathon, Ontario at 1642Z. At that same time, 1642Z, a C208 aircraft was cleared to depart and fly direct to Manitouwadge, Ontario at 4 thousand. The Superior controller released control of the C208 to Winnipeg Marathon Sector at the time the departure information was forwarded to Winnipeg. At 1629Z the pilot of the C208 contacted the Marathon controller and advised that she was level at 4 thousand.  Two minutes later she requested 6 thousand. The Marathon controller asked the pilot of the C208 to report her DME reading from Wawa.  The pilot indicated sixteen DME but the Marathon controller mistakenly heard fifty-six. He asked for a repeat. Once again the reply was sixteen but the controller still believed the pilot had said fifty-six. The controller requested a similar DME from the pilot of the CL215T aircraft and the response was 49 miles.  The controller believed the two aircraft had passed each other and the were tail to tail by more than 7 miles and he cleared the C208 to maintain 6 thousand. At 1636Z the pilot of the C208 reported level at 6 thousand. Neither aircraft were in radar coverage at the time. At 1647Z the C208 requested and was granted permission for descent into Manitouwadge and it was at this time that a corresponding radar target appeared on the radar screen at the Marathon sector.  The controller was surprised by the position of the aircraft on his screen and after he queried the pilot about the original DME report he realized an error had been made. He reported the situation to the supervisor. At the time the pilot of the C208 reported reaching 6 thousand it is estimated that aircraft was 28 miles northwest of Wawa and the CL215T was 36 miles northwest.  The two aircraft were estimated to have been laterally separated by 12 miles.The separation requirement with both aircraft on reciprocal track requires that a separation in altitude of not less than 1,000 feet is assured until both aircraft are past the same DME point plus 5 miles and the departing aircraft must be more than 15 miles  from the navigation aid providing the DME information.

A00Q0063: Le Cessna 182R était sur un contrat de patrouille de feu. La SOPFEU avait demandé au pilote d'aller vérifier, sans se poser, la condition d'une piste non utilisée depuis quelques années. Le pilote a effectué une passe et l'aile gauche a heurté la cime d'un arbre. Le pilote a été en mesure de revenir jusqu'à sa base de Val D'or où les dommages structuraux à l'aile ont été constatés par l'équipe de maintenance.

A00W0103: WHILE CONDUCTING FIRE FIGHTING TRAINING THE PILOT EXPERIENCED LOSS OF THE SLUNG LOAD (BAMBI BUCKET - EMPTY) IN FLIGHT. EXAMINATION OF THE HOOK AND RELEASE SWITCH AND WIRING DID NOT DETERMINE A CAUSE FOR THE SEPARATION. THE OPERATOR BELIEVES THAT IN FORWARD FLIGHT THE TWISTING OF THE BUCKET CAUSED THE HOOK KEEPER TO BE FORCED UP, ALLOWING THE BUCKET TO COME OFF THE LOAD BEAM.

A00C0112: The crew of a Manitoba Government Air CL215, C-FTUV, were conducting their 9th scoop from the surface of a river. They had just completed their second power reduction when they heard a backfire and noticed a BMEP split.  After confirming that the problem was with the right engine(Pratt & Whitney R-2800 -CA3), the crew maintained both engines at normal cruise power as they flew to Thompson where they landed safely at 1942Z.  Company maintenance personnel found that the N0-13 cylinder on the right engine had failed causing the backfire and BMEP split.  The cylinder was replaced and the aircraft was returned to service without further difficulty.

A00W0112: The helicopter, C-GLVJ was being used for fire fighting activities. While hovering for a landing in an unprepared helipad the main rotor contacted a pine tree located in about the pilot's eight o'clock position. The pilot immediately departed and landed in a larger are to inspect the damage. One main rotor blade was damaged. The blade was replaced and the helicopter was returned to service.

A00C0115: The pilot of a Province of Saskatchewan Northern Air Operations Tracker (TKR6), C-GEQE, was returning to land at Prince Albert with the right engine (Wright Cyclone 1820-86A) shut down.  While enroute to a fire, the aircraft developed a vibration and the right engine oil pressure was observed to be dropping.  The pilot advised that he had shut down one engine and that he would be returning to land at Prince Albert.  Another Tracker (TKR5), C-GEQD, had  also suffered an engine failure and was landing with one engine out.  The pilot of C-GEQE had to circle on one engine while arrangements were made to access and tow C-GEQD from the runway.  C-GEQE landed safely at 2147Z.  Company maintenance personnel determined that the No-1 cylinder had failed and metal-contaminated  the right engine for C-GEQE.  The engine is being replaced.

A00C0114: The pilot of a Province of Saskatchewan Northern Air Operations Tracker (TKR5), C-GEQD, was 30 miles northeast of Prince Albert when the left engine (Wright Cyclone 1820-86A) produced a series of loud bangs.  The pilot confirmed that the problem was with the left engine and he shut it down.  He then advised that he would be returning to land at Prince Albert.  The CFR responded and the aircraft landed safely at 21:32Z on runway 08. A second tracker (TKR6), C-GEQE, which had also suffered an engine failure, was delayed in landing and circled, while arrangements were made to allow a non-radio-equipped tow vehicle to access and remove C-GEOD from the runway.  Company maintenance personnel inspected the left engine of C-GEQD and determined that it had suffered the initial phases of an internal failure resulting in metal contamination. The engine is being replaced.

A00A0094: C-GFPL, a Grumman TBM 3E was landing after a fire-fighting practice flight out of Miramichi. The landing gear was not extended on touchdown and subsequently, the aircraft skidded along the runway on it's underside until coming to a stop. The underside of the aircraft and the propeller sustained damage; repairs will be carried out by the operator.The operator will be sending a copy of the pilot report to the TSB.

A00W0125: The tip cap separated from one tail rotor blade during a Rappel practice. The pilot noted a severe vibration in the tail rotor pedals and landed the Bell 205 immediately, without injury or damage. Both tail rotor blades were forwarded to the TSB Engineering Lab for analysis, and were examined as part of LP 064/00. The bond between the end closure surface and the blade interior surfaces on the failed blade appeared to have separated with little or no tearing of the adhesive, indicating that the bond was less than ideal. The tip region of the second blade exhibited a noticable buldge in the end face, probably as a result of an ingress of moisture into the blade.

A00C0136: The Manitoba Government Air Services CL215 water bomber was engaged in fire-fighting activities near Wintering Lake, Mb, when a GPU fire indication was noted.  The right engine was secured and the aircraft was diverted to Thompson with ERS standing by.  No fire was found; a malfunction of the fire warning system was noted.

A00W0130: The Air Spray B-26B was dispatched for forest fire fighting duties from Grande Prairie, AB. The pilot refuelled once during the mission at the Loon River Forestry Base. The B-26B left Loon River with 700 US gallons on board which would normally give 210 minutes flying time with no reserve. After the last drop on a fire by Lac La Biche, dispatch ordered the aircraft back to Grande Prairie. The pilot received a GPS distance from the bird dog aircraft and decided there was enough fuel on board based on the fuel gauges. The aircraft reached a 10 mile final for runway 25 in Grande Prairie  with a fuel gauge indication of 35-40 US gallons in each main tank. At this time the left Pratt and Whitney R2800 engine lost power. The pilot feathered the engine and declared an emergency. At five miles from the runway the pilot selected gear down and shortly after the right engine lost power. The pilot feathered the right engine and landed approximately one mile from the runway in a field. The landing gear did not complete a full cycle, and the aircraft slid along its belly coming into contact with a road. The left engine departed the aircraft and a small oil fed fire ensued. The pilot evacuated the aircraft and ERS vehicles extinguished the flames shortly after. The pilot received a minor cut over the left eye and bruises to his left arm; he was wearing a helmet. At the time of the accident the aircraft had been flying for 212 minutes.

A00W0141: The Buffalo Airways Consolidated PBY-5A departed Yellowknife, NT for Lutselk'e, NT on a fire fighting mission. The water bomber departed runway 15 and after the first power reduction the right Pratt and Whitney R-1830-92 engine began to shake. The crew secured the right engine, requested an immediate return to the airport and completed a successful single engine approach and landing onto runway 09. ERS was called out and standing by. Maintenance changed the number 10 cylinder which was cracked.

A00P0124: The Conair Aviation Firecat [C-GHPJ] experienced a propeller feathering oil line leak. The pilot was on approach for landing and observed an oil leak coming from the left side propeller.  The pilot pushed the feather button for that propeller and noticed oil gushing out from the feather line; he shut the engine down and declined the services offered by the E.R.S (Emergency Response Services).  The aircraft landed without incident but had to be towed off taxiway 'A' to the Air Tanker base.Company maintenance determined that the leak originated at the oil line fitting.

A00W0158: The Aerospatiale AS315B helicopter was fighting a forest fire south of Blairmore, AB. While hovering to fill the bucket from Lynx Creek, the helicopter drifted upslope and the main rotor struck a pine tree. After releasing the load, an uneventful landing was completed.The pilot was uninjured, although the helicopter was substantially damaged.

A00C0178: The Jackson Air Services DeHavilland DHC-3 Otter was departing from an outpost camp at Stevens-Nicklin Lake, MB with a pilot and two camp employees and some camp equipment on board.  The camp was being evacuated because of the threat of a nearby forest fire. During initial climb, at about 80 feet agl, the aircraft began to descend, despite the application of full engine power, and settled into the trees.  The occupants were reportedly not injured by the crash, but sustained minor injuries exiting the aircraft.  The aircraft was destroyed by the impact with the trees and a post-crash fire.The local temperature was 27 degrees C, and the aircraft was near its maximum gross weight.  It was reported that the aircraft had a headwind in proximity to the forest fire on takeoff, and that it flew into the area of a tailwind during initial climb.

A00W0169: The pilot of the Conair Firecat performed an in-flight precautionary shutdown of the No. 2 engine (Wright 1820) due to illumination of the low oil pressure light and low oil pressure and high oil temperature gauge indications. The aircraft landed in Rainbow Lake, Alberta without further incident. The operator has advised that the engine sustained a main bearing failure.

A00A0128: The Newfoundland Government CL 215, operating as TKR284, was working a fire when the crew noticed the hydraulic pressure was fluctuating. After consulting with maintenance the crew were discontinued fire operations and flew the aircraft to Gander for repairs. While entering the control zone at Gander the crew requested RWY 04. Gander tower stated RWY 04 was unavailable due to traffic. The crew then reported they were experiencing hydraulic fluctuations and again requested RWY 04. Priority was then given to TKR283 and the aircraft landed uneventfully with ERS at standby position.Maintenance reported that the main gear locked but the nose gear only extended half way during the approach into Gander. The crew then used emergency extension procedure to lock the nose gear. After inspecting the aircraft maintenance discovered a broken hydraulic line in the ski slope area which resulted in a loss of fluid to the main hydraulic system.

A00W0171: The Douglas B-26C was landing on runway 13 at High Level, Alberta, following the passage of a heavy rain storm. During the landing roll the aircraft hydroplaned and departed the right side of the runway. The aircraft struck and damaged one runway light and a "Taxiway A" fibre optic sign before coming to a stop on the infield approximately 375 feet west of the centreline and 400 feet from the threshold of runway 31. The aircraft sustained damage to one nose gear door and the nose wheel shimmy damper. The pilot was uninjured. The wind was 250 degrees at five knots, light rain was falling, and there was thunderstorm activity in the area at the time of the occurrence. The pilot reported that there was a sheet of standing water on the runway and that the B26 rotating tire hydroplane speed is 75 knots, with a tire pressure of 70 psi, and the aircraft touchdown speed is 91 knots.

A00W0241: The Boeing 737-300, N17345, was on descent into Calgary when the forward cargo compartment fire warning light illuminated, and the fire warning bell sounded. The crew discharged the fire extinguishers, but the fire warnings continued. An emergency was declared, and an uneventful landing was completed with ERS in attendance. No evidence of fire was found, and the aircraft departed after the cargo fire suppression system was put on MEL and the fire bottles and parts replaced. Maintenance determined that the false warning was caused by a warning switch cannon plug that was not fully seated. It was secured and the system checked normal.

A00P0224: During climbout from Vancouver International, the crew of the Boeing 737 (C-GIPW) noted a momentary flash of the No. 1 fire handle. The aircraft had been dispatched with an unserviceable No.1 engine overheat and fire protection system (under the authority of MEL 26-02). As the climb continued above 10,000 feet, the flashing of the fire handle became imtermittent and the crew decided to return an to Vancouver. The crew requested ERS support and received a clearance to return. During the descent, the fire handle light illuminated steadily, as did the Master Caution light. The crew completed the primary fire precaution checklist and the No. 1 engine (P&W JT8D) was shut down. Following this activity, the crew completed the full fire checklist. The flight landed normally, with the fire trucks in attendance. The aircraft was brought to a full stop on the runway and, once the fire crews cleared it, they proceeded to the terminal and de-planed the passengers using the bridge. The passengers had been briefed about the situation during the descent, and again on the runway. The flight attendants were given a full de-brief.

A01P0097:  The Conair CL-215 C-GFSM was on a flight from Abbotsford to Slave Lake, Alberta. While in cruise about 50 nm north of Kamloops, the number 1 engine (Pratt & Whitney R-2800) began to backfire with moderate vibration every 5 to 7 minutes. Later in the flight the Captain decided to shut down the engine in case it was incurring some damage. No emergency was declared and the aircraft landed at Slave Lake without difficulty. As of 16 May 2001 the backfiring is still occurring and maintenance are continuing to troubleshoot the problem. The aircraft will not be released to service until the problem has been eliminated.

A01Q0077: LE CL-215 EXPLOITÉ PAR LE SERVICE AÉRIEN GOUVERNEMENTAL DU QUÉBEC EFFECTUAIT UN VOL D'ENTRAÎNEMENT À PARTIR DE L'AÉROPORT DE ROBERVAL. EN VOL DE CROISIÈRE, LA PRESSION D'HUILE DU MOTEUR #2 (P&W R-2800-CA3) A CHUTÉ. L'ÉQUIPAGE A FERMÉ LE MOTEUR. L'APPAREIL A ATTERRI SANS AUTRE PROBLÈME À ROBERVAL. LE PILOTE N'A PAS DÉCLARÉ UNE URGENCE.

A01Q0094: Le Bell 412, exploité par Essor Hélicoptère effectuait un vol lors d¿une opération de  lutte contre les incendies de forêts. Au terme d'une approche au lac Culotte, le pilote ne pouvait pas atterrir sur l¿héliplate-forme aménagée à cette fin parce qu¿elle était encombrée d'objets laissés par les travailleurs précédemment débarqués. Par conséquent, le pilote a tenté de se poser dans un espace restreint qui n¿était pas aménagé. Pendant la descente, le rotor principal a percuté un arbre qui était situé à l'arrière de l'hélicoptère. Les pales en composite ont subi des dommages importants. Le pilote a alors mis fin à l¿atterrissage et a remis les gaz à la recherche d¿un site plus propice. L'appareil a atterri environ deux minutes plus tard.

A01W0118: The Cessna 310, C-FGZR, serial number 310Q1034, was working as a bird dog aircraft on a forest fire NE of Red Earth Creek, AB. During a turning manoeuver at low altitude, the aircraft descended into the trees and crashed. The pilot and the fire control officer were fatally injured, and the aircraft destroyed by fire.

A01W0121: The crew of the CL215 had just completed a water scoop when the No. 2 engine indicated high oil temp and low oil pressure. The No. 2 (Pratt and Whitney R2800) engine was shut down and the propeller was feathered. Company examination determined the oil cooler thermostat was unserviceable.

A01W0146: The Buffalo Airways Ltd. Consolidated Vultee PBY-5A was on approach to Defeat Lake, 20 nm east of Yellowknife, NT, when the right engine began to run rough. The flight crew aborted the approach and climbed to 1000 feet. The right engine was shutdown and the aircraft returned to the Yellowknife airport. The flight crew declared an emergency and requested AFF services for the arrival. The aircraft landed without further incident. Upon inspection, the number four cylinder on the Pratt and Whitney R-1830-92 engine had cracked from the spark plug hole to the intake valve. The right engine was replaced.

A01C0134: The Erickson Air-Crane Inc. S64E was performing fire-suppression work in the Quetico Provincial Park when the crew noted falling transmission oil pressure (20 psi) and rising transmission oil temperature.  The flight was diverted to a nearby bog, and landed with minor damage to the aircraft from small trees in the area, but no crew injuries. Transmission oil pump function and oil quantity were confirmed after the occurrence.

A01Q0105: Le Bell 212 immatriculé C-FXDS de la compagnie Canadian Helicopter effectuait du support local pour la lutte contre les incendies de forêt. L'appareil a subi une panne sèche et a effectué un atterrissage d'urgence dans la forêt.  L'appareil a été fortement endommagé.

A01C0150: Tanker 251, a Canadair CL215, was conducting fire suppression activities 65 nm east of Gimli, MB, when passing aircrew noted smoke trailing from the aircraft's right engine (P & W R2800-CA3). The crew was notified, and the aircraft diverted back to Gimli, where it landed without further incident.  Maintenance found that a BMEP plug in the engine had blown out, allowing oil to escape.

A01C0164: The Province of Saskatchewan Northern Air Operations Dehavilland CS2F Tracker, C-GEQC, was returning from a fire suppression mission when the airframe began to vibrate and the left engine (Wright 1820-82) began to fail. The left engine was shut down down and feathered. The aircraft landed successfully at Prince Albert and was shut down on the runway and towed in.  The left engine was found to be seized.

A01W0180: The pilot of C-FKBM, an A26B water bomber executed a go-around while on approach to the Whitehorse airport (CYXY) due to an indication of unsafe gear position. The aircraft landed uneventfully  with AFF standing by as a precaution.  Company maintenance has determined the problem to be a faulty gear indicator micro switch.

A01W0176: The crew of the PBY-5, C-FNJE was conducting a water pick up from Sitidgi Lake during fire suppression activities when they lost control. A wing tip dug into the water and the aircraft came to rest nose down in the lake. Another PBY which was in the area landed on the lake near the downed machine and picked up the crew before it sank in about 100 feet of water.

A01W0179: On the outbound flight approximately 10 nm from the departure airport, Norman Wells (CYVQ), the no. 2 engine of the McDonnell Douglas DC-4 developed an oil leak onto the exhaust, resulting in smoke. The engine, a Pratt & Whitney R-2000-7M2 reciprocating radial, was shut down and the aircraft returned to Norman Wells (CYVQ) for an uneventful landing.

A01A0092: WHILE ON CLIMB-OUT FROM HALIFAX FOR LBPIA, THE FLIGHT ATTENDANTS ON BOARD CMM 7164, A BOEING 737-200 (B732), REPORTED A BURNING SMELL IN THE CABIN. THE AIRCRAFT WAS APPROXIMATELY 7 MILES ON DEPARTURE FROM RWY 24 WHEN PILOT REQUESTED A RETURN TO LAND AT HALIFAX. A/C REQUESTED PRIORITY AND THE FIRE CREWS. TERMINAL VECTORED THE AIRCRAFT TO A LEFT DOWNWIND FOR RUNWAY 24.  AT APPROXIMATELY 3 MILES FINAL THE PILOT INFORMED TOWER THAT THE SMELL OF SMOKE WAS GONE. AFF ADVISED. AIRCRAFT LANDED SAFELY AT 193OZ. UPDATE O8/O8/01THE RIGHT AIR CONDITIONING PACK TRIPPED OFF PRIOR TO ROTATION POSSIBLY DUE TO INGESTION OF A SMALL BIRD. MAINTENANCE WAS UNABLE TO DETERMINE IF THE PACK FAULT CAUSED THE BURNING ODOUR; HOWEVER THEY BELIEVE THAT IT IS LIKELY THAT BIRD INGESTION CAUSED THE BURNING SMELL AS FLIGHT ATTENDANTS LIKENED THE SMELL TO BURNING HAIR. THE ENGINES WERE INSPECTED AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS SUBSEQUENTLY RELEASED TO SERVICE.

A01W0198: During forest fire suppression activities, the pilot of CRC567, a Conair Fire Cat observed a low oil pressure light and dropping oil pressure on No. 2 engine. He shut down the engine (Wright 982 C9 HE2-MR5) and advised Whitehorse Intl (CYXY) control tower of his situation, requesting AFF response. The aircraft landed uneventfully at 1605 PST.  Inherent difficulties in ground handling of the Fire Cat with one engine inoperative, necessitated a tow off the airport manoeuvring area. Initial inspection of the engine revealed that a valve had failed.

A01Q0142: Le Canadair CL-215 1A10 enregistré C-GFQB du Service Aérien Gouvernemental était de retour d'une mission d'arrosage de feux de forêt lorsque le moteur #2, un Pratt & Whitney R-2800 CA-3, a perdu de la puissance. Plusieurs détonations se sont produites. Après quelques vérifications, le pilote commandant de bord a décidé de monter à 3,500 pieds pour fermer le moteur afin de se rendre à destination. L'aéronef a atterri à l'aéroport de Roberval sans autre problème.Une vérification technique du moteur a permis de déceler que le cylindre #4 était à l'origine des problèmes. Il a été remplacé et l'aéronef a été remis en service.

A01P0198:  The Vancouver Island Helicopters Bell 212 (C-GTKE)(engine Pt6t-3/3b) departed Prince George for 108 Mile Airport and was 7 NM south of Prince George when the pilot reported an engine failure and declared an emergency. The aircraft was cleared to return to Prince George for a straight-in approach to runway 33 and landed safely at 10:41 PDT.Subsequent investigation revealed that the oil cap had been left off of one engine. The pilot had noticed falling oil pressure on one engine during the flight and elected to shut down that engine and return to the airport. Company maintenance inspected the screens and chip detectors on the affected engine and found no metal. Oil was added to the engine and a ground run performed before the aircraft was returned to service.

A01O0248: C-GOGW, a Canadair CL-215-6B11 aircraft, was on a forest fire fighting mission in northern Ontario. During final approach to land and pick up another load of water at a lake approximately 35nm south of Kapuskasing, the aircraft's left wing and sponson struck a tree. Due to the extensive damage to the aircraft, the crew elected to divert to Sault St. Marie. The aircraft landed without further incident. There were no injuries.

operation: AIR TRANSPORT; FIRE FIGHTING / FIRE MANAGEMENT
Summary: A01P0224:  The Boeing 737-200, C-GMWJ, WJA31, took off on runway 15 on a Kelowna 2 SID enroute to Vancouver. The crew were issued a traffic advisory on a Conair Air Tractor Aircraft, C-FXVF, CRC678, engaged in fire fighting in the Penticton area and advised the aircraft in sight. WJA31 subsequently received a TCAS RA and responded appropriately while keeping the aircraft in sight. The crew reported the Conair aircraft did not alter its flight path.

A02P0083: The Conair Firecat S2P aircraft, C-FOPY, CRC569, was on fire patrol in the Kamloops area when the low oil pressure warning light for the right engine (Wright R1820-82) illuminated. The oil pressure indicated 45 psi (below normal). The right engine was feathered and the aircraft returned to Kamloops airport with a request for airport CFR. The aircraft landed without further difficulty. The operator will provide information regarding the reasons for the oil pressure problem.

A02C0093: The Province of Saskatchewan Northern Air Operations Piper PA31-350, C-GVDQ, operating under CAR 702, was departing La Ronge, SK. At 3000 asl, about 16 nm south of the airport the aircraft struck a bird. The aircraft returned to La Ronge where repairs were made to the left stabilizer and inner left wing.

A02C0098: The Saskatchewan Northern Air Operations Canadair CL215, C-FYXG, was being used for fire suppression activities. After experiencing a loss of hydraulic pressure, the crew advised that they would return to land at La Ronge, and advised that the hydraulic problem would require that the aircraft be towed from the runway. The aircraft landed without incident and it was towed clear of the runway within a few minutes. Company maintenance personnel determined that a cracked hydraulic pump had allowed hydraulic fluid to leak from the system. The pump was changed, the system replenished, and the aircraft was successfully returned to service.

A02W0088: The flight crew of the Convair 340/580, registration C-FFKF, observed a reduction gearbox low oil pressure indication on the number two engine (Allison 501-D13H). They secured the engine and returned to Slave Lake without further incident. The reduction gearbox was inspected and no discrepancies that would account for low oil pressure were identified. Subsequent troubleshooting identified that the gearbox oil pressure transmitter was defective.

A02Q0090: Après le quatrième écopage, lors de l'inspection routinière des moteurs par l'équipage du CL-215 immatriculé C-GFQB, le premier officier a signalé une surchauffe sous le moteur droit.  Le capitaine s'est rendu dans la cabine et a remarqué par le hublot face au moteur de droite que le tuyau d'évacuation des résidus du compartiment moteur était au rouge vif et laissait s'échapper des bouffées d'étincelles.  La puissance a été réduite sur le moteur et une diversion vers l'aéroport de Rivière du Loup a été immédiatement initiée. Ce tuyau vidange un récipient à l'arrière du moteur recueillant tous les résidus d'huile provenant des accessoires.   Aucune fuite importante n'a été décelée, cependant une accumulation de carbone et de produit graisseux a été noté.  Le tuyau a été nettoyé et l'appareil remis en service sans autre difficulté.

A02W0095: After departing Slave Lake airport (CYZH), the crew of Convair 580 water bomber, C-FFKF, observed a gauge indication of low gear box oil pressure on the number 2 engine (Allison 501-D13H). The crew shut the engine down and returned to Slave Lake where the aircraft landed safely. In response to a similar incident (A02W0088), on the same aircraft 2 days prior to this occurrence, the gear box oil pressure transmitter was changed. After the second incident, company maintenance personnel determined that there was no fault with the transmitter but it had been installed with the improper type of fitting.

A02W0089: The Eurocopter AS350B helicopter, registration C-GBBX, was being utilized for forest fire water bucketing. The water bucket was fitted with a short lanyard and the pilot was watching the bucket in the mirror as he descended onto the lake. He did not arrest the forward speed during the final approach and he flared abruptly when the bucket contacted the water. The tail rotor struck the water during the flare and the helicopter began to rotate uncontrollably to the left. The pilot ditched onto the surface of the lake approximately 100 feet from shore, and the helicopter rolled onto the right side and sank in four feet of water. The pilot was uninjured and the helicopter sustained substantial damage. The surface of the lake was glassy, the ceiling was 500 feet and the visibility was approximately three miles in smoke at the time of the occurrence.

A02C0112: The Manitoba Government Air Services Canadair CL 215, C-FTXI, was proceeding to The Pas, MB, after fire suppression operations when the crew noted an oil leak at the left engine. The crew shut down the engine (Pratt & Whitney R2800) and carried on to destination where they landed without further incident.  Maintenance found that the left engine nose case had failed.

A02W0092: The Bell 206L3 helicopter, C-GRMH, was returning to the House River Fire Base to refuel when the engine failed due to fuel exhaustion. As the pilot was attempting to autorotate into a clearing, he noticed a power line crossing the clearing. The helicopter crashed into the trees when he turned to avoid the power line. The pilot was not injured, although the helicopter was substantially damaged.

A02C0114: The Bell 205A-1 helicopter, C-FMQN, was engaged in fire-suppression bucketing operations from a base at Tobin Lake, SK.  As the aircraft was transiting, the crew noted an engine fire warning and a burning smell. The pilot completed a landing in a field, activated the fire extinguisher, and shut the aircraft down.  The fire continued to burn until it was suppressed by several buckets of water from another helicopter. The helicopter sustained substantial damage.  There were no reported injuries.

A02W0096: Shortly after the CL215 water bomber, C-GFSN (CRC 204) reached cruise altitude while working a forest fire, a  "zone 1" fire warning light illuminated for the number 1 engine. When the crew reduced power on the engine (Pratt & Whitney WASP CA3), the warning light went out, then reappeared 10 minutes later. The engine was then shut down and feathered and the aircraft was flown to its base at Lac La Biche (CYLB). Maintenance personnel determined that an exhaust stack had split, allowing hot exhaust gasses to burn through the fire detection wiring loop.

A02W0098: The Bell 212, C-GRHA had conducted a sling load drop into a clearing during forest fire operations, and was hovering to allow a ground assistant to hook up the empty net, when the tail rotor contacted a tree. After four uncontrolled rotations to the right, the pilot put the aircraft on the ground with substantial damage to the tail boom and tail rotor drive train. There were no injuries to the pilot or the ground assistant who dove out of the way of the gyrating helicopter.

A02W0104: The Douglas B-26, registration C-FPGP, was on fire fighting operations near Fort Vermillion, Alberta when the engine, a Pratt and Whitney R2800, s/n FPO28246, started to backfire and run roughly. The flight crew shut the engine down as a precaution and proceeded to High Level, Alberta where an uneventful landing took place. Maintenance crews discovered a problem with one of the magnetos, and has filed an SDR with Transport Canada. The aircraft was returned to service.

A02W0100: The Eurocopter AS350B, C-GRHI, was landing on an access road to drop off a fire-fighting team. At an altitude of about 60 feet, the pilot reduced speed and began the flare for the landing. As he raised the collective to increase power for a controlled hover, he immediately noticed a lack of response from the engine (Turbomeca Arriel 1B S/N 4155), and lowered the collective to maintain rotor rpm, then raised the collective to cushion the landing. The "Low Rotor Warning" horn sounded just prior to impact as the aircraft began an uncommanded left turn. The tail boom separated from the fuselage during the two bounces on the road, and the engine appeared to accelerate as the helicopter made several counter-clockwise rotations before impacting in the grass beside the road on its RH side. Ground witnesses assisted the pilot and four passengers after they evacuated the wreckage, before a fire erupted and destroyed the helicopter except the engine and tail boom. The pilot and two passengers were uninjured, and the other two passengers sustained minor injuries.The engine (Turbomeca Arriel 1B S/N 4155), had 6152.2 hours since new, and was removed and shipped to the manufacturer, Turbomeca Engine Corporation, for examination. Present at the examination was an NTSB investigator (representing the  TSB), a Turbomeca accident investigator, two representatives from the operator, and a representative for  the Insurance company. No significant anomalies were found in the engine and components, with the exception of internal damage in the freewheel sprag clutch assembly, and deposits in the engine fuel control pressure relief valve. The sprag clutch assy was examined at the TSB Engineering Branch with a Turbomeca representative and an insurance company representative present, and concluded that the broken sprag and other damage was the result of overload from main rotor blade impact (Report LP65/2002). The components were then sent to the manufacturer for examination, under FAA oversight. Their findings were similar to the TSB report (Formsprag 1928ER.03).The pressure relief valve and deposits were examined at the TSB Engineering Branch in the presence of a Turbomeca representative and an insurance company representative. Detailed examination of the particles with a medium power optical microscope revealed that they were carbonaceous agglomerates easily crushed between two sheets of paper. The deposits were probably the results of carbonization from fire/heat damage.

A02W0107: The Douglas B-26 airplane, registration C-FOVC, was on water bombing operations when the right side engine (Pratt and Whitney R2800, s/n FPO27412) began backfiring and running rough. The engine was shut down as a precautionary measure and the aircraft landed at Whitecourt, Alberta without incident. Maintenance crews discovered a fault with one of the magnetos. An SDR has been filed with Transport Canada.

A02C0130: While en route from Lynn Lake to Gimli at 5500 feet, the crew of C-GBOW noticed that the right engine started backfiring with a loss of Brake Manifold Engine Pressure.  The crew initiated a precautionary engine shutdown (Pratt & Whitney R2800) and diverted to The Pas. A subsequent engine inspection revealed a faulty cylinder. The cylinder was replaced and the aircraft returned to service.

A02P0129:  The Conair Firecat S2P, C-FEFX, flight number CRC575, departed Prince George enroute to a forest fire. About 5 minutes after take-off, the low oil pressure light for the number 1 engine (Wright R1820) illuminated. The oil temperature was at the maximum (130 degrees Celsius) and the oil coolers were open with gills in trail. The pilot decided to return to Prince George and advised ATC. He attempted to feather the number 1 engine 3 or 4 times without success and landed with the propellor windmilling and CFR on standby. The initial reason for the high oil temperature has not yet been determined. The left engine feathering pump would not work on the ground although it was powered. Efforts are being made to determine if the pump was working in the air. The company will submit an SDR.

A02W0121: The Bell 212, C-GFDV, SN 30842, was on a local flight at Loon River, AB when the pilot experienced a loud bang, followed by power loss on the number 1 engine, and a significant yaw. A single engine landing was successfully carried out with no further incident, or injuries to the pilot, who was the only occupant. Inspection of the PT6-T-3, SN 61536, revealed that failure of a compressor blade resulted in destruction of the remaining compressor section as well as extensive damage to the power turbine.

A02W0114: The Buffalo Airways Ltd. C54E-DC (DC-4), registration C-GCTF, experienced a loss of hydraulic pressure while manoeuvring on the ramp in Manning, AB. The pilot lost nose wheel steering and braking and headed towards a parked Ontario Government CL-415, registration C-GOGE. The pilot slowed the DC-4 to a walking pace with the emergency air braking system and shutdown all four engines, but was unable to bring the aircraft to a complete stop. The CL-415 was having a left propellor prop blade seal worked on by two maintenance personnel, who were in a lift truck bucket. The DC-4's left wing contacted the lift truck and the left wing of the CL-415. The maintenance people jumped from the bucket anticipating a fire from the leaking fuel. The CL-415 sustained damage to the left winglet, wing fence, and vortex generators. The DC-4 sustained a three inch hole in the underside of the outboard portion of the left wing. Emergency services arrived to attend to the 25 gallons of fuel that was spilled and to tend to the minor injuries sustained by the maintenance personnel.Update 2 July: While the DC-4 was loading retardant, the flight crew noticed low hydraulic pressure. A hydraulic leak was observed and the fluid replenished. Hydraulic pressure returned to normal as the aircraft began to taxi for the fueling area. During the taxi the main hydraulic line failed at the hydraulic pump coupling and all contents were lost. The pneumatic accumulator for the emergency braking system normally supplies 1000 psi for the braking system which would allow for approximately five applications of the brakes. In this occurrence only one application occurred before the accumulator was depleted. Inspection revealed one crushed washer and a pinched O-ring in the system which prevented 1000 psi from being stored in the accumulator. The operator checked the emergency braking systems in the other DC-4 aircraft for similar problems, and none were found.

A02C0144: The crew of the Bombardier CL-415 was taxiing for departure at Pickle Lake, ON, for a local fire-fighting flight. As the aircraft was maneuvering, its left wingtip struck a standing Bell 205A, C-GFFY, which was parked on the ramp. No injuries resulted.  The CL-415 sustained damage to its left wing.  The Bell 205A sustained damage to its main rotor system.

A02Q0096: En approche vers une aire d'atterrissage étroite en forêt (vol local), le rotor de queue de l'Astar immatriculé C-FWAU, propriété d'Héli/Express inc. a touché un arbre. La perte du rotor de queue a immédiatement engendré une giration non contrôlable et l'hélicoptère a tourné 360 degrés avant de toucher durement le sol. A l'atterrissage les patins du train se sont affaissés.

A02W0123: Shortly after the Conair Firecat water bomber, C-GABC, operating as TNK567, took off from Whitehorse (CYXY), the pilot turned off the auxiliary fuel pump as part of the after takeoff checklist. Fuel pressure dropped and the engine, (Wright 982-C9 HE2, SN PC10114) immediately lost power. The pilot was able to restore power by turning on the auxiliary fuel pump, and after jettisoning the retardant load over an unpopulated area, returned to Whitehorse with AFF standing by. Company maintenance personnel determined that the engine driven fuel pump had failed.

A02C0157: The Manitoba Government Air Service CL215, C-FTUV, was water bombing a fire south of Thompson (CYTH). The crew had just completed scooping water and were en route to the drop area when it became apparent that oil was leaking from the nosecase of the starboard engine (P&W R2800-CA3). The crew dropped the water load and they manually shut down the engine. They then proceeded to CYTH where they landed without incident. There were no injuries incurred as a result of this occurrence. Company maintenance personnel determined that a nose case plug for an unused front case oil transfer tube port had failed in the plug threads. This plug is subject of P&W R-2800 service bulletin 1755 revision B. which requires a repair to the threads of the subject plug.  The Operator is submitting a service difficulty report to Transport Canada and the engine manufacturer has been advised.

A02Q0103: Le CL-215 des Services Aériens du Gouvernement du Québec, immatriculé C-GFQB, en provenance de Québec, était en base gauche pour atterrir à l'aéroport de Roberval, Québec, lorsqu'un des deux moteurs Pratt & Whitney Canada R2800, a subi une perte de puissance et de régime. Le pilote a déclaré une urgence, a demandé une priorité à l'atterrissage et s'est posé sans autre incident.La défaillance d'un des cylindres est à l'origine de la perte de puissance. Le cylindre a été remplacé et l'appareil est retrourné en service.

A02C0167: The Bell 206B was departing from a camp 25 nm nw of Big River, SK, when the right skid snagged a stump. The helicopter experienced a dynamic rollover and sustained substantial damage. The two crew members on board suffered minor injuries.

A02C0168: The Cypress Helicopters Ltd. Sikorsky S-58E, C-FFZM, was departing en route to a fire camp 25 nm nw of Big River, SK, on a cargo flight. During initial climb, the engine (Curtiss Wright R1820) backfired and momentarily lost power. It regained power, but backfired again and the pilot landed the aircraft in a marsh. The aircraft was consumed by a fuel-fed fire. The crew of two and the passenger evacuated the helicopter without injury and were evacuated from the marsh by another helicopter. The aircraft's engine had backfired 30 flight hours before the occurrence, and an inspection after that occurrence revealed a bent intake valve.

A03A0014: The Atlantic Coast Dornier 328, operating as BR6269, departed Runway 06 at Halifax for a scheduled flight to Boston. Two minutes after take-off the fire detection system indicatd a fire warning on the number one engine. The crew referenced the QRH and discharged both fire suppression bottles. The fire indication remained "on" and the crew declared an emergency. Crash alarm was activated and vehicles were in stand-by positions. The aircraft was vectored back to the airport where it landed safely on runway 24 at 07:16 AST. Maintenance inspected the number one engine (Pratt & Whitney Canada PW306B) and found no evidence of fire and they could not duplicate the fire indication. Maintenance replaced the fire control panel and one fire bottle for a ferry flight back to the Boston base.

A03W0075: The Air Spray Douglas A-26B, C-FPGF, had just departed Red Deer, AB for a local flight when the pilot observed smoke and oil streaming aft from the right engine (P&W R2800-79) power section. A precautionary engine shutdown was performed and the aircraft returned to Red Deer for a single engine approach and landing. Maintenance determined that the oil leak originated from a rocker box lid at the top of the engine.

A03C0102: The Bell 205A, C-FNMO operated by Yellowhead Helicopters, was conducting fire-fighting operations when the pilot inadvertently selected the bucket release switch rather than the water release switch and jettisoned the bucket.

A03P0090:  The Conair DC-6 aircraft, C-GKUG took off from Abbotsford on a local training flight. When climb power was selected the number 4 engine (P&W R2800) began backfiring which became progressively worse. The crew completed the QRH procedure which included shutting down the engine and feathering the propellor. The crew returned to Abbotsford and landed without further difficulty. No emergency was declared. The number 16 cylinder was found to have a cracked cylinder head.

A03P0094: The Canadair CL215 (C-GFSK) was conducting a flight test of the manual propeller feathering system. During the test, the propeller of the number 2 engine, Pratt and Whitney R-2800, failed to come out of feather. The engine was shut down and the aircraft returned to Abbotsford. The aircraft landed without further incident.

A03C0121: The Canadair CL215 aircraft, registration C-FAFN, was on its way to a drop zone to help suppress a forest fire. While en route, the right engine (P&W R2800) lost power and the propeller feathered. The pilot elected to fly clear of the community before he released his load. After releasing the load the engine was secured and the aircraft returned to the Hudson Bay tanker base were the aircraft landed safely. The operator advised that the FCU portion of the carburettor had failed.

A03W0097: The Air Spray (1967) Ltd. Douglas A-26B, C-GPTW, had departed the Red Deer Regional airport (CYQF) and just levelled off, when the right engine (Pratt and Whitney R2800-79) began to run rough. The pilot performed a precautionary shutdown and returned to Red Deer. Maintenance determined that the exhaust valve on the #13 cylinder had failed.

A03C0131: While conducting water bombing operations the crew of CL215, C-FAFP, noticed large quantities of oil spraying out of the nose case area of the left engine (Pratt & Whitney R2800 CA3). The engine was manually feathered and secured and the crew returned to the Meadow Lake tanker base. When turning on long final for the Meadow Lake Airport, the crew noticed that there was no hydraulic pressure. The crew overshot the runway and circled, while performing an emergency gear extension. The aircraft landed safely without incident.Maintenance personnel found that the nose case plug on the left engine had blown out causing a loss of oil and necessitating the replacement of the nose case. The loss of hydraulic pressure was traced to a failed engine driven hydraulic pump on the right engine (the left hydraulic pump was inoperative due to the engine being shutdown). The hydraulic pump was replaced.

A03C0133: The Provincial Helicopters Bell 204B, serial number 2043, registration C-FOKY had departed Norway House on a smoke patrol in support of forest fire fighting operations. The helicopter was established in cruise flight at 3000 ft (2200 ft agl) when, approximately 15 to 20 minutes into the flight, a banging noise was heard coming from the tail area followed by a slow and smooth 30 degree yaw to the left. The pilot gently applied opposite pedal and was able to correct the yaw. The banging was not repetitive, but appeared as pedal was applied. The pilot landed the helicopter straight ahead into a swampy area approximately 1/4 nm north of the Molsen Lake Lodge. The helicopter landed without incurring further damage or injury to the occupants.An examination of the helicopter revealed that one of the tail rotor pitch link bolts (AN 174-15 or subsequent) was missing and that the pitch link was hanging free from the tail rotor horn, but still attached on the opposite end to the crosshead assembly. One, or both of the tail rotors had struck the tail boom several times in flight causing the banging noise heard by the pilot and damage to the tail boom. The tail boom and tail rotor assembly is to be replaced in situ. More info to follow.Update:  The vertical stabilizer was struck several times by the disconnected blade only. An examination of the tail rotor blade grip horn pitch change bushings showed a wear lip on the outer circumference on the face of both bushings from movement or fretting with the pitch change link rod ends. The wear pattern was indicative of an under-torqued or loose bolt arrangement. Because of interference with the tail rotor trunnion spindle bearing caps, the pitch link change bolt would have to fail in order for the pitch change link to become disconnected in flight. As the bolt was not recovered, the mode of failure could not be determined. A TSB Occurrence Bulletin was issued.
