After the departure, FGD447 contacted the Vancouver Area Control Center (ACC) and was approved for flight following at 11 500 feet ASL on an eastbound track. After completing the turn to the east, the flight crew observed a target on their Traffic Collision Avoidance Device (TCAD) at 10 000 feet ASL and elected to stop their climb at 9 500 feet. At about the same time, the flight crew of the C-GCEU observed a target on their Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) and queried ATC about the potential conflict. ATC advised that it was the Convair and asked the flight crew of FGD447 if they were able to make a turn to the south, which FGD447 complied with. ATC then advised the flight crew of C-GCEU that the Convair was turning clear; however, C-GCEU was responding to a TCAS Resolution Advisory (RA) and was turning and climbing away from the conflict.

C-GJTZ, a Lockheed 188C Electra aircraft operated by Air Spray, was conducting flight Tanker 492 on a local flight from Prince George, BC (CYXS) in support of forest fire suppression activities. During a manoeuvre, the flight crew declared a PAN PAN due to an asymmetrical flap indication. The aircraft jettisoned the remaining load of retardant and returned to land at CYXS without further incident with emergency services standing by.

operation: AIR AMBULANCE/ EMERGENCY MEDICAL; FIRE FIGHTING / FIRE MANAGEMENT
Summary: C-FZVX, a Beech 200 King Air aircraft operated by North Caribou Flying Service, was conducting medevac flight NCA911 from Kamloops, BC (CYKA) to Vancouver Intl, BC (CYVR). At the same time as NCA911 was departing IFR on the Ashcroft One Departure from CYKA, C-FKFL, a Convair 580 air tanker aircraft operated by Conair, was conducting fire suppression flight FGD449 under VFR from Penticton, BC (CYYF), and was tracking southeast to northwest at an altitude of 10 500 feet ASL. The flight crew of FGD449 was in contact with Vancouver ACC and had requested flight following after becoming airborne.After being cleared to climb to 16 000 feet, the flight crew of NCA911 requested a turn away from the Ashcroft One Departure in order to proceed direct to the BOOTH intersection. Approximately at the same time, the flight crew of FGD449 advised ATC that they were initiating a descent from 10 500 feet to an area of fire fighting activities. Once ATC acknowledged the call from FGD449, NCA911 was notified of FGD449’s presence in the vicinity, and the flight crew confirmed that they had the traffic on their TCAS. Shortly thereafter, NCA911 advised that they were maneuvering to avoid the traffic as they were complying with a TCAS RA. The flight crew of FGD449 reported the traffic in sight at approximately three miles.

C-GJHC, an Aerospatiale AS 350 B-2 aircraft operated by Mustang Helicopters, was conducting forest fire suppression operations 14 nautical miles South West of Banff, AB (CYBA). During the approach for a landing to drop off 3 firefighters, the helicopter settled with power and struck the ground hard. The occupants were not injured, however the helicopter sustained substantial damage.

C-GDCL, a Conair Rockwell Commander 690 was returning to Kamloops airport (CYKA) for landing after fire suppression duties. When the aircraft touched down the directional control was lost. The pilot applied differential braking and reverse thrust, but the aircraft exited the runway onto the grass south of RWY 09/27. The 2 occupants were uninjured and there was no damage to the aircraft. A main landing gear tire was found deflated.

C-FZQB, a Bell 212 aircraft operated by Heliqwest Aviation, was returning to Fairmont Hot Springs, BC (CYCZ) when the pilot observed a chip light for the number 1 engine (Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6T-3). The engine was shut down as per the checklist and the pilot completed an uneventful single-engine approach and landing. The operator’s maintenance inspected the chip detector and removed the fine metal debris that had accumulated on it. The aircraft was then returned to service.

C-GENM, a Bombardier DHC-8-402 aircraft operated by WestJet Encore was conducting flight WEN3205 from Fort St. John, BC (CYXJ) to Vancouver Intl., BC (CYVR) with 4 crew members and 44 passengers on board. After departing CYXJ enroute to Vancouver, the #2 engine fire warning illluminiated. The flight crew shut down the engine and activated the fire suppression system. Both extinguisher bottles were discharged, however the #2 engine fire warning persisted. The flight crew advised air traffic control, declared an emergency and diverted to Prince George, BC (CYXS). The aircraft landed uneventfully at with airport rescue and fire fighting (ARFF) crews standing by. The operator’s maintenance established that there had not been an engine fire. The warning had been the result of a damaged wire in a connector within the fire detection system. The system was repaired and the aircraft returned to service.

C-GYHQ, a Bell 212 aircraft operated by Yellowhead Helicopters, was conducting water bucketing operations 50 nm North of Peace River, AB (CYPE), when the bucket and long line were unintentionally released. It is suspected that the manual release cable was rigged too short.

C-GMAN, a Rockwell Intl Aero Commander 690B aircraft operated by MAG Aerospace Canada, was conducting a Bird Dog operation from Red Lake, ON (CYRL) in support of aerial fire suppression 13 nautical miles South of Lac du Bonnet, MB (CYAX). During flight, there was an odour and associated smoke in the cockpit and cabin, that appeared to be unrelated to the smoke generated by the fire on the ground. The flight crew elected to divert to CYAX and noticed that, when the ground blower automatically shut down at 140 knots, the smoke cleared. The subsequent landing was uneventful. The operator's maintenance proceeded to replace the ground blower.

C-GMAN, a Rockwell Intl Aero Commander 690B aircraft operated by MAG Aerospace Canada, was conducting a Bird Dog operation from Red Lake, ON (CYRL) in support of aerial suppression of Red Lake Fire 23, 2.5 nautical miles North East of Pikangikum, ON (CYPM). The aircraft interior began to get warm regardless of the climate control selections and an odour and haze began to fill the cabin. The flight crew notified the Air Attack Officer that there was smoke in the cabin and that they needed to leave the wildfire. The flight crew depressurized the cabin, at which point the odour and haze cleared. The flight crew consulted the QRH and elected to continue to Red Lake, ON (CYRL).The operator's maintenance determined that the Blower Motor isolation switch was in the OFF position, allowing the climate control system to overheat. The switch, intended for use by maintenance personnel, is in a non-standard and exposed location on this particular aircraft. The switch has since been witness-wired to prevent inadvertent operation.

C-GNYH, a Bell 407 aircraft operated by Yellowhead Helicopters, was commencing water bucketing operations approximately 46 nm North West of Mackenzie, BC (CYZY) when the longline and bucket inadvertently released from the helicopter. Subsequent maintenance inspection revealed that the manual release cable was kinked.

C-GRHJ, an Aerospatiale AS 350 B-2 aircraft operated by Remote Helicopters, was conducting bucketing operations in support of forest fire suppression, 10 nm North of Calling Lake, AB (CFK4). While lifting the bucket from a water source, the engine (Avco Lycoming LTS-101-700D-2) experienced compressor stalls, followed by an engine deceleration. The engine RPM recovered during the landing on the shore of the lake.The operator’s maintenance replaced the power turbine governor and engine air flow modulator actuator before flying the aircraft back to CFK4.

C-GRHW, a Bell 205A-1 aircraft operated by Remote Helicopters, was conducting forest fire suppression operation South West of Loon River, AB (CFS6). When the pilot tried to release the load of water on fire SWF053, the water, bucket and longline were all released from the helicopter. No one was injured in the incident. Repairs to the long line and bucket wiring in the cargo hook area were carried out.

C-FFJL, un Cessna 310R exploité par Grondair Aviation, effectuait un vol d’aéropointage dans le cadre d’une opération d’extinction de feu de forêt selon les règles de vol à vue depuis l'aéroport de Val d’Or, QC (CYVO) avec un pilote et un coordinateur des opérations à bord. Lors du retour à environ 12 miles marins au sud-ouest de CYVO, la pression d’huile du moteur droit (Teledyne Continental IO-520-MB) a diminué à son minimum opérationnel et le pilote a fermé le moteur. L’appareil s’est posé sur la piste 36 sans encombre. Il n’y a eu aucun blessé ni dommage à l’appareil.

C-FRZE, un Cessna 182R exploité par Grondair, effectuait un vol de patrouille de feu selon les règles de vol à vue depuis l'aéroport de Val d’Or, QC (CYVO) avec seul un pilote à bord. En croisière, le pilote remarque que l’alternateur ne charge pas la batterie et décide de revenir à CYVO. Au retour, la radio ne fonctionnait plus, donc le pilote communique avec Rouyn Radio par téléphone, déclare un état d’urgence et avise qu’il revient à CYVO sans radio. La procédure d’extension manuelle des roues est utilisée et l’appareil se pose avec les volets rentrés sans encombre. Il n’y a eu aucun blessé ni dommage.

C-GBSC, un appareil de type Cessna R182 exploité par Exact Air, effectuait un vol selon les règles de vol à vue depuis Manic-5, QC (CMN5) à destination de Baie-Comeau, QC (CYBC) avec seul le pilote à bord. En raison des travaux de réfection de la piste à CYBC, la moitié sud (75 pieds) de la largeur de celle-ci était fermée sur toute sa longueur. Lors de l’atterrissage sur la piste 28, l’appareil a dévié à gauche et s’est posé sur la partie fermée de la piste. Il n’y a eu aucun blessé ni dommage. Le personnel au sol a aidé l’appareil à retourner sur la partie nord de la piste qui était ouverte.

C-FYHD, a Bell 205A-1 skid-equipped aircraft operated by Northern Shield Helicopters, was conducting belly-hook water bucket operations 24 nautical miles North West of Hudson Bay, SK (CYHB). The pilot was hovering the helicopter over Buckmayer Lake, SK with the bucket in the water while waiting for instructions from the bird dog aircraft when there was an abnormal noise, which was accompanied by a lateral vibration. The pilot began to manoeuvre the helicopter toward the shore and, after travelling approximately 100 metres, the vibration changed to a vertical vibration and worsened. The pilot informed the bird dog pilot that there was a drive train problem, then landed the aircraft in the lake close to shore. During the approach, the tail rotor contacted trees. Once on the water, the shaking caused both crew doors to pop open. The pilot shut the engine down and pulled collective pitch to slow the rotors. The helicopter floated and, after the rotor system came to a stop, the pilot exited the aircraft and swam about 15 metres to shore. The helicopter eventually rolled onto its side, and sank in about 6 feet of water. The bird dog aircraft was circling the site and initiated rescue operations. After firefighters cleared a landing pad, the pilot was recovered from the site. The pilot was uninjured, however was transported to hospital for observation. The helicopter sustained substantial damage and was recovered from the site. The investigation is ongoing.

C-GOJI, an Air Tractor AT402B aircraft operated by Fly On Ag Services Inc., was conducting a flight from Geraldton, ON (CYGQ) to Sioux Lookout, ON (CYXL). During the landing on Runway 34 directional control was lost. The aircraft exited the runway to the west, north of Taxiway A. The aircraft re-entered the runway and taxied to the apron. The winds were reported to be 260 degrees at 14 knots gusting to 27 knots. The tailwheel alignment required adjustment after a subsequent flight.

C-FTXK, un appareil de type CL-215 exploité par le Service Aérien Gouvernemental du Québec, avec à son bord 2 membres d'équipage de conduite effectuait un vol de combat de feu de forêt selon les règles de vol à vue. Lors d'un écopage sur le lac Skokiaan l'équipage a senti une perte puissance du moteur droit (Pratt & Whitney Wasp R2800-CA3) attribuable à une mise en drapeau non commandé. Lors de la décélération qui a suivi, l'aéronef s'est échoué sur un haut fond et y est resté immobilisé. Il n'y a pas eu de blessés.

C-FZCS, a Lockheed 188A  aircraft operated by Air Spray (1967), was operating as Tanker 487 on fire LWF179, 25 nm West of Fort McMurray, AB (CYMM). During the flight, the number 4 engine propeller experienced an over speed. The flight crew executed the checklist and, once the propeller was regulating, the decision was taken to fly to the abort area to dump the remaining retardant in the tanks. Once this was completed, the flight crew shut the number 4 engine down. An emergency was declared, and the aircraft returned to CYMM where it landed without further incident with ARFF attending.The operator’s maintenance found the propeller governor O-ring damaged. The mounting pad O-ring was replaced, and the engine was successfully run. The aircraft was returned to service.

C-FHHH an Aerospatiale AS 350 BA helicopter operated by Helicoptères Transit, was operating under a contract with the Société de protection des forêts contre le feu (SOPFEU) to transport firefighters in and out of their assigned area. The pilot landed the helicopter in a remote staging area established for fire #368, located 50 nm South East of Lebel-sur-Quévillon (CSH4), QC, in order to pick up firefighters. While lowering the collective lever and awaiting for firefighters to board, the tail rotor impacted a 2 to 3 inch wood log, which immediately caused noticeable vibrations. The pilot shut the engine down, and subsequent inspection revealed substantial impact damage to the tail rotor blades. Repairs were carried out in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions, and the aircraft was returned to service a few days later. The selected landing site was reportedly unprepared and covered with fallen wood debris.

C-FPPN, an Aerospatiale AS 350 B-2 aircraft operated by Dam Helicopters, was conducting fire suppression activities approximately 17 nm Southeast of Trail, BC (CAD4). During the landing phase, while dropping off an initial crew, the pilot heard a loud buzzing noise and felt a vibration in the tail rotor system. The pilot landed and shut down the aircraft. A visual inspection of the tail rotor system did not find any abnormalities. After consultation with maintenance personnel, the pilot completed a ground run, flight test and then flew the aircraft back to Castlegar, BC (CYCG). Further inspection of the tail rotor revealed that contact with an unknown object had occurred. The tail rotor blade assembly was replaced in accordance with the manufacturer.

C-GKFO, a Convair 340/580 aircraft operated by Conair Group, was conducting local flight FGD453 in support of fire-fighting operations from Slave Lake, AB (CYZH) with only the 2 pilots on board. During the takeoff, observers on the ground noted that one of the nose wheel came off on departure, and the flight crew was notified by radio. The flight crew extended the flaps and the landing gear, and the missing nose wheel was confirmed by the pilot of the birddog aircraft that was accompanying FGD453. The fire retardant was jettisoned, and the flight diverted to Edmonton Intl, AB (CYEG). An emergency was declared, and the flight landed uneventfully. The aircraft stopped on the runway, and was towed to a maintenance facility.The nose wheel was recovered from CYZH. The operator’s maintenance is investigating.

C-FAFC, a Cessna 208B aircraft operated by Conair Group, was conducting fire-fighting operations from Edson, AB (CYET) with 2 persons on board. Approximately 35 nm North of CYET while returning to the firebase, the autopilot system disconnected. The flight crew attempted to re-engage the autopilot, however without success. At that time, a burning odour was detected in the cockpit. There was no sign of visible smoke and no other system failures were detected. The flight crew selected the battery master, standby power and main generator to the off position, and circuit breakers to the autopilot system were pulled. The odour then began to dissipate. The main electrical power was restored, and the aircraft proceeded to land at CYET without further issues.

C-FAVT, a Bell 407 helicopter operated by Canadian Helicopters, was conducting forest fire control operations and was on approach to release a load of water from the suspended Bambi bucket, when the long-line was inadvertently released from the helicopter belly hook. The operator’s maintenance suspected the mechanical emergency release mechanism was not fully retracted. Electrical wires at the disconnect plug were re-routed to offload pressure on the release cable.

C-GHXO, a Cessna 180J aircraft operated by Trek Aerial Surveys, was conducting pipeline patrols approximately 30 nm East of Fort St. John, BC (CYXJ) with one pilot and one observer on board. The area of inspection features a significant amount of oil and gas production infrastructure. After flying for about 3 hours, the amount of forest fire smoke had increased significantly. Coincidentally, the pilot and the observer began to feel out of sorts; cognition was reduced. The pilot decided to head back to CYXJ out of precaution and while en route, the ability to concentrate became more difficult for both the pilot and the observer. ARFF was on standby for the landing, which was uneventful. Both the pilot and observer were met by EMS for observation and nothing significant was noted. The aircraft exhaust system was checked for leaks, and none were found.

C-FJUU, a Bell 212 aircraft operated by Campbell Helicopters, was conducting fire suppression activities near Vernon Lake, BC. During the final approach to a target on the side of a mountain, the helicopter began to settle in the down flowing air. The pilot released the long-line and bucket and returned to the staging area where it landed without further incident.

C-FOFI, a Bombardier CL-415 aircraft operated by the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, departed from Gander Intl, NL (CYQX) to conduct aerial firefighting operations near Whitehead Pond, NL. The flight crew inspected several lakes and selected Whitehead Pond for scooping water while fighting a fire approximately 8 nm to the South West. While making the sixth water scoop run along the lake, the flight crew heard a loud bang. The flight crew suspected that they had struck hidden rocks, so full power was applied and a go around was conducted. Both left water drop doors indicated open, and the hydraulic quantity indicated low. The hydraulic pressure was normal, and airspeed below maximum open door speed was maintained for the return to CYQX. While enroute, attempts to close the doors were unsuccessful. The flight crew completed the checklist related to the low hydraulic quantity, manually jettisoned the remaining water, and landed without further incident at CYQX.The aircraft's lower left hull sustained substantial damage.

C-GWCY, a Boeing 737-600 aircraft operated by WestJet, was conducting flight WJA137 from Calgary Intl (CYYC), AB to Vancouver Intl (CYVR), BC with 5 crew members and 99 passengers on board. Approximately 5 minutes prior to the top of descent, the lead flight attendant informed the pilots that a sulphur like smell was observed in the overhead bins, in the vicinity of Row 2. The flight crew declared a PAN PAN, and landed without further incident. Once at the gate, a fire crew proceeded on board and identified a smell from a WestJet commissary cooler bag in the overhead bin, above Row 2. The bag was removed and searched with no heat source identified. The aircraft was returned to service.

C-FBRP, a Cessna 525B aircraft operated by Tricycle Lane Aviation, was conducting a private flight from Scottsdale (KSDL), AZ to Calgary Intl (CYYC), AB with 2 pilots and 4 passengers on board. During the turn to final approach at CYYC at approximately 2000 feet AGL, the flight crew received a BAGGAGE SMOKE indication. The flight crew carried on with the approach, and declared an emergency. The aircraft landed without incident, vacated the runway, and was met by ARFF. No smoke was present; the flight crew elected not to evacuate the aircraft. Fire crews inspected the aircraft and no heat source was detected. The operator’s maintenance inspected the forward and aft baggage compartment smoke detection system. No faults were found. The issue was entered into the operator’s Safety Management System (SMS) for tracking, and the aircraft was released back to service.

C-GYSK, a Convair CV340/580 aircraft operated by the Province of Saskatchewan/Northern Air Operations, was conducting a local flight as TKR474 from Prince Albert (Glass Field) (CYPA), SK with 3 crew members on board. During the initial climb after the takeoff, the flight crew noted an issue with the number 1 engine propeller (Hamilton Standard 54H60-77), and decided to do a precautionary engine (Allison 501-D22G) shutdown. The flight crew declared an emergency, and returned to CYPA where the aircraft landed without further incident.An inspection of the propeller system by the operator's maintenance revealed defective o-rings inside the propeller hub. The operator has filed a Service Difficulty Report (SDR) with Transport Canada.

On 04 May 2019, the Lakes District Air Service Ltd. Cessna 182E (registration C-FLVN, serial number 18253755) was conducting a fire surveillance flight under daytime visual flight rules. The flight was being conducted on behalf of the BC Wildfire Service in the vicinity of Smithers, British Columbia, with the pilot and 3 crew members on board. Approximately 3 hours into the flight, the pilot transmitted a Mayday before communication was lost. The 406 MHz emergency locator transmitter activated on impact and its signal was received by the Canadian Mission Control Centre. A helicopter search was conducted and the aircraft wreckage was located in a forested area approximately 50 nautical miles north of Smithers, 500 feet north of the Babine River, 5.6 nautical miles east of the Silver Hilton Lodge airstrip. The aircraft had collided with trees and terrain. One crew member survived the crash and was transported to hospital by helicopter. The pilot and the other 2 crew members were fatally injured. The aircraft was destroyed; there was no post-impact fire.UPDATED: 26 MAY 2020
confirmed_note: fire surveillance flight for BC Wildfire Service

Summary: C-GMAF, a Canadair CL215 1A10 water bomber aircraft operated by Air Spray Air Tankers, was conducting flight Tanker 250 in support of firefighting/fire management activities in the area of West Hawk Lake, MB with 2 pilots on board. During an active firefighting operation at approximately 3 nautical miles east of West Hawk Lake, the left wing sponson struck the tip of a tall spruce tree as the aircraft was in a left hand turn. The aircraft departed the fire area, and landed without further incident at Winnipeg/James Armstrong Richardson Intl (CYWG), MB. There were no injuries.The operator's maintenance inspected the aircraft and replaced the left wing sponson due to damage. The aircraft was returned to service.

C-GCGB, a Bell 212 aircraft operated by Star Helicopters, was conducting bucketing operations in support of forest fire fighting activity, approximately 15 nm south east of Lac La Biche (CYLB), AB. During a lift of water from a pond, the pilot experienced difficulties in controlling the yaw. The collective was reduced, and a power loss of the number 1 engine (Pratt and Whitney Canada PT6T-3B) occurred. The pilot returned to the staging area, and conducted an uneventful single-engine approach and landing. The operator’s maintenance observed damage to the number 1 engine. The engine was removed for replacement. There was no other damage to the helicopter.

C-GSLI, a Bell 212 aircraft operated by Skyline Helicopters, was conducting aerial firefighting operations from a lease site located 22 nm south southwest of High Level (CYOJ), AB with only the pilot on board. After the operation was completed, the pilot returned to the lease site, placed the water bucket on the ground, and maneuvered the helicopter in a rearward direction to put the longline down. The helicopter began to descend, and the pilot increased the collective and power in an attempt to arrest the descent. The helicopter continued to descend and struck the ground. The landing gear skid tubes broke free of the cross tubes, and the helicopter began to pitch forward. The pilot was able to gain altitude, stabilized the helicopter, and released the longline. The helicopter was manoeuvered away from the detached skid tubes, and the pilot was able to settle it on its belly. The engines were secured, and the pilot evacuated. There were no injuries.

C-FFKA, an Aerospatiale AS350 B3 aircraft operated by Airspan Helicopters, was conducting operations in support of forest fire fighting in the vicinity of Manning, AB with 1 pilot and 4 passengers on board. While maneuvering near a fire, a risk of collision occurred with C-GIRZ, a Bell 212 aircraft equipped with a long line and bucket, operated by Alpine Helicopters. C-GIRZ was approximately 450-600 feet to the left and slightly higher than C-FFKA, who maneuvered to the right to reduce the potential for a collision.

C-FYDN, a privately registered Piper PA-12 aircraft on floats, was conducting a flight from an outpost camp at Domain Lake, ON to another outpost camp at Optic Lake, ON with 1 pilot and 1 passenger on board. The aircraft was reported overdue at destination, and was found near the shore of Domain Lake the following day by another aircraft. C-FYDN collided with terrain, and the accident caused a forest fire. The Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources responded to the forest fire, and the Ontario Provincial Police subsequently attended to the scene. The 2 occupants were fatally injured, and the aircraft was destroyed. No ELT signal was detected.

C-GOGZ, a Bombardier CL-415 water bomber aircraft operated by the Province of Ontario, was conducting fire suppression operations near Pikangikum (CYPM), ON with 2 pilots on board. While scooping water on a lake, the flight crew heard a bang and immediately received failure indications on the bomb system panel. The flight crew aborted the pickup, climbed out of the lake, and returned to Dryden Regional (CYHD), ON where the aircraft landed without further incident. The aircraft sustained minor damage to the hull and water bombing system.

operation: AIR TRANSPORT; FIRE FIGHTING / FIRE MANAGEMENT
Summary: C-GNYI, a Bell 212 aircraft operated by Airspan Helicopters, was operating on a forest fire approximately 23 nm north west of Manning, AB. C-GNYI was dispatched along with 4 other medium size helicopters to rescue firefighters that had become trapped by a forest fire. While approaching the area, C-GFHP, an Aerospatiale AS350 B2 aircraft operated by Highpoint Helicopters, passed above C-GNYI with only 100 to 150 feet of separation. At the time of the occurrence, there were three radio frequencies in use with significant frequency congestion. Visibility varied from unlimited to 2-3 nm in smoke.

C-FJUU, a Bell 212 aircraft operated by Campbell Helicopters, was conducting local aerial firefighting operations from High Level (CYOJ), AB with only the pilot on board. During the first flight of the day, the pilot inadvertently depressed the cargo release button. The Bambi bucket and longline jettisoned from the helicopter, and landed in a wooded area. There was no damage or injuries to any ground based structures, or personnel. The helicopter returned to CYOJ and was not damaged.

C-FHKF, a Convair 440 aircraft operated by Conair Group, was conducting flight FGD455 on a fire suppression mission from Calgary/Springbank (CYBW), AB with two crew members on board. Shortly after the departure from CYBW, the flight crew observed a fire warning light for the number 1 engine (Allison/Rolls Royce 501-D13D). The power was reduced on the affected engine, and the light extinguished; consequently, the flight crew elected to return to CYBW. The load of fire retardant was released into a forested area prior to the return. During the initial approach at CYBW, the fire warning light illuminated once again. The flight crew shut the number 1 engine down as per the QRH, and completed an uneventful single-engine approach and landing.The operator’s maintenance observed that a clamp associated with the number one engine exhaust duct had failed, allowing hot exhaust gases to be directed at the fire sensors in zone 1. The clamp was replaced, and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-FVTS, a Bell 212 aircraft operated by Tasman Helicopters, was conducting forest fire-fighting operations near Steen River (CFB7), AB with 1 pilot on board. During bucketing operations at approximately 300 feet AGL, the pilot observed that the number 2 engine fire light had illuminated. The pilot followed the emergency procedures for an engine fire indication, and subsequently discharged both fire retardant bottles. The right engine (Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6T-3) was shut down, and a successful single-engine approach and landing was completed.The operator’s maintenance found that a fire detector amplifier was unserviceable.

C-FHTS, a Bell 214ST helicopter operated by Héli-Transport, was conducting aerial firefighting bucket operations approximately 25 nm east south-east of High Level (CYOJ), AB with only the pilot on board. During the flight, the number 1 engine (General Electric CT7-2A) chip detector light came on briefly. All engine indications were normal, so the pilot continued the flight. Shortly thereafter, the number 1 engine chip detector light intermittently illuminated for 30 seconds, and remained illuminated. The pilot left the bucket circuit, reduced the power, and initiated a return to CYOJ. The checklist was actioned, and the number 1 engine was shut down. A PAN PAN was declared, and the aircraft returned to CYOJ without further incident. There were no injuries to the pilot, and the helicopter received no damage. The operator’s maintenance found a carbon particle on the number 1 chip detector.

C-FKFM, a Convair 580 aircraft operated by Conair Group, was conducting local aerial firefighting operations as flight FDG454 from Whitecourt (CYZU), AB with only the 2 pilots on board. Shortly after the IFR departure in clouds, the flight crew noticed that the cabin started to fill with smoke. The cockpit remained relatively clear of smoke. The flight crew declared an emergency, and returned to CYZU. During the descent as power was reduced, the smoke was observed to reduce. When power was increased, the smoke began to increase again. The flight crew actioned the checklist, and conducted an uneventful landing. The aircraft was able to taxi back to the apron and shutdown normally. The operator’s maintenance found burnt duct tape on the insulation of the tail de-icing ductwork.

C-GZCF, a Lockheed 188C Electra aircraft operated by Air Spray (1967), was conducting ferry flight ASB490 from Slave Lake (CYZH), AB to Red Deer Regional (CYQF), AB with 2 pilots and 2 aircraft maintenance engineers on board. During landing gear retraction on departure from CYZH, the left main landing gear did not retract properly. As the flight crew continued the flight to CYQF, various attempts to extend the landing gear were made while troubleshooting, however none were successful. Subsequently, the decision to land the aircraft with all landing gears retracted was made. In preparation for the landing, the aircraft dumped fuel and ARFF was placed on standby for the arrival. The aircraft touched down on Runway 35, and came to rest approximately half way down the runway, with the right wing in the grass on the east side of the runway. The flight crew evacuated; there were no injuries or post-landing fire. There was some minor damage to the belly mounted retardant tank and to all blades on the four propellers.Update 5 July 2019. The operator's maintenance determined that the forward door mechanism (P/N 810265) and gear roller (P/N S14-7625) clearance were found to exceed the requirements described in service bulletin  88/SB-558 and maintenance manual 32-0, paragraph 1.C (f).

C-GAVQ, a Bell 407 aircraft operated by Summit Helicopters, was conducting forest fire suppression operations 30 nm north of Terrace (CYXT), BC with only the pilot on board. While attempting to release the load of water on the fire, the pilot inadvertently depressed the cargo hook release button, resulting in the release of the bucket and longline. There were no injuries.

C-FAWQ, un appareil de type Canadair CL-215-6B11 CL251T exploité par le Service aérien gouvernemental (SAG) du Gouvernement du Québec, effectuait le vol Q239 selon les règles de vol à vue depuis Roberval (CYRJ), QC à destination d’un feu de forêt situé environ 45 milles marins au nord-ouest de CYRJ, avec 2 pilotes à bord. Lors d’une manœuvre d’écopage sur un lac, la coque de l’avion est entrée en collision avec un haut-fond, causant des dommages à celle-ci. L’équipage a cessé les opérations de lutte contre les incendies, et est retourné à CYRJ où l’aéronef s’est posé sans encombre. Une fois les dommages évalués, un permis de vol a été délivré afin de ramener l’aéronef à la base d’opérations principales du SAG pour y être réparé.

C-FTXJ, un Canadair CL-215 exploité par le service aérien gouvernemental avec à son bord 2 pilotes effectuait un vol local au départ de Val-d'Or (CYVO) QUE lorsque l'équipage de conduite a observé une indication anormale des paramètres du moteur droit sans perte de puissance. Le moteur (PWC R-2800) a été arrêté par précaution, une urgence a été déclarée et l'appareil est revenu se poser à CYVO sans difficulté.

C-GCGB, a Star Helicopters Ltd. Bell 212, was conducting forest fire fighting operations 92 nm NW of Fort McMurray (CYMM), AB with one pilot on board. While in the hover just prior to touch down, the tail rotor struck a tree damaging one tail rotor blade. The pilot landed the helicopter without further issues.

C-GMHT, a Bell 206L helicopter operated by Canadian Helicopters Ltd, was conducting forest fire control operations near Pasadena, NL. The pilot attached the water bucket to the hook and proceeded to pick up a bucket of water. The water would not release when the water release button was pressed. After landing and checking that the cables were not tangled, the pilot departed and decided to check if the release would work, but hit the cargo release button instead. The water bucket released and fell into a pond. It was later determined that the water release button was incorrectly wired.

C-GOVT, a Rockwell Commander 695A operated by the Province of Saskatchewan as flight BD167, landed on runway 26 at Prince Albert/Glass Field (CYPA), SK with only the pilot on board. After turning off the runway onto taxi way Delta, the nose gear collapsed. The aircraft came to a sudden stop and the engines were then shut down. There were no injuries and the aircraft sustained substantial damage. The aircraft was removed from the taxi way and taken to the tanker base. The operator will advise of their findings.

C-GYSK, a Convair CV340/580 aircraft operated by the Province of Saskatchewan/Northern Air Operations, was conducting a local flight as TKR475 from Prince Albert/Glass Field (CYPA), SK with 2 crew members on board. While joining downwind in the circuit, the flight crew noted an issue with the right engine propeller. The flight crew actioned the checklist, shut down and secured the right engine, declared an emergency and returned to airport. The aircraft landed safely with emergency services standing by. No impact on operations.The operator's maintenance identified that the control valve of the propeller controller unit had failed. The control valve was replaced and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-FBRH, un Cessna 337G exploité par MAG Aerospace Canada Corp effectuait un vol selon les règles de vol à vue depuis l’aéroport de Sudbury, ON (CYSB) à destination de Val-d’Or, QC (CYVO). Lors de son atterrissage sur la piste 18, une rafale de vent a contribué à faire rebondir l’aéronef sur la piste. Suite au rebond, l’aéronef a touché durement le sol ce qui a provoqué l’affaissement du train d’atterrissage avant causant le heurt de l’hélice au sol. L’aéronef s’est immobilisé sur la piste. Le pilote seul à bord n’a pas été blessé. L’aéronef a subi des dommages importants. La compagnie a temporairement suspendu les vols de ses autres Cessna 337G afin de procéder à une inspection détaillée des trains d’atterrissage avant et aucune anomalie n’a été rapportée.

C-GFPP, a Rockwell International Aero Commander 690 operated by Air Spray (1967) Ltd., was conducting a local flight 17 nm east of Gimli Industrial Park Airport (CYGM) MB. During cruise the pilot noted a rapid rise in ITT on the number 2 engine. The pilot elected to shutdown the engine and returned to CYGM. The aircraft landed safely without further incident.The operator's maintenance identified the a fault in the engine temperature indicating system.

C-FBRG a MAG Aerospace Cessna 337G aircraft, was returning from a fire detection patrol, to Chapleau, ON (CYLD) and joined the circuit for Runway 23. The aircraft bounced on touch down and the landing gear didn't feel correct after the bounce. A second approach and touchdown was conducted on Runway 23 and again the aircraft bounced and the pilot conducted an overshoot. C-FBRG left the zone to troubleshoot the situation and confirmed that the gear was down and locked. C-FBRG returned and conducted a normal full stop landing on Runway 28.After shutdown, a MAG Aerospace AME noticed that the front propeller had been damaged. A thorough maintenance inspection of the landing gear system was completed which included multiple swings of the landing gear with no faults found. The front propeller was damaged and no other structural damage was found. The front propeller and engine was replaced, and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-GKGA, a Beech 1900C operated by Skylink Express Inc. as flight SLQ720, was enroute from Winnipeg/James Armstrong Richardson INTL (CYWG), MB to Regina INTL (CYQR), SK with a crew of 2 onboard. During descent into CYQR, the crew heard a thump followed by a split in engine RPM and a slight yaw movement of the aircraft. Efforts to correct the split in engine RPM revealed the right propeller lever was jammed. The crew noticed the right engine (PT6A-65B) cowling had dislodged and remained only partially in place. The crew declared a PAN PAN with CYWG center and continued on to CYQR. The aircraft landed safely and came to a stop on the runway where they were met by fire crew for inspection. The aircraft then taxied off the runway. An inspection of the aircraft confirmed the right upper engine cowl had dislodged and interfered with the propeller governor, jamming the propeller control arm.

C-GNYI, a Bell 212 helicopter operated by Airspan Helicopters Ltd. was engaged in forest fire fighting operations at the end of Butte Inlet. C-GNYI departed the fire location for fuel in the Toba Inlet with a Bambi Bucket attached.  On short final to the fuel barge, the pilot unintentionally pressed the belly cargo release button and jettisoned the slung load (Bambi Bucket) short of the fuel barge.  The bucket landed in the water and could not be retrieved. The helicopter landed on the fuel barge without further event. There was no injury, damage to property or the environment, beyond the loss of the Bambi Bucket.

C-FAHG, a Bell 212 operated by Alpine Helicopters was conducting operations in support of forest fire fighting in the vicinity of Ghost River, Alberta. The pilot was repositioning the helicopter to a location previously utilized. During the approach for landing, the pilot noticed a tree top that appeared to have been recently broken off. An uneventful landing and shut down was completed. Upon further inspection of the helicopter, the pilot noticed that the main rotor blades had sustained damage consistent with a tree strike. The aircraft was subsequently inspected by maintenance personnel, and ferried to a maintenance location for repair. There were no injuries.

N806NW, an Airbus A330-323 aircraft operated by Delta Air Lines, was conducting flight DAL30 from Hartsfield/Jackson Atlanta (KATL), GA to London/Heathrow (EGLL), England. When in cruise flight at about 233 nm east-southeast of St. John’s (CYYT), NL, the flight crew smelled a wood smoke odour in the cockpit. The flight crew contacted cabin crewmembers, who confirmed smelling the odour in the cabin as well. The flight crew subsequently declared an emergency, began descending and completed the quick reference handbook (QRH) procedure for smoke and fumes; however, the odour did not dissipate. Following a discussion with company maintenance personnel, the flight crew decided to divert to CYYT where the flight landed without further incident. Maintenance personnel inspected the cabin, cargo, and avionics compartments and reported no finding of smoke or haze. No faults were recorded by aircraft systems. On 22 October 2020, multiple flights across eastern Canada reported the detection of smell related to smoke carried aloft at high altitude in Canadian airspace, which originated from ongoing wildfires in Colorado.

The Sky Regional Airlines Embraer 175 (AC7505, C-FXJC) was parked at the gate in Ottawa/ MCIA (CYOW)and was boarding for the flight to Toronto/ LBPIA (CYYZ). Approximately half of the passengers were boarded when the flight crew heard "FIRE" from the cabin and noticed smoke coming from the heater attached to the bridge. Boarding was stopped, and the ground crew began to use fire extinguishers on the heater; ARFF also responded to the scene. The captain decided not to deplane the passengers due to the location of the faulty heater underneath the bridge, but had passengers deplane after it was safe to do so. The aircraft was covered on the left side with the retardant residue, and after company maintenance was contacted it was decided to remove aircraft from service until a thorough inspection of the aircraft was completed. No damage was found and after cleaning the aircraft it was returned to service.

C-GYLD, a Rockwell International 690B aircraft operated by Mag Aerospace, was conducting a local training flight from Dryden Regional (CYHD), ON as flight BD160 with 2 crew on board. During the initial takeoff, the crew selected landing gear up and heard a bang followed by an in-transit landing gear indication. The crew then decided to select the landing gear down and received an unsafe nose gear indication. The crew conducted a fly-by and received notification that the nose gear seemed to be extended. An emergency was declared and the crew proceeded to land the aircraft on Runway 30. During landing, the aircraft settled on the main gear and the crew then received a nose gear safe indication. As the nose gear settled the aircraft immediately veered to the right and came to a stop with the right main gear off the side of the runway. An inspection by the operator revealed that the nose gear wheel was turned to the right and did not centered.

C-GOGH, a Canadair CL-215-6B11 (Series CL-415) operated by the Province of Ontario, Ministry of Natural Resources, was conducting a local training flight at the Sault Ste. Marie Airport, ON (CYAM). While conducting the third circuit on runway 12, the flight crew inadvertently landed the aircraft with the landing gear retracted. The aircraft came to a stop on the runway surface. There was significant damage to the belly of the aircraft. There were no injuries.

C-GOSX, a Piper PA-60 aircraft operated by Forest Protection Limited, was returning to Fredericton Intl (CYFC), NB on a VFR flight after conducting night currency circuits at Saint John (CYSJ), NB with one pilot onboard. While on final approach to Runway 27 in CYFC, the pilot felt an impact on the left side of the aircraft and believed that a possible bird strike had occurred. After landing, company maintenance personnel inspected the aircraft and it was determined that the aircraft had come in contact with trees. The aircraft sustained minor damage. No injuries were reported.The operator’s maintenance department will be removing the left engine and propeller for inspection and making minor repairs to the left landing gear door assembly.

C-FCHD, a Bell 205A-1 helicopter operated by Custom Helicopters Ltd, was conducting water bucket operations near the fire base at Marchand, MB. The cargo-hook release switch had been de-activated prior to bucket operation in accordance with the operator's standard operating procedures. While in the climb at 70 knots, after releasing a full load of water onto a fire, the cargo hook released un-commanded. The water bucket fell into an open area and was retrieved un-damaged. During the previous 2 days the helicopter had made 129 drops with the occurrence hook and bucket. The operator's maintenance personnel duplicated the un-commanded release while testing with a spare bucket. The cargo hook was replaced and operations resumed without further incident.

C-FSPM, a Gulfstream American Corporation 690D Aero Commander aircraft operated by the Saskatchewan Public Safety Agency (Air Operations), was conducting flight BD161 from Prince Albert/Glass Field (CYPA), SK to La Ronge/Barber Field (CYVC), SK. During the initial climb after taking off from Runway 08, the cabin air became hazy and smoky. The flight crew communicated with Prince Albert Radio FSS and advised that the aircraft would perform a 180 degree turn and return to Runway 26. The flight crew conducted the actions for smoke in the cockpit and closed the bleed air valves. The smoke subsequently began to clear. The flight crew declined emergency services and the subsequent landing was uneventful. The operator's maintenance personnel determined that the environmental system turbocharger oil-pump seal had failed allowing oil mist to enter the cabin air system. The turbocharger was replaced. The operator submitted a SDR (20210514012).

C-GRWK, a Bell 205A-1 helicopter operated by Custom Helicopters Ltd., was transporting 5 members of a Helitac crew from the Gypsumville Fire Base, MB to a fire near Barker Lake, MB. When the helicopter was approximately 30 nm NW of Gypsumville, the occupant of the left cockpit-seat noticed smoke in the left chin bubble area. The pilot conducted a precautionary landing and contacted the operator's maintenance personnel. The No. 2 battery relay was determined to be at fault. The No. 2 battery was de-activated and the aircraft returned to service with the item deferred. The relay was replaced upon return to the Gypsumville Fire Base. The operator submitted a Service Difficulty Report (SDR) concerning the failed relay.

At 1640 on 07 June 2021, the Helicopter Transport Services (Canada) Inc. (HTSC) Bell 214ST helicopter (registration C GDYZ, serial number 28109) with only the pilot on board departed from the Nipigon, Ontario, fire base on a forest-fire suppression flight to wildfire Nipigon 8, located approximately 28 nautical miles northeast of Nipigon. The pilot was flying the helicopter from the left seat and was wearing a lap belt and helmet. The aircraft was equipped with a 550-gallon collapsible water bucket on a 150-foot long line. The pilot conducted approximately 45 drops before informing the fire boss on board the bird dog/spotter aircraft that the helicopter was low on fuel and that the end of his duty day was nearing.The return trip from Nipigon 8 to the Nipigon fire base was flown at 3000 feet above sea level, about 1600 feet above ground level. The helicopter was travelling at 70 to 74 knots in a nose-down attitude of roughly 7° due to the empty water bucket when the pilot was alerted by a vibration in the tail rotor pedals and a grinding noise. Moments later, the 42° BOX OIL PRESS and 90° BOX OIL PRESS annunciators for the 2 tail rotor gearboxes illuminated, and there was an audible engine overspeed noise. The helicopter yawed to the right and the nose began to pitch down.The pilot lowered the collective control and moved the cyclic control aft to counteract the nose-down tendency, increase the main rotor rpm, and enter autorotative flight. As the helicopter began to spin, the pilot released the long line and water bucket by kicking the manual cargo release pedal. The pilot transmitted a Mayday call on the enroute frequency (126.7 MHz) and informed other aircraft working on the same fire that he had lost tail rotor control. While the helicopter was descending at approximately 1000 to 1500 fpm, the pilot made 3 attempts to use some engine power to fly the helicopter to a suitable landing area near a small lake. He was able to regain some control over the adverse yaw via airflow acting on the vertical stabilizer. As the helicopter descended below treetop height, he raised the collective control to cushion the landing, at which point the low rotor rpm horn activated. At 1924, the helicopter landed on its left skid gear with almost no forward speed. The emergency locator transmitter activated automatically and there was no fire. The helicopter was substantially damaged.The pilot shut down the engines and electrical systems and was able to climb out of the right-side cockpit door. Another helicopter with fire fighters on board responded to the Mayday call and, within a few minutes, landed near the accident site. The seriously injured pilot was transported directly to a hospital in Thunder Bay, Ontario.

C-GBSC, un Cessna R182 exploité par Exact Air, effectuait un vol selon les règles de vol à vue depuis l’aérodrome de Lachute (CSE4) QC, à destination de Manic-5, QC (CMN5) avec seul le pilote à bord. Alors que l'appareil était en vol de croisière, à une altitude de 3000 pieds ASL, à environ 20 NM au nord-nord-ouest de La Tuque, le moteur a perdu de la puissance. Le pilote a effectué les vérifications d’urgence et déclaré un MAYDAY. Après avoir appliqué du réchauffe carburateur, le moteur a eu quelques ratées et la puissance normale est revenue. L’appareil s’est arrêté à l’aéroport de St-Honoré (CYRC) Qc, où une inspection a été effectuée et aucune anomalie n’a été détectée.

C-GGZQ, a Bell 206LR helicopter operated by Canadian Helicopters Limited, was conducting a flight from Fredericton International Airport, (CYFC), NB to Grand Falls Airport (CCK3), NB. In cruise, the pilot noticed the engine oil pressure intermittently showing above the maximum pressures of 130 psi. The pilot planned to carry out a precautionary landing in a field to check the oil levels. On the approach to landing, as the pilot raised the collective, the main gear box (MGB) pressure dropped below minimum and the caution light illuminated for 4 seconds. At this point the pilot transitioned to a no hover landing. After landing, the collective was reduced to full down and the MGB pressure returned to the normal range.After shut down, the pilot noticed that the main gearbox had no oil in the sight glass. An AME checked the chip plugs and removed 3 quarts of oil from the engine oil reservoir as it was over full from the transfer of oil. The MGB was topped up with 4 quarts of oil and a ground run was completed before the helicopter transited to Woodstock NB. The company completed a full serviceability check on the MGB, chip plugs and freewheel unit.

On 28 June 2021, the Yellowhead Helicopters Ltd. Bell Textron Inc. model 212 helicopter (registration C-GYHQ, serial number 30933) was conducting operations in support of forest fire fighting efforts approximately 4 nautical miles west-northwest of Evansburg, Alberta. At approximately 1800 Mountain Daylight Time, the helicopter departed the staging area to complete a series of 3 flights transporting groups of forest fire fighters back to the staging area. The first 2 trips were completed uneventfully. During the last trip, as the helicopter was approaching the landing area to pick up the final group of fire fighters, one of the main rotor blades separated from the rotor head assembly. The second rotor blade and rotor head assembly then broke free from the helicopter and the helicopter crashed. The pilot, the sole occupant on board, was fatally injured. There was a post-impact fire that destroyed the helicopter. A signal from the 406 MHz emergency locator transmitter was not received.UPDATED 02 JULY 2024

C-FHKF, a General Dynamics Convair 440 aerial fire fighting aircraft operated by Conair, was conducting flight TANKER455 from the Penticton airport (CYYF), BC tanker airbase with 2 flight crew members on board. C-FKFL, another General Dynamics Convair 440 operated by Conair, was not operating and was parked at the north end of the tanker base near Taxiway C. As TANKER455 was taxiing northbound for departure towards Taxiway C its left wingtip contacted the left wing of C-FKFL. There were no injuries. C-FHKF received minor damage. C-FKFL received substantial damage.

C-FVAS, a Cessna 337 aircraft operated by Can-West Corporate Air Charters Ltd., was conducting an aerial fire detection/bird dog operation in the Stoney Rapids (CYSF), Saskatchewan area with the pilot and one passenger on board. After completing the aerial fire detection operation, the crew returned to CYSF where the pilot selected landing gear down during final approach to Runway 24. During initial touchdown, the landing gear collapsed and the aircraft came to a stop on the centerline of the runway. The pilot and passenger were able to evacuate the aircraft without injury. The aircraft sustained significant damage.

C-FIKM, a Cessna 337G aircraft operated by Mag Aerospace Canada, was conducting fire detection/bird dog operations in the vicinity of Pickle Lake (CYPL), ON with only the pilot onboard. While in cruise, the rear engine RPM began to fluctuate. The pilot conducted a precautionary shutdown of the rear engine and returned CYPL. AARF was put on standby and the aircraft then landed safely. A subsequent inspection of the system revealed an indication issue with the RPM gauge.

C-GVSK, a Convair 340/580 aircraft operated by the Saskatchewan Public Safety Agency-Air Operations, was en route from Buffalo Narrows (CYVT), SK to La Ronge (CYVC), SK via the Forks wildfire. After finishing wild fire suppression activities, while en route to CYVC, the crew of C-GVSK observed fluctuations in the propeller rpms and that the propellers were out of sync. They attempted to manually sync the props, which resulted in the right-hand propeller (Hamilton Standard 54H60-77) going into an overspeed condition and an associated pitch lock. The crew made attempts to recover from the pitch lock but were unable. They then shut down the right-hand engine (Allison 501-D22G) as per the checklist. The flight crew declared an emergency and carried out an uneventful landing in YVC with the right-hand engine inoperative.During a subsequent inspection,  maintenance crews troubleshot the snag and replaced the R/H valve housing on the prop governor and the propeller synchronization box.  The aircraft was returned to service the following day.

C-GIPL, an Airspray 1967 Ltd. Aero Commander 695B, was operating as ASB062 from Prince George International Airport (CYXS), BC with 2 crew members on board conducting fire suppression south of CYXS. During the operation, the crew became aware of a possible hydraulic failure. Within a short time, the hydraulic failure was confirmed through the hydraulic pressure gauge. The crew completed the hydraulic failure checklist and decided to return to CYXS. As the aircraft approached CYXS the crew reviewed the flapless landing and emergency braking procedures. The crew then completed the landing gear emergency extension checklist and declared a PAN PAN with the CYXS tower. The aircraft landed safely without further incident with ARFF on standby. There was no fire and no injuries.Upon inspection, the maintenance staff found the auxiliary hydraulic pump pressure switch leaking causing a loss of hydraulic pressure. The switch was replaced and the system tested successfully. The aircraft was returned to service.

C-FGPC, a privately registered Cessna 185F on amphibious floats, departed Prince George International Airport (CYXS), BC  to Mackenzie (CYZY), BC  with 2 persons on board. The flight was occurring under special VFR with forest fire smoke in the area limiting the visibility to 2 1/4 sm. Upon departure, the visibility deteriorated as the aircraft climbed. CYXS ATC asked the pilot to deviate their heading to accommodate inbound traffic. The deviation placed the aircraft in an area with even less visibility so the pilot elected to descend and follow the Fraser River northbound. As the river became more difficult to follow, the pilot elected to land on it. The landing gear had not been retracted after take off and upon touchdown the aircraft flipped over. Both occupants managed to egress the overturned aircraft and climb onto one of the floats while waiting for rescue. The pilot received minor injuries and the passenger received serious injuries. The aircraft was substantially damaged.

C-FTXK, a Canadair CL-215 operated by Gouvernement du Québec (Service aérien gouvernemental), was conducting a flight from Dryden Regional (CYHD) ON. to The Pas (CYQD) MB. When applying power for takeoff, the right engine (Pratt and Whitney-USA R2800 CA3) shutdown, the propeller feathered, and the takeoff was discontinued.The operator's maintenance found that the accelerating pump on the carburetor was at fault. The unit was replaced and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-GRHJ, an Aerospatiale AS 350B2 SD-2 helicopter, operated by Remote Helicopters, was engaged in aerial fire suppression 42 NM WSW of Big River (CKX8), SK. While water bucketing, the engine (Avco Lycoming LTS-101-700D2) lost power. The pilot jettisoned the bucket and conducted a successful autorotative landing near a slough. The pilot was uninjured and was extracted from the site by another helicopter. The helicopter was undamaged.The operator's maintenance personnel identified a problem was with the engine airflow modulator. The helicopter was repaired temporarily and then flown to Meadow Lake (CYLJ), SK under a special flight permit. The airflow modulator actuator was replaced. A detailed inspection of the tail rotor system was conducted with nil damage noted.

C-FRMH, a Canadian Helicopters Limited Sikorsky S-61N, was conducting bucketing operations in support of forest fire suppression activity southeast of Penticton (CYYF), BC with 2 crew on board. After lifting the water bucket out of the lake, the helicopter transitioned into forward flight. As they accelerated through approximately 30 knots, at an estimated 100 feet above the lake, the crew felt the bucket release. They confirmed that both the bucket and the long line assembly had fallen in to the lake. The crew then returned to CYYF and landed. Maintenance examined the manual hook release cable assembly and found that it had been assembled incorrectly. This allowed for the cable assembly to inadvertently activate the manual release mechanism in the cargo hook. The manual hook release cable assembly was put together correctly and returned to service.

C-FVHS, a Bell 212 helicopter operated by Vortex Helicopters Inc., departed Kenora (CYQK), ON. to conduct forest firefighting duties approximately 35 NM north of Kenora equipped with a 150 foot long line and water bucket attached. The helicopter completed a cycle of bucketing and was returning to a staging area for fuel. During the return flight the pilot noticed the bucket was twisted. The pilot decided to stabilize the bucket by adding water from a nearby lake. During the process, the pilot lost sight of the bucket and the helicopter began to drift to the right. The pilot then felt a tug on the helicopter and seconds later the helicopter impacted the water. The pilot, who was seated in the left seat, exited the helicopter, swam to shore and was picked up by a passing helicopter and transported to the staging area and was then transported to the local hospital with minor injuries. The helicopter was substantially damaged. The visibility in the area was reported as being reduced to 2 to 3 miles in smoke and the winds were reported as calm.

C-GZIV, an Aerospatiale AS350 B3 helicopter, operated by Canadian Helicopters Limited (CHL), was dispatched to fire #G12340 approx. 36nm SSW of Prince George Airport (CYXS), BC. Shortly after starting water bucketing operations on the fire, the pilot smelled an acrid smoke. He elected to terminate the operation and pulled out of the dip, released the water in the bucket, and the smell of smoke became stronger. He initiated a 360 degree turn to assess whether the helicopter was on fire, and as he pulled out of the turn, acrid smoke started to billow over the instrument panel. He immediately turned off all unnecessary electronics and headed for the cut-block area where he'd previously set down, and declared an emergency. Once over the cut-block (approx. 3/4-1 km from the fire), he set the bucket down, released the longline, landed, and shut down. After doing an initial inspection he contacted the CHL aircraft maintenance engineer. The directional gyro was discovered to have failed and the rear of the instrument was split. The Company will file a Service Difficulty Report (SDR) with Transport Canada.

C-GJJX, an Air Tractor AT-802 operated by Forest Protection Limited, operating as Tanker 624, was conducting forest fire fighting operations out of the Miramichi (CYCH), NB Airport with 1 crew member on board. At approximately 1553 ADT, while conducting the fourth bombing run of the day, the aircraft impacted the hillside of a heavily wooded area of northern New Brunswick. The pilot sustained minor injuries and was able to walk to a nearby road, where he was taken by helicopter and ambulance to a local hospital.There was no post accident fire, however, the aircraft was destroyed.UPDATED 05 AUGUST 2022

C-GIPL, an Air Spray 1967 Limited Gulfstream Commander (Twin Commander) 695B, operating as flight ASB062, was conducting fire suppression operations from Prince George International Airport (CYXS), BC, with 2 crew members on board. During the operation southwest of CYXS, the crew became aware of a possible hydraulic failure. Within a short time, the hydraulic failure was confirmed with reference to the hydraulic pressure gauge. The crew completed the hydraulic failure checklist and decided to return to CYXS. As the aircraft approached CYXS, the crew completed the landing gear emergency extension checklist and declared an emergency with the CYXS tower. The aircraft landed safely with ARFF on standby. There were no injuries. A maintenance inspection determined that the auxiliary hydraulic pressure switch had a leak which caused a loss of hydraulic pressure. This pressure loss resulted in damage to the engine driven hydraulic pump due to lack of lubrication. The switch and pump were replaced and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-GGFP, a Jazz Aviation LP. De Havilland DHC-8-402, operating as flight JZA416, was en route from Vancouver Int'l (CYVR), BC, to Kelowna (CYLW), BC, with 4 crew members and 38 passengers on board. The initial approach, approximately 23 nautical miles North of CYLW, was in the vicinity of the White Rock Lake forest fire. During this approach, the flight experienced severe turbulence in instrument meteorological conditions while in descent through 10000 feet above sea level. The flight crew discontinued the approach. The flight diverted to CYVR and landed without further incident. There were no injuries. Subsequent to the flight, maintenance actions included a severe turbulence inspection with no faults being found. The aircraft was returned to service.See occurrences A21P0085 and A21P0087 in relation to the same turbulence event.

C-FCMR, a Central Mountain Air Beech (Textron) 1900D was operating as flight GLR728 from Prince George (CYXS), BC to Kelowna (CYLW), BC, with 2 crew members and 12 passengers on board. The initial approach, approximately 24 nautical miles North of CYLW, was in the vicinity of the White Rock Lake forest fire. The flight experienced severe turbulence in instrument meteorological conditions while in descent between 12000 feet and 11000 feet above sea level. The flight crew discontinued the approach. The flight diverted to Penticton (CYYF), BC, and landed without further incident. There were no injuries. See occurrences A21P0085 and A21P0086 in relation to the same turbulence event

C-FQWE, a WestJet Encore De Havilland DHC-8-402, operating as flight WEN3324, en route from Vancouver Int'l (CYVR), BC, to Kelowna (CYLW), BC, with 4 crew members and 46 passengers on board. The flight's initial approach, approximately 24 nautical miles north of CYLW, was in the vicinity of the White Rock Lake forest fire. During the approach, the flight experienced severe turbulence in instrument meteorological conditions while in descent through 9500 feet above sea level. The flight crew discontinued the approach. The flight diverted to CYVR and landed without further incident. There were no injuries. Subsequent maintenance actions included a severe turbulence inspection; no faults were found. The aircraft was returned to service.See occurrences A21P0086 and A21P0087 in relation to the same turbulence event

C-GLYO, an Airspan Helicopters Limited Bell 212HP, was conducting water bucketing operations 45 nautical miles east-northeast of Williams Lake Airport (CYWL), BC, with 1 pilot on board. During initial approach to a water source, the pilot felt stiffness in the tail rotor pedals and aborted the approach to diagnose the problem. Shortly thereafter, the pilot felt stiffness in the cyclic and collective that was followed by an audible bang and a squealing noise. The helicopter hydraulic caution light illuminated on the caution panel and the pilot confirmed the #1 hydraulic pressure gauge was indicating below normal operating pressure. The pilot communicated the hydraulic problem to a Bell 206 helicopter pilot operating in the vicinity and then selected the #1 hydraulic system switch to the OFF position. The stiffness felt in the cyclic and collective controls subsided while the tail rotor pedals remained stiff for the remainder of the flight. The Bell 206 pilot transmitted a MAYDAY message to the fire centre and assisted the incident pilot in finding a suitable landing location. The Bell 212 pilot performed a successful precautionary landing in a farmer's field and the MAYDAY was canceled. There were no reported injuries and no damage to the aircraft.Maintenance discovered a ruptured hydraulic pressure line immediately downstream of the #1 hydraulic pump. Additional investigation revealed metallic debris in the pressure and return ports of the #1 hydraulic integrated valve assembly.

C-GYLD, a Rockwell International Commander 690B aircraft operated by Mag Aerospace Canada as flight BD160, began its takeoff roll on Runway 12 at Thunder Bay (CYQT) ON with only the pilot on board. Shortly after rotation, the aircraft rolled into a left bank, continued to roll, and then struck the surface of Runway 07 in an inverted attitude. The pilot sustained fatal injuries. The aircraft was destroyed by the impact and a post-impact fire. AARF responded and Runway 12 and 07 were closed. The TSB deployed investigators and the investigation is ongoing.

C-FCGK, a Bell 206B helicopter operated by Heli-Recon Aerial Support Services Inc., was engaged in forest fire support approximately 18 nautical miles west of Hudson Bay (CYHB), SK. While reconnoitering a fire guard at low level, there was a loud pop and the engine (Rolls-Royce 250-C20) lost power. The turbine outlet temperature (TOT) spiked to full scale on the TOT gauge. The pilot initiated autorotation and maneuvered the helicopter to a creek south of the fire area. The pilot extended the glide and conducted a successful run-on landing onto a gravel bar. During the landing the helicopter rocked from the heels of the skids to the toes and a main rotor blade made light contact with the tail rotor driveshaft cover. The pilot and 2 passengers were uninjured. The helicopter was transported from the site and is undergoing repairs. Initial inspection by the operator's maintenance personnel identified damage to the compressor beginning near the 3rd or 4th stage .

C-FRJA, a Bombardier CL-600-2D24 (Series 900) aircraft, operated by Jazz Aviation LP (JZA7461), departed Toronto/Lester B. Pearson International Airport (CYYZ) ON, destined for Chicago O’Hare International Airport, Chicago (KORD). After leveling off at FL380 the flight crew observed a flap caution message. They actioned the appropriate QRH checklist, contacted maintenance and decided to return to YYZ. The flight crew declared a PAN PAN in order to ensure they would get runway 23 for a long final approach, and requested emergency equipment on standby. The aircraft landed without further incident. After exiting the runway, fire crews inspected the brakes and tires with no damage or heat concerns noted.

C-GJJK, an Air Tractor AT802 aircraft operated by Forest Protection Ltd was conducting a local training flight at Fredericton International Airport (CYFC), NB. The crew was conducting circuits on Runway 27 and on downwind, when checking the brake pressure, the right brake felt soft. However, the pressure came back to normal when the pilot pumped the pedal with toe pressure. On the landing rollout the aircraft slowed, however began drifting left due to weather-cocking. When the pilot corrected by depressing the right brake, the pedal went to the floor. The pilot used power and reverse to maintain directional control. The aircraft continued to drift left and exited the side of the runway into the grass, approximately 10 feet from the edge. The tower asked if the crew required assistance, and the decision was made to shut down and be towed back to the hangar by maintenance.Maintenance noted the O-ring was kinked on the right brake cylinder and fluid had leaked. The brake was secured and towed back to the hangar. No injuries or any other damage to the aircraft was noted.

C-FTXK, un Canadair CL215-1A10 exploité par le Service aérien gouvernemental sous l’indicatif QUE231, effectuait un vol local d'entrainement selon les règles de vol aux instruments depuis et à destination de l’aéroport de Québec/Jean Lesage, QC (CYQB). Alors que l’appareil revenait du lac Montauban où des exercices d'entrainement à l'eau ont eu lieu, un retour de flamme s'est produit sur le moteur de gauche. Le moteur a été éteint par mesure de précaution et une urgence (PAN PAN) a été déclarée. L'appareil s'est posé sans encombre. Il n’y a eu aucun blessé. La cause du retour de flamme est sous investigation par l'opérateur.

C-GQBA, un Viking Air Limited CL215-6B11(CL-415) exploité par le Service aérien gouvernemental sous l'indicatif GRFEU06/QUE240, effectuait un vol local d'entrainement selon les règles de vol aux instruments depuis l'aéroport de Québec/Jean Lesage, QC (CYQB). Alors que l'appareil était en vol, les pilotes ont noté un problème du système hydraulique qui indiquait un bas niveau et une basse pression. La liste de vérification du Manuel de référence rapide (QRH) a été complétée et l'équipage de conduite a déclaré une urgence (PAN PAN). L'appareil s'est posé sans encombre à CYQB. Aucun blessé. Une fuite au niveau d’une bague d’étanchéité sur le train d’atterrissage gauche a été trouvée.

C-FDOD, a Bell 412 helicopter operated by Wisk-Air Ltd., was returning 4 drums containing Jet A-1 (UN 1863) fuel from a cache near Prospect Lake, ON to the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (OMNR) fire base at Red Lake, ON. The pilot supervised the loading and the sling gear had been inspected and found serviceable prior to departure. After takeoff the pilot de-activated the electrical release on the cyclic control. Approximately 8 minutes later the load of 4 fuel drums fell to the ground. All of the drums were damaged and 3 released their contents. The remaining drum still held fuel. The fuel drums were retrieved by OMNR personnel on 12 June and remediation of the site was conducted. Details of the event were reported to CANUTEC. The operator reported that abrasion to the retaining strap connecting the load to the belly hook indicated that it had worked itself around and under the hook keeper. The hook and release mechanism were inspected and found serviceable. The emergency foot release had not been used. The operator's aircrews that used the same helicopter type and hook system were notified.

C-GSAO, a Beech 95-B55 aircraft operated by Saskatchewan Public Safety Agency, was conducting birddog flight BD154 from Buffalo Narrows (CYVT), SK. During the approach to CYVT, the aircraft landing gear would not extend. The flight crew conducted an emergency landing gear extension procedure, declared an emergency, and diverted to La Ronge (CYVC), SK. The aircraft landed safely and without incident.The operator's maintenance discovered the landing gear "gear down microswitch" was stuck. The switch was cleaned and tested, and the gear was cycled as per Aircraft Maintenance Manual. No additional faults were found and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-GSHD, a Skyline Helicopters Ltd. Agusta AW119 MK II (Koala), was conducting bucketing operations in support of wildfire management (wildfire MWF052) in the vicinity of Birch Mountains, Alberta. The pilot departed the fire area and was proceeding to refuel at Birch Mountain when he observed that the "Cargo Open Hook" caution light had illuminated. The collective load release switch was guarded and the manual floor release was fully down. The pilot started slowing down and that is when the external load (Bambi Bucket and longline) departed the helicopter. The pilot diverted to Ft. McMurray to assess the issue.Company maintenance observed that a crimp on the manual cable release had failed. The cable was removed and a serviceable unit installed and the helicopter was returned to service.

C-GBOW, a Canadair CL215-1A10 aircraft operated by Air Spray (1967) Ltd., was conducting fire suppression operations in the vicinity of Pukatawagan, MB. After a water pickup, the crew noticed excessive oil on the right engine cowl. The water load was dropped and the aircraft climbed to 5500 feet ASL. The right engine was shut down per the emergency checklist and the aircraft diverted to The Pas (CYQD), MB for an uneventful landing.The operator's maintenance inspected the aircraft and identified an oil leak coming from the right engine nose case. The nose case was replaced and the engine was subsequently ground run with no further faults identified.

C-FVFH, a Lockheed 188A (Electra) operated by Air Spray (1967) Ltd, was conducting aerial firefighting operations from West Kootenay Regional Airport (CYCG), BC, with 2 pilots on board. During takeoff, the No. 2 engine (Allison 501-D13) suffered a power loss when take off power was set. The flight crew rejected the take off at approximately 50 knots and taxied off the runway. There were no injuries.The operator's maintenance replaced the propeller governor and propeller regulator which were found to have malfunctioned. The engine was successfully run and the airplane was returned to service.

C-FFQS, a Conair Group Incorporated Air Tractor AT-802A on amphibious floats, was conducting forest fire fighting operations from the Canadian Rockies International Airport (CYXC), BC, with 1 crew member on board. After releasing his payload on the Connell Ridge wildfire, the pilot applied power for the climb out but the engine power rolled back to idle. The pilot selected the Emergency Power Lever but no more power was produced. The pilot selected an area for a forced approach and landed in a logged area with newly planted trees. The pilot sustained minor injuries and was taken by helicopter to receive medical aid. There was no post impact fire. The aircraft was substantially damaged.

C-FTXA, a Viking Air CL215 operated by Buffalo Airways, was conducting operations as Tanker 293 from Yellowknife, NT (CYZF) with 2 crew members on board. During the cruise portion of the flight, the left engine (Pratt & Whitney R2800) quit operating. The flight crew performed the actions required by the emergency checklist, and elected to return to CYZF. An uneventful landing was performed.Subsequent inspection by company maintenance personnel determined that the engine driven fuel pump had failed. The fuel pump was replaced, ground runs were performed and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-FTHY, a Talon Helicopters Limited Airbus AS350-B2 (A-Star) helicopter, was conducting external load operations 46 NM NW of Vernon (CYVK), BC, in support of forest fire suppression operations with 1 pilot on board. During cruise, the empty net which was attached to the long line, inadvertently released onto a steep hillside within the fire area. There were no injuries.The hook was inspected and the keeper was found to be sticky. The keeper was lubricated and function tested. Ground crews received additional briefings on sling operations.

The BC Ministry of Forests was conducting fire management operations 7 nautical miles northwest of Kamloops (CYKA), BC, with an Autel Evo II Enterprise V2 RPAS with an operator and an observer. Due to environmental conditions, the RPAS was being recovered using hand catches rather than landing on a surface. After landing on the observer's hand, the RPAS operator shut down the RPAS. During shutdown, the RPAS spun and a rotor struck the observer's hand causing a serious injury. The RPAS sustained minor damage.

C-FBNX, a Cessna 337G operated by Mag Aerospace Canada Corp., was conducting a flight from Buffalo Narrows (CYVT), SK to Ile-à-la-Crosse (CJF3), SK. Just prior to the approach to CJF3, the aircraft returned to CYVT due to weather conditions. On approach to CYVT, the landing gear failed to extend and the landing gear circuit breaker was tripped. The QRH was consulted and an alternate gear extension was attempted; however, only the nose landing gear extended while the main landing gear did not. The pilot subsequently landed the aircraft on the nose gear only and the aircraft sustained damage to its belly and rear propeller. The pilot exited the aircraft without injury.The aircraft was subsequently removed from the runway and the operator's maintenance personnel noted that a hydraulic leak was found in the nose landing gear actuator and that the hydraulic reservoir was depleted.

C-GNTM, an Air Tractor AT-802 operated by Forest Protection Limited, was conducting fire suppression training flights about 20 nm southwest of Fredericton (CYFC), NB. It was planned to have the aircraft land at Brockway (CCX3) Airport, NB for fuel, and as the aircraft touched down on Runway 22 at CCX3, the aircraft began to drift to the left. The pilot applied right rudder, and when the yaw to the left continued, the pilot began adding right brake pedal pressure in an attempt to arrest the left yaw. It was not possible for the pilot to arrest the left yaw with right rudder and brake pedal force, and the left yaw increased until the aircraft nose was 90 degrees left, relative to the runway. The tailwheel pylon separated during the skid to the left, and the aircraft came to rest with the main landing gear off of the runway surface. The pilot was uninjured.
