Summary: C-GZCF, a Lockheed L188C operated by Air Spray (1967) Ltd., was operating as ASB490 engaged in forest fire suppression operations based out of Fort McMurray Airport (CYMM), AB. After the second drop of the day, while returning to base, the crew observed that the No. 2 engine (Allision/Rolls Royce 501-D13) had fluctuating then dropping oil pressure and quantity. The flight crew consulted the quick reference handbook and shutdown the No. 2 engine, declared an emergency, and returned to CYMM. The 3-engine landing at CYMM was uneventful.Company maintenance is evaluating and troubleshooting the engine.

C-FSHC, a Sierra Helicopters Aerospatiale AS 350 B-2 departed Squamish Municipal Airfield (Don Patrick Field)(CYSE), BC, on a British Columbia Wildfire Services (BCWS) tasking, to a fire on Mount (Mt) Currie under visual flight rules with 1 pilot and 3 passengers on board. The 3 passengers on board were an initial action firefighting crew deploying to fight the fire on Mt Currie. The pilot gave a safety briefing, and the crew lead a hover exit walk through prior to takeoff. The pilot and the crew lead were in the front seats, and the other two members were in the rear left and rear center seat. The equipment was strapped in the rear right seat. The drop off location was a steep talus field on the northern face of Mt Currie. The pilot and crew lead agreed on a large flat rock for the drop off position. The pilot did an overhead recce and completed an approach to the rock. He repositioned once for a more stable position and had the toe of both skids resting on the rock. The crew member in the left rear seat removed his headset, put on a hardhat, and exited the aircraft. The second crew member in the back removed his seatbelt and headset, put on his hardhat, and began passing equipment to the outside member in packages that were less than 20lbs. All crew members heard a sharp noise, and the aircraft pitched nose high and to the left. The outside person leapt down and away from the aircraft. The helicopter turned 180° and rolled down the slope. During the roll down the slope, the crew member in the back seat was ejected from the helicopter and the pilot's helmet came off. The helicopter came to rest in an upright, nose down attitude. The pilot and passenger were both able to exit the aircraft prior to the airframe being engulfed in flame. The crew member who had been outside the aircraft called a Mayday on his handheld radio and started downhill toward the wreckage. The four members grouped together and started to climb back up the slope, away from the burning helicopter. The crew lead used his cell phone to call in to dispatch and advise the status of the helicopter and crew. A BCWS team was dispatched for the rescue and recovered the crew to the Pemberton Aerodrome (CYPS), BC. All four occupants had minor injuries. The helicopter was destroyed.

C-GYHF, a Yellowhead Helicopters Ltd. Bell 212 was conducting a crew transfer flight in support of firefighting operations. While on approach to a remote landing site, the pilot observed the number 1 engine (Pratt and Whitney Canada PT6T-3B) RPM begin to roll back to idle. Suspecting a governor failure, the pilot aborted the landing, issued a MAYDAY call, and activated the ELT. The aircraft was switched to manual mode, returning the engine to operation. The aircraft returned to Red Earth Creek Aerodrome (CEH5), AB, uneventfully. There were no injuries.Maintenance completed troubleshooting and found a faulty torque control unit (TCU). The affected part was replaced and tested, and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-GKKB, a Kenn Borek Air Ltd. Douglas DC-3C Basler BT-67, was conducting a visual flight rules flight in support of firefighting operations from the Fort St. John Airport (CYXJ), BC, to a remote site approximately 57 nm southwest of CYXJ. While in a holding pattern waiting for guidance from the bird dog aircraft, the flight crew noticed a decreasing oil pressure indication on the number 1 engine (Pratt and Whitney Canada PT6A-67R). The crew elected to divert back to CYXJ and declared a PAN PAN. The crew then observed oil streaks on the nacelle of the affected engine, actioned the appropriate checklists to shut down the engine, and declared a MAYDAY. The aircraft conducted an uneventful single-engine approach and landing.Company maintenance determined a cracked vent tube was leaking oil. The affected part was replaced, the engine ground run, and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-FDCH, a Canadian Helicopters Ltd. Sikorsky S-61N was operating on a local fire suppression mission to wildfire SWF-092-2025 U18, approximately 61 NM NNW of Slave Lake Airport (CYZH), AB. During firefighting operations, the helicopter was 1.9 hours into the first 3.3-hour tanking cycle of the day. While on short final to the dip site, the flight crew noticed a burning smell that entered the cabin, which was shortly thereafter followed by the No. 2 engine (General Electric CT58-140-2) fire light illuminating. A climb was initiated as the dip site was not suitable for landing. The flight crew actioned the engine fire checklist, extinguished the fire and shut down the No. 2 engine. A PAN PAN was declared and the helicopter returned to CYZH where it landed uneventfully on the runway. There were no injuries. Company maintenance removed the No. 2 engine, and it has been routed to an engine shop for examination.

C-GIAF, a Conair Group Limited Cessna 525B (Citation CJ3), was being operated as flight FGD116 from Spokane International Airport (KGEG), WA, U.S., under instrument flight rules to Abbotsford Airport (CYXX), BC, with 1 flight crew member and 1 passenger on board. During approach to CYXX, when the landing gear was selected down, the left main gear down indicator light did not illuminate. A missed approach was conducted and the applicable checklist was performed. An emergency was declared as a precautionary measure. The aircraft landed without further incident. Following the flight, the left main landing gear light bulb was found to be burnt out. The lightbulbs for all gear lights were replaced and the system was function tested with no faults found.

N347CM, a Boeing 767-323 aircraft operated by Amerijet International Airlines, was conducting flight AJT8620 from Brussels International Airport (EBBR), Belgium, to Gander International Airport (CYQX), NL. During the landing rollout on Runway 13 at CYQX, smoke began accumulating in the cockpit. The crew brought the aircraft to a full stop before reaching the intersection of Runway 03/21 and donned their oxygen masks. The crew then received a forward cargo fire warning, followed by an aft cargo fire warning. The crew declared a MAYDAY, requested emergency rescue services (ERS), and began the quick reference handbook procedures for fire indications and smoke removal. The fire suppression systems were discharged, and the smoke and the fire warnings were cleared. Following an exterior inspection by ERS the crew continued to use oxygen and taxied to the apron to shut down. The crew received medical assessment by first responders and were also given a detailed medical examination at the local hospital before being released.The subsequent inspection of cargo and cargo hold areas revealed no sign of fire.

C-GFQB, un CL215 1A10 exploité par le service aérien gouvernemental du Québec, sous l'indicatif QUE237, effectuait un vol selon les règles de vols à vue de formation depuis l’aéroport de Québec/Jean Lesage, QC (CYQB) avec 2 membres d’équipage. Après la sortie de l’eau pendant l’écopage au lac Montauban, l’équipage a remarqué des variations d’indications du moteur droit et a ouvert les portes pour vider l’eau embarquée. À environ 200 pieds le moteur droit a fait des ratées (Pratt & Whitney USA R2800 CA3), l’équipage l’a fermé, a mis l’hélice en drapeau et s’est dirigé vers CYQB. Une urgence a été déclarée et l’aéronef s’est posé sur la piste 24 sans encombre avec les services de Sauvetage et lutte contre les incendies d’aéronefs (SLIA) en alerte.

C-GMAK, a Canadair CL-215 operated by AirSpray (1967), had departed the The Pas Airport (CYQD), MB and was conducting aerial fire operation water scoops at Egg Lake, MB. During the 34th scooping operation, the flight crew observed low #1 engine (Pratt & Whitney USA R-2800) brake mean effective pressure (BMEP) and an engine oil temperature of 100°. As the aircraft was climbing, the oil temperature increased to 115°. The flight crew jettisoned the load and diverted to CYQD. During the diversion, the oil temperature climbed to 125°. The flight crew proceeded to feather the #1 propeller and shut down the #1 engine. An emergency was declared and the aircraft subsequently landed safely at CYQD.

C-FRYP, un Cessna 182RG exploité par Grondin Transport Inc., effectuait un vol selon les règles de vol à vue pour une patrouille de feu depuis et à destination de l'aéroport de Val-d’Or, QC (CYVO). Après environ 2 heures de patrouilles à 1500 pieds AGL, le moteur a commencé à perdre de la puissance. La pilote a effectué les actions d’urgence et s’est dirigée vers l’aérodrome de Lebel-sur-Quévillon, QC (CSH4). Le moteur tournait à 1500 RPM et l’aéronef perdait de l’altitude graduellement. À environ 25 NM de CSH4, le moteur s’est arrêté et la pilote a effectué un atterrissage d’urgence sur une route forestière. En raison du temps disponible, la décision a été prise de se poser sur le ventre de l’aéronef. L’atterrissage s’est bien déroulé et les dommages ont été limités à l’hélice, le revêtement sous la cabine et un saumon d’aile. La pilote n’a pas été blessée et a pu appeler des secours. Un hélicoptère est venu récupérer la pilote environ 1 heure plus tard. Selon les informations de l'exploitant, aucune anomalie n'a été trouvée sur le moteur, du givrage carburateur est suspectée.

C-GDDR, a WestJet Boeing 737-8 was operating flight WJA65 from Glasgow International Airport (EGPF), Scotland, to Toronto/Lester B. Pearson International Airport (CYYZ), ON. With about 3 hours remaining in the flight, all 4 flight attendants (FA) experienced shortness of breath due to fumes detected in the aft cabin. Two passengers in the aft cabin experienced similar symptoms. The flight crew contacted MediLink before deciding to divert to Goose Bay Airport (CYYR), NL, which was about 113 NM southeast of their position. The FA maintained their safety related duties and the aircraft landed at CYYR without incident where ATC had deployed emergency services to meet the aircraft. The crew and passengers were assessed by paramedics and released. Fire crews inspected the aircraft for the source of the fumes and tested the air quality in the aircraft. Maintenance personnel identified the source of the fumes as a faulty aft galley oven.

C-FNRP, a Rockwell International 690C, was operating as an air attack/bird dog flight originating out of Fort Simpson Airport (CYFS), NT, with 1 pilot and 2 crew on board. While providing tactical support for forest fire fighting 28 NM west of CYFS, the aircraft collided with terrain. The aircraft was destroyed and all 3 occupants were fatally injured.

C-GBDC, an Air Spray (1967) Ltd. Gulfstream-USA 690C (Twin Commander), was operating as flight ASB050 from the Yellowknife Airport (CYZF), NT, in support of forest firefighting activities. While turning final for Runway 16 in CYZF, the right engine (Garrett TPE331-10T) demonstrated an intermittent fuel flow and lost torque. The pilot shutdown the engine, declared a MAYDAY and requested aircraft rescue and firefighting to stand by. The pilot completed an uneventful single-engine approach and landing. Company maintenance is investigating and will report back to the TSB.

C-GSCI, un Cessna 182R exploité par Exact Air inc. effectuait une patrouille de feu selon les règles de vol à vue depuis l'aéroport de Roberval, QC (CYRJ) avec seul le pilote à bord. Durant le montée initiale, un bruit a été entendu et de la fumée est apparue dans la cabine du côté passager. Les équipements électriques non essentiels ont été fermés et un retour à CYRJ a été amorcé. Le pilote a déclaré une urgence et l’aéronef s’est posé sans encombre. Suite à une vérification, il a été trouvé qu’une résistance du système d’allume-cigarette avait surchauffée.

C-GMAF, a Canadair CL215 1A10 operated by Air Spray (1967) Ltd, was conducting VFR aerial firefighting flight TKR250 from the The Pas Airport (CYQD) MB. During the flight, the #2 engine (Pratt & Whitney - USA R-2800-CA3) was backfiring and the flight crew observed fluctuating brake mean effective pressure (BMEP) indications. The flight crew shut down the engine and diverted to the Flin Flon Airport (CYFO), MB, where the aircraft landed without further incident.An inspection performed by the operator's maintenance discovered a broken exhaust pushrod and a bent intake pushrod. Both pushrods were replaced and the engine was subsequently tested serviceable.

C-FFUC, an Airspan Helicopters Airbus AS350-B3 (AStar) helicopter, was conducting firefighting operations approximately 17 nautical miles southeast of Williams Lake Airport (CYWL), BC, with only the pilot on board. While conducting fire suppression activities with a Bambi Bucket on a longline, the pilot unintentionally actuated the belly release control instead of the intended remote release to drop water on a fire. As a result, the bucket and longline were unintentionally released. There were no reports of injuries or damage.A maintenance inspection confirmed the correct function of switches and hook releases. The bucket and longline were subsequently recovered and are being inspected.

C-GAAL, a Conair Group Inc. North American Rockwell 690A (Turbo Commander) airplane, was being operated as flight FGD131 from Cranbrook Airport (CYXC), BC, under instrument flight rules, to Abbotsford Airport (CYXX), BC. During the pre-descent checklist, the flight crew observed an abnormal increase in the right engine (Garrett TPE331-5) interstage turbine temperature (ITT) and engine power indication. Minor fluctuations in engine power and ITT had been noted earlier in the flight despite a constant power lever setting. The flight crew was able to reduce the ITT below the maximum authorized limit (redline), but the engine power remained unresponsive to power and condition lever inputs. The right engine was shut down as a precaution in accordance with the quick reference handbook, and the aircraft landed without further incident. Maintenance personnel were able to recreate the issue during a high-power ground run. The fuel control unit on the right engine was replaced. The aircraft was returned to service.

C-GGMZ, a Jazz Aviation DHC-8-402 (Dash 8 Q400), was being operated as flight JZA366 from Fort St. John Airport (CYXJ), BC, under instrument flight rules, to Vancouver International Airport (CYVR), BC. After retracting the landing gear after takeoff, the flight crew noticed the No.2 hydraulic fluid hot (HYD FLUID HOT), No.2 engine (Pratt & Whitney Canada, PW150A) hydraulic pump (ENG HYD PUMP), and the elevator pressure (ELEVATOR PRESS) caution lights illuminate. The hydraulic fluid level was observed to have dropped to 40%. The flight crew actioned the quick reference handbook, spoke with company maintenance, and planned to continue to CYVR. Approximately 8 minutes south of Prince George Airport (CYXS), BC, the flight crew noticed the hydraulic fluid level had dropped to 35%. They decided to divert to CYXS, declared an emergency, and landed safely on Runway 33. The flight crew stopped the aircraft on the runway, set the park brakes, and feathered both propellers. Fire trucks inspected the aircraft and could not see any visible signs of a fluid leak. The flight crew decided to taxi to the ramp. After the aircraft was parked on the ramp and as the passengers were deplaning, the fire crews noticed that there was hydraulic fluid on the ground underneath the No.2 engine. The flight crew confirmed the hydraulic leak. There were no reported injuries or damage to the aircraft.Maintenance personnel found the hydraulic fluid leak was coming from the No.2 hydraulic engine-driven pump (EDP). The EDP was replaced and flushing carried out. All associated filters were also replaced. The aircraft was returned to service. Reference SDR 20260805006.

C-FRCW, a Mustang Helicopters Incorporated Bell Helicopter 212, departed Lillooet Aerodrome (CYLI), BC, for a repositioning flight in support of BC Wildfire Service, under visual flight rules, to South Cariboo / 108 Mile Aerodrome (CZML), BC, with only the pilot on board. Approximately halfway through the flight, the pilot started to encounter lowering visibility due to heavy smoke. As the smoke intensified and visibility continued to worsen, the pilot attempted to find a route around the fire. The pilot descended and slowed to accommodate for the lower visibility. When the pilot found himself in less than 1 statute mile of visibility, he attempted to land the helicopter but was unable to find a suitable landing site. While transiting southbound over Alberta Lake, BC, the pilot lost visual references. Soon after, a main rotor blade struck the lake’s surface and the helicopter came to an abrupt stop, upright, in the shallow lake. The pilot had undergone recurrent instrument flight rules training as per the company's annual low visibility flying training. The pilot had minor injuries. The helicopter was substantially damaged.

C-GTWL, a Transwest Helicopters Limited Bell Helicopter of Textron 214B-1, was being flown to conduct longline activities in support of firefighting operations out of Cache Creek Aerodrome (CAZ5), BC. Shortly after departure, the helicopter had a loss of engine (Avco Lycoming T5508D) power, and the pilot conducted an autorotation to landing. The pilot was unable to jettison the bucket that was suspended on the longline. There were no injuries and the aircraft had only minor damage.

C-GRHN, a Eurocopter AS 350 B-2 operated by Helicopters Canada, was operating VFR fire suppression external load (water bucket) operations from the Armstrong Aerodrome (CYYW), ON.After completing a bucket cycle, the pilot filled the bucket for the return trip to CYYW. Once over CYYW, the pilot attempted to drop the water load from the bucket on to the aerodrome's infield grass prior to landing; however, he inadvertently released the long line and bucket from the belly hook. No persons were near the drop area. The water bucket was damaged and there was no reported damage to the helicopter.
